en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Pañcaka-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
1. The First Fifty [Discourses] 1.
The Chapter on the Powers of the Trainee 1.
Commentary on the Short Discourse (Saṃkhittasutta)

1. In the first sutta of the *Pañcakanipāta*, while it is true that stability among associated states is indeed the meaning of "power" (*bala*), it is stated—specifically with regard to being unshakable by opposing factors—that this is the preeminent sense of power: "He does not waver in the presence of lack of faith.
The commentary on the *Saṃkhittasutta* is concluded.
2–6. Commentary on the *Vitthatasutta* and the following suttas.

2–6. In the second [verse], *hirīyati* means he feels shame (*lajjati*) and becomes dispassionate (*virajjati*). Since *hiri* has the characteristic of loathing evil, it is said that its meaning is "he loathes. *Ottappati* means he fears; for *ottappa* has the characteristic of dread of evil.
*Paggahitavīriyo* means one whose energy has not fallen into contraction. Therefore he said, "with a mind free from despondency. *Pahānatthāya* means for the sake of total eradication.
The "attainment" (*upasampadā*) of wholesome states is indeed their acquisition; thus he said, "for the sake of obtaining."
Since words denoting elements (dhātu) have the sense of going (gati), they possess the sense of understanding (buddhi);
thus he said, "capable of penetrating both arising and passing away. This teaching is presented according to the mixed method; thus he said, "by way of suppression and by way of eradication.
Therefore he said, "by means of both insight-wisdom and path-wisdom," because of the act of suppressing by means of insight-wisdom.
And as for the phrase "that indeed is partial," it was stated—"because it leads to the acquisition of path-wisdom"—in order to show that it is not exhaustive.
The same principle applies to its being the state of leading to the destruction of suffering. "Correctly" means according to reality (*yāthāvato*).
For by way of the unshakable nature of path-wisdom, what has been discarded is truly discarded; there is no further need to discard it. Thus, by means of the method and the principle...
"It proceeds" means "by way of cause and method. There is nothing further to be said regarding the third and subsequent [sections].
The commentary on the *Vitthata-sutta* and others is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Kāma-sutta*.
7. It is *asita* because they cut it with an *asita* (sickle); that is, it is reaped. It is *byābhaṅgī* because they variously break it and hang the burden [of grain] upon it;
that is, it is a variety. Regarding the term *kulaputta* (son of good family), there are two kinds of *kulaputta*: the *kulaputta* by birth and the *kulaputta* by conduct. In this context:
"Now at that time, a *kulaputta* named Raṭṭhapāla was in that very Thullakoṭṭhika..."
One who has come from such a lineage as "the son of the head of the clan" is called a *jātikulaputta* (one born into a noble family).

However, those sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—as described in the passage beginning "those sons of good family"—are called *ācārakulaputta* (sons of a family perfected in conduct), even if they are born into any kind of family whatsoever.
Here, however, the *ācārakulaputta* is intended. Therefore, he said: "a son of good family."
“A son of good family who observes proper conduct. “Appropriate” (*yutta*) means suitable; the sense is that he is worthy of being addressed in such a manner. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Kāmasutta* is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Cavanasutta*.
8. In the eighth [verse], by the word "faith" (*saddhā*), faith as realization (*adhigama-saddhā*) is shown. For faith is fourfold:

faith that is to be arrived at (*āgamanīya-saddhā*), faith as realization (*adhigama-saddhā*), faith as serene confidence (*pasāda-saddhā*), and faith as conviction (*okappana-saddhā*). Among these, faith that is to be arrived at occurs in the case of omniscient Bodhisattvas.
For the faith that has come through the path to be arrived at is preeminent in Great Bodhisattvas, having been attained through the instruction of others.

It is so called because of resolving by grasping things that are to be believed without error, even in their absence. Faith that has come through the penetration of truth (*saccappaṭivedha*) is faith of attainment (*adhigamasaddhā*), such as that of Suppabuddha and others.

Confidence (*pasāda*) arising toward the Buddha and the rest—such as the thought, “The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened one”—is faith of clarity (*pasādasaddhā*), such as that of King Mahākappina and others.
It is [also] the plunging [into the Dhamma] with the thought, “This is indeed so.”
*Okappanā* is the fixing [of the mind] by way of leaping forward through the act of believing; that itself is faith, thus it is "faith as fixing" (*okappanasaddhā*).
In this context, faith as clarity (*pasādasaddhā*) is of a nature to be led by others, because one has confidence merely by hearing.
Faith as fixing, however, proceeds as if making the object of belief directly evident, having plunged into and entered into it, thinking, "It is exactly so."
The commentary on the Cavanasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the First Agāravasutta:
Regarding the ninth [sutta], *appatissayo* is a designation for *appatissavo*, formed by changing the letter *va* to *ya*. [It means] not showing respect toward anything regarding one’s teacher.
"Respectful" (*patissava*) refers to anything that constitutes respect—whether it be the act of listening out of reverence, the state of being respectful, or the very nature of such reverence.
"Disrespectful" (*appatissava*) means one in whom such respect is absent; thus, one who is devoid of reverence. Therefore, he said: "He is not the eldest, nor does he behave with humility.
The commentary on the first sutta on lack of reverence is finished.

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Reverence (Dutiya-Āgāravasutta) Regarding the tenth discourse, in the phrases beginning with "growth" (*vuddhi*), there is growth by means of virtue (*sīla*), increase by means of the path (*magga*), and abundance by means of Nibbāna.

Alternatively, there is growth by means of virtue and concentration (*samādhi*), increase by means of insight (*vipassanā*) and the path, and abundance by means of the fruit (*phala*) and Nibbāna. And herein, for one who possesses the fourfold...

Virtue, when perfectly purified through its occurrence in an unbroken and other such states, brings about the path and its fruits without difficulty because it partakes in distinction, as in the case of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
One who possesses such virtue will attain growth in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Therefore it was said: "Growth by virtue. But for one in whom the Noble Path has arisen, he is like a tree with well-established roots.
Because it is well-established, the tree attains growth within the Dispensation; therefore it is said: "growth by means of the Path.
He who has attained the Nibbāna that extinguishes all defilements—that Arahant—attains abundance through the fulfillment of the aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and the rest;
therefore it is said: "abundance by means of Nibbāna. This is the meaning in the second interpretation.
It is to be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the second Discourse on Lack of Respect is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee is finished.
2. Balavagga 1.
Ananussutasuttavaṇṇanā 11.
In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], "abhijānitvā" means having known by means of superior knowledge (abhivisiṭṭha-ñāṇa). There are eight reasons [for this].
“Of the Tathāgata”: “He has come thus, therefore he is the Tathāgata. He has gone thus, therefore he is the Tathāgata. He has come to the true characteristic, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
He has perfectly awakened to true phenomena as they really are, therefore he is the Tathāgata. Because of his seeing thus, he is the Tathāgata. Because of his speaking thus, he is the Tathāgata.
Because of his acting thus, he is the Tathāgata. In the sense of overcoming, he is the Tathāgata.”
By these eight reasons thus stated. "Āsabhaṃ" (the bull-like) means that which belongs to a bull (usabha); it is the pre-eminent position. Therefore he said:
"The bull-like position means the pre-eminent position. By virtue of the power demonstrated hereafter, he lets out a fearless roar, saying, "I am one possessed of the ten powers.
Regarding the term "Brahmacakka," here the word *brahma* has the sense of "pre-eminent. He said "the pre-eminent wheel" (*seṭṭhacakka*) because of the word *brahma*. And this is a wheel.
The Wheel of Dhamma is intended here.
The commentary on the *Ananussuta Sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Saṃkhitta Sutta*.

13. In the third [case], while it is true that the state of stability among the associated states is indeed the sense of strength, it is stated that "it is not shaken by forgetfulness" because being unshakable by opposing factors is the preeminent sense of strength.
The commentary on the *Saṃkhitta-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Vitthata-sutta*.
14. In the fourth [phrase], *satinepakkena* means by mindfulness and by discernment (*nepakka*); the meaning is "by way of being sharp, clear, and resolute.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, with the intention that "discernment" (*nepakka*) is wisdom (*paññā*), it is said: "Discernment is called wisdom.

If this were so, then [wisdom] would be something other than what was already indicated [by the term "mindfulness"]. By the phrase "possessing mindfulness" (*satimā*), a distinguished kind of mindfulness is taken; thus, even further on, [it says]: "Even what was done long ago..."
By stating, “Even what was spoken long ago is remembered and recollected,” only the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is indicated, not the function of wisdom (*paññā*).
Therefore, it can indeed be understood that "by mindfulness and discernment" (*satinepakkena*) means by the state of mindfulness’s discerning quality (*nepakkabhāva*).

The power of mindfulness is independent of other factors due to the specific nature of its conditions; for instance, even with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta-citta*), recitation and reflection are possible.

"Even that which was done long ago by oneself or by another" refers to the fulfillment of major duties such as the observance of the *cetiyangaṇa* (shrine-yard) and other rites performed with the body.

"Even that which was spoken long ago by oneself or by another" refers to verbal action (*vācīkamma*) set in motion through careful recitation, causing others to recite, reminding them of the Dhamma, teaching the Dhamma, informal discourses while seated together, expressions of appreciation, and so forth, performed with speech.
"Remembered and recollected" means that regarding that bodily act done long ago, "body" refers to bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
Speech uttered over a long time is called vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*); both of these are material form (*rūpa*), while the mind and mental factors that originate them are immaterial (*arūpa*).
Thus, one both remembers and recollects that "these material and immaterial phenomena have arisen in this way and ceased in this way";
the meaning is that one arouses the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*satisambojjhaṅga*). For it is mindfulness that arouses the factors of enlightenment which is intended here.
By that mindfulness, it should be understood that this [mindfulness] is "remembered" through remembering once, and "recollected" through repeated remembering.
The commentary on the *Vitthata-sutta* is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the *Daṭṭhabba-sutta*, etc.
15–20. "In the fifth [chapter], 'only within their own respective domains' means precisely within each one's own domain.

'To speak of mundane and supramundane phenomena' means to speak of mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena according to their various specific modes of occurrence. 'The four factors of stream-entry' are:
association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma."

Regarding these four causes for the path of stream-entry: while it is certainly true that states such as mindfulness and the rest must also be desired among them—since they cannot occur without those [other qualities]—nevertheless, it should be understood that faith (*saddhā*) is specifically what performs the function here.
For only one who possesses faith attends upon true persons, hears the true Dhamma, and applies the mind wisely to the impermanent nature of things and so forth.
One acts in accordance with the noble path and practices its natural law; therefore it is said, "herein the power of faith is to be seen.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood for the remaining powers as well.
Regarding "the four right endeavours," this refers to the cultivation of the fourfold right endeavour. Regarding "the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth...

The same method applies here. Furthermore, just as faith is required among the factors of stream-entry, and just as energy is required for the development of the right efforts, so too—for the sake of the development of the foundations of mindfulness—mindfulness must be emphasized in terms of its function during the preliminary stage, because of the statement: "Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
Likewise, concentration is required for one whose task is concentration, and the development of the Noble Truths...
Having stated, "the development of wisdom," it is evident that in that context wisdom is intended to be predominant during the preliminary stage.
However, at the moment of actual attainment, an evenness of all the powers—faith and the rest—is intended, just as with concentration and wisdom.
For this reason, the word "here" (*ettha*) is used in various places in such passages as, "herein the power of faith."

Now, in order to clarify by means of a simile the specific, superior functions of faith and the other [faculties] in their respective roles, the passage beginning with "Just as" was spoken. Herein, this is the correlation of the simile:
the five powers that bring about the maturation of liberation are like the companions with the king as the fifth.
Their entering together onto a street for the purpose of recreation is like the entry of the powers together onto the street of insight (vipassanā).

Among the companions, just as the first and the others each have their respective deliberations within the house, so too do faith and the other faculties attain the state of being forerunners upon reaching the factors of stream-entry and so forth.

Among the companions, just as the others remain silent here and there, so too do the remaining powers follow after that [faith] in various instances, conforming to the function of that forerunning power;
for at that time, they do not [function] in relation to the earth and so forth together with their constituent parts.

The function of faith and the other [faculties] remains manifest, whereas the function of the faculties beginning with confidence (saddhā) stands clearly evident because the mental continuum has been previously conditioned by such conditions.
And here, in order to show that for one who practices insight (vipassanā-kammika),
cultivation is specifically dominated by wisdom (paññā), the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is presented using the king as an illustration.
It has been stated. The sixth and subsequent sections are easy to understand.
The commentary on the suttas to be examined is finished.
The commentary on the Balavagga is finished.
3. The Chapter on the Five Factors (Pañcaṅgika-vagga) 1–2. Commentary on the First Discourse on Lack of Respect, etc.

21–22. Regarding the first discourse of the third section: *Ābhisamācārika* means that which exists in *abhisamācāra*, that is, in the highest conduct. What, then, is that? He says: "The virtue prescribed by way of formal duties (*vatta*). The rest is easily understood. In the second discourse, there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the first *Agārava-sutta* and others is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the *Upakkilesa-sutta* and others. 23–24.
In the third [sutta], "nor shining forth" (*na ca pabhāvantam*) means not endowed with radiance. "Having the nature of breaking apart" (*pabhijjanasabhāvam*) refers to having heated it.
"Frail as a palm leaf or a reed. "The remainder is iron" refers to all types of iron mentioned as the remainder:
namely, iron of its own kind (*sajātiloha*), iron of a different kind (*vijātiloha*), *pisācaloha*, and artificial iron (*kittimaloha*). Regarding the phrase "by not allowing [it] to arise":

is it not the case that even a mundane wholesome consciousness, though perfectly pure, possesses defilement simply by virtue of not being allowed to arise? True, this is so; however, in whatever mental continuum—
When the hindrances have gained a footing, there is no possibility even for sublime wholesome states, let alone supramundane wholesome states. However, limited wholesome states,
arising according to their conditions within a continuum impaired by the hindrances,
are called "defiled" because they are impure in their arising— just like a lamp’s oil, wick, and vessel when supported by an impure base.
Like a lamp. Furthermore, showing that they are called "defilements" precisely because they do not allow [the mind] to arise in its primary sense, he says, "By which [factor]," and so forth.
Their state of being "pulverized and scattered" should be understood by way of their occurring in a distracted manner toward the object.
In the fourth [case], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta and others is finished.
5. Commentary on the Anuggahita Sutta:
Regarding the fifth [sutta], "right view" refers to the right view of insight (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi), according to the opinion of the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
This commentary on the meaning has begun; however, regarding this point, the Majjhimabhāṇakas explain the meaning differently. For it is said in the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:
“‘Supported’ means having received assistance. ‘Right view’ refers to the right view of the path of arahantship. At the moment of the fruit...”
That which has the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) as its arisen fruit is "having the liberation of mind as its fruit" (*cetovimuttiphalā*).

That which has that very fruit—designated as the liberation of mind—as its benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) is "having the liberation of mind as its fruit and benefit" (*cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā*). The same method applies to the second phrase as well.

Here, it should be understood that the wisdom of the fourth fruit is called "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*), while the remaining factors are the "liberation of mind. Regarding the phrases beginning with "supported by virtue" (*sīlānuggahitā*):
“Virtue” (sīla) refers to the virtue of the fourfold purification. “Learning” (suta) refers to listening to the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress].

“Discussion” (sākacchā) refers to discourse concerning stumbling, slipping, and cutting off in regard to the meditation subject. “Tranquility” (samatha) refers to the eight attainments that lead to insight.

“Insight” (vipassanā) refers to the seven kinds of contemplation. For one who fulfills the virtue of the fourfold purification, listens to the learning of the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress],...
For one who cuts off stumbling and tripping regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), who applies effort toward the eight attainments that establish insight,
and who develops the sevenfold contemplation, the path to Arahatship arises and bestows its fruit.
Just as, for example, one desiring to eat a sweet mango fruit might construct a water-reservoir all around the young mango tree—
He makes it firm and binds it; taking a jar, he pours water into it from time to time;
and to prevent the water from leaking out, he makes the embankment firm.
Whatever creepers, dry sticks, ant-hills, or spiderwebs are nearby, he removes them; and taking a spade, he digs around the roots from time to time.
Thus, for one who is diligent and performs these five actions, that mango tree grows and yields fruit;

it is in this way that this matter should be understood. For virtue (sīla) is to be seen as the fence-binding all around the tree, listening to the Dhamma as the sprinkling of water from time to time, and making the boundary firm.

Just as the clearing away of creepers and such from the vicinity [of a mango tree] is like serenity (*samatha*), the cutting away of stumbling and wavering in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is like that;
and the digging up of the roots by taking a spade from time to time is like the cultivation of the seven contemplations (*anupassanā*).
For one who is assisted by these five factors, it is like the time when the mango tree yields its sweet fruit.
"It should be understood that for a bhikkhu supported by these five qualities, right view yields the fruit of arahantship.
And here, "having obtained assistance" means having obtained the necessary conditions through dependence (*nissaya*) and so forth as appropriate.

Because it is grasped by way of being assisted by insight-right-view (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*), it refers to right-views of the path, specifically the right-view of the path of arahantship. Of the [two] immediate [factors],...

For indeed, whether it be an injunction or a prohibition, the term "knowledge of others' minds" (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) is established exclusively in reference to the concentration of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala-samādhi*) and the states that serve as its requisites.

"Right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) refers to the right view of the path of Arahantship. "At the moment of the fruit" (*phalakkhaṇe*) means at both types of moments of fruition: the immediate [moment] and at a subsequent time.
It is called "liberation of mind" (*ceto-vimutti*) because by means of this [right view], the mind is liberated from all defilements through the process of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).
The liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) consists of all remaining states of fruition (*phala-dhamma*), setting aside the wisdom of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala-paññā*). Therefore, he said:

"That which has liberation of mind as its fruit is the benefit (*ānisansa*) designated as liberation of mind. The construction is: the abandonment (*pahāna*) known as subsiding (*paṭippassambhana*), which is the liberation of the mind from all defilements, is both the fruit and the benefit. Here, by the term "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti-sadda*):

Only the abandoning is mentioned here, whereas previously the factors that abandon were stated. Otherwise, if the benefits were understood as being merely the resultant states themselves, the subsequent mention would be redundant.
The same meaning should be understood here for the phrase "the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom" (paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsa).
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood, because they are of the nature of virtue (sīla), are particularly helpful to concentration; likewise is right intention.
Because it has the nature of jhāna; for that [jhāna] is designated as "absorption" (appanā). However, since right mindfulness and right effort belong to the side of concentration, he said:
"The remaining states should be understood as liberation of mind.
"Fourfold purification of virtue" refers to the fourfold purification of virtue that serves as the proximate cause for the attainment of the Noble Path.
The same method applies to the Suttas and so forth as well. "Discourse" (*saṃkathā*) is speaking together by way of announcing the movement of one's own mind;
"discussion" (*sākacchā*) is simply such discourse. However, since this [context] is connected to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he says: "discourse on the meditation subject," and so on.
"Stumbling" (*khalana*) is failing to carry out the procedure for that meditation subject even once; "faltering" (*pakkhalana*) is doing so many times.
It is a discourse that cuts through and removes both of these; it is a discourse that severs stumbling and tripping.
"Of one who fulfills" means of one who maintains and increases [the practice] by making it dependent upon turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭa).

"Of one who hears" means of one who hears in such a way that the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) as it was received will reach full development. For this very reason, it is called "hearing the Dhamma that is suitable."

"Of one performing kamma" means of one performing the kamma of devotion to meditation (bhāvanānuyoga). In all five instances, the word *anta* should be understood as indicating a causal sense (*hetuattha*).
For it is only in this way that the mango simile being stated with "Just as," and so forth, would be appropriate.
"A water-trench" means a moat for water. "He binds it firmly" means he ties it not loosely, but tightly and not too large.

He joins [the parts] without making them too small. "He makes it firm" means that at the time of pouring water, he makes the embankment of the water-channel more solid so that the water does not escape by flowing away here and there.
"A dry stick" refers to the withered tip of a branch of that very mango grove. "An ant's nest" refers to a nest of copper-colored ants. "A spade" means...
The hoe: virtue is like the binding of the trench because it serves as the root for the method of increasing right view.
Hearing the Dhamma is like the pouring of water because it nourishes development (*bhāvanā*).

Tranquility (*samatha*) is like the making firm of the boundary because it brings about the strengthening of the boundary of virtue, which is the aforementioned basis for development. For one who is concentrated...

For virtue becomes more stable. This is because, by removing the obstacles to the development of what is desired, it prevents stumbling, slipping, and cutting off in the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), just as the removal of creepers and the like from nearby areas [ensures a firm footing].
And the development of the seven contemplations is like the digging up of roots, because it uproots craving, conceit, and views, which are the very roots of those obstacles. And here—

Since one who is thoroughly purified in virtue and devoted to the meditation subject must desire to hear the Dhamma that is conducive to it, from that comes engaging in discussion regarding the meaning as it has been heard;
from that comes the development of serenity through the purification of the meditation subject;
from that comes the fulfillment of insight for one who is concentrated and has begun insight; and when insight is fulfilled, it becomes right view of the path.

It should be understood that this sequence has been explained because these factors are supported in their successive order by being brought face-to-face; thus [the Blessed One] says, "He causes them to increase.
The commentary on the *Anuggahita Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Vimuttāyatana Sutta*.

26. In the sixth [section], he says "bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatana*) because they are the bases or causes for being liberated from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). He explains this as "the causes of liberation.

"For one who knows the meaning of the text" means for one who knows the meaning of each respective portion of the text exactly as it is, according to such passages as, "Herein comes virtue; herein comes concentration; herein comes wisdom," and so forth. "For one who knows the text" refers to that which brings about the understanding of its meaning.
For one who is investigating the Pāli exactly as it is, "nascent rapture" arises—a soft rapture that has merely begun to be born.

How does it arise? As one investigates the Dhamma exactly as it was taught and examines one’s own conduct of body, speech, and mind accordingly, there arises in one who has attained gladness a joy characterized by exhilaration. It is the manifestation of a state of being satisfied.
"Powerful rapture" means that because it has gained habitual practice through the influence of the rapture previously arisen,
there arises a powerful rapture capable of becoming a condition for *passaddhi* (tranquility)—

which is the capacity to allay the agitation of body and mind and which constitutes an extreme state of gladness. Since the material body (*rūpakāya*) becomes tranquil when the mental body (*nāmakāya*) is tranquil, therefore...
It is said simply that "the mental body subsides.
"He obtains happiness" means he obtains and experiences a non-material (nirāmisa) mental happiness capable of serving as a condition for the concentration of mind that will be discussed later.
As for the phrase "he becomes concentrated," it is not just any kind of concentration that is intended here.
Then, demonstrating that it is "unsurpassed concentration," he said: "He attains arahantship... [and so on] ...he becomes concentrated.

The passage beginning with "For this" explains, within that teaching, the causal nature for such a person to obtain the aforementioned concentration, which is the state of being a basis for liberation (vimuttāyatana).
It is shown that [the mind] inclines toward it. Concentration itself is the sign of concentration (samādhinimitta).

Concentration itself, having ascended the text of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), is the sign of concentration (samādhinimitta) because it serves as the cause for the concentration of further development that arises subsequently.
Therefore he said, "In the presence of the teacher," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Vimuttāyatana Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta 27.
In the seventh [sutta], it is stated that "there is an especially superior happiness here because of the complete absence of the distress and fever of the defilements," and thus it is said:
"It is pleasant in the present because it is pleasant at every moment of absorption. This is by way of each preceding [moment].
Because each subsequent [moment] reaches a state that is more peaceful and more refined through the process of repeated cultivation (*laddhāsevanatā*), it is said:
"The preceding... [is] of pleasant result. "By the subsiding of the defilements" means because it is obtained through the calming of the defilements.
"'The state of the subsiding of the defilements' means the state of the calming of the defilements. Because it is obtained, because it is reached."
Because it has attained that state. The hindrances, the attachment to the first jhāna, and so forth—which are the opposites of mundane concentration—must be suppressed;
other defilements must be warded off. But since all defilements have been stilled in this concentration of Arahantship, there is nothing to be suppressed or warded off;
thus, immediately after the path and at the moment of attainment, it occurs without effort.

Because it has been attained and because it has been entered into, or because it has been entered into by way of non-decline, it does not involve the suppression and warding off of effort (*sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagata*).

By the phrase "because of having reached the fullness of mindfulness," he shows that even when mindfulness is not actually occurring, one is still called "mindful" due to the abundance of mindfulness.
By the phrase "by way of the time delimited," he shows that one is mindful through mindfulness that has been delimited. "In the rest" refers to the various types of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
The commentary on the *Samādhi-sutta* is finished.
8–9. Commentary on the *Pañcaṅgika-sutta*, etc. 28–29.
In the eighth [sutta], "kara" refers to that which arises from a flower; it is so called because it is produced within the womb. From *kara*.
The "born body" is the body produced by kamma; it is the aggregate of the fourfold continuity of form that has that [kamma] as its decisive support.
Granted, the mental body (*nāmakāya*) also receives such assistance from the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, according to the statement beginning with "it moistens";

nevertheless, because of the specific wording here, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is intended, which is why he says, "this body produced by kamma. "Moistens" means it performs the act of moistening. And as for that moistening:
Because the physical body is brought to a state of saturation by the rapture and happiness born of jhāna, its dryness is entirely removed;

thus he said, "it moistens," and so forth. This "moistening" (abhisandana) should be understood, in terms of meaning, as the suffusion of the body by sublime material forms produced by the aforementioned rapture and happiness.
The same method applies to the terms "it drenches" (parisandetī) and so on. All of this...
“Of all” (*sabbāvato*) means “of that which is all. In the context of a relationship between a part and the whole, the genitive case is used for the whole;
thus, the word “all” (*sabba*) refers to the parts. Therefore, it is said: “of that which possesses all constituent parts.

There is nothing that is not pervaded wherever there is matter born of kamma, because matter born of consciousness permeates every such place. Hence he says: “in the continuity of what is clung-to,” and so forth.
He is skilled (*kusala*). That skill of his should be understood as the capacity for preparing bath-powders and kneading them into balls; thus he says, "capable" (*paṭibala*), and so forth.
The word *kaṃsa* occurs in the sense of gold in such passages as "in a large bronze bowl" (*mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā*).

In such passages as "as a bronze vessel is struck" (*kaṃso upahato yathā*), it refers to bell-metal (*kittimaloha*). In some instances, it is used merely as a designation (*paṇṇattimatta*), as in "a minor bronze vessel" (*upakaṃso*).
“...you are named King, the son of Mahākaṃsa,” and so forth. But here, regarding the phrase “by whatever metal,” he says:
“in a vessel made of any kind of metal. “Followed by moisture” means entered or approached by way of the penetration of water-moisture.
“Enveloped by moisture” means surrounded by water-moisture, pervaded on all sides. For that very reason, it is both internal and external.
“Saturated with moisture” (*phuṭā snehena*). By this, he expresses the state of being completely drenched by water. “And not dripping” (*na ca pagghariṇī*):
by this, he speaks of its dense and solid nature even though it is moist. Therefore, he said: “not drop by drop,” and so forth.
It is called *ubbhida* because it breaks out through various water-veins; that which has such bursting-out water is *ubbhidodaka*.
"Water that wells up" (*ubbhinnaudaka*) is like a well dug on the bank of a river from which water rises up. "Water that rises up" (*uggacchanaudaka*) is water that emerges in the form of a stream.
Why, then, is only a lake with water that wells up mentioned here, and not the others? He says:
"Because the water below rises up," and so forth. "By the falling of streams and water-bubbles" means by the falling of streams and by water-bubbles.
And it should be said: “and with masses of foam. The intended meaning is that it is settled, motionless due to its lack of agitation, and perfectly clear.
“The rest” refers to the passage beginning with “it moistens. “Uppalāni” means lotus thickets.
“In white, red, and blue” refers to the lotuses; that is, white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses.
The meaning is as follows: whatever is a blue lotus (*uppala*) is simply called "blue lotus" because of the grasping of its common characteristic.

Regarding the term *satapatta*, here the word *sata* is a synonym for "many," as in expressions such as *satagghī* ("worth a hundred"). By this, the inclusion of even those with many hundreds of petals is established.
In the world, however, the red lotus is called *paduma* and the white one *puṇḍarīka*. [It is that which is] from the tip down to the root, by water...

The mention of "not emerging from the water" is for the purpose of showing the arising of [the state] beginning with the intention (*abhisandana*). Here, the body born of karma (*karajakāya*) is like the *uppala* and other lotuses, while the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.
Since he says "with a purified mind," he refers to the consciousness of the fourth jhāna; and that is because of the departure of the stains of defilements such as lust (*rāga*).
It is without defilement and stainless; therefore, he said, "it is purified in the sense of being without defilement.

Furthermore, since it is precisely through the specific condition of purification that there is a specific mode of occurrence—just as the brightness of well-polished gold results from its rubbing—it was said, "it should be understood as luminous in the sense of being radiant. This...
“White” (odāta) refers to the word. “For the purpose of pervading the temperature” means for the purpose of showing the pervasion of the temperature.
The intention is that there is no further pervasion of temperature. Therefore he said: “At that moment... it becomes powerful. Like a cloth, the body born of kamma (karajakāya):
the yogi’s body born of kamma should be regarded as being like a cloth, because it is to be pervaded by the bliss of the fourth jhāna, which is similar to the pervasion of temperature.
The fourth jhāna should be regarded as being like a person’s body, because it serves as the basis for the happiness that takes the place of the pervading temperature.
Therefore he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. And therein, by the mention of “mind” in the phrase “with a purified mind,” it should be understood that the jhāna-happiness is meant.
Thus he said, “the happiness of the fourth jhāna is like the pervading temperature.”
But is it not the case that there is no pleasure at all in the fourth jhāna? True, there is none;

however, because equanimity here has the characteristic of being peaceful and its intrinsic nature is tranquil, it is intended by the term “pleasure. Therefore, it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*: “But because equanimity is peaceful, it is spoken of as ‘pleasure.’”

Because it is the condition for seeing the specific nature of each respective concentration, reflective knowledge is the "sign of reflection" (*paccavekkhaṇanimitta*). "Evenly filled" (*samabharita*) means completely full.
"The level ground" (*maṇḍabhūmi*) refers to a flat, even terrain where crops flourish and remain stable even without the pouring of water.
"Charioteers" (*yoggā*) are those to be yoked to the yoke; their teacher is the "charioteer" (*yoggācariya*). Because he trains them, elephants and other animals are also [included].
“They are called ‘the fit’,” thus it says in the text: “charioteers of horses to be tamed. “By whichever [way]” means by whichever path among the four paths.
“Whichever destination” means whichever destination among the destinations distinguished as swift, moderately swift, and so forth. There is nothing further to be said regarding the ninth [chapter].
The commentary on the Pañcaṅgika-sutta and others is finished.
10. Nāgitasutta Commentary 30.

Regarding the tenth [sutta], "loud-voiced and noisy": because their sound rises upward (*uddhaṃ uggata*), it is "high" (*ucca*); it is "extended" (*patthaṭa*) and "great" (*mahanta*), such that it cannot be grasped by being separated into its components;
thus they are "loud-voiced and noisy. For even the sound of speech, when produced together by many people, is loud and noisy.
When it is set in motion, it is difficult to understand either in meaning or in sound; it reaches the range of hearing as nothing more than a great roar.
"In the catching of fish" (*macchavilope*) means: like the seizing [of fish] after they have been plundered, or in the plundering of fish.
For when a great crowd of people has gathered at the place where fishermen have set out their fish-traps, [they say]: "Give us one other fish here, one..."
“Give me a fish-slice! and “A large one was given to you; mine is small,” they cry out in this way with loud voices and great clamor.
Even when the net has been cast for the purpose of catching fish, the fishermen and others at that spot raise a great shout, saying, “It has entered!
It is caught! It is with reference to this that it was said. “Impure pleasure” is so called because it is dependent upon the impurity of the body.

And because it is dependent on the impurity of the defilements, it is the happiness dependent on impurity. "Of the happiness of renunciation" means the happiness of one who has emerged from sensual desire.
"Of the happiness of seclusion" means the happiness of one who is free from the company of crowds and the company of defilements.
"Of the happiness of peace" means the happiness that brings about the subsiding of lust and so forth. "The happiness of enlightenment" refers to that which is designated as the Path.
It is happiness for the sake of reaching the culmination of full enlightenment. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Nāgita Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Pañcaṅgika Vagga is finished.
4. Sumanavagga 1.
Sumanasuttavaṇṇanā 31.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth [vagga]: *Satakkaku* means "having a hundred peaks"; the sense is that it has many summits. This is a demonstration of its nature as a great cloud.
For indeed, it rains heavily. Therefore he said: "The meaning is that he is possessed of hundreds of cloud-masses arisen from here and there.
Regarding the term "endowed with vision" (*dassanasampanna*), "vision" here refers to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*). For that is called "vision" because it first sees Nibbāna.
Even though the state of lineage (*gotrabhu*) sees it slightly earlier, once [the path] has seen [Nibbāna], the function to be performed...
Because it does not effect the abandoning of the defilements, that knowledge is not called "vision" (*dassana*). For that knowledge stands in the place of adverting (*āvajjana*).
This is stated because of its commonality with the Path in having Nibbāna as its object, but not because of its penetration of Nibbāna;
therefore, vision—which has not yet reached the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by being generated again and again—is the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*). And the Dhamma-eye...
The realization of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths through the performance of the task of full understanding and so forth is what constitutes "clear comprehension" (abhisamaya);
thus, there is no attainment of the state of seeing on the part of the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhū) here. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary to the Sumanā Sutta is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Cundīsutta 32.
In the second [sutta], in the passage beginning with “endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones,” the virtues dear to the noble ones (*ariyakantāni*) are the five precepts (*pañcasīla*).
For the five precepts dear to the noble ones are beloved and cherished by the noble ones; even when the noble ones have passed into other existences, they [remain] those [virtues].
They do not abandon them. However, because it was said here: “Cunda, as far as there are virtues beloved by the noble ones (ariyakanta-sīla), these are declared the foremost...
[etc] ... you are those who fulfill the foremost,” he stated: “‘Virtues beloved by the noble ones’ means virtues associated with the paths and fruits.”
The commentary on the Cundīsutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Uggahasutta 33.
Regarding the third [discourse], "first of all, those who are habituated to rising": at the time when night turns to dawn, while the owners and the household attendants are still in bed...

They are "early risers" (*pubbuṭṭhāyiniyo*) because they are habitually the first to rise before everyone else has risen; or alternatively, because upon seeing their husband, they rise from their seat even before him, as if scorched by fire. "What is to be done?

(*kiṃkāraṃ*) means "what task is there to be performed"; having asked this, they perform the services that ought to be done—that is the meaning. They wander about responding to such [calls], thus they are "those who respond to what is to be done" (*kiṃkārappaṭissāviniyo*).

They are called "those of pleasant conduct" because they perform only agreeable actions by way of virtue. They are called "those of pleasant speech" because they speak only what is dear by way of virtue.

"By means of the appropriate method" means by means of the investigation that serves as the method for accomplishing that task. Therefore he said: "In that arrangement of wool and cotton," and so forth.
"Able to do" means capable of doing. "Able to arrange" means capable of deliberating. Therefore he said: "Able..."
“‘Able to do’ and ‘capable of arranging’ means being able to do it oneself as well as having others do it,” and so forth. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Ugga Sutta is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta, etc.

34–35. In the fourth [verse], "visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means that it is to be seen by oneself because it does not pertain to a future life. It is to be experienced by oneself, directly perceived;
this is the meaning of "pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*). It does not remain by mere faith alone:
it does not persist merely through the thought, "Giving is good and beautiful; it is praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others."
"Whatever gift he gives" means whatever object of charity he gives to another.
"Being its master" means that, having thoroughly overcome the greed directed toward that object, he gives as its lord; because he cannot be overcome by it, he is neither a slave nor a companion.
In this regard, the passage beginning with "For he who... is stated to demonstrate both of these points through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya and vyatireka).
One gives as a slave because of having entered into the slavery of craving. One gives as a friend because of not relinquishing one's affection for that person.
One gives as a master because of acting after having liberated oneself from the slavery of craving therein and having overcome it.

Alternatively, a person who is a giver by virtue of generosity and morality is called a "slave of giving," a "companion of giving," or a "lord of giving" according to the specific mode of their engagement in giving.

It is of three kinds. To analyze and demonstrate this threefold nature of his, the passage beginning with "For he who... was stated. In the sense of being given, *dāna* refers to food, drink, and so forth.
Among these, that which one consumes oneself becomes like a slave because one must act under its influence due to being overwhelmed by craving (*taṇhādhipannatā*).
Regarding that which is given to others, this was said even there—by way of the commonality of food and drink—"of that which is designated as giving..."
"Having become a slave to the gift. He gives as a friend because he places on an equal footing what he himself should enjoy and what he must give to others.
He gives as a master because, instead of remaining subject to the gift, he brings it under his own control.
Another method: one who, having enjoyed fine things for himself, [gives to others...]
One who gives what is inferior is called a "slave to giving" because, by reason of that [inferior gift], one falls into an inferior state.
One who gives others exactly what one enjoys oneself is called a "companion in giving" because, by avoiding both inferiority and superiority through that [act], one attains a state of equality.
One who, having enjoyed what is inferior oneself, gives what is excellent to others is called a "master of giving" because, by reason of that, one attains a state of excellence.
“Become lusterless” means having attained the loss of luster. “Sahabya” (companion) means one who goes together;
it is that which functions together. Its state is “sahabyatā,” meaning co-functioning. Thus he said, “they have attained companionship, a state of oneness.
“Of the unattached” means of the unbonded; the meaning is, of one unbonded by the fetter of craving. The fifth [verse] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sīhasenāpati-sutta* and others is concluded.
6–7. Commentary on the *Kāladāna-sutta* and others. 36–37.

In the sixth [sutta], "from the grove" (*ārāmato*) means from the grove of fruit. "First arisen" (*paṭhamuppannāni*) means those that have first appeared, being well-born (*sujātāni*). "One who understands what is said" (*bhāsitaññū*)...
Although the bhikkhus standing at the door of a house remain silent, in substance they are indeed saying, "Give alms," by means of the noble way of begging.
For this has been said: "The Noble Ones stand with reference [to a specific person]; this is the begging of the Noble Ones.

In that regard, those who think, "We cook, but these do not cook; having reached those who cook, if they do not receive anything there, where will they find it? [should be known as those who obstruct].
They share out the things to be given; they are called "knowers of what has been said" because they act upon what must be done after having understood it.
"At the proper and opportune time" means at the time suitable for giving. "With a mind that does not turn back" means with a mind that does not retreat. The seventh [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Kāladāna-sutta* and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Saddha Sutta 38.
In the eighth [verse], "having compassion" means they favor others by extending a wish for their welfare, thinking, "May all beings be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction.
Furthermore, it refers to those who, taking other virtuous fellow-celibates with them, enter the house of their supporters.
"Show favor" means to show compassion. "A humble manner of life" means a disposition characterized by prostration. "Free from the rigidity of anger and pride":
the meaning is that it is devoid of that state of rigidity in the mind—which arises through anger and pride and has the characteristic of inflation—that is absent here.
"By means of gentleness (*soracca*)": in this regard, what is gentleness? It is non-transgression of body, non-transgression of speech, and non-transgression of both body and speech.
Non-transgression—this is called gentleness (*soracca*). By means of this state of gentleness, which is designated as the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), as it has been handed down thus:
"All restraint of virtue is gentleness," [one speaks of] being "courteous" (*sakhila*). Regarding that: "What is courtesy (*sākhalya*)?
It is the abandoning of such speech as is stiff, harsh, rough, bitter, provocative, bordering on anger, and not conducive to concentration."
"Whatever speech is blameless, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, heart-stirring, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people—one speaks such speech.
Whatever gentleness of speech, amiability of speech, and lack of harshness of speech there is in that—this is called 'gentleness' (sākhalya).
Thus, it is endowed with the quality of being friendly and soft as described; therefore, he said:
“‘Sakhila’ means ‘affectionate.
The commentary on the Saddha Sutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Putta Sutta and others.

39–40. "Nourished by us" means he was supported. To show that this support proceeded from the time of birth through the provision of conditions for happiness and the removal of conditions for suffering, the phrase beginning with "by us" was stated. By the word "etc.
in "by the growth of hands and feet, etc.," one includes such acts as removing mucus from the mouth, bathing, and adorning [the child]. Of the mother and father...

He said, "Our property... our family lineage will endure for a long time," because fields and other assets, when preserved without being destroyed, serve as the cause for their continued existence through successive generations.

"Without interrupting the *salākabhatta* and so forth" means without discontinuing the *salākabhatta* and other such provisions; for one must remain engaged in conduct that makes one worthy of receiving an inheritance.
He said, "He will deal with the inheritance, not the other," by means of the phrase "by conduct befitting his family lineage" and so forth.
"Making himself worthy of the inheritance" means making oneself deserving of the inheritance.
For when children do not abide by their parents' advice and follow wrong practice, the parents may take them to court and disinherit them; such children are not worthy of the inheritance.
But while the exhortation is being given, they act as the owners of what belongs to the family.
"Starting from the third day" means starting from the third day after the day of death. The rest is easy to understand. The tenth [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Puttasutta* and the others is finished.
The commentary on the Sumanavagga is finished.
5. Muṇḍarājavagga: 1–2.
Commentary on the Ādiyasutta and others.
41–42. Regarding the first [jhāna] of the fifth [dhyāna], it is said: "attained through exertion and energy" (*uṭṭhāna-vīriyādhigata*). That is, attained by means of both exertion and energy.

In this context, they say that "exertion" (*uṭṭhāna*) is bodily energy (*kāyika-vīriya*), while "energy" (*vīriya*) is mental (*cetasika*). Alternatively, "exertion" is the state of being engaged and intent upon the production of wealth;
"energy" is the corresponding effort (*ussāha*). "Refreshed" (*pīṇita*) means nourished and well-satiated. One who has become thus...
Because he has a stout body, it is said that "he makes [himself] stout. The second [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Ādiyā-sutta and others is finished.
3. Commentary on the Iṭṭha-sutta.
43. "In the third [verse], they praise heedfulness" means that the wise praise heedfulness alone, thinking: "Heedfulness must be practiced by one who aspires for these things, such as long life.
Or, because the wise praise heedfulness in the performance of meritorious deeds, the meaning is:
therefore, heedfulness alone must be practiced by one who aspires for long life and the rest. This refers to the first alternative of meaning.
The word “in meritorious deeds” (*puññakiriyāsu*) is connected with the word “heedful” (*appamatto*).

Since the wise praise heedfulness, and since one who is heedful in performing meritorious deeds attains both goals, therefore, by one who aspires for long life and the other [qualities], heedfulness alone must be practiced.
In the second interpretation of the meaning, the wise praise heedfulness.
"In what? means "in meritorious deeds. "Why? means "because the wise person who is diligent attains both benefits";
this is the meaning. "By the acquisition of benefit" means by the acquisition of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth.
The commentary on the *Iṭṭhasutta* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the *Manāpadāyīsutta* 44.
Regarding the fourth [sutta], he says, "A mind-made [body] is that produced by means of jhāna," referring to "one class of devas among the Suddhāvāsa [heavens] produced by means of jhāna.
For although all beings are indeed produced by the volitional mind (*abhisaṅkhāramanas*), [this specific case is distinguished].
Because they are produced by the mind alone, without external conditions, beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are called "mind-made" (manomaya).
If it is argued that, in this case, it would follow that spontaneously born beings (opapātika) in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) are also mind-made, we say no;

for in that case, there is no possibility of the restriction "produced by the mind alone," since there is no suspicion whatsoever that they must be produced by external conditions. This term is conventional (niruḷha).
Furthermore, this designation "mind-made" (*manomaya*) is used in the world with respect to beings in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

For even those who maintain the authority of the Vedas speak of the self as fivefold: "consisting of food, consisting of breath, consisting of mind, consisting of bliss, and consisting of consciousness. Even the proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) say:
"divine, material, mind-made. Or, [it refers] to the three successions of families, namely those designated as Brahmins, Khattiyas, and Vessas.
"Among families of noble birth. Or "in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure" means among the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The commentary on the *Manāpadāyī Sutta* is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the *Puññābhisanda Sutta* and others.
45–46. "Incalculable" (*asaṅkheyya*) in the fifth [case] means incalculable by the calculation of *āḷhaka* measures.

However, it does have a reckoning in terms of *yojana*, because it is delimited—by the great earth below, by space above, by the Cakkavāḷa mountains all around, and in the middle by the islands and mountains situated here and there—for one who knows it, it is measured in *yojanas*.
"Can be calculated" means it is possible to count them. It is "very terrifying" by way of many fearful objects:

conscious beings such as large-bodied fish, crocodiles, *kumbhīla* water-monsters, *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, great *nāgas*, and *dānavas*; and unconscious things such as powerful mouths [of rivers] and abysses (*pātāla*).
"Many" means numerous. "Flowing" means streaming. "Approaching" means coming near. The sixth [chapter] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Puññābhisanda-sutta* and others is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the *Dhana-sutta* and others. 47–48.
In the seventh [verse], "faith" (*saddhā*) refers to faith attained by means of the Path. "And whose virtue is noble" (*sīlañ ca yassa kalyāṇaṃ*) refers to noble virtue (*kalyāṇasīla*).

This is called the noble disciple’s virtue dear to the noble ones (*ariyakanta-sīla*). Although there is not even a single aspect of virtue that is not dear to the noble disciple, in this context, what is intended is the fivefold virtue that has not been abandoned even in other lives.
The eighth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Dhanasutta and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the Kosala Sutta 49.

In the ninth [sutta], "with drooping shoulders" means having his face cast downward because he is unable to look directly at anything. "Lacking eloquence" means being without ready wit (*paṭibhāna*), because he is incapable of saying anything consistent with the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Kosalasutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Nāradasutta 50.

In the tenth [verse], “intoxicated” (*ajjhomucchito*) means being stupefied by an excessive intoxication of craving (*taṇhāmucchā*); that is, having fallen into a state of delusion (*muccha*), confusion (*moha*), and negligence (*pamāda*).
He has fallen [into that state]. Therefore he said: “Having swallowed... endowed with an excessive intoxication of craving. “Greatly” means “with great [intoxication].
This was stated by means of a change in grammatical gender. Therefore he said: “With great royal majesty.
The commentary on the Nārada Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Muṇḍarājavagga is finished.
The First Fifty [Discourses] is finished.
2. The Second Fifty [Discourses].
(6) 1. The Chapter on Hindrances (Nīvaraṇavagga). 1–2.
Commentary on the Discourses on Obstructions, etc. (51–52).

Regarding the first [discourse] of the second [chapter]: they "obstruct" (*āvaranti*), thus they are "obstructions" (*āvaraṇā*); they "shut off" (*nīvārayanti*), thus they are "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇā*). And herein, "they obstruct" means...
They surround the arising of wholesome states from the very beginning. "Nīvārayanti" means they ward off them completely;
therefore, "by way of obstruction" (*āvaraṇavasena*) means by way of obstructing the initial arising of the wholesome.

"By way of hindrance" (*nīvaraṇavasena*) means by way of warding them off without remainder—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Because when the five hindrances arise, they [obstruct] that which has not yet arisen...

They do not allow mundane or supramundane wisdom to arise; even when the eight attainments or the five higher knowledges have arisen, they cut them off and cause them to fall away. Therefore, they are called "the weakeners of wisdom.
Here, "cutting off" and "causing to fall away" mean precisely the non-arising of those types of wisdom that have not yet arisen. Thus, [they obstruct] sublime and unsurpassed wisdom.
Furthermore, because the hindering states— which act as causes for the non-attainment of certain limited wisdom—
destroy the capacity of others, they are described as "weakening wisdom.
A "human quality" (*manussadhamma*) is a state that can be produced by humans by nature, or a state that brings about a human existence.
It is a limited wholesome state that is not exalted. It is that which continues to exist even when a Buddha has not appeared in the world, and with reference to which it is said:
"By a lowly holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas. "Ariya" means "sufficient for the state of an Ariya";

what is meant is that he is capable of attaining the state of an Ariya. "Knowledge and vision" itself is the "distinction of knowledge and vision"; thus, he is an "alamariya," meaning he is the distinction of knowledge and vision who is sufficient [for the state of an Ariya].
And this is a distinguished noble knowledge and vision (*ariya-ñāṇadassana-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*) refers to the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), insight (*vipassanā*), the path (*magga*), the fruit (*phala*), the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*), and even omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*).
For in the passage, "Being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision," it is the divine eye that is meant.
“Knowledge and vision” (ñāṇadassana). In the passage, “He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision,” it refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
In the passage, “They are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,” it refers to the path (magga).

In the passage, “This is another distinguished attainment of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a superhuman state, a superior dwelling more peaceful than before,” it refers to the fruit (phala). And furthermore, “As for my knowledge... [the text continues].
In the passage, “Vision arose: ‘Unshakable is my liberation; this is the last birth; now there is no further existence,’ ” it is the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
In the passage, “And the knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago,’ ” it is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
However, here the supramundane state (*lokuttaradhamma*) is intended. And herein, the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*)...
"Knowledge-vision" (ñāṇadassana) refers to the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), which knows and sees just as visual consciousness does.
Furthermore, "knowledge-vision" refers to insight (vipassanā), which likewise knows and sees the three characteristics of phenomena during the stages of comprehension (sammasanūpacāra).
Finally, "knowledge-vision" refers to the path (magga), which knows and sees Nibbāna or the Four Truths through penetration characterized by non-delusion.
The fruit, however, should be associated with Nibbāna alone. Reviewing is "knowledge and vision" in the sense of illuminating in every way the goal attained through the Path.
It is "knowledge and vision" by virtue of its omniscience, its unobstructedness, and its quality as the universal eye.
"Time exhausted" means time consumed. The second [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Āvaraṇasutta and others is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the Padhāniyaṅgasutta and others. 53–54.
In the third [sutta], one who exerts himself is a "striver" (padahana); he is a yogi devoted to cultivation (bhāvanā). His state is "devotion to cultivation" (bhāvanānuyoga).
The state of striving (*padhāna*). One who possesses striving is a *padhānika*; by changing the letter *k* to *y*, it is stated as “*padhāniyo*.

Because it is said, “because it has come from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*),” the faith that has come from the aspiration of both *paccekabodhisattas* and *sāvakabodhisattas* is indeed a term for “coming” (*āgamana*);
however, by way of an exalted description, it says “of all-knowing bodhisattvas (*sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ*).”

It has been said. Because it has been attained through realization (*adhigama*), that which is associated with the supreme path and fruit is also called "faith through realization" (*adhigama-saddhā*), which is stated to be a constituent factor of the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).

"By way of immovability" means by way of being unshakable, because it cannot be overcome by opposing factors. "Resolute confidence" (*okappanā*) is the act of leaping forward and resolving upon an inspiring object through the arising of serene confidence (*pasāda*).
"Confidence alone. "Well-penetrated" means thoroughly penetrated. It was penetrated in such a way that, by that penetration, omniscient knowledge came into his hands;

it was penetrated accordingly. For one whose faith is unshakable and unwavering due to the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, that faith does not remain so [unwavering] with respect to the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature or the Saṅgha’s perfect practice, because of that [specific] penetration.
This is impossible, this has no occasion. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, he who is confident in the Buddha, confident in the Dhamma, confident in the Saṅgha,” and so forth.
Exertion through striving succeeds because of striving with diligence, thinking: “Surely by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.”
The word *appa* has the sense of "absence," as in such passages as "of one who is quiet... or again... and so forth; thus he said, "healthy.

"Samavepākiniyā" means having the nature of digesting food exactly as it is eaten in a balanced manner. For if the stomach (*gahaṇī*) digests by making [the fire] too intense, it produces disease through the corruption of bile and other humors due to its fierce state;
if it digests by making [the fire] too weak, it does so through the corruption of wind and other humors due to its sluggish state.
Therefore he said, "neither too cold nor too hot. Because of the dullness or sharpness of the fire-element (*gahaṇiteja*) within beings, they respectively endure cold and heat;

thus he said, "one who is sensitive to extreme cold," and so forth. Since confessing one's transgression as it truly is is called "self-disclosure," he said, "one who reveals one's own lack of virtue as it really is.
[The phrase] "leading to arising and passing away" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).
"Those who penetrate both arising and passing away"—this is the meaning here; thus he said, "Both arising," and so forth. "Pure" means free from defilements.
"Capable of piercing through" means capable of abandoning [the defilements] with distinction by way of their specific factor (tadaṅga).
"Leading to the destruction of that suffering" refers to whatever suffering would otherwise continue as long as this knowledge has not been attained.
It does not occur once that [state] has been attained; it is with reference to this that he speaks. For thus this practitioner is called a "minor stream-enterer.
The fourth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Padhāniyaṅga Sutta* and so forth is finished.
5. Commentary on the Mātāputtasutta 55.

In the fifth [verse], "confidence" (*vissāsa*) refers to a state of being characterized by a clear appearance. "Entry" (*otāra*) means the mind's penetration into that [state]. "Having taken" (*gahetvā*) means having taken its own opportunity. "Having exhausted" (*khepetvā*) means having exhausted the wholesome phase (*kusalavāra*).

"It would strike" (*ghaṭṭeyya*) means it would afflict by way of stepping upon it and so forth. "By the three full understandings" (*tīhi pariññāhi*) refers to those consisting of knowledge (*ñāta*), investigation (*tīraṇa*), and abandoning (*pahāna*).
By means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). "Fearless from any quarter" (*akutobhaya*) means that there is no fear for them from anything; the sense is that they are without fear.
They have gone to the further shore, the limit, of the four floods (*ogha*), or indeed of the great flood of saṃsāra. Therefore he said: "The further shore is called Nibbāna," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Mātāputtasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Upajjhāya Sutta 56.
In the sixth [sutta], "sweetness" (madhurakabhāva) refers to the rigidity of the body;
however, since that is preceded by a sense of heaviness, it says, "having become heavy. "They do not fly apart" means they do not manifest, nor do they appear due to various causes.
Therefore he said, "The four quarters and the intermediate directions do not appear to me. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Upajjhāya Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭṭhāna Sutta.

57. In the seventh [verse], in the phrase "subject to aging" (*jarādhammo*), the word *dhamma* has the sense of "nature," as in such expressions as "nibbāna, which is of a nature not subject to confusion.

Therefore, the meaning is "one whose nature is aging" or "one whose inherent character is decrepitude. For this reason, he said, "the nature of aging," and so forth. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
One who takes up what is to be given by karma is a "heir to karma" (*kammadāyādo*); that is, one who partakes of the fruit of the karma accumulated by oneself.

This is the meaning. Speaking of that inheritance by way of figurative designation for its cause, he said: "The meaning is that 'action is my inheritance, it is my property. This is just as it is said:
"Monks, through the undertaking of wholesome states, in this way this merit increases.
Although the fruit is distinct from its sources in terms of its intrinsic nature, it becomes mixed with them as if it were not distinct. Therefore he said:
“Kamma is my womb, kamma is my cause. Relatives and blood kin are called *bandhu* because they are bound together by the sense of “mine-ness” (*mamatta*).
However, since kamma is an absolute bond, he said, “Kamma is my relative (*bandhu*). A support (*patiṭṭhā*) is a refuge;
for there is no support for sentient beings equal to kamma.
Pride arisen concerning youth is the act of becoming conceited by disregarding one's youth, thinking, "We shall perform meritorious deeds when we are old;
for now we are still young. Or, "I have passed sixty or seventy years free from illness;
I do not need to eat even a fragment of *harītaka* fruit, whereas these others [think], 'Such-and-such a part of our body hurts; we must take medicine.'"
“I eat,” they wander about, thinking, “Who else is like me, being called ‘healthy’? Such making of pride is the intoxication with health (*ārogyamada*).

Life, for all beings, is indeed fragile and followed by suffering; yet, without considering either of these two, and relying instead on its apparent continuity and the ease with which conditions are obtained, one thinks:
“I have lived long, I am living long, I shall live long; I have lived happily.”
“I live happily, I shall live happily”—this kind of prideful attitude is the intoxication with life (*jīvitamada*).

“Free from substrate” (*upadhirahita*) means free from the substrate of sensual desire (*kāmūpadhi*). For there are four substrates: the substrate of sensual desire, the substrate of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*), the substrate of defilements (*kilesūpadhi*), and the substrate of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārūpadhi*).
Sensual desires are also [defined as]: “Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence upon the five strands of sensual pleasure...”

Because it serves as the basis for the pleasure described in the words, "This is the gratification of sensual pleasures," the term "upadhi" is used in the sense of that wherein pleasure is founded; likewise,
the aggregates (khandhas) are so called because they serve as the basis for the suffering rooted in the aggregates,

the defilements (kilesas) because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the woeful states, and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāras) because they serve as the basis for the suffering of existence.
Because it is a state of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*). The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭṭhāna-sutta* is finished.
8–10. Commentary on the *Licchavikumāraka-sutta*, etc.
58–60. Regarding the term *sāpateyyaṃ* in the eighth [case]: here *saṃ* means wealth (*dhana*); its master (*pati*) is a *sapati*, that is, the owner of wealth.

Because it brings about his welfare, it is *sāpateyyaṃ*; the meaning is "property," "substance," or "wealth. One who leads the affairs of the village according to his own preference is a *gāmaṇi*; a *gāmaṇi* himself is a *gāmaṇiko*.
"Those who live in dependence upon and by relying on [another] are 'dependents' (anujīvino)," thus he said: "and those who live depending upon this.
This was said with reference to people where, depending on a single great family, even thirty or sixty families live;
the rest is easily understood. The ninth and following sections have their meaning already explained.
The commentary on the Licchavikumārakasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Nīvaraṇavagga is finished.
(7) 2. Saññāvagga (The Chapter on Perception)
1–5. Commentary on the Saññā-sutta, etc. (61–65).
Regarding the first [discourse] of the second [chapter], the phrases "of great fruit" (*mahapphalā*) and "of great benefit" (*mahānisaṃsā*) are identical in meaning; only the phrasing differs.
Thus he said, "of great fruit," and so forth. In such passages as "Householders, there are these five benefits" (*pañc’ime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā*), the word *ānisaṃsa* [is used].
There is also the sequence of the fruit (*phala-pariyāya*). They are of great benefit because they serve as conditions for the great supramundane happiness (*lokuttara-sukha*).
They are "plunged into the Deathless" (*amata-ogadhā*) because they are within the Deathless, have entered into the Deathless due to having seen Nibbāna, and do not go beyond it.

Therefore it is said, "having the Deathless as their consummation" (*amatapariyosānā*). That which has the Deathless as its consummation, end, and limit is "having the Deathless as their consummation."

The perception of death (*maraṇasaññā*) is the perception arising through the knowledge of contemplation of death. The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*) is the perception that arises in one who comprehends nutriment as repulsive by way of its going into the body and so forth.
"Of one who is weary" means of one who is disenchanted and not attached to anything whatsoever.
The second and subsequent [perceptions] have meanings that are already evident.
The commentary on the Saññāsutta and others is finished.
6–10. Commentary on the Sājīvasutta and others (66–70).
In the sixth [sutta], it is called *sājīva* because they live together (*saha ājīvanti*) therein; it refers to the posing of the question and its resolution. Therefore he said:

“‘Sājīva’ means both the posing of a question and the answering of a question,” and so forth. “Abhisaṅkhataṃ” means accumulated. The seventh [discourse] and the others have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sājīvasutta* and the rest is concluded.
The commentary on the *Saññāvagga* is concluded.
(8) 3. Yodhājīvavagga 1–2.
Commentary on the First Discourse on the Fruit of Liberation of Mind, etc. 71–72.

In the first [discourse] of the third [vagga], regarding the phrase "the bar of ignorance" (*avijjāpaligha*): here, "ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the ignorance that is the root of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭamūlikā*). This...
Because it cannot be lifted by ordinary people, it is called a "cross-bar" (*paligha*) in the sense of being difficult to lift and because it acts as an obstruction to entering the door of Nibbāna;
thus it is said to be "like a cross-bar. Therefore, because that [craving] has been lifted, he is called "one who has lifted the cross-bar" (*ukkhitapaligho*).

That which has the nature of producing renewed existence, or which deserves the fruit of renewed existence, is "leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavikā*), meaning it gives rise to renewed existence.

Meaning: "The cycle of birth" (*jātisaṃsāra*) refers to the formative volitional action of karma (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*), which is the condition for the aggregates of renewed existence that have thus acquired their name by way of both being born and wandering on.
For "the cycle of birth" is stated as the cause by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
Indeed, because it stands surrounding [existence] by way of being the cause for repeated arising, it is called a "moat" (*parikhā*), owing to its encircling of the continuum.
Because it was strewn, scattered, completely cast about, and ruined, it is called "one with a strewn moat" (*saṃkiṇṇaparikha*). Regarding the phrase "reckoned as craving" (*taṇhāsaṅkhāta*):
here, "craving" refers to the craving rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For this [craving] is called a "stake" (*esikā*) in the sense that it has gone deep down.

"Having pulled out" means having extracted it. "Belonging to the lower portion" (*orambhāgiyāni*) means those which produce the lower portion—namely, the conditions for rebirth in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*).
The fetters such as the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*). For these are called "bolts" (*aggaḷā*) because they stand closing off the mind, just as a bolt closes the gate of a city.

Therefore, because he has emerged from and broken through them, he is called "boltless" (*niraggaḷa*). One whose banner of conceit (*māna-ddhaja*) has been lowered and discarded by means of the supreme path is "one who has lowered his banner" (*pannaddhaja*).

"One who has laid down the burden" (*pannabhāra*) refers to the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*), the burden of the defilements (*kilesa*), and the burden of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"One who has laid down the burden" means one whose burden has been set down. "Dissociated" means dissociated from the four bonds and from all defilements.
"The conceit ‘I am’" refers to the conceit "I am" in regard to form; the conceit "I am" in regard to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
For here, what is intended by "the conceit ‘I am’" is that which proceeds by grasping the five aggregates collectively as "I am."

He says, "the pillar-standards raised at the city gate," because one plants and sets up pillar-stands on both sides for the purpose of warding off dangers and for the purpose of clearing [the way] from the city gate.
He says, "having broken down the wall and leveled the moat," because by the very act of destroying the wall, the ground of the moat becomes level. "In this way," and so forth.
