The correlation of similes: "Sakkāya" (personality) refers to the collection of phenomena that exists as a real body; it is the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
The "masses of suffering" include the sufferings mentioned in the *Dukkha-khandha-sutta* arising from the thirty-two causes of action, such as eye-disease, headache, and so forth;
the ninety-eight diseases; and the twenty-five great fears, beginning with fear of kings. The second [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the first sutta on the fruit of liberation of mind is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the first two suttas on dwelling in the Dhamma, 73–74.
In the third [sutta], "within one's own internal continuity" means within one's own mental continuum (*santāna*). It refers to one seeking welfare by way of bringing forth loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"By means of compassion" means by one who feels sympathy. "Having embraced" (*pariggahetvā*) means having grasped all around; the meaning is "having pervaded.
"Having encompassed" (*pariccatvā*) means having made it all around; the meaning is simply "having pervaded from every side. There is also a reading, "having depended upon" (*paṭicca*).
"Do not neglect" means [do not neglect] by not devoting yourself to the serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) mentioned as "you should meditate," or by any other [means].

"Do not fall into negligence through the cause of negligence. In the Dispensation that leads to liberation, negligence consists both in doing what should not be done and in failing to do what should be done.
"At a time of failure" means at a time characterized by the seven kinds of failure, such as unsuitable conditions and so forth.

He said, "Meditate; do not be negligent... [etc. ...this is the instruction," because all the virtues in the Dispensation are included right here. There is nothing further to be said regarding the fourth verse.
The commentary on the first *Dhammavihārisutta*, etc., is finished.
5. Commentary on the first *Yodhājīvasutta* (75):
In the fifth [sutta], "fighting" (*yujjhana*) is "war" (*yodha*); those whose livelihood (*ājīva*) is this are "warriors by profession" (*yodhājīva*). Therefore, he said, "those who live by war."
“Unable to stand firm after steadying himself” means that one who is bound, though endowed with fortitude, is unable to remain steady.

“Having come together” means having arrived. “Becomes afflicted” means it undergoes a transformation; therefore he said, “it abandons its natural state. “In a cloud of dust” is a locative used in the sense of the accusative;
thus he asked, “What is this so-called ‘cloud of dust’ for that person? “Having disentangled” means having caused the grasping to be released. “Having freed” means having removed it from the body.
The commentary on the first *Yodhājīva-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the second *Yodhājīva-sutta*. 76.

In the sixth [sutta], by the word "leather" (*camma*), one refers to that which is made of leather, or what is sewn together as "leather," or other items such as shield-boards (*keṭaka-phalaka*) and so forth.
He gathers [them] together. "Having fastened on his quiver and bow" means having fastened and prepared both the bow and the quiver.
For even the act of making the string dependent upon the staff of the bow is called "fastening the bow. Therefore he said:
"having fastened on the bow and the arrow-quiver. "Standing in a battle formation" means according to the method of arranging the arrays (*vyūha*) of two armies.
"By way of its arrangement" means it stands by way of that particular formation; what is meant is that it is arrayed according to the disposition of a military phalanx.
"Exerts zeal and effort" means he exerts zeal and effort for the purpose of fighting.
"They bring to completion" means they lead [the life] to its limit, which is death. Therefore he said, "bringing to completion," referring to life.
"They bring about ruin" means they cause one to undergo death.
Regarding the phrases "with an unguarded body," and so forth: one who plays with the hands and feet or twists the neck is said not to guard the body.
One who engages in various kinds of wicked conduct is said not to guard speech. One who entertains thoughts such as sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) and the like [is said not to guard the mind].
"Does not guard the mind" means that mindfulness established in the body is not established.
"Followed by lust" means overcome by lust; or "overpowered by lust" means touched by lust, like being bitten by a snake with virulent venom.
"In the sense of burning after" refers to the practice of improper means, which brings about great torment both in the present and in the future, due to its lack of stability in nature.
In the sense of being a temporary manifestation; in the sense of being momentary due to its charm for only a brief instant;

in the sense of crushing all limbs and members because it can be overcome by the skilled; in the sense of striking, because it resembles a blow due to its nature as a basis for cutting, breaking, and so forth;
and in the sense of piercing through, because its inherent nature is to enter inside after producing a wound in what was previously unwounded.
In the sense of being accompanied by risk and danger, because they are signs of harm pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
The commentary on the second *Yodhājīva-sutta* is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the first *Anāgatabhaya-sutta*, etc.
77–78. "For the sake of attaining distinction" means for the purpose of reaching a higher state. "Energy" (*vīriya*) refers to the energy of striving (*padhāna-vīriya*).
Furthermore, when it is practiced by way of walking meditation (*caṅkama*), it may also be described as "bodily"; thus he said, "both kinds.
"Knife-winds" (*satthaka-vātā*) are winds that blow like a butcher’s knife cutting through the joints and ligaments. Therefore he said, "a knife..."
"By those who have performed [the deed]," etc. "By those who have performed the deed" means by those who have committed the act of robbery.
It is said that those who have performed the deed, having invoked a deity so that their task might be accomplished, kill men and take their throat-blood for the sake of assisting that deity.
They think, "If other men were being killed, a great clamor would arise; therefore, we shall seek out one who has gone forth (a monk)."...
Thinking, “They do not exist,” they seize and kill monks; it is with reference to this that it was said.

“By those who have not performed the ritual” means by those wishing to perform an offering beforehand for the sake of ensuring the success of their task when returning from the forest to the village. For this very reason he said:
“Those who have gone out after committing a robbery are called ‘those who have performed the ritual,’ and so forth. Regarding the eighth [offense], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the *Paṭhama-anāgata-bhaya-sutta* and others is concluded.
9. Commentary on the *Tatiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta*. 79.
Regarding the phrase "the text is profound" (*pāḷi-gambhīrā*): by way of its textual content, it is profound, bottomless, difficult to fathom, and similar to the *Salla-sutta*.
For the *Sallasutta* is profound by way of its textual phrasing (*pāḷivasena*), such as in the passage beginning “the signless, the unknown,” but it is not profound in meaning (*atthagambhīra*).
For in that text, various verses remain difficult to comprehend. Indeed, what is difficult to comprehend is called “profound” because it is hard to penetrate with knowledge.
Here too, due to the difficulty of comprehending certain verses in their sequence, they are indeed hard to penetrate.
Therefore, they are profound by way of the text (*pāḷi*). They are "profound in meaning" (*atthagambhīrā*) because they are profound by way of their meaning, like the Mahāvedalla Sutta;
for the profundity of the Mahāvedalla Sutta by way of its meaning is indeed evident. It transcends the world, thus it is "supramundane" (*lokuttara*);
those that possess this as their meaning are "supramundane. Hence he said: "They illuminate supramundane states. They are "connected with emptiness" (*suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttā*).
They reveal the phenomena of the emptiness of the seven [bases]. Therefore he said:
"Connected with the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and modes of conditionality. As for the terms "to be learned" and "to be mastered," they are stated with a change of gender and number;
thus he said: "both to be learned and to be employed. Poetry is the work of a poet (*kavi*). Furthermore, whatever is the work of someone, that is called "done by him."
He says, "It is called *kavitā* (poetry), meaning 'made by poets' (*kavīhi katā*). *Kāveyya* means *kabya*; the sense is that *kabya* is what is spoken by a poet (*kavinā vutta*).
Therefore he says, "it is a synonym for that. *Cittakkharā* means letters of variegated form. The other [term] is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Standing outside the teaching" means they do not belong to the sphere of the teaching (*na sāsanāvacarā*). "By the external disciples" refers to those who say, "We are Buddhas."
"Among those disciples of whom nothing has been prescribed"— this refers to novices, young monks, women, great householders, and so forth. "They will wish to listen" means that,
being delighted by the beauty of the syllables and the excellence of the voice, they will gather together thinking, "This one is a preacher of the Dhamma," and become desirous of hearing it.
The commentary on the Third Discourse on Future Dangers is finished.
10. Commentary on the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers 80.

Regarding the tenth [discourse], "by means of fivefold association": "association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversation, [association by touch, and association by using things in common]."

By the fivefold contact mentioned as "contact through hearing (*savanasaṃsagga*), contact through seeing (*dassanasaṃsagga*), contact through conversation (*sākacchāsaṃsagga*), contact through association (*sambhogasaṃsagga*), and physical contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*).
Contact (*saṃsagga*) is that by which one comes into contact; it is passion (*rāga*). Contact through hearing is contact that has hearing as its cause, or contact that proceeds by way of hearing.
This same method applies to the others as well. Physical contact, however, is the grasping of the body. Among these, [one hears] the excellence of form and so forth being described by others...
Lust that arises by way of the cognitive process of ear-consciousness in one who hears sounds of singing, whether cool or pleasant, is called "contact through hearing.
Lust that arises by way of the cognitive process of eye-consciousness in one who gazes upon an unwholesome form is called "contact through seeing.
Lust that arises by way of mutual conversation and chatter is called "contact through conversation. [In the case] of a bhikkhu [and] a bhikkhunī...
Taking what belongs to a nun and taking what belongs to a monk for the purpose of personal use, arising from lust, is called "sexual contact" (*sambhoga-saṃsagga*).
Lust arising through grasping the hand and so forth is called "bodily contact" (*kāya-saṃsagga*).
"In various ways" refers to the storage of food, the storage of drinks, the storage of clothing, the storage of vehicles, the storage of bedding, and the storage of perfumes.
It is of many kinds by way of the storage of material goods (*āmisa*).

By the word "of what has been stored" (*sannidhikatassa*), he shows that in the expression "enjoyment of what has been made into a store" (*sannidhikāraparibhoga*), the word *kāra* has the sense of an object (*kamma*).

Or, just as when it should have been said "leading to accumulation" (*ācayaṃ gāmino*), the designation "leading to accumulation" (*ācayagāmino*) is made by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*), so too, when it should have been said "enjoyment of what has been made into a store" (*sannidhikāraṃ paribhogaṃ*), [it is stated as *sannidhikāraparibhogaṃ*] by eliding the nasal vowel.
“Consumption of what has been stored” (sannidhikāraparibhoga) is said; the meaning is: consumption after having made a store.
Regarding the phrase “consumption of what has been stored,” there are two ways of explaining it:
according to the Vinaya and according to the principle of austerity (sallekha). First, according to the Vinaya: whatever food was received today becomes “stored” on the following day.

If one consumes it oneself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, if one gives what was obtained by oneself to novice monks (sāmaṇera) and eats on the following day what they have received or what has been made available by them, it is permissible;
yet, there is no purification (sallekha). The same principle applies to the storage of drinks (pānasannidhi).
Regarding the storage of robes (vatthasannidhi), if a robe is neither formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) nor assigned to another (avikappita), there is both storage and a lack of purification.
He causes agitation. This is the literal explanation. But according to the figurative sense, one should be content with the three robes; having obtained a fourth, it should be given to another.

If one is unable to give it to anyone at all, yet wishes to give it to someone who has gone for the purpose of receiving a recitation or for the purpose of inquiry, it should be given as soon as that person returns; one must not fail to give it.
It is permissible. However, if robes are insufficient, or if there is a reasonable expectation [of obtaining more], it is permissible to set aside [the robe] for the permitted period.

If one cannot find a needle, thread, or a robe-maker, it is also permissible to set it aside after performing the formal act (vinayakamma) [of postponement], thinking, "When this one is worn out, where else shall I obtain such as this again?

But it is not permissible to set it aside [merely] thinking, "When this is worn out, where shall I obtain such again? For in that case, there is storage (sannidhi), and it violates the austerity (sallekha).
Regarding the "storing of vehicles": a vehicle consists of a cart, a chariot, a wagon, a carriage, or a small chariot.
However, these are not vehicles for one who has gone forth; rather, sandals are the vehicle.
For a single bhikkhu, at most two sets of sandals are permitted—one for dwelling in the forest and one for washing the feet. Having obtained a third, it must be given to another.
It should be given away. It is not permitted to set it aside [thinking], "Where else shall I find another when this one has worn out?";
for that constitutes storing up and violates the practice of effacement (*sallekha*). Regarding the storage of bedding: "bedding" here refers to a bed.
For a single monk, two beds at most are permitted—one in his sleeping chamber and one in his daytime resting place. If he should obtain more than that, [it must be disposed of].
It should be given to another bhikkhu or to a group; it is not permissible not to give it, for there would be both storage and the violation of the practice of effacement (*sallekha*).
Regarding the storage of scents: when a bhikkhu suffers from ailments such as boils, itch, or skin diseases, scents are permitted.
One who needs a scent may have a scent brought, and once that illness has subsided, or for others who are afflicted, [it may be used].
It should be given away, or placed at the door, or used for things such as fumigating the five-finger marks on the walls.
It is not permitted to set it aside with the thought, "It will be useful when there is illness again," for that constitutes the storage of perfumes and undermines effacement (*sallekha*).
By "material goods" (*āmisa*), one should understand what remains after what has been mentioned; namely: here, a certain bhikkhu, at such a time...
Thinking, "These will be for my benefit," he had sesame, rice, mung beans, peas, salt, fish, ghee, oil, earthenware vessels, and so forth brought and set aside.

During the rainy season, having had rice-gruel cooked by the novices at an early hour and having consumed it himself, he would say, "Novice, it is difficult to enter the village because of the water and mud; go to such-and-such a family and [bring back] for me from my monastery..."
“Inform her that you have sat down, and bring curds and other provisions from such-and-such a family,” he sent word.
When the monks asked, “Venerable sir, shall we enter the village? he replied, “Friends, it is difficult to enter the village now. They said, “Very well, venerable sir;
you stay here, and we will go and bring back almsfood,” and so they departed. Then the novice...
Having brought curd and other items, and having prepared both the meal and its condiments, he serves them;
while he is eating, his attendants send further food, so that he eats what is both pleasing and unpleasing from that source as well.
Then, when monks arrive bringing alms-food, he likewise eats what is both pleasing and unpleasing from that too. In this manner, he passes even the four months of the rainy season.
This is called a monk who lives the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse. Such is what is known as the storage of material goods (*āmisasannidhi*).

However, it is permissible for a monk to store in his dwelling place one measure of rice, one lump of sugar, and a small amount of ghee—just enough for the purpose of providing hospitality to thieves who may arrive unexpectedly. For they [the monks] provide such hospitality with these material goods.
If they were unable to obtain it, they might deprive one of life; therefore, if such an amount is not available, it is permissible to have it brought and set aside.
Furthermore, during times of discomfort, whatever among these items is allowable (kappiya) may be consumed by oneself.
However, even for one who stores a great quantity in a storehouse for allowable goods (kappiyakuṭi), there is no such thing as "hoarding" (sannidhi).
The commentary on the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers is finished.
The commentary on the Warrior Chapter is finished.
(9) 4. The Chapter on Elders.
1–2. Commentary on the *Rajanīyasutta* and others. 81–82.

The first [verse] of the fourth [sutta] is easy to understand. In the second, "deceit" (*makkha*) is so called because, like excrement striking a person who is smearing themselves with it, it first smears the one who performs the action even while it is directed toward smearing another's virtues; since he possesses this, he is [called] deceitful.
*Makkhī*. *Paḷāsa* means he envies; the meaning is that he snatches away another’s virtues as if biting them. One who possesses this is a *paḷāsī*.
For a person who is envious does not give way to a second person, but stands there having pushed him aside.
Therefore it is said: "endowed with envy characterized by grasping at the yoke."
The commentary on the *Rajanīyasutta* and others is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Kuhakasutta*. 83.

In the third [sutta], "by means of three grounds for hypocrisy" refers to the classification into: (1) hinting (*sāmantajappana*), (2) reliance on deportment (*iriyāpathasannissita*), and (3) the use of requisites (*paccayappaṭisevana*).

By means of the three types of grounds for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*). One who deceives and deludes the world by means of these three grounds for hypocrisy, causing others to wonder of him, "Oh, what a marvelous person!
and thus arousing their amazement within themselves, is called a hypocrite (*kuhaka*).
Being desirous of gain and honor, he prattles, either exalting himself or disparaging the donor, so that the latter might give something; having thus made a display (*ukkācetvā*), he speaks.
One who talks is a talker (*lapaka*). One whose habit is signs is a sign-taker (*nemittika*);
or, one who acts by means of signs, or one who makes signs, is a sign-taker. A "sign" refers to bodily or verbal action that produces in others the perception that they should give requisites.
One whose habit is disparagement is a disparager (*nippesika*). Or, that which disparages is disparagement; one who is simply disparagement is a disparager.
*Nippesa* means, like a fraudulent person, reviling, mocking, backbiting, and so forth for the sake of gain and honor.
The commentary on the *Kuhaka-sutta* is finished.
6–7. Commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāppatta-sutta*, etc.
86–87. Regarding what should be said concerning the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) in the sixth [chapter], that has already been stated above. "High and low" means high and low.
Therefore, he said, "great and small. "Duties" (*kiṃkaraṇīyāni*) refers to tasks to be performed after saying, "What shall I do?
Among these, "high duties" are the making of robes, dyeing them, plastering work at a shrine (*cetiya*), and [work] in the Uposatha hall, the shrine house, and the Bodhi house.
"Tasks to be performed" refers to such things as these. "Minor tasks" (avaca-kamma) means small duties such as washing and anointing the feet.
"Those who are fit for those [tasks]" (tatrupāyā) means those who are suitable for them;
the sense is that they approach each respective task—whether great or small—as a means of accomplishment. What is meant is that they are capable of bringing each particular task to completion.

"By means of the appropriate method" (*tatrupāyāya*) means by means of that which serves as the method for accomplishing this or that particular task. "Able to do" (*alaṃ kātuṃ*) means he is capable of doing it.
"Able to arrange" (*alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ*) means capable of deliberating upon it. The seventh [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Paṭisambhidāppatta-sutta* and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Therasutta* 88.
"One who has attained stability" means one who has reached a state of firmness and non-retrogression within the Teaching.
"One who knows the nights" (*rattaññū*) means one who has known many nights since becoming a renunciant. Therefore he said: "From the day of his going forth," and so forth. "Renowned" (*pākaṭo*).
It is arisen through both qualities that are not as they truly are and qualities that are as they truly are. One who possesses fame (*yaśas*) is "famous" (*yasassī*);
one who is attached to or dependent upon fame is "famous. Therefore, he said, "dependent on fame. The qualities of the non-existent, the unwholesome, are "unrighteous qualities" (*asaddhammā*);
or alternatively, those qualities that are non-existent, unsightly, censurable, and base are "unrighteous qualities. By contrast, the "true qualities" (*saddhammā*) should be understood accordingly.
The commentary on the *Therasutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Paṭhamasekhasutta*: 89.

In the ninth [verse], one who has work (*kamma*) as his delight (*ārāma*)—in the sense of that which is to be delighted in—is called a "work-delighter" (*kammārāma*); the state of being such is "delight in work" (*kammārāmatā*).
In this context, "work" (*kamma*) refers to work that must be done. That is to say:
the sorting of robes, the making of robes, providing support, and the making of bowl-bags, shoulder-straps, waistbands, Dhamma-wrappers, water-strainers, foot-stands, sandals, brooms, and so forth.
For someone who, while doing these things, spends the entire day doing only these very tasks—it is with reference to such a person that this prohibition is made.

But he who performs those very tasks at the time they are to be done—taking up the recitation at the time for recitation, reciting at the time for recitation, performing the duties in the shrine courtyard at the time for the shrine courtyard duties, and applying attention at the time for application—is not one "delighting in work. Regarding "delighting in talk":
herein, [it refers to] one who [engages in talk] by way of the beauty of women, the beauty of men, and so forth.
One who spends both day and night merely engaging in conversation and idle talk does not set a limit on speech;

such a person is called "one who delights in speech" (*bhassārāma*). However, one who preaches the Dhamma and answers questions both by night and by day is one who speaks little and indeed sets a limit on speech. Why? [Because it is said: "For you who have assembled..."
Because it has been said: “Monks, two things are to be practiced: either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
Regarding “delight in sleep”: here, one who—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—is overcome by sloth and torpor and simply sleeps, is called a “delighter in sleep.
However, he whose mind sinks into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) due to illness in his physical body is not [considered such].

Delighting in sleep. For this very reason he said: "I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of summer, after my meal and having returned from the alms round, I would spread out my outer robe folded fourfold and lie down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, to fall asleep.
Delighting in company: herein, one who is the second to one, or the companion of two...
"Third," "of three, fourth"—thus he dwells in company; he does not find satisfaction being alone. This is one who delights in society (*saṅgaṇikārāma*).
However, he who finds satisfaction being alone even in the four postures (*iriyāpatha*)—this should not be understood as one who delights in society.
Because it is impossible for those in training (*sekha*) to fall away from qualities already attained, the words "by higher qualities" and so forth are stated.
The commentary on the First Discourse on the Trainee is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Trainee: 90.
In the tenth [discourse], "too early" means having slept through the entire night, [to rise] at a strong dawn and [begin] a little with the *koṭisammuñjanī* broom.
Having swept [the dwelling] and washed his face, he enters the village early in the morning for the sake of alms-food consisting of rice-gruel.
"Having passed that time" means that, by associating with householders, he passes the time and departs after the midday period has elapsed.
For indeed, having entered the village early in the morning, taken rice-gruel, gone to the sitting-hall, drunk it, and lain down in one place to sleep, he falls asleep.
At the time when people are eating, thinking, "I shall receive choice almsfood," he rises as midday approaches,
takes water with a water-strainer, cleans his eyes, and after wandering for alms and eating as much as needed,
he spends the day in close association with householders; then, once midday has passed, he returns.
“Discourse on fewness of wishes” (*appicchakathā*) refers to a discourse proceeding in such a manner as: “Friend, these states—excessive wishing and evil wishing—are to be abandoned”;
having shown the danger in those, it continues: “One should live having undertaken such fewness of wishes,” and so forth.

“By means of the three kinds of seclusion” (*tīhi vivekehi*) refers to these three: seclusion of body (*kāyaviveka*), seclusion of mind (*cittaviveka*), and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*). Therein, one...

One goes, one stands, one sits, one lies down, one enters a village for alms, one returns, one resolves upon the walking meditation path, one wanders alone, and one dwells alone—this is called bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
The eight attainments (*samāpatti*), however, are called mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). Nibbāna is called seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*). As it has been said:

This is what was said: “Physical seclusion belongs to those whose bodies are secluded and who delight in renunciation; mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity;
and seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons who are without acquisitions and have reached the state beyond conditioned formations.
Energy is twofold: bodily energy and mental energy. Virtue is the virtue of the fourfold purification. Concentration is...
The eight attainments are the basis for insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, "discourse on liberation" refers to a discussion concerning the noble fruit (ariyaphala).
The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the second Sekha-sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Theravagga is finished.
(10) 5. Kakudhavagga: Commentary on the first ten suttas, beginning with the *Paṭhama-sampadā-sutta*.

91–100. Regarding the first and second [sections] of the fifth, there is nothing further to be said. In the third, "higher knowledge" (*aññā*) is so called because it is a knowing distinct from the initial comprehension;
this refers to the wisdom of the higher paths, since they know through the full understanding of what has been known (*ñātapariññā*) by means of the lower path.

Furthermore, because it constitutes the fruit, the wisdom of the path and its fruit, along with the right intention and other factors associated with it, are here termed "higher knowledge. The "declarations of higher knowledge" (*aññābyākaraṇāni*) are the declarations made by means of that higher knowledge.
For this very reason it was said: "The declarations of final knowledge" means "the declarations of Arahantship. "With the conceit of attainment" means:

having the perception of having attained what has not been attained, or having the perception of having attained what has not been attained, one acts with the conceit, "It has been attained by me. The fourth and subsequent sections have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the first *Sampadā-sutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Kakudhavagga is finished.
The Second Fifty is finished.
3. The Third Fifty.
(11) 1. Phāsuvihāravagga 1–4.
Commentary on the Sārajjasutta and following suttas 101–4.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter], there is nothing further to be said. Regarding the second, [it concerns] approaching for the sake of alms-food and so forth.

A suitable place is the proper resort; "one who has prostitutes as his resort" means one who should approach them by way of friendship and intimacy—this is the meaning. Those called "prostitutes" are women who live off their beauty;

they should not be approached by way of friendship and intimacy because it creates an obstacle to the state of a recluse and because it is a cause for reproach even for one of pure intention. Therefore, [one should approach them] with mindfulness by way of giving a gift.
Having waited upon them, one should approach them. "Widows" refers to those whose husbands are dead or those whose husbands have gone abroad.

"Old maidens" refers to grown-up girls who have not been married. "Eunuchs" refers to those who are neuter; for they have intense defilements, their fever has not subsided, and they are full of talk concerning worldly gain;
therefore, one should not approach them. "Bhikkhunīs" refers to those in whom the holy life is predominant.

The same applies to monks as well. Because they constitute a mutually inappropriate basis for intimacy, approaching them on account of such familiarity could lead to an obstacle to the holy life within just a few days;
therefore, one should not approach them. However, when approaching them for the purpose of inquiring after their health and so forth, one must act with mindfulness.
The third and fourth [sections] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the Sārajja-sutta and others is finished.
5. Commentary on the Phāsuvihāra-sutta: 105.
In the fifth [verse], that which possesses loving-kindness (*mettā*) is "loving" (*metta*); bodily action originating from that is "loving bodily action" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*).

This same method applies to the remaining two [types of action] as well. *Āvi* means manifesting. And here, the state of being manifest refers to the presence of the person for whose sake that bodily action is performed;
thus he said "in the presence" (*sammukhā*). *Raho* means non-manifesting.
And the state of being non-manifest refers to the absence of the person for whose sake that bodily action is performed; thus he said "in the absence" (*parammukhā*).

These acts of loving-kindness, such as bodily action and so forth, are presented here with reference to monks because they constitute the foremost assembly; however, they are certainly found among laypeople as well.
For monks, the fulfillment of the higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) through a mind of loving-kindness is called "loving-kindness as bodily action.
For laypeople, it is the going for the purpose of worshipping a shrine (*cetiyavandana*), for the purpose of worshipping the Bodhi tree, or for the purpose of inviting the Saṅgha.
Seeing monks who have entered a village for alms, going out to meet them, receiving their bowls, preparing a seat, and following them—
such acts as these are called loving bodily action (*metta-kāyakamma*). Teaching the monks the rules of conduct with a mind of loving-kindness,

explaining meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), giving Dharma teachings, and even the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas— these are called loving verbal action (*metta-vacīkamma*).
To householders [he says]: "We are going to pay homage at the cetiya; we are going to pay homage at the Bodhi tree; we shall listen to the Dhamma;
we shall offer lamps and flowers as an act of worship; we shall conduct ourselves by undertaking the three types of good conduct;
we shall give food tickets and other offerings; we shall give the rains-retreat gift; today we shall provide the four requisites for the Saṅgha; having invited the Saṅgha..."
When one says, "Prepare the solid foods and so forth; arrange the seats; set out the drinking water; go out to meet the Saṅgha and lead them here;
have them sit on the prepared seats; with hearts full of faith and zeal, perform service," this is called verbal action of loving-kindness.
[Likewise,] when one rises early in the morning, attends to the body, and goes to the shrine courtyard for the monks...
Having gone and performed the duties and so forth, and having sat down in a secluded lodging, the thought, "May the bhikkhus in this monastery be happy, free from enmity,
and free from affliction," is called loving-kindness as mental action; likewise, the thought toward householders, "May the noble ones be happy, free from enmity,
and free from affliction," is called loving-kindness as mental action.
In this context, for novices, assisting in tasks such as the making of robes is called "bodily action in person.
For elders, however, all forms of respectful service—including washing and pouring water for their feet, fanning them, and so forth—is called "bodily action in person.

Furthermore, when both [novices and elders] encounter wooden articles or other items that have been poorly placed, they should not show contempt toward those who placed them poorly, but rather [treat them as if they were their own].
Acting as if one were pacifying [an offense] while facing away from the person is called bodily action of loving-kindness (*mettā-kāyakamma*) behind their back.

Speaking words of praise such as “The Elder Deva” or “The Elder Tissa,” as already mentioned, is called verbal action of loving-kindness (*mettā-vacīkamma*) in their presence. However, for one who is not present in the monastery and asks about them, saying, “Where is our Elder Deva? Where is our Elder Tissa? When will he perhaps arrive?”—thus [is it called verbal action of loving-kindness behind their back].
Speaking kind words in another's absence is called loving verbal action (*metta-vacī-kamma*).
However, opening one’s eyes with a gaze moistened by the affection of loving-kindness and looking upon someone with a serene face is called loving mental action (*metta-manokamma*) in their presence;
while the mental application of thought, such as "May the Elder Deva and the Elder Tissa be healthy and free from affliction," is called loving mental action in their absence.

In this context, while the opening of eyes moistened by the oiliness of loving-kindness (*mettā-sineha*) and looking with a serene face are indeed bodily actions of loving-kindness, it is with reference to that state of mind by virtue of which the eyes become moist with the oiliness of loving-kindness and the face becomes serene that it is said:
"It is called mental action of loving-kindness. [The] purposes conducive to concentration (*samādhi*).
"Conducive to concentration.
"Having attained conformity in virtue" means having attained conformity in virtue with those bhikkhus who dwell in various directions and regions.
"That which" refers to this very [path] which is manifest both to me and to you. "View" means right view.
"Noble" (ariya) means faultless. "Leads out" (niyyāti) means it emerges from and departs from the suffering of saṃsāra.

For it is said that while it itself is being led out, it leads the person possessing it out from the suffering of saṃsāra. "One who acts accordingly" (takkara) is one who performs what has been instructed by the Teacher;
the meaning is: of one who practices according to the instruction. "For the destruction of suffering" (dukkhakkhayāya).
"For the sake of the destruction of all suffering. "One who has attained the commonality of view" means one who has entered into a state of shared view.
The commentary on the *Phāsuvihāra Sutta* is finished.
6–10. Commentary on the *Ānanda Sutta*, etc.

106–110. In the sixth [verse], the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimittatthe*); the meaning is that he does not revile or criticize the cause of virtue (*sīlanimittaṃ*). He is called "one who reflects upon himself" (*attānupekkhī*) because he reflects repeatedly upon himself by means of virtue (*sīlena*). The seventh and following verses have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Ānandasutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Phāsuvihāravagga* is finished.
(12) 2. The Chapter on Andhakavinda.
1–4. Explanation of the *Kulūpaka-sutta* and others, 111–114.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the second [chapter]: one who has confidence in families with which he is not intimate is called "one who trusts in non-intimate families" (*asantthavavissāsī*).
One who, being independent, habitually makes arrangements and makes agreements is an *anissara-vikappī*.
One who, by habit, attends upon families that have become estranged, scattered, and separated for the sake of reconciling them is a *vissaṭṭhupasevī*.
The meanings of the second and subsequent terms are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Kulūpaka-sutta* and others is finished.
5–13. Commentary on the *Maccharinī-sutta* and others (115–123).

In the fifth [sutta], the five types of stinginess, beginning with *āvāsamacchariya* (stinginess regarding dwellings), are presented here from the perspective of a bhikkhunī; for a bhikkhu, they are as follows: [text continues].

They should also be understood by way of their function. For a bhikkhu who possesses stinginess regarding dwellings, upon seeing a visitor, might say things such as, "The requisites for the shrine or the Saṅgha have been placed here," and thus does not give up the communal dwelling.
A bhikkhu who possesses stinginess regarding families, having shown the disadvantages through various reasons...

He prevents others from entering his own family circle even when they are his attendants. Possessed of stinginess regarding gains (*lābhamacchariya*), he acts so as to prevent others from receiving even what belongs to the Saṅgha, due to his own dependence on the unrighteous and his reliance on the powerful.
Possessed of stinginess regarding praise (*vaṇṇamacchariya*), he praises his own virtues while [suppressing] those of others.

Regarding appearance, one speaks of various faults, asking, "What kind of appearance does he have? Here, "appearance" (vaṇṇa) should be understood as both physical appearance and the appearance of qualities.
One possessed of stinginess regarding the Dhamma thinks, "Having mastered this Dhamma, he will surpass me," and thus does not give it to another.
Furthermore, one who thinks, "This person, having learned this Dhamma, will misinterpret its meaning..."

It is not stinginess when one does not give [the teaching] out of support for the Dhamma, thinking, "If he learns this Dhamma, he will become arrogant, conceited, and unpeaceful in mind, and will produce demerit," or out of support for the person; nor is it stinginess when one thinks, "He will destroy [this Dhamma].
And here, by "Dhamma" the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) is intended. For the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-dhamma) belongs only to the Noble Ones, and they do not...
Because stinginess has been entirely abandoned, they do not act with stinginess; thus, its non-existence is certain.

In that regard, through stinginess regarding dwellings (*āvāsamacchariya*), one is cooked in an iron house, or having become a *yakkha* or a *peta*, one wanders about carrying the refuse of that very dwelling on one’s head.

Through stinginess regarding families (*kulamacchariya*), one becomes one of little wealth. Through stinginess regarding gains (*lābhamacchariya*), one is reborn in the Excrement Hell (*gūthaniraya*).
Having been stingy with the gains of the Saṅgha or a group, or having consumed them for one's own private use, one is reborn as a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or a great python.
One who is reborn among the various states of existence due to stinginess regarding physical beauty lacks beauty itself.
Due to stinginess regarding the Dhamma, one is reborn in the Kukkuḷa hell. The sixth and subsequent [factors] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Maccharinīsutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Andhakavindavagga* is finished.

124–130. The third chapter has its meaning already explained. (14) 4.
The Chapter on Kings (Rājavagga). 1.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Following the Wheel (Paṭhamacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā).
131. In the first [verse] of the fourth [chapter], "one who knows the benefit" (*atthaññū*) means one who knows what is beneficial (*hitajñū*).
Here, the word *attha* is a synonym for *hita*, as in such expressions as "one's own welfare" (*attattha*) and "the welfare of others" (*parattha*).

Because he, knowing the welfare of others, causes them to rejoice in himself, it is said that "he knows how to make them rejoice. "In punishment" (*daṇḍe*) refers to the infliction of punishment according to the offense. "In strength" (*balamhi*) refers to the military force. Five.

"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the fivefold classification of meaning: one's own welfare, the welfare of others, the welfare of both, welfare pertaining to the present life, and welfare pertaining to future lives.

"Four things" (*dhamma*) refers to the four truths, or alternatively, to the four things classified as the realms of sense-desire, form, formlessness, and the supramundane. Through moderation alone in receiving and using [things], there is also moderation in seeking and relinquishing them.
"They have been awakened" means it is simply stated that "they know the mere act of receiving and using [the gift].
It is called *uttara* because it crosses over (*uttarati*), transcends, or overcomes; it is *anuttara* because there is nothing superior (*natthi ettha uttaraṃ*) to it.
It is unsurpassed (*anatisayaṃ*) or peerless (*appaṭibhāgaṃ*), by way of accomplishing the penetration of the Noble Truths for them hundreds of times amidst many assemblies of gods and humans.
The turning of the wheel of Dhamma is the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Moreover, that teaching of the Dhamma which, for the first time ever, brought about the penetration of the Four Truths for the eighteen assemblies headed by Aññāta-Koṇḍañña and for the millions of Brahmās, is preeminently designated as the "Wheel of Dhamma" (Dhammacakka).
In this context, the Dhamma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth is the wheel in the sense of being a "turning" (pavattana).

“Wheel” (*cakkam*) refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). Alternatively, it is called a “wheel” because it is an authoritative command that does not deviate from the Dhamma; thus, being both Dhamma and a wheel, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.

It is also the Wheel of Dhamma because it is a wheel by means of the Dhamma, according to the right method. As it has been said: “It sets in motion the Dhamma and it is a wheel, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma;
it sets in motion a wheel and it is the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma; it sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma.”

“Dhammacakka,” and so forth. “Irresistible” (appaṭivattiya) means that it cannot be countered because the Wheel of Dhamma of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Lord of Dhamma, is unsurpassed.
To the question of by whom it is irresistible, he says: “By a recluse (samaṇa),” and so forth.

Therein, “by a recluse” means one who has entered the life of renunciation. “By a brahmin” means a brahmin by birth. For [this refers to] recluses and brahmins in the ultimate sense of the Dispensation.
There is no contrary thought at all. "By a deva" means by a deva of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). "By anyone" means by any remaining member of the assembly.
Up to this point, the inclusion of all eight assemblies without exception should be understood. "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings (sattaloka).
The commentary on the First Discourse on Turning the Wheel is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Following the Wheel (Dutiyacakkānuvattanasutta-vaṇṇanā) 132.
In the second [discourse], "the duty of a wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavatti-vatta*) refers to the tenfold or twelvefold conduct that brings about the status of a wheel-turning monarch.
In this regard, it includes the provision of righteous protection, defense, and security for the inner retinue and the army.

Among the khattiyas, the followers, the brahmins and householders, the town-dwellers and country-folk, the ascetics and brahmins, and even among the beasts and birds—there is the rejection of unrighteousness, the bestowing of wealth upon the poor, and approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions:
this is the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch. And this very same [duty] applies to householders and those born as birds.
And by taking them separately, there are twelve kinds according to their mode of grasping.

Alternatively, there are ten or twelve kinds of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-vatta*); when the son, having fulfilled these duties, sits [on the throne], another [wheel] appears to him, and he sets it in motion.
However, because it is made of jewels, it is considered identical in essence; thus, it is said to be "set in motion by the father."
It has been said. Or rather, because he said, "O King, you may remain at ease;
I shall rule," it should be understood that the meaning here is that he causes the wheel of authority set in motion by his father to continue turning.
For that Wheel-Treasure (cakkaratana), which is accomplished through the power of his own merit, is what is called "set in motion" by him in the primary sense.

The first method was stated [in the sense that] they do not lead [others]. Since there is only a following of what has already been set in motion, and the first method was stated by way of applying that designation to something similar to it, the second method was stated without taking that [first method] into account.
The commentary on the *Dutiyacakkānuvattanasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Yassaṃdisaṃ* Sutta. 134.
In the fourth [verse], when it is said, “Well-born on both sides,” one might conceive of being well-born by means of any two factors whatsoever;

however, since the word *sujāta* (well-born) in such passages as “well-born and beautiful to behold” is a synonym for excellence of physical proportions (*ārohasampatti*), here it refers to being well-born by way of birth (*jāti*).
To clarify this, it is said: “from the mother and from the father. In the world, the designation “mother” and “father” is also seen in reference to non-biological children;
however, here it is intended in the sense of biological children, as shown by the phrase “one who has taken up a pure conception.
One “takes up” (gahaṇī) means one “carries” (dhāreti); thus, the *gahaṇī* is that portion of the mother’s womb designated as the seat of the embryo. Therefore he said:

“Endowed with a thoroughly purified mother’s womb. Because it receives and does not reject food according to how that food has been consumed, by way of digesting it, it is the *gahaṇī* (the digestive organ);
[it is] the fire element (*tejodhātu*). Both father and mother are the parents (*pitaro*). The parents of the parents are the grandfathers (*pitāmahā*).
Their pair is the grandfather-pair (*pitāmahayugo*); thus, from the grandfather-pair up to the seventh generation, it is the “grandfather-couple,” and so it is here.
The meaning should be understood thus: for in this way, by the mention of the grandfather alone, the maternal grandfather is also included;

therefore, he is not mentioned separately in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). Furthermore, the word *yuga* (pair) here should be understood according to the method of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*) as "the father and the grandfather are both [called] *yuga*.
For in this way, two individuals are effectively included in each instance. Thus he said: "Beyond that, all ancestors..."
“They are included by the mention of the grandfather alone. And here, the mention of the male should be understood as being made by way of an inclusive (ukkaṭṭha) description;
for in this way, the scriptural expression “on the mother’s side” (mātito) is justified.
“Unthrown” (akkhitto) means one who has not been thrown out [of the lineage]. “Uncast off” (anavakkhitto) means one who has not been cast off or abandoned in disputes and the like that have arisen.
To show that the instrumental case in the phrase "by way of birth" (*jātivādena*) expresses the cause, the words "for what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) and so forth were spoken.

Here, by the phrase "from both sides... from the lineage of great-grandfathers," the absence of any defect in the womb (*yoni-dosa*) of the Khattiya is shown, because it describes his state of being born of a pure lineage.
By the word "uncensured" (*akkhitta*), the absence of any fault in action (*kiriyā-parādha*) is indicated; for it is through a fault in action that beings incur censure.
“Unreproached”: by this is meant the absence of improper association; for it is in dependence upon improper association that beings receive abuse.
“Wealth” means the possession of property; since that is spoken of in relation to various degrees, he says: “anyone who is wealthy by means of some property belonging to himself.
Likewise, in order to show that [wealth] has reached its highest degree, he speaks of “great riches.”
"It is said that he was endowed with great, immeasurable wealth.

Because they are to be enjoyed and utilized, and specifically because they are objects of sensual desire, he says "by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. A *koṭṭha* is called the place where grain is stored;
a house that serves as such a storehouse is a *koṭṭhāgāra*. Therefore, he says "with a storehouse full of grain."
Having thus shown that a sheath (*kośa*) is the inner core of strength and a storehouse (*koṭṭhāgāra*) is a place for storing grain,
the passage beginning with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) is now stated to show it in another way. In this context,
just as a covering that protects the sharpness of a sword is called a "sheath," so too the fourfold army (*caturaṅginī senā*) maintains the king's state of sharpness [and thus is his sheath].
"What is the treasury? he asked; [the answer was] "The fourfold treasury: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Since the mention of the "storehouse" and the "granary" already includes every place where goods are stored, it is said that "the storehouse is threefold.
Regarding the wisdom by virtue of which a person is called "wise," he said: "By means of wisdom..."

"Endowed with": skillfulness (*veyyattiya*) is the state of being clever and proficient in various duties that ought to be performed. *Medhā* is so called because it destroys and dispels delusion (*sammoha*);
one who possesses this is "wise" (*medhāvī*). *Ṭhānuppatti* means having its arising in the appropriate instances;
it is wisdom that arises according to the occasion (*ṭhānaso*). "In the matter of growth" means in the matter known as growth (*vaḍḍhi*).
The commentary on the *Yassādisaṃ* Sutta is finished.
5–9. Commentary on the *Patthanā* Sutta and others. 135–9.

In the fifth [verse], “in elephant-training” (*hatthismiṃ*) means in the art of elephants (*hatthisippe*). For it is called “elephant” (*hatthī*) because it pertains to the domain of elephants and because it is dependent upon elephants.
And the art of elephant-training was mastered. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Vaya" means age;
the meaning is that one who does not stumble or falter in any of the beautiful [arts] is able to sustain them. "Na vaya" is "avaya";
one who is unable to sustain them both in meaning and in word is "avaya. "Not being avaya" is "anavaya. Two negations restore the original state.
He says "it goes" (*gacchati*) in the sense that "it is capable" (*anavayo*). The sixth and subsequent [verses] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the *Patthanā-sutta* and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Sota-sutta*.

140. "Sharp" (*tikkhānaṃ*) means piercing. "Harsh" (*kharānaṃ*) means coarse. "Bitter" (*kaṭukānaṃ*) means dreadful. "Disagreeable" (*asātānaṃ*) means not pleasant, that is, unlovely. They are called "unpleasant" (*amanāpā*) because the mind does not incline toward them, nor do they cause the mind to incline—that is, to increase [in attachment].
The commentary on the Ear Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Royal Chapter is finished.
(15) 5. The Chapter on the Three Stumps (Tikaṇḍakīvagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Disparaging (Avajānāti-sutta). 141.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "having given, he disparages": here, there was a certain bhikkhu of great merit who was a recipient of the four requisites.
There is one who, having obtained robes and other requisites, asks another person of little merit [to share them]. Even though that person asks again and again, he simply takes them for himself.
Then the other, becoming slightly angry and wishing to cause him embarrassment, says:
"This man does not obtain robes and other requisites by his own nature; he obtains them only by depending on us. Thus, even after giving, he treats the donor with contempt.

This is what is meant by "by name. However, one person who has lived with another for two or three years, having previously held that person in high esteem, fails to show respect as time goes on and does not even go to offer a seat or a place to sit.

This person, too, is said to "despise through co-residence. "One whose mouth is directed toward what was received at first" means one whose mouth is directed [toward contempt] from the very beginning; that is, at the very first word.
The meaning is "one who has set aside his own opinion. Herein, this is the method: A certain person describes a monk who is indeed worthy as "unworthy.
Having heard this, he reaches a conclusion; even when another monk of similar standing says, "This one is worthy," he does not accept that person's word.
[He thinks: "By such-and-such a person it was said, 'This one is unworthy'—to us..."
"Spoken of": one takes up the report of a previous bhikkhunī. Another person then tells her that he is immoral, yet she calls him "virtuous.
Having placed faith in his words, even when another later says, "This bhikkhu is unsuitable;
he is not fit to approach you," she does not accept that latter statement but continues to hold only to the former report.
Another person takes up both praise when spoken and blame when spoken.
This too is called "one whose mouth is open for receiving" (ādheyyamukha), meaning one whose mouth is set to receive whatever he hears; wherever he hears something, there his mouth is placed.

"Fickle" (lola) means that because faith and the other [faculties] are established only for a short time, he is fickle due to being shaken by lack of faith and so forth. Regarding the terms "of limited devotion" (ittarabhattī) and so on:
Through repeated association, there arises faith, devotion, and affection. Both affection born of faith and affection based on worldly attachment are appropriate;
clarity is "clarity born of faith. Thus a person is called "fickle" (lola);
because of such fleeting faith and the like, the person is said to be fickle—like turmeric dye, like a wooden pestle struck against a heap of husks, or like a gourd placed upon the back of a horse.
And like [the wind], it becomes agitated in an instant in an unsteady place. "Dull and deluded" means dull due to the state of ignorance (*aññāṇa*), and deluded due to the lack of an object;
the meaning is "greatly bewildered.
The commentary on the *Avajānāti-sutta* is finished.
2–3. Commentary on the *Ārabhati-sutta* and others. 142–3.
Regarding the second [sutta], in the phrase "he undertakes" (*ārabhati*), the word *ārambha* (undertaking) refers to action, performance, injury, exertion, provocation, transgression, and violation.
For instance, it occurs in the sense of action in the passage: "Whatever suffering arises, all of it has undertaking as its condition."

“Great undertakings, great sacrifices, these do not bear great fruit”—this refers to ritual action (*kiriyā*). “They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama”—this refers to violence (*hiṃsana*).
“Exert yourselves, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching”—this refers to energy (*vīriya*).
“He abstains from the destruction of seeds and the destruction of living plants”—this refers to irritation (*kopana*). “He undertakes [an action] and feels remorse.”

"And he becomes remorseful"—this, however, refers to the transgression of an offense; therefore, the meaning here is that he both initiates [the act] by way of transgressing an offense, and because of that, he becomes remorseful.

"He does not understand it as it really is" means that because it has not been attained, he does not know it according to its true nature (*yathāsabhāva*). "In which [place] for him" means in whatever place for him, having reached which place...
The meaning is that for this person, arisen evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.
But having reached what do they cease? They cease upon reaching the path of arahantship; however, for one who has attained the fruit, they are said to have already ceased.
Even so, it should be understood that here, by way of the function of the path, the fruit itself is what is spoken of.
"He undertakes [an action] and does not feel remorse" means that he incurs an offense, yet he seeks out a person of similar standing to confess it;

therefore, he does not feel remorse. "He does not undertake [an action] and feels remorse" means that he does not incur an offense, but because he is unskilled in the formulation of the Vinaya rules, he perceives what is not an offense as an offense and thus feels remorse.
"Occurs"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. As for the person described as "neither undertaking [the practice] nor feeling remorse," who is that person?
It is the person of slackened energy. For even though his virtue is purified, he does not fulfill the practice, thinking:
"What is the use of my attaining final Nibbāna at this time? I shall attain final Nibbāna in the future, at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Metteyya."
For he should indeed be exhorted thus: "For what purpose do you dwell in negligence? The destiny of an ordinary person is unfixed;
therefore, may you obtain the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One Metteyya, and develop insight for the sake of Arahantship."
“Sādhu” is a particle used in the sense of a request. This is what is meant: “How much we have been wronged indeed by the Venerable One!

Nevertheless, even so, we entreat the Venerable One—to teach that which is fit to be taught, to emerge from that which is fit to be emerged from, and to reveal that which is fit to be revealed—by abandoning the taints born of exertion and by reflecting upon the state of standing in the pure end.”
"Having dispelled and removed the taints born of remorse, may he increase both the mind of insight and the wisdom of insight.
By "this fifth person," it means by this fifth person who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
"He will become exactly equal" means he will become equal precisely through the state of equality in supramundane qualities; thus should one who has destroyed the taints be exhorted.
The meaning [is as follows]. The third [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Ārabhati-sutta* and others is finished.
4–6. Commentary on the *Tikaṇḍakī-sutta* and others.

144–6. Regarding the fourth [meditation subject], "repulsive" means disagreeable, unpleasant, or undesirable. "Perceiving it as non-repulsive" means that the mind functions in a manner that treats it as desirable.
One either pervades a desirable object with the perception of foulness (*asubha*), or one applies and directs it toward it by way of impermanence (*anicca*).
"In an undesirable object" refers to an undesirable object consisting of a sentient being. "Or pervades it with loving-kindness" means [one pervades it] with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Either he applies it there by bringing to mind what is beneficial everywhere, or he applies it "by way of elements" (dhātu),
meaning that through reflection on the specific nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) and through reviewing by way of elements, he directs attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra) therein.
"Avoiding both of these" refers to the repulsiveness of the object as it presents itself by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and its functional power (ānubhāva).
"And by not taking up the state of being non-repulsive"—that is to say, having abandoned both of those and not grasping them, but rather remaining neutral toward all of it;
this is what is meant. But what does one who wishes to dwell as neutral do?
When desirable or undesirable objects come into range, he is neither elated nor dejected. He should dwell equanimous.

Not being attached to the desirable and not being repelled by the undesirable, one should dwell equanimous toward the six objects of experience through the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*), without generating delusion in the manner that others do by failing to maintain such observation. For this very reason it is said: "The fifth [jhāna] is by way of the sixfold equanimity.
This refers to that which has the characteristic of not abandoning its naturally pure state even when confronted with the course of the six desirable and undesirable objects.

The meaning is that the fifth section is stated by way of equanimity regarding the state of affairs (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*), which has acquired the name "sixfold equanimity" because it occurs at the six doors. The fifth and sixth sections are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Tikaṇḍakī Sutta* and others is concluded.
7–10. Commentary on the *Asappurisadānasutta* and others (147–150).

In the seventh [sutta], "without respect" (*asakkacca*) means having acted with disregard. Regarding the lack of respect shown toward the gift to be given (*deyyadhamma*), it is said that one makes it incomplete;
thus he says: "he does not give having honored it or made it pure," meaning free from faults such as unhusked rice and the like.
The meaning is: "having made it complete and pure, he does not give. "Without honoring" (*acittīkatvā*) means not placing it in the mind, that is, not worshipping it.
For one who worships places the object to be worshipped within the mind; he does not cast it outside of it.

Alternatively, "honoring" (*cittīkaraṇa*) is the act of esteem consisting in a transformation of practice through a sense of wonder; its opposite, "not honoring" (*acittīkaraṇa*), is the act of non-esteeming.

"He gives without respect" means that, showing no regard for the person, he gives a gift after failing to sweep the seating area, having someone sit down here or there at random, or having placed just any old support there.

"Not with his own hand" means he does not give with his own hand, but causes it to be given by slaves, laborers, or others. "He gives what has been cast away" means he gives what has been discarded or interrupted in the interim.

He gives after having [prepared it]. Therefore he said, "he does not give continuously. Alternatively, "he gives what is cast away" means he gives it having treated it like something to be discarded, such as leftovers and the like. Therefore he said, "he gives as if wishing to discard it.
One who possesses the view of the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*)—thinking, "Surely the fruit of this gift will come to him"—is one who holds the view of its arrival. This...

But because he does not hold such a view, he is one who does not believe in the coming-to-be [of results]. Therefore he said, "How indeed will the fruit of what has been done come to be? and so forth.
There is nothing further to be said regarding the eighth and subsequent verses.
The commentary on the *Asappurisadānasutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Tikaṇḍakīvaṅga is finished.
The Third Fifty is finished.
4. The Fourth Fifty.
(16) 1. The Chapter on the True Dhamma (Saddhamma-vagga), 151–160.
The first chapter is self-evident in meaning.
(17) 2. The Chapter on Resentment (Āghāta-vagga).
1–5. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Removal of Malice, etc. (161–165).

Regarding the first [discourse] of the second [section], there is nothing further to be said. Regarding the second: it is called *āghātapaṭivinaya* because malice (*āghāta*) is removed (*paṭivinayati*) therein, or by means of these [factors]. Therefore he said: “Malice is to be removed by means of these,” and so forth. *Nantaka*:
this means endless (*anantaka*), a piece of cloth devoid of an end. For if it had an end, it would not be designated as a “rag” (*pilotika*).
“With *sevāla* moss” means with *sevāla* moss, which is divided into types such as seeds, tubers, and filaments.

“With water-moss” (*udakapappaṭaka*) means with water-moss that has arisen covering the surface of the water, having the color of the back of a blue frog. “Pursued by heat” means touched by and overcome by heat.
“The arising of consciousness” means the arising of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).

It is called *ābādha* because it afflicts (*ābādheti*) and oppresses (*pīleti*), cutting off the maintenance of the postures (*iriyāpatha*) by means of the arising of discordant feelings, as if with a saw;
one who possesses that is *ābādhika*. "Afflicted" (*dukkhita*) means one for whom suffering has arisen due to its origination. "Severely ill" (*bāḷhagilāna*) means extremely sick.
"One who leads to the village boundary" (*gāmantanāyaka*) means one who brings [the patient] to the vicinity of a village.
The clarity of the water is to be understood through its state of being serene; thus he said, “*Acchodakā* means having clear water. Because of its excellent flavor, it is constant;
thus he said, “*Madhurōdakā* [means] having sweet water. The water is specifically thin and cool, not thick;
thus he said, “*Tanusītasalilā* [means] having thin, cool water. “*Setakā*” means free from mud; for the discoloration of water occurs due to the presence of mud and such.
By its very nature, however, it is white in color. The third and subsequent sections have their meanings self-evident.
The commentary on the first discourse, the *Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta*, is concluded.
6. Commentary on the *Nirodha Sutta*.
166. In the sixth [case], "amarisaṇattha" means "in the sense of not enduring. Regarding the phrase "anāgatavacanaṃ kataṃ":
the application of the word *anāgata* (future) has been made, yet the meaning is actually present-tense.

For grammarians, in such instances, by way of the sense of "not tolerating" (*anokappana-amarisaṇa*), they employ the future tense even when the auxiliary verb *atthi* (is) indicates the present time.
The commentary on the Nirodhasutta is finished.
7–9. Commentary on the Codanāsutta and others. 167–169.
In the seventh [sutta], "pointing out the basis" (*vatthusandassanā*) means the showing, in its specific form, of the particular matter upon which an offense is based.

"Pointing out the offense" means the pointing out of whichever offense he has committed. "Refusal of communal living" means the refusal or non-performance of communal living such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies.
"Refusal of respectful conduct" means the non-performance of acts of respect such as prostrations.
"By one who reproves" means by one who accuses. "The time for the one being reproved" means the time when the one being reproved should be reproved. "A person" means...
The person to be charged. "Having investigated" means having examined whether or not this person stands within the characteristics of one who has been charged.
"He brings infamy upon himself" means he brings infamy upon the monks, thinking, "These people, by falsely misrepresenting me, are causing me infamy and ruin.
The eighth and ninth [offenses] have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the *Codanāsutta* and others is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Bhaddajisutta*. 170.
In the tenth [verse], the intention is: "He stands having overcome these beings. For he, by virtue of being praiseworthy—
And because he stands having surpassed all beings through his supreme state, he conceives of himself [as such]; therefore it is said, "the eldest.
Furthermore, by the statement "he sees" (*dasa*), he declares his unobstructed vision through the absence of any impediment to seeing and through his capacity to grasp specific objects of knowledge;
thus it is said, "the intention is that he sees everything."
The commentary on the Bhaddaji Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Āghāta Vagga is finished.
(18) 3. The Upāsaka Vagga.
1–6. Commentary on the *Sārajja-sutta* and others, 171–176.
Regarding the first, second, third, and fourth [sections] of the third [chapter], there is nothing further to be said.

In the fifth, the phrase "the lowest of lay followers" (*upāsaka-pacchimako*) refers to one who is inferior among lay followers. This refers to that which is designated as "superstition" (*kotūhala*)—as imagined by foolish people—thinking, "By means of this view or other such factor, such-and-such an auspicious omen (*maṅgala*) will come to pass."
One who possesses omens consisting of what is seen, heard, or thought is a "superstitious omenist. Therefore, he says: "By this, this will come to pass," and so forth.

"He relies on omens" means he merely hopes for omens divided into categories such as those seen and so on. "Not [relying] on action" means he does not hope for the ownership of one's own deeds (*kammassakata*).
"From this teaching" means from this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha. "Outside" means in the systems of outsiders (*bāhiraka*).
“He seeks one worthy of offerings” means he searches while perceiving that those who have entered upon a wrong course are worthy of offerings.
Here, by counting the preliminary act of seeking offerings as one, five factors are to be understood. The sixth is self-evident.
The commentary on the Sārajja-sutta and others is concluded.
7–8. Commentary on the *Vaṇijjā-sutta* and others. 177–8.
Regarding the seventh [precept], "the trade of weapons": this refers to the selling of weaponry after having had it made, caused to be made, or obtained already made.
The phrase "having had weaponry made and then selling it" is merely an illustration; [it includes] pigs, deer, and so forth.
"Rearing them for sale" means rearing pigs, deer, and so forth, and then selling their meat after it has been prepared.
In this context, the trade in weapons is said to be improper because it is the cause of harming others; the trade in living beings is improper because it renders them non-independent;
the trade in meat and poison is improper because it is the cause of killing; and the trade in intoxicants is improper because it is a basis for negligence. The eighth [trade] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Vaṇijjā-sutta and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the Gihī-sutta (179).
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "of the higher mental states" (*ābhicetasika*): *abhiceto* refers to the excellent, purified mind; it is called *adhicitta*.
Or, they are called *ābhicetasika* because they have arisen in a superior mind (*abhicetasi*), or because they are dependent upon a superior mind;

for this very reason, he said, "dependent on the supreme mind. Regarding the phrase "pleasant dwellings in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ*): it means pleasant dwellings in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamme*).

"Present life" (*diṭṭhadhammo*) refers to the directly perceived personal existence (*attabhāvo*); the meaning is "pleasant dwellings therein. This [refers] to the fine-material-sphere absorptions (*rūpāvacarajjhāna*).
This is a designation. For those meditators who have sat down after partaking of these [drinks] experience, even in this very life, the undefiled bliss of renunciation;
therefore, they are called "abidings in happiness in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā*).
They intoxicate in four ways: namely, the fourfold division consisting of flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, molasses-liquor, and honey-liquor.

“Merayan” means liquor. And as for the five kinds of *sura*: cake-liquor, flour-liquor, rice-liquor, that into which grain has been put, and that mixed with various ingredients—such is *sura* with its fivefold division.
“Puññattho” means one for whom merit (*puñña*) is the purpose (*attha*).
Since he is indeed one who seeks merit, therefore it is said, “of one who seeks merit. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Gihisutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Gavesīsutta 180.
"A good reason" means a certain and beautiful cause for the ripening of enlightenment. "A gentle smile" means...

"A slight smile" (*īsakaṃ hasitaṃ*). "Kahaṃ kahaṃ" is an imitation of the sound of laughter. "Mere appearance of being joyful and exultant" (*haṭṭhappahaṭṭhākāramattaṃ*) means the mere appearance of one who is joyful and exultant.
Just as those who have grasped the conventional designation recognize [the Buddha] as "the Blessed One is exultant," so too it is merely an indication of the appearance.
Now, in this context, the following passage beginning with “And what is called laughter” is undertaken to show the classification of that which originates from laughter (*hāsasamuṭṭhāna*).
In this regard, laughter does not even arise by way of equanimity (*ajjhupekkhanavasena*), let alone by way of displeasure (*domanassavasena*);
thus he says, “by thirteen consciousnesses accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagatacitta*). But is it not the case that some people laugh even by way of anger (*kodhavasena*)?

No; they do not experience joy regarding the object of anger because laughter arises from a state of mental gladness that is difficult to discern, with the thought: "Now we shall act according to our own desires.
"Among these" refers to the five functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-kiriyacitta*).
"With a powerful object" means with an exceedingly sublime object, such as the Twin Miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*). "With a weak object" means with an unexalted object.

“However, in this place... [and so on] ...he produces [it],” this was stated because it is recorded as such in the *Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā* (the Ancient Commentary), not for the purpose of showing that the Blessed One’s smile does not occur with consciousness accompanied by joy and accompanied by roots.
In the *Abhidhammaṭīkā*, however, after stating that the Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past and so forth, [it says]: “For a Buddha endowed with these qualities...”

It is said: "Because of such statements as 'all bodily action of the Blessed One is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge,' the statement that 'this thought arises in the Blessed One' must be investigated.

In this context, even though the Blessed One’s act of smiling occurs through this smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppādacitta*), it nevertheless conforms to his knowledge of past lives, his knowledge of the future, and his omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

"Only in accordance with knowledge": thus, when there is this state of being in accordance with knowledge, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the Canon and the commentaries. For instance, it is said in the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*: "When those knowledges have reached their limit of practice, this consciousness arises.
And this must necessarily be accepted as such; otherwise, even for the Buddha’s advertence-consciousness (*āvajjana-citta*), [the same difficulty would apply].
It would not be appropriate [to claim] such a time [as the moment of consciousness], for its status as the producer of intimation (*viññatti*) has been definitively established.
For it has been stated: "And by doing so, it is established that even the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) possesses the quality of producing intimation.
Furthermore, regarding its status as the producer of intimation, there is no [lack of] bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and so forth in the bodily intimation produced by it.
The state of occurrence is abandoned.
By "laughing," he speaks with reference to smiling alone. Therefore he said, "even such a slight trembling. The lightning flashes have converged;
for unlike other lightning flashes, they do not cease quickly due to a momentary duration, but rather they cease slowly.
And it is not present at all times; it issues forth from either a great cloud of the world-system of three suns or a great cloud of the four continents.
Therefore he said, "from the mouth of a great cloud of the four continents. It is said that this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of those rays:
namely, that after circumambulating the head three times to the right, they vanish right into the tips of the fangs. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Gavesī Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Upāsaka Vagga is finished.
(19) 4. The Arañña Vagga.
1. Commentary on the Āraññika Sutta 181.
Regarding the first [section] of the fourth [chapter], in the passage beginning with "relying solely upon fewness of desires," etc., [it means]:
"Thinking, 'In this way I shall be one of few desires,' this factor of forest-dwelling of mine will lead to fewness of desires; thinking, 'In this way I shall be content,' this..."

"The forest-dweller's factor will lead to contentment for me; 'thus I shall scrape away the defilements'—this forest-dweller's factor will lead to the scraping away of defilements for me"—thinking thus, he becomes a forest-dweller.
"Foremost" means the eldest. The remaining terms are synonyms for that same quality.
"Milk from a cow" is called *gāvito khīraṃ*; it does not mean curd from a cow. The same principle applies to expressions such as "curd from milk," and so forth.

This is the method.
