"In the same way" means: just as among these five products of the cow, the cream of ghee (*sappimaṇḍa*) is the foremost, even so, among these five kinds of forest-dwellers, he who becomes a forest-dweller by relying on fewness of wishes and so forth is the foremost, the best, the most liberated, and the most excellent.
Among these forest-dwellers, one should understand the "forest-dweller by birth," and not one who is a forest-dweller merely by name.
They should be understood as forest-dwellers (*āraññika*). The same method applies to the refuse-rag wearers (*paṃsukūlika*) and the others.
The commentary on the *Āraññika-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Arañña-vagga* is finished.
(20) 5. The Chapter on Brahmins. 1.
Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta. 191.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "by means of affection alone" (*sampiyena eva*) means by means of mutual love alone; they have become blended together both in body and in mind.
Having come together and associated, they live in community; it is not by means of unpleasant restraint, so it is said. Therefore he says “dear,” and so forth.
It fills, accumulates, and satisfies the belly, thus it is *udarāvadehaka*. This is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*);
having made [the state of] *udarāvadehaka*, that is to say, having filled the belly—this is the meaning. Therefore he says “having filled the belly,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Soṇa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Doṇa Brāhmaṇa Sutta: 192.
"In the second [verse], 'those who propagate' means those who maintain [the tradition] as sacred scripture (*pāvacana*); for they are the ones who cause those mantras to circulate."
Therefore, it says: “those who cause it to proceed. Because they are to be spoken in secret, excluding the *sudras*, they are called *mantras*.

They are *mantapadas* (words of *mantra*) because they are the cause for the practice of their respective goals. They are the means for attainment through an activity to be performed in secrecy (*rahassa*), due to their being unshared with those not yet initiated.
“Recited” (*sajjhāyita*) means recited by way of chanting. That, moreover, occurs only through the perfection of vowels such as the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*).
Regarding "desired," he said, "by way of the perfection of the essence. "Stated by others" means stated by others by virtue of being the oral tradition (pāvacana).
"Compiled together" means gathered and arranged in successive layers. "Collected into a mass" means collected into a mass by way of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and so forth;
therein also, each by way of the mantras, the brāhmaṇas, and so forth, and by way of the chapters (ajjhāya), sections (anuvāka), and so forth. "Of them" refers to...

Of the composers of the mantras. "Having observed with the divine eye" means: having observed, by means of the knowledge of the destination according to karma—which is like a fringe to the divine eye—the fact that beings are the owners of their own karma and so forth;

and having observed, by means of the knowledge of past lives—which is similar to the divine eye in the sense of seeing directly—the procedure for the mastery of the brahminical mantras in past aeons. "Having compared it with the Pāvacana" means: [having compared it] with the word of the Buddha.
Having made it non-contradictory with whatever teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa was dependent upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For the meaning dependent upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*) was not directly evident to them.

"Successively" means those who arose later than Aṭṭhaka and others, during the time of King Okkāka and subsequent periods. "Having inserted" means [having inserted] into the sections of the mantras composed by Aṭṭhaka and others.
Having inserted words dependent on the defilements (*kilesa*) here and there into the respective passages.
"They made them hostile" means they made them into adversaries, because they illuminate the meaning of defilement according to the method found in such suttas as the *Brāhmaṇadhammika-sutta*.
"Archery" (*issattha*) is the act of shooting with arrows; it is a livelihood by the craft of the bow. But here, it is called "archery" (*issattha*) because it is like archery.
"All those who live by weapons" refers to "those who live by the work of warriors"; the meaning is: by the work of attending [to others] while having taken up weapons.
"Royal service" means attending upon the king by performing royal duties such as the work of a commander-in-chief or a minister, without using weapons.

"By some other craft" means by whatever remains after those already mentioned, such as the crafts of elephant-riding, horsemanship, and so forth. "From the time of being a youth onwards" refers to their conduct.
The lifelong celibacy of a youth.

"Giving after pouring water" means that while standing at the door, they pour water into the hand of the Brahmin and say, "Brahmin, we give this to you for the purpose of supporting a wife," and then they give it. But why do they observe such celibacy?
"Even after practicing [the religious life], they seek a wife and do not remain celibate for their entire lives"?
This is due to wrong view. For they hold such a view as this: "He who does not procreate a son is one who breaks the lineage of the family;
therefore, he is roasted in hell. It is said that there are four who fear what should not be feared: the gadfly, the hen, the female dog, and the nun.
"Brāhmaṇa": It is said that the *gaṇḍuppāda* insects, out of fear of the destruction of the great earth, eat only their fill and do not consume much clay.
The *kikī* bird, out of fear of falling from the sky, lies on her back upon her eggs.
The *kontinī* bird, out of fear of the shaking of the earth, does not step firmly upon the ground with her feet. The brāhmaṇas [do not marry] out of fear of the extinction of their family lineage.
They seek a wife. And regarding this, they say:
"Gaṇḍuppāda, Kikī, Kontī, and Brāhmaṇadhammika—these four deluded persons fear even what is not to be feared."
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Doṇa Brāhmaṇa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta.
193. "In the third [case], 'the very first indeed' means precisely beforehand;
the non-appearance of mantras that have not been recited is established as the very first, so there is nothing further to be said regarding that—this is the intended meaning.
'Obsession' (pariyuṭṭhāna) means overcoming or seizing; thus he says, 'by one obsessed with sensual lust' means 'seized by sensual lust. It suppresses."
It is called *vikkhambhana* because it removes; it is called *nissaraṇa* because one escapes from [the defilements] by means of its opposite.
Thus, *vikkhambhananissaraṇa* means both that suppression and that escape. Therefore he said, "In that regard," and so forth. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
One's own purpose (*attattha*) is the goal to be attained by oneself. Likewise, the purpose of others (*parattha*) should be understood.

In such passages as, “Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence,” because ill-will (*byāpāda*) and the other hindrances have not yet arisen, escape by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-nissaraṇa*) is not mentioned in the section on ill-will.

Although it is not explicitly mentioned there, it can be understood that escape by substitution of opposites is indeed applicable, since those states must be dispelled through the power of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).
The perception of light (*ālokasaññā*) may be either at the level of access concentration (*upacāra*) or at the level of absorption (*appanā*).

Or: whatever serenity (*samatha*) there is, such as the various types of kasiṇa-jhānas. The "determination of phenomena" (*dhammavavatthāna*) should be understood by way of its attainment of access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*).
"Burning with heat" (*kudhito*) means heated. "Having become hot" (*ussūrakajāto*) means having reached the extreme heat of that very state of burning;

thus he said, "having become steaming" (*usumakajāto*). "By way of the distinction of sesame seeds, etc. means by way of the distinction of sesame seeds, husks, filaments, and so forth, [as found] in algae (*sevāla*).
"Paṇaka" means slippery with water. "Appasanna" means turbid. "Asannisinna" means settled into a state of mud. "Anālokaṭṭhāne" means in a place devoid of light.
The commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kāraṇapālīsutta.
194. Regarding the phrase "In the fourth [verse], he conceives himself wise": here, *maññeti* is a particle (*nipātapada*) synonymous with *maññati*.
Showing its meaning by bringing in the word *iti*, it says, "He conceives himself to be 'wise'.
This is stated by way of a question seeking consent; therefore, he asks, "Or rather not? [And: "What does the venerable Piṅgiyānī conceive regarding the ascetic..."
By repeating the very point already stated regarding "the clarity of Gotama’s wisdom," he said, "I consider him wise.
Therefore, it was asked: "Does Master Piṅgiyānī consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or not?
The intention was: "Speak to him as you see fit. [The other replied: "Who am I? This is beyond my scope," thereby showing that it was not within his domain.

Regarding the phrase "Ko ca" (And who?), since it is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the ablative (*hetunissakke*), he said, "From where? (*Kuto ca*). Likewise, he said, "By what means shall I know?
The intention is that the specific cause by which one might know the clarity of the ascetic Gotama’s wisdom does not exist within me. Only a Buddha could [know this];
for one who is not a Buddha, the power of a Buddha’s knowledge is entirely beyond reach.
"Because it is impossible to know. For this has been said:
"But this, monks, is a mere trifle, a mere pittance, a mere matter of virtue, by which an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.
There are, monks, other states that are profound, hard to see, difficult to understand... [and so on]... by which the Tathāgata’s praise may be spoken of according to reality."
And: "One speaking rightly should say thus. Regarding the phrase "In this case": "He too would surely be such as that.
"Praised by the praised" means he is praised by his own praiseworthy qualities, not by his reputation; the sense is that he is praiseworthy by the very nature of his praise.
Therefore he said, "Of all virtues," and so forth. "The jewel-treasure" refers to the jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).
The second alternative, "or by those who are praised," is taken in order to show that he is praised even among those praised within the world including its devas.
"Araṇīya" means purpose; that which dwells (vasati) in that very [purpose] is "vasa" (abode).

He says, "atthavasa means the benefit (ānisamsa) of the purpose," because it is the fruit that constitutes the benefit of each respective application. Alternatively, "attha" is the fruit, and "vasa" is that which depends upon it for its existence.
*Etassa* means "of this," referring to the purpose or the cause.
*Khuddakamadhū* is honey made by small bees. *Aneḷakaṃ* means faultless, being free from bee-fragments.
It is called *udāna* because it is uttered by way of uplifting joy; or rather, *udāna* is that which is thus uttered. Therefore he said: "*Udāhāraṃ*..."
"...was uttered. To show how that speech is called an *udāna*, the passage beginning with "For just as...
was stated. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Piṅgiyānī Sutta 195.
In the fifth [verse], "comprehensive" (*sabbasaṅgāhika*) means a term that encompasses all states of blue, both those pertaining to the body and those pertaining to clothing and ornaments.
"Of that very same" (*tasseva*) refers to the meaning already stated by way of encompassing all [states] such as blue.

"Seeing the division" means seeing the differentiation. Just as those Licchavi kings appeared to be of yellow and other colors naturally, yet some appeared to be of yellow and other colors due to the application of ointments, so too, some who were naturally not blue and other such colors appeared to be blue and other such colors due to the application of ointments.
It is said that because of the luster of their jewels variegated with gold, they appeared as if they were entirely blue.
Or, *kokanada* is a qualification of the lotus, as in the term “*kokāsaka*. It is said that this [lotus] has many petals, is endowed with color, and is exceedingly fragrant.

This is the meaning here: just as the lotus known as *kokanada*, when it blooms and opens at dawn at the time of the sun’s rising, would be radiant and its fragrance unabated, so too [is he] by the fragrance of his body.
And one sees the Fully Enlightened One, Aṅgīrasa, who is fragrant with the scent of his virtues, who blazes with his own splendor like the sun in the sky during the autumn season,
and who is called Aṅgīrasa because of the radiance streaming from his limbs.
The commentary on the Piṅgiyānī Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mahāsupina Sutta 196.
In the sixth [case], the condition known as "that which causes disturbance of the elements" refers to conditions such as unwholesome medicine, lodging, food, and so forth.
"Whether out of a desire for welfare or a desire for harm": those who are confident do so out of a desire for welfare, while those who are angry do so out of a desire for harm.
"For benefit or for harm" means for the sake of that which ought to come to pass by its own nature, whether it be beneficial or harmful.
"They bring forth" means they cause [the child] to approach by means of their own divine power. It was like the mother of the Bodhisattva regarding the sign of obtaining a son;

for it is said that at that time, starting from the seventh day before the full moon, [the city] was free from the drinking of intoxicants and was endowed with the splendor of garlands, perfumes, and other luxuries.

While experiencing the festival of the constellations, the Bodhisatta’s mother rose early on the seventh day, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all her ornaments, and having eaten excellent food, undertook the observances of the Uposatha.
Entering the inner chamber and lying down upon her splendid bed, as she fell asleep, she saw this dream: "Four, it is said..."

Then the great kings, lifting him up along with his couch, led him to Lake Anotatta, bathed him, dressed him in celestial garments, anointed him with celestial perfumes, and adorned him with celestial flowers. Not far from there was a silver mountain;
within it was a golden palace, and there they laid him down to rest with his head toward the east. Then the Bodhisatta—
Having become a noble white elephant, he wandered not far from there upon a certain golden mountain;
descending from there, he ascended a silver mountain, entered a golden palace, circumambulated his mother, and—as if splitting her right side—entered her womb.
It was with reference to this dream that it was said: "The mother of the Bodhisatta..."
“...as if for the sake of obtaining a son.
Regarding the sixteen dreams of the King of Kosala:
“The bull, the trees, the cows, and the cow...”
The horse, the bronze vessel, the female jackal,
and the jar; the lotus pond, the raw sandalwood,
the gourds sink, and the stones float.
“Frogs swallow black snakes;
golden birds surround crows;
and fish flee out of fear of the otters.”
Like the King of Kosala who saw these sixteen dreams.
1. It is said that one day, while the Great King of Kosala was asleep at night, he saw sixteen great dreams during the last watch.
Among them, four black bulls, the color of collyrium, [came] from the four directions to the royal courtyard, thinking, "We shall fight."
Having arrived with the thought, "We shall watch the bull-fight," when the great multitude had gathered, they displayed the manner of fighting, bellowed, and thundered;
yet, without fighting at all, they retreated. This was the first dream he saw. 2.
Small trees and shrubs, having burst forth from the earth, flowered and bore fruit without rising even a span or a cubit above the ground. This was the second [dream] he saw.
3. He saw cows suckling the milk of calves born that very day. This was the third dream.
4. He saw men yoking young, untrained bullocks to the yoke in succession instead of large, full-grown oxen capable of bearing the burden;
unable to pull the load, they stood there having abandoned it, and the carts did not move forward.
This was the fourth dream. 5. He saw a horse with two heads; fodder was given to it on both sides, and it ate from both mouths. This was the fifth dream. 6.

A great multitude of people, having swept out a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand pieces, presented it to an old jackal, saying, "Empty your excrement here. He saw it emptying its excrement therein. This was the sixth dream.
7. A man wound a rope and placed it at his feet. While he was unaware, a famished female jackal lying beneath the seat where he sat devoured it. He saw this as the seventh dream. 8.
At the king’s gate, he saw one large full jar surrounded by many empty jars.
Furthermore, people of the four castes, bringing water in jars from the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions, [were pouring it in].
They fill only those jars that were already full; having crossed over the water that was already full, it flows away.
They pour the water back into those very same places again and again, yet even though they look for them, there are no empty jars. This is the eighth dream. 9.
He saw a deep lotus pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, with a landing-place on every side. On all sides...
Bipeds and quadrupeds descend there and drink the water.
In its deep central part the water is turbid, but in the areas near the banks where bipeds and quadrupeds tread, it is clear, serene, and undisturbed. This was the ninth dream. 10.
He saw rice being cooked in a single pot, yet it remained uncooked. Having reflected on this as "uncooked," he divided it [into parts].
It was as if being cooked in three ways: in one part it was overcooked, in another part it was undercooked, and in another part it was perfectly cooked. This was the tenth dream. 11.
He saw people selling the finest sandalwood, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], for rotten gruel. This was the eleventh dream.
12. He saw empty gourds sinking in the water. This was the twelfth dream. 13.
He saw massive boulders, as large as gabled houses, floating on the water like boats. This was the thirteenth dream. 14.

He saw frogs the size of small madhuka flowers rapidly pursuing large black snakes, cutting them like lotus stalks, and devouring their flesh while swallowing them whole. This was the fourteenth dream.

15. He saw golden royal swans, surrounded by ten qualities contrary to the True Dhamma, which were named "Suvaṇṇa" (Golden) because they possessed the color of gold; these were the village-roaming crows. This was the fifteenth dream. 16.
Previously, leopards used to eat goats. But he saw those leopards pursuing the goats and devouring them with a "muramurā" sound.
Then other trembling crabs, having seen the goats from afar, became terrified and seized with fear out of dread of the goats.
Having fled and entered into dense thickets, they hid there. This was the sixteenth dream.

1. Therein, when unrighteous kings and unrighteous people prevail, when the world is undergoing transformation, when wholesome qualities have declined and unwholesome qualities have increased, and at a time of decline for the world, the rain does not fall properly; the clouds do not... [continue as in the source].
The crops will be cut short, the grain will wither, and there will be famine.
When clouds, as if desiring to rain, arise from the four quarters and the women, fearing that the rice and other grains spread out in the sun will become damp, have brought them inside;
and at the moment the men, taking spades and baskets, go out to bind the embankments, the [clouds] display the appearance of raining and thunder.
"Having discharged flashes of lightning like bulls that neither yoke nor shed their seed, they will flee away. This is the first result.
Second: In an age when the world has declined and the lifespan of humans is short, beings will possess intense lust;
even while still young girls, they will go to other men, and having become menstruating and pregnant, they will increase through sons and daughters."
For their state of menstruation will be like the flower of small trees, and sons and daughters will be like the fruit.
This is the second result.
3. When the practice of honoring one’s elders among humans has perished, beings [will behave] toward their mothers and fathers, or toward their mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law...

Or, failing to establish a sense of shame, while they themselves manage the household, those who wish to give even a mere measure of food and clothing to their elders will give it; those who do not wish to give will not.
Thus the elders, being left without support and lacking self-control, will live by gratifying their children, like great cows that drink the milk of calves born on that very day.
This is the third ripening.
4. In the time of unrighteous kings, those unrighteous kings do not grant honor to great ministers who are wise, skilled in traditional lineages, and capable of accomplishing their duties;
nor do they [honor] the wise who are skilled in legal procedure within the Dharma assembly or at the place of judicial decision.

They will not appoint elderly ministers, but will instead bestow honor upon those who are quite young and contrary to that [ideal], and they will appoint such persons to positions of judicial authority.

Being ignorant of what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding royal affairs, they will neither be able to maintain their own prestige nor carry out the duties of the state. Being unable to do so, they—
They will abandon their administrative duties; even the elder wise ministers, though capable of accomplishing their tasks, will receive no honor and will think, "What use have we for these?
We are outsiders; the young men of the inner circle will know how to handle this," and thus they will not perform the duties that arise. In every way, there will be only decline for those kings.
It will be like the time when young bullocks, incapable of bearing the yoke, are first harnessed to it;
or like the time when great oxen, accustomed to long journeys, are harnessed in a continuous succession of yokes. This is the fourth result. 5.
Only during the time of unrighteous kings will foolish and unrighteous kings appoint unrighteous and greedy men to the office of judges.
Those fools, indifferent to both demerit and merit, sit in the assembly hall and deliver judgments;
having accepted bribes from the hands of both the plaintiff and the defendant, they will consume them like a horse eating fodder from two mouths. This is the fifth ripening.
6. Furthermore, unrighteous kings of low birth, out of suspicion toward noble sons of pure lineage, will not grant them honor.
They will give their daughters only to those of low birth. Thus, great families will become impoverished, while base families will become powerful.
Those men of noble birth, being unable to make a living, will give their daughters to those of low birth, thinking, "We shall live by depending on them.
In this way, the union of these daughters of noble families with those of low birth is like the old jackal with the golden bowl.
It will be like a drainage ditch. This is the sixth ripening.
7. As time goes on, women will become lustful for men, lustful for liquor, lustful for ornaments, lustful for the streets, and lustful for material gain;
they will be immoral and of evil conduct. Having performed such tasks as plowing and tending cattle for their husbands, they...
Having acquired wealth with great difficulty and hardship, they drink liquor with their lovers;
wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments, they disregard even urgent duties within the house; they watch for their lovers through the upper parts of the house walls and even through cracks;
and having pounded seeds fit to be sown the very next day, they prepare rice gruel, cooked rice, and snacks.
Having cooked it, they will devour it, plundering it like a famished female jackal lying beneath a seat, rolling and rolling over a rope placed at her feet.
This is the seventh ripening. 8.
As time goes on, the world will decline; the kingdom will become devoid of essence; and the kings—
They will become miserable and wretched. Whoever becomes the lord will have a storehouse containing about a hundred thousand [measures].
All those people, being thus miserable, will be made to perform labor for their own sake;
oppressed, the people will abandon their own work and, for the sake of the kings alone, will sow, protect, and reap the primary and secondary crops.

Crushing [sugarcane], planting it, cultivating fields of sugarcane, operating machines, boiling down molasses and other products, and establishing flower gardens and fruit orchards, they will bring back the rice and other crops produced here and there to fill the king’s storehouses alone.
Even looking at their own empty storehouses in their homes, they will not exist; they will not even look at empty jars.
It will be just like filling a vessel that is already full. This is the eighth ripening. 9.
As time passes, kings will become unrighteous; acting out of favoritism and other such motives, they will govern by following improper courses.
They will not administer justice according to the Dhamma, but will become seekers of bribes.
Greedy for wealth, they will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion toward the inhabitants of the realm;
harsh and cruel, they will oppress the people like sugarcane in a sugarcane press, and having levied various kinds of taxes, they will seize their riches.
Oppressed by these taxes and unable to give anything further, the people will abandon their villages, market towns, and other settlements.

Having gone to the borderlands, they will establish their dwellings there. The central provinces will become empty, while the borderlands will become densely populated—just as in a lotus pond, the water is turbid in the center but clear at the edges. This is the ninth ripening. 10.
As time passes, kings will become unrighteous; when those kings are unrighteous, so too will those appointed by the king.
"Both the brahmins and householders, as well as the people of the towns and the countryside—in short, all humans including recluses and brahmins—will become unrighteous (*adhammika*).
Consequently, their guardian deities, the deities who receive offerings, the tree deities, and the deities dwelling in the sky—all such deities will likewise become unrighteous.
Under the reign of unrighteous kings, winds that are irregular and harsh will blow."
They will cause the sky-dwelling celestial mansions to tremble. When those tremble, the deities, becoming angry, will not allow the rain to fall.
Even if it does rain, it will not fall all at once throughout the entire kingdom;
and even when it rains, it will not do so in a way that is beneficial for agriculture or sowing everywhere. And just as it is with the kingdom, so too—
In some districts and in some villages, even within a single reservoir or lake, it will not rain at once;
raining on the upper part of the reservoir, it will not rain on the lower part, and raining on the lower part, it will not rain on the upper part.
In one area the crops will be destroyed by excessive rain, in another they will wither from lack of rain, and in another they will thrive through proper rainfall.
As it rains, it will fall perfectly. Such is the ripening of the crops grown during the reign of one king.
There will be three kinds [of results], like rice from a single pot. This is the tenth ripening.
11. As time goes on and the Dispensation (Sāsana) declines, many monks will become greedy for requisites and shameless.

They will exist. Having crushed out the Blessed One’s teaching on the Dhamma—which was spoken after crushing greed for requisites—they will teach it to others for the sake of the four requisites, such as robes.
Being infatuated with requisites, though they stand on the side of those seeking deliverance, they will not be able to teach while directing [the mind] toward Nibbāna.
They will do so merely by hearing the excellence of the words and phrases and the sweet sound [of the teaching].

“They will teach, saying: ‘They will give costly robes and so forth. Others, sitting on the crossroads, at the junctions of four roads, at royal gates, and so on, will teach by means of even coins, half-coins, quarter-māsakas, and rūpakas.
Thus, the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—having been made priceless as Nibbāna—is [now used] for the sake of the four requisites and for the sake of coins and such.
Teaching while selling [the Dharma] will be like selling the essence of sandalwood, worth a hundred thousand, for rotten juice.
This is the eleventh ripening result. 12.
While the world is revolving in times of unrighteous kings, kings [will treat] sons of noble family who are endowed with a good birth...
They will not grant honor to [the noble], but will grant it only to those of low birth. They will become masters while others remain poor.

Whether in the presence of the king, at the king’s gate, in the presence of ministers, or in the seat of justice, the speech of those of low birth—who are like empty gourds—will remain as if submerged, motionless, and firmly established. Even in an assembly of the Sangha...

In matters of formal acts of the Saṅgha and the Gaṇa, as well as in decisions regarding alms-bowls, robes, monastic courtyards, and so forth, only the talk of immoral and wicked individuals will lead to liberation, not that of modest bhikkhus;
thus, in all such places, it will be like the time when empty gourds sink. This is the twelfth result.
13. At such a time as that, unrighteous kings will grant honor to those of low birth.
They will become the masters, while those of noble birth fall into misfortune. No one will show respect toward them; rather, they will show respect only toward others.

Whether in the presence of the king, in the presence of ministers, or in the place of legal judgment, [they will favor] those sons of good family who are skilled in adjudication and resemble solid rocks.
Their discourse will not reach a firm foundation after being investigated. While they are speaking, others will merely mock them, asking, "What are these people talking about?

Even in the assembly of monks, at the aforementioned places, they will not consider the virtuous monks worthy of respect, nor will their discourse reach a firm foundation after being investigated; it is like the time when stones float.
It will be as if [this were so]. This is the result of the thirteenth [perfection].

14. While the world is indeed declining, humans will be born with intense passion and other such defilements; following after their own afflictions, they will remain under the control of their young wives.
Even the slaves, laborers, and others in the household, as well as the cattle, buffaloes, and even the gold and silver, [will likewise fall under their sway].
"Everything will depend on them alone. When asked, "Where is such-and-such gold, bullion, or household goods?
she will say, "Let it be wherever it may be! Why do you concern yourself with this?
Have you become one who wishes to know whether what is in my house exists or not? Having spoken thus, she will revile him in various ways and strike him with the weapons of her mouth.
Having crushed them and brought them under their control like slaves and servants, they will exercise their sovereignty.
Thus, it will be like the time when female frogs the size of *madhuka* flowers are swallowed by venomous black snakes. This is the fourteenth ripening. 15.
But in times of weak kingship, kings will be unskilled in the arts of elephants and so forth, and lacking confidence in battles.
Fearing the loss of their own royal sovereignty, they will not grant power to young men of similar birth,
but will instead give it to those who serve at their feet, such as bath-attendants and barbers. Consequently, young men of noble birth and lineage,
unable to find a footing in the royal court and thus incapable of maintaining a livelihood, will remain in positions of power while those inferior in birth and lineage take their place.
Those of low birth will wander about serving [the king]; it will be like the time when a crow was surrounded by golden royal swans.
This is the fifteenth ripening.
Furthermore, during the reign of an unrighteous king, only those of low birth will become the king’s favorites and lords, while those of noble birth will remain unknown.
They were miserable. Having caused the king to adopt their own arguments, they became powerful in the courts of justice and other such places;
they then brought charges against those who were weak, claiming that ancestral fields, lands, and so forth belonged to them, saying, "These are ours, not yours.
When the weaker parties came to the courts of justice and other such places to dispute this, [the former] had them beaten with cane whips and other instruments.
Having seized them by the neck and dragged them away, they will threaten them, saying: "You do not know your own measure; you quarrel with us!
Now we shall have you beaten, report it to the king, and have your hands, feet, and other limbs cut off!
Out of fear of them, they will hand over their own property, saying: "These belong to you; take them."
Having entered their own homes, they will lie down in fear. Even wicked monks will harass the virtuous monks according to their pleasure.
Finding no refuge, the virtuous monks will enter the forest and hide in dense thickets.
Thus, for those sons of noble family who possess birthright and are oppressed by those of low caste as well as by wicked monks—
It will be like the time when well-behaved monks flee out of fear of wild sheep and predatory beasts.
This was the sixteenth fruition. Thus he saw these sixteen great dreams, which served as omens of various misfortunes.
Therefore it is said: "Like the King of Kosala, [he saw] sixteen dreams. And herein, from the perspective of the omen regarding himself—
One who sees a dream indicating benefit or harm does so through the power of one's own karma.
However, it should be understood that one who sees a dream indicating the benefit or harm of the world, such as the King of Kosala, sees it through the power of karma common to all sentient beings.
"Angry deities" refers to the deities who were angry with the Great Elder at the Mahānāga Monastery.
It is said that at the Mahānāga Monastery in Rohaṇa, the Great Elder had a banyan tree (*nāgarukkha*) cut down without even consulting the Saṅgha of monks.
The deity dwelling in that tree became angry with the Elder; first, she tempted him with a dream of truth, and afterwards [she declared], "Seven days from now..."
The attendant announced in a dream, "The king will die. The Elder brought this report and informed the king’s women.
They all broke out into a great wailing at once. The king asked, "What is this?
They reported, "It was spoken thus by the Elder. The king calculated the days, and when seven days had passed, [he cut off] the Elder's hands and feet.
He had it cut down. It is said that "it was entirely true" because the fruit [of the dream] was real; however, the vision itself was indeed distorted (*vipallattha*).
For this very reason, those who have abandoned distortions do not see even a dream that serves as a precursor.
One may sometimes see a dream due to two or three causes; thus he says, "from the breaking of associations. "The Asekhas do not..."
Based on the statement, "They see [objects] because they have abandoned the perversions," it should be understood that for all four [types of dreams], the perversions themselves are the root cause.

"That" refers to the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) occurring at the time of sleep. "An object such as a visible sign" means there is no object such as a visible sign other than kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny.
"Such as these" refers to objects such as visible forms that were previously experienced through direct perception or are merely imagined.
And those associated with lust and so forth. "By the ordinary consciousness" means by the natural (pakati) consciousness.
"Released from two extremes" means released from the two extremes known as the wholesome and the unwholesome.
"At the moment of adverting and its object" is said with reference to the series of consciousnesses that proceed until the arising of the registration (tadārammaṇa). "Even as in a dream..."

They say: "But at the time of saying 'it is as if seen by me' or 'it is as if heard by me,' it is indeed indeterminate (abyākata), because it arises merely as an adverting consciousness (āvajjana-matta).

For those who speak thus, it is intended that even in the mind-door (manodvāra)—just as in the second section on the flood-gates (moghavāra) regarding the five doors—the adverting consciousness arises two or three times, stands in the place of the impulsion (javana), and then sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

It must be seen [as such] because, at the moment of the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) which lasts for a single thought-moment, the conceptualization "it is as if seen by me" or "it is as if heard by me" is impossible.

And here they say: "Even in a dream, because of the statement that it has that as its object, real phenomena (*sabhāvadhammā*) exist as objects in a dream, whether by way of the present or the past. "Even if in a dream..."
They say: "It is said that when the object-base such as visible form has appeared after having become manifest, it is called 'having that as its object';
nevertheless, because the sign appearing at the end of a dream must be grasped through conceptualization, it is weak, and thus it is said to have a weak object-base.
However, some say: "Because the body born of karma has reached a state of quietude devoid of activity, the heart-base supported by it is not very clear."
Because it exists, the mental process supported by that [heart-base] is not very clear, like the light of a lamp situated in a turbid pool;
therefore, regarding the phrase "because its basis is weak," they explain the meaning as "because its heart-basis is weak.
Having investigated this, one should accept what is most appropriate.
"Volition in dreaming" refers to volition occurring by way of mind-door impulsion during sleep.
For one seeing a dream sees it only through mind-door impulsion, not through the five doors; and when waking up, one wakes up only through the mind door, not through the five doors.
Indeed, while one is sleeping, even if a great fire is lit and a lamp is brought close to the eye—
When [the object] is presented, the first adverting consciousness pertaining to the eye-door does not turn back the life-continuum; it turns back only the mind-door.
Then, after the impulsion has impelled, it sinks back into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the adverting consciousness pertaining to the eye-door turns back the life-continuum;
thereafter, the eye-consciousness and the others proceed until the conclusion of the impulsion, immediately following which—
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned back by mind-door adverting consciousness, mind-door impulsion (javana) impels.
By that consciousness, one knows: "What is this light in this place?
Likewise, for one who is sleeping, when musical instruments are played near the ear, or when fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near the nose—

When [objects] are presented—such as when ghee or molasses is placed in the mouth, or when a blow is struck on the back—the advertings (*āvajjana*) belonging to the ear-door and so forth do not cause the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) to turn back;
rather, it is only the mind-door adverting that turns it back, and then, having performed the impulsion (*javana*), it sinks back into the life-continuum.
On the second occasion, the advertings belonging to the ear-door and so forth [do turn back the life-continuum].
They cause the stream to turn back; then, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses, ending with the impulsion (javana), proceed, after which the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) flows on.
On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned back by mind-door adverting consciousness, mind-door impulsion impels;
having known through that consciousness, [one wonders]: "What is this sound in this place? Is it the sound of a conch, or the sound of a drum?"
Or he might say, "What is this fragrance in this place? Is it the scent of roots? or "What has been put in my mouth?
Is it ghee or molasses? or "Who struck me on the back? The blow was very heavy.
Thus one awakens by means of the mind-door javana alone, not by the five sense-doors. Even a dream occurs through that same [process].
He sees by means of the mind-door, not by means of the five doors. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Mahāsupina Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Vassa Sutta.
197. "In the seventh [case], 'arisen through the season' means that which arises during the four months of the rainy season. 'Even out of season' means even during the months of Cittā and Vesākha.
For when the sons of the gods who are rain-clouds give rise to a thought desiring to sport for their own pleasure, it rains even out of season.
Here is an account of this: it is said that a certain son of the gods who was a rain-cloud once [visited] a *khīṇāsava* elder living at Vākarakuṭaka..."
Having approached and paid homage, he stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you? "Venerable sir, I am the divine son Vassavalāhaka," he replied.
"Is it said that the rain-god rains according to your mind? "Yes, venerable sir. "We wish to see him. "Then you shall be drenched, venerable sir.
"Neither the crest of the cloud nor the thunder is perceived; how shall we be drenched? "Venerable sir, for us..."
"The deity rains by means of his mind; you should enter the leaf-hut. "Very well, young deity," he replied, and having washed his feet, he entered the leaf-hut.
As soon as he had entered, the young deity sang a song and raised his hand;
an instant cloud arose over an area of three leagues on every side. The Elder entered the leaf-hut while still half-soaked with rain.
The commentary on the Vassasutta is finished.
8–9. Commentary on the Vācāsutta, etc. (198–9).
In the eighth [sutta], "by means of factors" (*aṅgehi*) means by means of causes (*kāraṇehi*). They are called "factors" (*aṅgāni*) because they are known as causes; that is, they are the reasons.
The word *aṅga* is used here in the sense of cause (*kāraṇatthe*). In the phrase "by five" (*pañcahi*), the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetumhi*).

"Endowed with" (*samannāgatā*) means accompanied by, occurring together with, or joined with. "Speech" (*vācā*) refers to the speech of conversation; it is that which is described as "speech, utterance, expression," and also as "gentle and pleasant to the ear.

Furthermore, it includes the intimation (*viññatti*) expressed by the words, "if an action is performed through speech," and that which [is defined] by the four types of verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita*).
In this context, "right speech" is not intended to refer to abstinence—as in the passage, "Abstaining from [unwholesome speech]...
this is called right speech"—nor to volition—as in the passage, "Bhikkhus, harsh speech, when practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in, leads to rebirth in hell. Why?
Because it cannot be spoken. For it is said: "It is well-spoken, not ill-spoken."
"Subhāsitā" means well-spoken; by this, it indicates that it brings about benefit. "Anavajjā" means free from the faults of passion and so forth;

by this, it indicates purity of cause and the absence of defects such as falling into wrong courses, for when one speaks free from passion and hatred, because of being devoid of partiality, falling into wrong courses is far removed indeed. "Ananuvajjā" means free from reproach.
By this, he illustrates her perfection in every respect; for when there is perfection in every respect, there is no fault.
"Of the wise" means of the learned. By this, he shows that fools are not the standard in matters of blame and praise.
With the words "By these," and so forth, he concludes that speech by directly pointing out those factors. And whatever others...

They imagine that even speech such as lying, if it is endowed with the members [of a syllogism] beginning with the proposition (*paṭiññā*), with words beginning with names (*nāma*), and with the perfection of gender, number, case, tense, and grammatical relation (*kāraka*), is well-spoken; he refutes that.
For even speech of such a kind, though endowed with the members and so forth, is indeed ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others. But by these...
If one possesses five qualities, even if they are included among the speech of non-Aryans (*milakkhu*) or included among the songs of slave-girls,
it is nevertheless well-spoken because it brings about mundane and supramundane welfare and happiness. For instance,
there was the sound of a Sinhalese slave-girl guarding the standing crop by the side of the road, singing a song in the Sinhalese language concerning birth, aging, and death.
Having heard this, about sixty bhikkhus practicing insight while traveling on the road attained arahantship.
Likewise, a bhikkhu named Tissa, who had begun the practice of insight, was walking near a lotus pond; having broken off some lotuses from the pond, he thought:
"The red lotus that blossoms at dawn..."
It is shattered by the light of the sun;
even so, beings who have attained human status are crushed by the force of old age.
Having heard this song from the maidservant who was singing it, he attained Arahatship.
Furthermore, during the interval between Buddhas, a certain man came from the forest with seven sons and saw a certain woman pounding rice with a pestle, [saying]:
"This is worn out by old age, clinging to withered skin."
“This is destroyed by death; it is the bait and food for the Lord of Death.
It is an abode of worms, filled with various kinds of filth;
it is a vessel of impurity, equal to a heap of refuse.”
Having heard this song and reflecting upon it, he attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha together with his sons.
Thus, speech endowed with these five factors should be understood as well-spoken, even if it is included in a foreign tongue or contained within the song of the pot-girl.
Such well-spoken words alone are blameless and beyond reproach to the wise.
"For clansmen who seek the goal and rely on the meaning, not on the letter. The ninth [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Vācāsutta* and others is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Nissāraṇīyasutta*.

200. Regarding the phrase "escaping in the tenth": although it should be stated as *nissaraṇīyā* (those that lead to escape), it is expressed with a long vowel (*nissaraṇīyā*) for metrical reasons. This suffix *-anīya* denotes the agent, as in the word *niyyāniyā* (those that lead out).
Therefore, he says "escaped" (*nissaṭā*). From what, however, have they escaped? From their respective opposites.

Since they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*), he says "having a nature empty of self. In terms of meaning, however, they are specific instances of the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) and the element of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
“For such a bhikkhu there is no attention directed toward sensual pleasures by way of defilement”; thus he said, “for the purpose of investigation. The meaning is:
for one who is investigating, thinking, “My mind is now fixed on renunciation; will a thought of sensual desire perhaps arise?
“Pakkhandana” means entry. Since that is not present there, he said, “it does not enter.”
“Pasīdana” means delight; “santiṭṭhana” means establishment; “vimuccana” means resolution.
Rejecting all of these, he says, “he does not attain confidence,” and so forth. To the question, “How then does his mind abide when it has become thus? he says, “Just as...,” and so on.
This refers to the first jhāna. "Of him" means of the bhikkhu. "The mind leaps forward" (pakkhandati):
this is said by treating the preparatory consciousness and the jhāna-consciousness as one through their unity. "Because it has gone into its own range" means because it proceeds upon its own object.
"Because it partakes of non-decline" means because it partakes of stability. "Well-liberated" means by way of suppression-liberation (vikkhambhana-vimutti).
It is rightly liberated. It is "affliction" (*vighāta*) because it causes the destruction of both mind and body.

It is "fever" (*pariḷāha*) because it burns all around. One does not experience sensual feeling because it does not arise. It is "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because they escape from it. What escapes? Sensual desires (*kāmā*).
And thus, the genitive case expressing the agent—“of sensual desires”—is perfectly appropriate. To the extent that sensual desires...
"Therefore they are called 'escaped from that'; by that same principle, even *jhāna* receives the designation 'escaped from sense-desires' (*kāma*), which is why it is said:
'because of being escaped from sense-desires' (*kāmehi nissaṭattā*). Having thus explained the escape from sense-desires by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), he now says "But he who...
and so forth, in order to show the ultimate escape by way of eradication (*samuccheda*). "In the remaining sections" means in the other divisions.

However, this is the distinction: when stating the distinction, the phrase "making that jhāna the basis," and so forth, was not mentioned at all in the second and third sections because it is considered a non-distinction;
but in the fourth section, in order to show that even this is a distinction, it is said:
"And here, the fruit of arahantship, which is ultimate deliverance, should be connected. This is because the formless jhāna...
Having made [the lower stages] the basis and having attained the highest path, the mind of one established in Arahantship is said to be entirely detached from forms (*rūpa*).
For when such a person, having emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), directs the mind toward forms for the purpose of investigation, this is explained.
Thus, the four preceding sections were taken by way of those whose vehicle is serenity (*samathayānika*). This...
However, he said "in pure formations," and so forth, with reference to the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*).
"The further existence of identity (*sakkāya*) does not exist" arises for one who investigates, thinking, "Now, the continuity of my identity no longer exists.
The commentary on the *Nissaraṇīya Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇavagga is finished.
The Fourth Fifty is finished.
5. The Fifth Fifty.
(21) 1. The Kimila Chapter. 1–4.
Commentary on the Kimila Sutta and others. 201–4.
The first and second [suttas] of the fifth [chapter] have their meanings already explained. In the third, *adhivāsana* means forbearance; toward others...
Adhivāsanā means enduring by taking upon oneself wrongs, insults, and opposition;
that very thing is patience, thus it is called *adhivāsanakkhanti*. One who delights in what is beautiful is *sūrato*; or, one who is well-restrained (*orato*) from evil is *sorato*.
The state of being such is *soracca*. Therefore he said: "By *soracca* means by purity of virtue (*sucisīlatā*). For that is delighting in beautiful deeds.
Or, it is the state of being well-restrained from evil, which is abstinence. There is nothing further to be said regarding the fourth [precept].
The commentary on the Kimila Sutta and others is finished.
5. Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta.
205. In the fifth [chapter], the "mental barrennesses" (*cetokhila*) are, in meaning, doubt and anger.
However, when they arise in a particular mental continuum, they stand as a state of harshness and rigidity toward that continuum, let alone toward the consciousness associated with themselves;
thus it is said, "due to the stiffened state of the mind. Just as the entire splendor of the Teacher’s physical body is grasped through the perfection of its characteristics...
"Just as [the head] is indeed grasped, so too the glory of the body of all phenomena is indeed grasped by omniscience.
Showing doubt regarding the basis for both of these, he said, "doubting about the body," and so forth.

"Investigating" means examining the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*). "Is distressed" means becomes weary. "Unable to resolve" means unable to reach a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhātuṃ*).

He is unable [to do so]. It scorches and burns away the defilements (*kilesa*), thus it is "ardor" (*ātappa*); he said "for the sake of ardor" (*ātappāya*) meaning "for the purpose of exerting energy that scorches the defilements.

"For repeated application" (*punappunaṃ yogāya*) means for the repeated engagement in cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "For constant practice" (*satatakiriyāya*) means for the uninterrupted application of cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "one who has doubt concerning the state of penetration" (*paṭivedhadhamme kaṅkhamāno*): how does doubt arise here with respect to the supramundane state (*lokuttaradhamma*)? Not by way of making it an object (*ārammaṇakaraṇavasena*).
Showing that doubt arises regarding a conceptually constructed form acquired through reflection on what has been heard, he said: "Insight...
[they say], one doubts whether that exists or does not exist. And here, "training" (sikkhā) should be understood as training in the prior stage (pubbabhāga-sikkhā).
Although it is true that, due to the arising of specific distinctions and because of its great blameworthiness, it is the cause for joining together with the purpose of communal living;
Some say that by specifying "toward fellow celibates" (*sabrahmacārīsu*) due to its frequent occurrence, anger is distinguished as its specific object;
thus, it cannot be understood that anger toward other things is not a "mental wasteland" (*cetokhila*). If this were so, the same logic would apply to doubt (*vicikicchā*) as well.
Therefore, it should be understood according to the literal expression.
The commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta is finished.
6–8. Commentary on the Vinibandha Sutta, etc. 206–8.
In the sixth [sutta], they are called "mental bondages" (cetasovinibandhā) because they bind the wholesome mind by way of preventing it from proceeding.
Furthermore, since those who bind it become like those who take a firm grip with their fists, he said, “having bound the mind,” and so forth.
A person greedy for sensual pleasures relishes and delights both in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) and in defilements (*kilesakāma*); thus it is said, “in sense-objects as well as in defilements.
“In one’s own body” means in one’s own mental body (*nāmakāya*), or in one’s personal existence (*attabhāva*). “External form” refers to that of others.
And in the body, which consists of matter not bound to a sense faculty. "Udarāvadehakaṃ" means that which swells, accumulates, and fills the belly.
"Seyyasukhaṃ" is the pleasure arising from the state of lying down on a bed. "Samparivattakaṃ" means having turned over.
"Paṇidhāya" means having directed [the mind] by way of craving alone. Thus, these five kinds of specific greed are indeed called "fetters of the mind."
It should be understood as "spoken. There is nothing further to be said regarding the seventh and eighth [suttas].
The commentary on the Vinibandha-sutta and others is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Gītassara-sutta and others.
209–210. Regarding the ninth [fault], called *āyataka* (protracted): it occurs when one breaks the respective rhythm (*vatta*) and destroys the syllables as they proceed;
thus he says, "by means of *āyataka*," and so forth. There is indeed a rhythmic pattern for prose (*sutta-vatta*) among the teachings, and there is a rhythmic pattern for verses (*gāthā-vatta*).
It is not permissible to destroy that [rhythm] and make [the recitation] excessively long. For one speaking the Dhamma should do so with clarity (*caturassa*).
The words and phrases should be displayed with circular movements according to the *vatta* (ritual procedure).
Furthermore, because of the statement, “I allow you, monks, the *sarabhañña*,” it is permissible to recite the Dhamma with a melodic chant (*sara*).

It is said that in the *sarabhañña*, there are thirty-two *vattas*, such as the *taraṅgavatta*, the *dhota-vatta*, the *bhāgaggahaka-vatta*, and so forth. Among these, one may perform whichever one desires. Regarding the tenth [precept], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Gītassara Sutta and others is completed.
The commentary on the Kimila Vagga is completed.

1–2. Commentary on the *Akkosakasutta* and others. 211–2.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the second [chapter]: "One who reviles by means of the ten grounds for reviling" refers to one who reviles using the ten grounds for reviling, such as: "You are a fool! You are deluded!
You are a camel! You are an ox! You are a donkey! and so forth. "Be off, shaveling ascetic!"... [and so on].
One who says things such as, "You strike me without a staff; now, having gone to the royal court, I shall have you punished," is called a reviler;

thus it is said, "by way of seeing [him as] a source of fear, he is a reviler. Because the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) constitute an obstacle to the path leading to the lower realms (apāya), they are called an "obstacle";
thus it is said, "because the obstacle to the supramundane has been severed," referring to that which is designated as supramundane.
The meaning is: "because the obstacles on the path to the states of loss have been cut off. There is nothing further to be said regarding the second [sutta].
The commentary on the *Akkosaka-sutta* and others is finished.
3–10. Commentary on the *Sīla-sutta* and others.
213–220. Regarding the third [term], *dussīla*: here the prefix *du-* has the sense of absence (*abhāva*), as in the case of *duppañña* and similar terms, and does not have the sense of censure.
Thus he says, "one who is without virtue, devoid of virtue" (*asīlo nissīlo*). Regarding *bhinnasaṃvara*: here one who has undertaken the precepts has reached a breach of virtue due to some cause;
let him for now be called *bhinnasaṃvara*. However, one who has not undertaken the precepts at all and is deficient in conduct—[he too is included].
How, then, is one said to have "broken restraint" (*bhinnasaṃvara*)? Because he has broken the good conduct that ought to be maintained, he is indeed called one who has broken restraint;
for what is meant is that his restraint is ruined, that he is devoid of restraint. [This refers to] various crafts or occupations.
On the day of the proclamation of the *māghāta*—that is, on the day when the proclamation "Do not kill living beings! has been made. He goes forth.
There is an evil reputation. Because of the state of remorse, he is indeed dejected in his underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
"Of him" means of the immoral one. "The place where he has acted after undertaking [the precepts]" refers to the purpose performed by rising up again and again.

"It comes into the range of vision" means it presents itself to the mind. "Opening [his eyes] to this world" means, at the time of opening them, [he sees it] by way of his own children, wife, and so forth.

He sees this world. Having closed his eyes, he sees the other world; that is, at the time of closing his eyes, he sees the other world by way of the appearance of the sign of his destination (*gatinimitta*).
Therefore, he said, "The four states of misery," and so forth. "The fifth section" refers to the fifth portion of the dangers, stated by the words "with the breakup of the body," etc.
"By way of the reverse of what was stated" means by way of the opposite of the discourse on the dangers whose meaning has already been stated.
“Being diligent, one is able to accomplish various tasks such as farming and trade at the proper time,” and so forth. One who possesses praiseworthy virtue is called *sīlavā*.

As for the explanatory synonyms such as *sīlasampanno* (endowed with virtue), *sīlena samannāgato* (possessed of virtue), and *sampannasīlo* (one whose virtue is perfected), these are easy to understand and have not been explicitly analyzed here.
The fourth and subsequent terms have their meanings already explained.

1. The Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings (Āhuneyyavagga) 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Paṭhama-āhuneyyasuttavaṇṇanā) 1.

In the first [discourse] of the Section of Sixes (Chakkanipāta), the phrase "having seen a form with the eye" is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the support (*nissaya-vohāra*). This is a description that includes the constituent factors (*sasambhāraka-niddesa*).

Just as in the expression "he pierces with a bow," one should understand that by way of the support (nissaya), there is the grasping of that which is supported (nissita). Therefore, the meaning is this:
"When a visible object has come into the range of the eye-door, having seen that form with eye-consciousness.
"He is not even glad" means that at the moment of impulsion (javana), he does not produce lust toward a desirable object, nor is he even glad by way of affection rooted in the household life.
Because greed has been completely eradicated by the Path. "Not dejected" means not being angry toward what is undesirable;

thus, through the absence of any alteration in his serene confidence, he does not grasp at desirable, undesirable, or neutral objects with equanimity, correctly, or improperly—that is, he does not view them in a biased manner.
And this practice of his is due to the attainment of fullness in mindfulness and the attainment of fullness in wisdom.

Thus he said, "having become mindful and clearly comprehending. He is *sato* because of being endowed with mindfulness (*sati*). He is *sampajāno* because of being endowed with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
It is stated that "the constant abiding" is taught because it occurs even at times when the conditions for the arising of knowledge are absent, owing to its distinct mode of occurrence.

"Constant abiding" refers to the perpetual abiding of one whose taints are destroyed, an abiding that proceeds at all times—except, of course, during the moments of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Those whose taints are destroyed dwell by means of this very dwelling in the sixfold equanimity.
Herein, the "sixfold equanimity" is stated by the phrase, "he dwells equanimous even at the six doors.
Furthermore, because of the word "clearly comprehending," four types of consciousness associated with knowledge are obtained, since clear comprehension is impossible without them.
Because they exist as a constant state of dwelling, the eight great functional consciousnesses (*mahā-kiriyacitta*) are obtained.

Because of the statement, "Neither joyful nor dejected," ten consciousnesses are obtained: the eight great functional consciousnesses, the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*), and the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhapana*).
Since the absence of joy and grief—which are co-nascent with greed and hatred—is common to them as well, [they are included] by way of the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*).
If it is asked, "How is joy obtained by these who have arrived at the constant abidings?"— it is through cultivation (*āsevana*).
Although one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) dwells mostly in equanimity (*upekkhaka*) toward both desirable and undesirable objects—

as if indifferent— because he does not abandon his own naturally purified state, nevertheless, when there is occasionally no such mental volition (*cetobhisaṅkhāra*), that [joy] which exists by its very nature...
Even with respect to a desirable object, by way of grasping its true nature, the Arahat’s consciousness still proceeds accompanied by joy due to the force of previous habituation.
The commentary on the first *Āhuneyya Sutta* is concluded.
2–7. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings, etc. 2–7.
In the second [discourse], "in many ways" (*anekavihitam*) means manifold or of various kinds. "The modes of supernormal power" (*iddhividham*) refers to a portion of supernormal power.
"He experiences" (*paccanubhoti*) means he experiences; the meaning is that he touches, realizes, and attains it. Now, as for its state of being manifold:

Demonstrating this, he says, "Having become one," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "having become one," it means that even though he was originally one by nature prior to performing the act [of transformation], he becomes many.

"He becomes many" means that, desiring to walk to and fro, or desiring to recite, or desiring to ask a question in the presence of many people, he becomes a hundred or a thousand. Regarding the phrase "manifestation and disappearance": here...
The meaning is: "he makes manifest" and "he makes invisible. Indeed, it is with reference to this very point that it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"'Manifest' means it is not covered by anything, unobscured, open;
'invisible' means it is covered by something, obscured, shut away, closed off. [He passes] through walls, through enclosures, through mountains.
"He moves without adhering, just as if in space. Here, "through walls" (*tirokuṭṭa*) means through another wall;
what is meant is the far side of a wall. The same method applies to the others. "Wall" (*kuṭṭa*) is a designation for the wall of a house.
"Rampart" (*pākāra*) is the surrounding rampart of houses, monasteries, villages, and so forth. "Mountain" (*pabbata*) refers either to a mound of earth or a mountain of rock.
"Not clinging" (*asajjamāno*) means not adhering, just as if in the air.
"Emerging and submerging" (*ummujjanimujja*): here, "emerging" (*ummujjanti*) refers to rising up; "submerging" (*nimujjanti*) refers to sinking down.
"Emerging and submerging" is the compound of both emerging and submerging. "Even while piercing through the water": here, that water which one steps upon and sinks into is meant.
That which is being broken is called "breakable," while the opposite is "unbreakable. He goes by means of a cross-legged posture. "A winged bird" means a bird endowed with wings.
Regarding the phrase "he touches even these sun and moon, so powerful and majestic, with his hand":
here, their great power consists in their movement forty-two thousand yojanas above [the earth].

The greatness of his majesty is to be understood by his ability to produce light simultaneously across the three continents. Thus, he possesses great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*) through such upward movement and the production of light.
"Grasps" (*parāmasati*) means he takes hold of it, or touches it in one part. "Polishes" (*parimajjati*) means he polishes it all over, as if on the surface of a mirror.
"Even as far as the Brahma-world" (*yāva brahmalokāpi*) means taking the Brahma-world as the limit.
"He exercises mastery with the body" means that there, in the Brahma-world, he exercises mastery over himself by means of the body.
Regarding the phrase "with the divine ear-element": here it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine.

For the ear-elements of deities, produced by well-performed kamma, are unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth; being free from such defilements, they are capable of receiving objects even at a great distance.
It is a divine faculty of the ear. And this faculty of knowledge-ear produced by the power of this bhikkhu’s development of energy is exactly like that;

thus, because it resembles the divine, it is "divine. Furthermore, it is "divine" because it is obtained through the mode of divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*) and because it itself is supported by divine abiding.
It is a "faculty of the ear" (*sotadhātu*) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*).
It is also called the "ear element" because it performs the function of the ear element, just like the ear element itself; [the phrase] "by that ear element" refers to this.

"Purified" means clean and free from defilements. "Transcending the human" means having transcended the range of humans and, in the hearing of sounds, having surpassed and gone beyond the human fleshly ear element, it remains so. "Hears both kinds of sounds" refers to two...
He hears sounds. Which two? Celestial and human; that is to say, the sounds of both devas and humans.

By this, it should be understood that the scope [of his hearing] is fully encompassed. "Those far and near" means he hears those sounds that are far away, even across another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), as well as those that are near, including even the sounds of minute creatures inhabiting his own body. By this...
It should be understood as a complete and exhaustive inclusion.
"Of other beings" means of all beings excluding oneself. "Of other persons"—this also has the same meaning as the former.
However, a difference in phrasing has been made due to the capacity of those to be trained and for the sake of elegance in the teaching. "Mind with mind" refers to one's own...

"By means of his own mind, he [knows] their minds. "Having delimited" (*paricca*) means having circumscribed. "He understands" (*pajānāti*) means he knows them in their various modes, such as being with lust and so forth.
Furthermore, in the passages beginning with "a mind with lust," the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood as "a mind with lust.

The remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is "free from lust. This includes the two types of consciousness associated with displeasure, and the two types of consciousness associated with doubt and restlessness.
However, these four types of consciousness do not fall within this dyad. Some elders, nevertheless, include them as well.
The two-fold mind of displeasure (*domanassacitta*) is called "mind with hatred" (*sadosa*).
All wholesome and indeterminate consciousness belonging to the four planes is "free from hatred" (*vītadosa*). The remaining ten unwholesome types of consciousness do not fall within this dyad.
They proceed. However, some elders include those [two] as well. Regarding the terms "with delusion" (*samoha*) and "free from delusion" (*vītamoha*):
here, according to the method of individual classification (*pāṭipuggalikanaya*), only the two types accompanied by doubt and restlessness are "with delusion.

But since delusion is possible in all unwholesome states, it should be understood that all twelve kinds of unwholesome consciousness are "consciousness with delusion. The remainder is "free from delusion. That which is accompanied by sloth and torpor...
Furthermore, that which is contracted is distracted when accompanied by restlessness. That which pertains to the fine-material and immaterial spheres is sublime;
the remainder is not sublime. All that belongs to the three planes is surpassable; the supramundane is unsurpassable. That which has reached access or reached absorption is concentrated;
that which has not reached either is unconcentrated. [It may also be classified as] liberation by substitution of opposites, suppression, eradication, tranquillization, and renunciation.
This fivefold attainment (patta) should be understood as either liberated (vimutta), or not having reached liberation (vimutti), it is unliberated (avimutta).
"In many ways" (anekavihita) means of many kinds, or the meaning is that it has proceeded or been described in many modes.

"Past lives" (pubbenivāsa) refers to the continuum (santāna) that dwelt here and there, beginning with the immediately preceding past existence. "He recollects" (anussarati) by way of the succession of the aggregates (khandha).

Furthermore, it should be understood that a kalpa in decline is a *saṃvaṭṭakappa* (a contracting kalpa), while one in increase is a *vivaṭṭakappa* (an expanding kalpa). In this context, by the term *saṃvaṭṭa*, the period of contraction (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is included because it is rooted in that; and by the term *vivaṭṭa*, the period of expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is included. For this being so, as it is said: "Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of a kalpa. Which four? [The passage continues: "The period of contraction, the period of remaining contracted, the period of expansion, and the period of remaining expanded.

Each of these lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakappa*). Thus, eighty intermediate kalpas constitute a great kalpa (*mahākappa*). It is with reference to this that it was said: "Monks, the lifespan of Brahmā Sahampati is a hundred thousand great kalpas and another forty thousand kalpas. This is how the duration of a kalpa should be understood. Furthermore, regarding the statement: "Monks, these four things are difficult to obtain in the world," the first is the arising of a Tathāgata, the second is the teaching of the Dhamma, the third is the attainment of human birth, and the fourth is the acquisition of the opportunity to hear the Dhamma. Among these, the arising of a Tathāgata and the teaching of the Dhamma are dependent upon the expansion of the world-system (*vivaṭṭa*). Human birth occurs during both the contraction and the expansion. However, the hearing of the Dhamma occurs only when a Tathāgata has arisen and is teaching the Dhamma. Therefore, all four are dependent upon the expansion of the world-system. Consequently, it is said: "Monks, these four things are difficult to obtain in the world. This is how the meaning of a kalpa should be understood. Furthermore, the Blessed One has taught that there are three kinds of kalpas: the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*), the kalpa of formation (*vivattakappa*), and the kalpa of duration (*ṭhitikappa*). Among these, the kalpa of destruction is the period from the time the world begins to contract until the final dissolution of the realm of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). The kalpa of formation is the period from the time the world begins to expand until the completion of the formation of the realm of nothingness. The kalpa of duration is the period from the time the realm of nothingness is fully formed until the world begins to contract again. Of these, the kalpa of destruction consists of twenty intermediate kalpas, as does the kalpa of formation. The kalpa of duration consists of twenty intermediate kalpas for the realm of nothingness, twenty for the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), twenty for the realm of non-perception (*asaññāyatana*), and twenty for the realm of the infinity of space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). Thus, the kalpa of duration consists of eighty intermediate kalpas. Together with the twenty intermediate kalpas of the kalpa of formation and the twenty of the kalpa of destruction, the total duration of a great kalpa is one hundred intermediate kalpas. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Monks, the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is a hundred thousand great kalpas. This is how the meaning of a kalpa should be understood. Furthermore, regarding the statement: "Monks, there are these four incalculable periods of a kalpa. Which four? The period of contraction, the period of remaining contracted, the period of expansion, and the period of remaining expanded"—each of these lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas. Thus, eighty intermediate kalpas constitute a great kalpa. It is with reference to this that it was said: "Monks, the lifespan of Brahmā Sahampati is a hundred thousand great kalpas and another forty thousand kalpas. This is how the duration of a kalpa should be understood. Finally, regarding the statement: "Monks, these four things are difficult to obtain in the world," the first is the arising of a Tathāgata, the second is the teaching of the Dhamma, the third is the attainment of human birth, and the fourth is the acquisition of the opportunity to hear the Dhamma. Among these, the arising of a Tathāgata and the teaching of the Dhamma are dependent upon the expansion of the world-system. Human birth occurs during both the contraction and the expansion. However, the hearing of the Dhamma occurs only when a Tathāgata has arisen and is teaching the Dhamma. Therefore, all four are dependent upon the expansion of the world-system. Consequently, it is said: "Monks, these four things are difficult to obtain in the world. This is how the meaning of a kalpa should be understood.
The terms "contraction," "the period of contraction," "expansion," and "the period of expansion" have been mentioned; these are now fully grasped. "I existed there" means:

in that particular eon of contraction, I existed in such a state of being, or in such a womb, or in such a class, or in such a station of consciousness, or in such an abode of beings, or in such a category of beings.
"With such a name" means Tissa or Phussa. "Of such a clan" means Gotama.
“...or Kaccāyana, or Kassapa. This was said by way of his recollection of his own name and clan in a past existence.

However, if at that time he wishes to recollect the excellence of his physical appearance, whether his mode of livelihood was coarse or refined, the abundance of his pleasure and pain, or whether his life span was short or long, he recollects that as well. Therefore he said: “Of such a complexion... [and so forth].”
"Thus is the limit of his lifespan. In this context: "Thus is his complexion" means he is either white or dark.
"Thus is his food" means his food consists of rice and meat, or he subsists on wild fruits.

"Thus is his experience of pleasure and pain" means that in this manner he experiences physical and mental pleasures and pains, distinguished as being with or without material sustenance, and so forth. "Thus is the limit of his lifespan" means that the limit of his lifespan is measured at one hundred years.
Or with a life span of eighty-four thousand eons as its limit. "Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere":

having passed away from that existence, womb, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings, I was born again in such-and-such an existence, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings named so-and-so. "There too I was... [and so on].
There too, in that existence, birth, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings, I was again.
"Of such a name," and so forth, is exactly as previously described.
Furthermore, "I lived there" refers to the recollection of one ascending step by step for as long as desired. "From there... [and so on].
