There is a reviewing of one who is turning back; therefore, it should be understood that the statement "he arose there" was spoken with reference to the place of rebirth immediately following this present birth, in the sense of "having been born here.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "there he was such-and-such" is intended to demonstrate the recollection of his name, clan, and so forth, regarding the places of rebirth within the interval between this present birth and that previous one.

It is said: "Having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. This means: "Having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, I have been born here in such-and-such a clan of Kṣatriyas or a clan of Brāhmaṇas.
Thus (*iti*) means in this way. "With its aspects and its details" (*sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ*):
it is "with its details" by way of name and lineage; it is "with its aspects" by way of complexion and so forth. For by name and lineage a being is known as "Tissa Kassapa."

It is pointed out by means of color and so forth as being distinct, such as "he is dark" or "he is fair"; therefore, name and clan constitute the "pointing out" (uddesa), while the others are the "modes" (ākāra).

Regarding the phrase "by the divine eye" and so on: it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine. For the divine eye of the deities—produced by well-performed kamma, unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, and capable of receiving objects even at a distance due to its freedom from defilements—is the divine faculty-eye (pasādacakkhu).
This eye of knowledge, produced by the power of the development of energy, is just like that; thus, it is "divine" because it resembles the divine eye.
It is "divine" also because it is obtained through the mode of divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*) and because it is supported by one's own divine abiding.
It is "divine" also because of its great radiance due to its mastery over light. It is "divine" also because of its great range due to seeing forms located beyond walls and other such obstructions.
It is divine. All of that should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing.

It is also "eye" because it performs the function of the eye, as if it were an eye. It is "purified" (*visuddha*) because it is a cause for the purification of view through the seeing of passing away and rebirth.
For he who sees only passing away and not rebirth adopts the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*); he who sees only rebirth... [and so on].
He does not adopt the view of the manifestation of new beings after death.
But he who sees both of these, because he transcends both those types of views, that vision becomes a cause for the purification of views.
And the sons of the Buddha see both of these. Therefore it was said: "Because seeing the passing away and reappearance is a cause for the purification of views..."

"Purified": having transcended the human range by seeing forms, it should be understood as "transcending the human" because it has surpassed the human fleshly eye. By means of that divine eye, purified and transcending the human.
"He sees beings" means he looks at beings with his human flesh-eye as if with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). Regarding the phrase "passing away and being reborn":
it is not possible to see them with the divine eye at the precise moment of death (*cutikkhaṇa*) or the precise moment of rebirth (*upapattikkhaṇa*).
However, those who are near to death and will die shortly are called "passing away," while those who have already taken rebirth and have just been born are called "being reborn."
"Those being reborn" is what is intended. He shows that one sees them thus passing away and being reborn.
"Inferior" means despised and held in contempt by way of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so forth, because they are associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha*).

"Exalted" means the opposite of that, because they are associated with the outflow of non-delusion. "Beautiful" means endowed with a desirable, lovely, and pleasing complexion because they are associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*).
"Ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) means possessing a color that is undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant due to being associated with the outflow of hatred; it also means deformed or misshapen.
"Well-gone" (*sugata*) means having gone to a good destination, or, because of being associated with the outflow of non-greed, being wealthy and possessing great riches.
"Ill-gone" (*duggata*) means having gone to a bad destination, or, because of being associated with the outflow of greed, being poor and lacking food and drink.
"According to their deeds" (*yathākammūpaga*) means that they have gone according to whatever karma has been accumulated.

Regarding "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) and so forth: it is called misconduct because it is a bad conduct due to being rotten with defilements. Bodily misconduct is that which is misconduct by way of the body, or misconduct arisen from the body;
the same method applies to the others as well. "Endowed with" (*samannāgatā*) means having become possessed of. Of the Noble Ones...

"Accusers" means those who, being ill-wishers toward the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, including even lay stream-enterers—accuse them by means of a final charge or by the destruction of their virtues; that is to say, they are abusers and revilers.
"Holding wrong views" means having perverted vision. "Adopting actions based on wrong views" means [acting] by way of wrong view.
They undertake various kinds of actions, and they also encourage others to engage in bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view.
"With the breaking up of the body" means the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped. "After death" means the taking up of the newly produced aggregates immediately following that.
Alternatively, "with the breaking up of the body" means the cutting off of the life-faculty. "After death" means after the moment of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).

"Apāya," and so forth—all these are synonyms for *niraya* (hell). For it is called *apāya* because it is devoid of "good fortune" (*aya*), which consists of merit that serves as the cause for heaven and liberation;
or else, because there is an absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness, it is an "absence. It is called *duggati* because it is a destination (*gati*) of suffering, or a refuge (*paṭisaraṇa*);
or else, because it is produced by defiled (*duṭṭha*) karma due to an abundance of hatred, it is a "bad destination. There, beings fall down helpless.
"Those who have committed misdeeds" refers to the *vinipāta*. It is called *vinipāta* because those who are perishing fall into it with their limbs and members shattered.
It is called *niraya* because there is no "essence" (*āya*) here that is characterized as a gratification.
Alternatively, by the mention of the "woeful states" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm; for the animal realm is a woeful state because it is departed from the happy destinies (*sugati*).

There is no miserable destination (*duggati*) for those of great authority, such as the Naga kings and others, because of their possibility of rebirth there. By the inclusion of "miserable destination," the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*) is also included;
for that is both a state of loss (*apāya*) and a miserable destination, since it is departed from the happy destinations (*sugati*) and has become a resort of suffering.

However, it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because [the Naga kings] do not fall like the asuras. By the inclusion of "fall," the host of asuras is meant; for that, in the sense already stated, is indeed a fall.
The term *vinipāta* (fall) refers to the states of loss (*apāya*) and miserable destinies (*duggati*), because of falling away from all elevations.

By the mention of "hell" (*niraya*), it is intended that there are many varieties of hell, such as Avīci and others. "Reborn" (*upapanna*) means having arrived; the intention is that they have been produced there through rebirth.
The "bright side" (*sukkapa-kkha*) should be understood by reversing what has been stated. However, this is the distinction: therein, by the mention of "a happy destination" (*sugatigga-haṇena*)...

The human realm (*manussagati*) is also included [in the term *sugati*], while by the mention of "heaven" (*sagga*), only the divine realm (*devagati*) is meant. Therein, a beautiful destination is a "good destination" (*sugati*).

It is a "heaven" (*sagga*) because it is an excellent (*su*) summit (*agga*) with respect to sense objects such as forms. All of that, in the sense of being subject to breaking up and disintegration, is the "world" (*loka*);
this is the summary here. However, the detailed exposition in all its aspects should be taken from the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
The third and subsequent sections have their meanings explained in plain terms.
The commentary on the second *Āhuneyyasutta* and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Anuttariyasutta*.

8. In the eighth [section], they are called "unexcelled" (*anuttara*) because there are no others superior or more distinguished than them. They are "unexcelled states" (*anuttariya*) simply because they are unexcelled, just as one says "the infinite itself is the infinite state" (*anantariya*);
thus he says "unsurpassed" (*niruttara*). What is called the "unexcelledness of vision" (*dassanānuttariya*) is so named because it brings about a distinction in the fruit (*phala*).

This same method applies to the remaining [unexcelled states] as well. "The acquisition of the sevenfold noble wealth" refers to the acquisition of the sevenfold supramundane wealth, beginning with faith (*saddhā*).

"Completion of the three trainings" means the fulfillment of the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue. Therein, completion should be understood in its primary sense by way of the Arahants.

For, starting from the noble ordinary person (kalyāṇaputhujjana), the seven types of trainees (sekha) are said to "fulfill" the three trainings, whereas the Arahant is one whose training is perfected. Thus, these are the unsurpassed states.
The mundane and supramundane [states] have been explained.
The commentary on the *Anuttariya-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Anussatiṭṭhāna-sutta*.
9. In the ninth [section], the recollections (*anussati*) are called "bases" (*ṭhāna*) because they are the causes for welfare and happiness pertaining to the present life and the future life;

thus, they are the "bases of recollection" (*anussati-ṭhāna*). "Mindfulness having the qualities of the Buddha as its object" means that just as the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) is a basis for the attainment of distinction, so too is the mindfulness that arises by taking the qualities of the Buddha as its object, beginning with the words, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One. For one who recollects in this way...
For when rapture arises, he establishes that rapture in its state of exhaustion and vanishing, and thereby attains Arahantship.

This proximate meditation subject (upacārakammaṭṭhāna) is available even for laypeople. "Proximate meditation subject" means a sequence of meditation subjects that brings about access concentration through direct experience, and which, by way of successive insight (sammasana), brings about mundane and supramundane distinctions all the way up to Arahantship. This method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the *Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Mahānāma Sutta*.
Regarding the tenth [sutta]: "At that time" means at the time of recollecting the qualities of the Buddha. "Overwhelmed by lust" means by lust (*rāga*).
"Overwhelmed" (*pariyuṭṭhita*): even the state of having reached an obsession; it is said that the mind associated with lust is "overwhelmed" by it, just as a forest is overwhelmed by bandits.
Furthermore, because it is the locus for that obsession, the meaning is "one whose lust is overwhelmed.
However, disregarding the literal phrasing and showing merely the sense, [it means] "having arisen by means of the lust that is arising."

"It has been grasped," he said. "Straight indeed" means that it has attained a state of straightness because bodily crookedness and the like have already been removed, because of the absence of pride and other factors that cause the mind to be unstraight, or because of the lack of the obsession of lust and so forth, which is free from leaning to one side or the other.
Alternatively, "straight indeed" means that the meditation subject has become straight through the disappearance of both laxity and agitation caused by sinking into sloth and torpor.
It has indeed attained straightness through the practice of the sign of middling serenity.

"Relying on the commentary" means relying on the meaning of such words as *bhava*, *jāti*, and so forth. Or, "joy in the meaning" (*atthaveda*) refers to the satisfaction that arises dependent upon cause and fruit;

"joy in the Dhamma" (*dhammaveda*) refers to the satisfaction that arises dependent upon the cause. For one who recollects, "He is an *Arahat* because of his being far removed," this [is what occurs] regarding the Blessed One...
Being far removed from the defilements (*kilesa*)—that is the cause. And here, the "cause" intended is one that makes known, not one that acts or brings about.
From that, the goal of Arahantship, being made known by it, is the fruit. By this method, the fruit as the result of the cause should be understood in the remaining phrases as well.

For even in the case of the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*) and so forth, such qualities as being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and right practice (*suppaṭipatti*), and so on, exist therein.
In this context, [the term] is indicated precisely by way of its being the cause. "Connected with the Dhamma" means endowed with the qualities comprised of the aforementioned causes and fruits.
The commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Āhuneyya Vagga is finished.
2. The Chapter on Recollections (Sāraṇīyavagga) 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Recollections (Paṭhamasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā) 11.

Regarding the first [discourse] of the second [chapter]: "Worthy of being remembered" (*saritabbayuttaka*) means they are fit for recollection (*anussaraṇārahā*). It is so called because by means of it one is moistened (*mijjati*) and softened (*siniyhati*).

Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the state of being a friend. That which possesses loving-kindness is "loving" (*mettaṃ*); this refers to bodily action (*kāyakamma*). Since that [action] is originated by a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, it is therefore said:
"Bodily action should be performed with a mind of loving-kindness. This same method applies to the other two [types of action] as well. "These" refers to loving-kindly bodily action and so forth.
They are presented from the perspective of the monks because they constitute the most excellent assembly. Furthermore, just as...

Since these qualities are found among the bhikkhunīs as well, and likewise among householders, because they are common to all four assemblies, he says "For the bhikkhus... and so forth to demonstrate this.

He says "Bodily action with a mind of loving-kindness... and so on, because for a bhikkhu, every blameless bodily action is indeed included within the category of conduct pertaining to higher practice (*ābhisamācārika*). Regarding the veneration performed toward the cetiyas and bodhi-trees...

Having established that the accomplishment of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is achieved through veneration, going for the sake of that [veneration] is called "loving-kindness as bodily action" (*mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ*). By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), there is included the bodily activity proceeding by way of loving-kindness toward the remaining objects of respect—such as shrines (*cetiyas*), the Bodhi tree, and monks—as previously mentioned.

The intention is that even the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) consisting of the Three Piṭakas is being recited. Even the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Piṭakas is [included] by way of questioning and explaining the meaning.

Vocal action (*vacīkamma*) is indeed that which is being performed as loving-kindness (*mettā*), because it must proceed with the intention for the welfare of others. "The three good conducts" (*sucarita*) refers to the good conduct of body, speech, and mind.
By the word "thinking" (*cintana*), he shows that even mere mental reflection is mental action (*manokamma*), let alone the actual practice of meditation.
"Openly" (*āvī*) means manifestly; and here, the state of being manifest refers to the presence of the person for whose sake that bodily action is performed.
He said, "In the presence. "Secretly" means out of sight. And because that bodily action is performed with respect to someone who is not present before one's eyes, he said, "in the absence.
"Going to the state of being an associate" means in their presence.
For indeed, going to the state of being an associate while they themselves are performing [the act] is what is called "bodily action in the presence. "By both" refers to the novices.

And by those [words]. "Taking up" means having grasped and raised it; it refers to the speech that takes up the expression "Deva Thera," which—rather than merely saying "Deva"—illuminates his stability through his virtues. "Speech that makes known 'mine'" is speech of possessiveness.
For mental action (*manokamma*), which is entirely turned away [from the object], its state of being "in the presence" occurs by way of generating a manifestation (*viññatti*).
And that is indeed known and recognized in the world as "bodily action. Without referring to the movements of the hands and so forth, he said, "opening the eyes," and so on, in order to show this.
Granted, the opening of eyes that are moistened with the oiliness of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and looking with a serene face are indeed bodily actions of loving-kindness;
however, it is by virtue of which mind that the eyes become moistened with the oiliness of loving-kindness [that is the primary factor].
And because of the clarity of the face, it was said with reference to that: “It is called loving mental action.
The word *lābha* (gain) functions as a noun (*kamasādhana*), as in such expressions as “O, what a gain has been obtained!

Since it is stated here, “obtained in accordance with the Dhamma,” it refers to the past tense; thus he says, “the requisites such as robes that have been obtained. They are *dhammika* (righteous) because they have come from the Dhamma.

The requisites are obtained through a pure means of livelihood; therefore, it is said, "righteously acquired" (*dhammaladdhā*). Indeed, it is precisely to demonstrate this meaning that the passage beginning with "by means of hypocrisy, etc.
was spoken. For things obtained improperly are not called "righteously acquired"; thus, in order to exclude such cases, the word "righteously acquired" is stated in the Canon.
One who enjoys what has been given without making a distinction between the donor and the recipient is called "one who enjoys without making distinctions" (*appaṭivibhattabhogī*).

This is the name. Therefore he said, “Two names are distinguished,” and so forth. By the phrase “distinguishing by means of the mind,” he shows that even by a mere arising of consciousness there is a distinction called “distinguished” (*paṭivibhatta*), let alone by the preliminary effort (*payoga*).
Or, “distinguishing by means of the body preceded by distinguishing by means of the mind” was stated in order to show the very root [of the process]. By that...
This shows that a distinction must be made merely by the arising of the thought. "Indivisible" (*appaṭivibhatta*) is a description in the neuter gender of the abstract noun;
or it is a description of the object, meaning "he enjoys the gain indivisibly. He does not give that to householders for the sake of purifying his own livelihood.
Nor does he consume it himself [thinking], "May there be no state of exclusive enjoyment on my part. And while receiving it... [etc.]
By the word "sees," he establishes a sense of commonality starting from the moment of arrival.
For in this way, sharing together becomes easy for him, and his quality of "remembering" (sāraṇīya-dhamma) is fulfilled.
Alternatively, by the phrase "accepting... [and] seeing," he establishes the commonality of that gain throughout the three periods of time.
The setting aside [of the robe] has been shown. By the phrase "and while receiving it, let it be common to the Saṅgha," the time of receiving is shown.
By the phrase "having taken it... he sees," the time after it has been received is shown.
Since both of these do not occur without a prior stage of that nature, the preceding time is established by implication. This indeed occurs for him even before the receiving: "By the Saṅgha..."

Thinking, "May it be common property; I shall accept it," while accepting it he thinks, "I accept it so that it may be common property for the Saṅgha," and having accepted it, he thinks, "It has been accepted by me so that it may be common property for the Saṅgha.
Having thus made it endowed with these three characteristics, one should handle the gain obtained without violating the characteristic of its inclusion [in the Saṅgha].
While enjoying [the requisites], one is a sharer of enjoyments and one who does not partition out enjoyments.
This, however, is the "conducive-to-remembering quality" (sāraṇīya-dhamma)—this fourth quality that is appropriate to be remembered. For... [as previously stated] ...they do not take it up;
therefore, since the state of being a sharer of enjoyments does not exist for the immoral person, even the undertaking [of this practice] is impossible, let alone its fulfillment.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). By the phrase "one of pure virtue," he shows that the gain is righteous (*dhammika*).

By the phrase "not breaking the observances" (*vattaṃ akhaṇḍento*), he shows the practice of not consuming things separately and the practice of sharing [the gains] in common. Since the quality of being "courteous" (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) is fulfilled when both of these are present, he says "he fulfills it.
By the expression "having made it specific," he implies [the opposite], namely, having made it non-specific with respect to one's father.
This shows that for one who gives starting from the senior seat of the teachers, preceptors, and so forth, it is indeed a *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (a duty of courtesy).
"To be given" means it must necessarily be given. However, it does not constitute a *sāraṇīya-dhamma* for him because it is given specifically designated for the place of maintenance.
Therefore he said: "It is called 'the maintenance of impediments. It is permissible for one whose impediments have been released.
Because it is impossible to fulfill [the requirements] for one whose impediments (palibodha) have not been relinquished.

If this is so, does it follow that for one who fulfills the qualities conducive to harmony (sāraṇīya-dhamma) in every respect, specific giving (odissaka-dāna) is permissible or not? It is not impermissible;
showing that it is appropriate in the proper place, he said, "But by that... and so forth. By this, he shows that specific giving is not prohibited for him in all circumstances.
For a gift made specifically for those who are ill and so forth is on the side of non-distribution, because there is no exclusion such as, "I will not give to such-and-such a person.
For the counterpart (paṭibhāga) is characterized by its contrast (byatireka). Therefore he said, "the remainder," and so forth.
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even if one does not give," he shows that it is also permissible to give; however, this is by way of compassion, not by way of fulfilling one's formal duties.
Therefore, even for one who is immoral, if there is need and the possibility exists, a gift should be given; for indeed, giving is not forbidden to anyone.
"Well-trained" means well-trained in the method of fulfilling the *sāraṇīya* (courteous) duties; the meaning is that she is highly skilled. Now, in order to demonstrate her proficiency, it was said:
"For one who is well-trained," and so forth. She should fulfill [the duties] in twelve years, and not beyond that.
By this, he shows its difficulty to fulfill. For it is of great fruit and great benefit, accompanied by results and benefits that are even more exalted than those pertaining to the present life;

and the person who possesses it is a special attainer, like a noble person (ariyapuggala), endowed with qualities that are wonderful and marvelous in the world. For likewise, [it is superior] to the gift consisting of what is difficult to abandon...
Having suppressed far away the factors that are the opposites of merit consisting in virtue, he dwells having become manifest and renowned in the world with a purified mind.
To clarify this matter both by way of contrast and by way of agreement, the passage beginning with “If indeed... was spoken. That is easy to understand.
Now, in order to demonstrate his benefits both in this present life and in future lives, it is said:

“For one who has thus fulfilled the qualities that are conducive to being remembered,” and so forth. Neither envy nor stinginess arises because these have been shaken off through long-term cultivation.
He becomes dear to people because he is renowned for his character of generosity. Thus it was said: “Giving, he becomes dear; many resort to him,” and so on.
The condition is easily obtained because, through the act of giving, the acquisition of requisites possesses the nature of a benefit here for those with lofty aspirations.
What is given from his bowl is never exhausted, because it is replenished by the uninterrupted offering of the twelve-year-old Great Vow itself.
He receives the finest portion daily, starting from the foremost among those worthy of offerings.

Because of having given gifts. Or in times of fear... [they] incur [these results] because their minds have been extended through the long-term fulfillment of giving with a mind free from attachment to themselves, without making a distinction between the giver and the receiver.
"Therein" refers to when those benefits are to be made manifest. These are the fruits, the bases, and the causes. [This concludes] Mahāgirigāma.
There was a certain village on the side of Nāgadīpa. "Even though they did not obtain [alms]" means that, due to their lack of merit, they were unsuccessful in obtaining them.
"Knowing the path of alms-round to be similar" means they knew the path of alms-round to be common to, or of the same nature as, that [other] one.

Because it was a superhuman state (anuttara-manussa-dhamma), and for the purpose of dispelling the Elders' doubt, he said: "Venerable sir, I have fulfilled the duty of courtesy. For likewise, in the second case as well:
The Elder has made himself known. It is said that even in his youth he was one who fulfilled the qualities of endearment (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*).

This story serves both to show his popularity among people and the ease with which he obtained the necessary requisites. However, because it specifically illustrates the excellence of his lack of fear regarding the bowl, it is stated:
"This, first of all... [etc. ...is the story in this regard."

"By means of the Great Festival of Mountain Offerings (Giribhaṇḍamahāpūjā)" refers to the great festival performed with island-flowers, perfumes, and so forth, on Cetiya Mountain, throughout the entire island of Laṅkā measuring one *yojana*, and across the ocean, including the fleets of ships and other vessels.
And in order to demonstrate that this practice is not barren [of fruit], he said, "These will come to me. By way of sequence and even by way of brevity.
"Worthy" (*anucchavika*) means "one who fulfills the qualities conducive to mindfulness" (*sāraṇīyadhammapūraka*).
The meaning is: "Knowing things as they truly are is suitable for you.
Out of fear of thieves, they fled without having reported [the matter]. Some also say it was because of their own difficult livelihood. She said, "I am one who fulfills the duties of endearment;
even with what is contained in my bowl, all these bhikkhunīs will survive," and she added, "Do not you [be afraid] of them..."
"He reflected on the state of having gone [to Nibbāna]. "It will exist" means it will endure. The Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*);
however, the deity became diligent solely through the power of the Elder’s virtue.
"They have no breakage" means they are unbroken. To demonstrate that breakage of theirs, the passage beginning with "Of her... was spoken.

In this context, the beginning and end of the precepts for those who are fully ordained (upasampanna) should be understood according to the order of their recitation. Therefore, he said, "in seven," and so forth.
For there is no other sequence for the classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha);

even for the precepts of those not fully ordained, the beginning and end are obtained according to the order of their undertaking. "Like a garment cut at its edge" means like a cloth that has been torn at its border or its hem.
This is an example of a dissimilar case (*visadisa-udāharaṇa*), because of the addition of the word "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍāni*).
The same applies to the remaining examples. "Brokenness" (*khaṇḍikatā*) is "fragmentation" (*bhinnatā*); that which possesses this is "broken" (*khaṇḍa*), namely, virtue (*sīla*).

The same method applies to "with holes" (*chidda*) and so forth. "Broken in the middle" refers to being pierced through by way of penetration. The connection is: "like a cow [pierced] by a dissimilar-colored [arrow]."
"Of mixed color" means having a half or a third part of a dissimilar color; "spotted" means variegated with spots of dissimilar colors interspersed here and there.
This is the distinction between these two. Those devoid of spots are "unspotted," and likewise those devoid of speckles are "unspeckled.
The liberation of virtue from the slavery of craving consists in making it a necessary condition for the turning away from existence (nibbāna); therefore—
By the statement "liberation from the slavery of craving," he indicates that those virtues are a necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).

With the phrase "making one free" (*bhujissabhāvakaraṇato*), he shows that this is an analysis [of the term] using elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*), meaning "those which make one free" (*bhujissakarāni*) are "the free ones" (*bhujissāni*).
Or alternatively, because a person possessing them is called "independent," "self-mastering," and "free," they too are "the free ones. For those who lack understanding...
Because they are immeasurable, it is said that they are "praised by the wise. Alternatively, because they are perfected through their state of extreme purity, they are praised by the wise;
thus, they are "praised by the wise" (*viññuppasatthāni*).
Because they are not clung to by craving or views, [one does not think]: "By this virtue, may I become a god or some other kind of deity."
Because it is not adhered to through adherence to craving—thinking, "By means of this virtue, having become a deva, I shall there be permanent, stable, and eternal"—nor through adherence to views.
"To adhere" means to adhere by pointing out any one of the four failures, saying, "This is a fault in your virtues"; the meaning is to revile, to accuse, or to reproach.
"Virtue" (sīla) is for the purpose of achieving concentration (samādhi) through the succession beginning with non-regret; thus he said, "conducive to concentration.
Those whose function is to lead to concentration are "conducive to concentration" (samādhisaṃvattanikā).
The state of being the same is "commonality" (sāmañña); by way of the state of the fourfold complete purity, it is like gold that has been melted in the middle.

Because there is no difference [in it], it is "commonality of virtue" (*sīlasāmañña*) due to its commonality with virtue; one who has gone to, or approached, that is "one who has attained the commonality of virtue" (*sīlasāmaññagata*). Therefore he said, "one whose virtue has attained the state of equality.

The meaning is: one whose virtue has attained the state of equality through the perfection of virtue, one who shares in the same conduct. Granted, there may be no diversity even among ordinary worldlings regarding the fourfold purification of virtue, yet that is not absolute.
He said, "There is no diversity in the virtue of the Path," because this [virtue] is absolute and of a fixed nature.
It was said with reference to that; namely, with reference to the virtue of the Path, it was stated: "Those virtues which... and so forth.
"By which" means by this [view] which is directly evident to both myself and you. "View" means the right view of the Path.
"Free from defilements" (*niddosa*) means those whose defilements have been removed; the meaning is that their evil states, such as lust and so forth, have been utterly cut off.

"It leads out" (*niyyāti*) means it escapes from and departs from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). For while it is itself being led out, it is said to lead the person endowed with it out from the suffering of the round of existence.
"One who acts accordingly" (*takkara*) is one who performs what has been instructed by the Teacher; [the phrase refers to] him who practices in accordance with the instruction.
The meaning: "A state of shared view" means a state of similar views, a state of non-differentiated views through the full penetration of truth.
The commentary on the first *Sāraṇīya-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *Sāraṇīya-sutta*.
12. In the second [verse], "of fellow-celibates" (*sabrahmacārīnaṃ*) means of those who share the same Dhamma. "Making dear" (*piyakaraṇā*) means making what is already dear even more dear.
"Making respected" (*garukaraṇā*) means making what is already respected even more respected. "For the sake of holding together" (*saṅgaṇhanatthāya*):

the connection is that they lead to the holding together of fellow-celibates because they constitute specific bases for such gathering (*saṅgahavatthu*). "For the sake of non-dispute" (*avivadanatthāya*): this is because they serve as bases for gathering.

It is not for the sake of causing dispute. And since they possess the quality of being a cause for non-dispute and for bringing about unity, the state of concord and the absence of schism among fellow celibates (sabrahmacārīs) is established by virtue of them;
thus he said, "For the sake of concord," and so forth.
The commentary on the second *Sāraṇīya-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Nissāraṇīya Sutta* 13.
In the third [verse], "increased" (*vaḍḍhitā*) means fully nourished by way of the completion of cultivation.

"Repeatedly performed" means set into motion again and again through the frequent practice of cultivation. "Made like a harnessed noble steed chariot" means just as a noble steed chariot that has been properly harnessed...
Just as a chariot controlled by a skilled charioteer proceeds according to his wish, so too "proceeding according to one's wish" is what is meant here.
Or, it is said that she is "made into a basis" (*vatthukata*) in the sense of being established;

for, through the complete purification of all defilements and the attainment of distinguished psychic power (*iddhi*), she has been made into a state of proceeding like a well-cleansed site free from obstacles.

It exists. "Established" means that because the opposing factors have been distanced through the state of being well-cultivated, it has been placed in a state of fitness for its respective foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"Accumulated on all sides" means it has reached the height of development in every respect; therefore, he said "accumulated" (*upacita*).
"Well undertaken" means it has been properly cultivated until reaching the pinnacle of the development of supernormal powers (*iddhi*). False proclamation.
"He declares" means he utters a proclamation of qualities not actually existing within himself, such as "Indeed, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed by me.
It is said "escaped" in relation to the term "liberation of mind. "Furthermore, there is no ill will" means having understood that now, for him, what is called ill will is entirely non-existent.

“Powerful insight” (*balavavipassanā*) is a designation for four types of knowledge: the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāne ñāṇaṃ*), the knowledge of contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassane ñāṇaṃ*), the knowledge of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ*), and the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅgañāṇaṃ*).

To show that the signless state (*animittatā*) of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship exists through the absence of certain signs, it is said, “For that...,” and so forth. In this context, the sign of lust, or lust itself, is [the sign].
The sign (*nimitta*) is the sign of lust. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the signs of hatred and so forth should be understood.
The sign of form, feeling, and other formations is the "sign of form" and so on. Their appearance as permanent and so forth is the "sign of permanence" and so on.
Since this sign does not exist at all in the fruit of Arahantship, it is said: "For that... is signless (*animittā*). The sign.
It is called *nimittānusārī* because it recollects, follows along with, and proceeds by means of a sign (*nimitta*) as its habit. Therefore, he said:
"The sign, which has the aforementioned divisions, has the nature of following.

"Asmimāna" (the conceit "I am") is the conceit directed toward the self that proceeds as "I am. This [conceit]—namely, "I am such-and-such"—is characterized by form (*rūpa*) among the aggregates such as feeling (*vedanā*).

Or, [thinking] "I am this self" characterized by one or another [of these marks]. "The eradication of the conceit 'I am'" (*asmimāna-samugghāta*) means that by means of this, the conceit "I am" is uprooted;
it is the path of Arahantship. Furthermore, by stating that the conceit "I am" no longer exists, he clarifies its very state of eradication by pointing out the fact of its non-arising.
The commentary on the *Nissaraṇīya Sutta* is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Bhaddakasutta, etc. 14–15.
In the fourth [verse], one who has work as his pleasure (*ārāma*)—in the sense of that which is to be resorted to—is "one whose pleasure is in work" (*kammārāma*).

One who delights in work, and not in the task of study (*ganthadhura*) or the task of insight (*vipassanādhura*), is "one who delights in work" (*kammarata*). One who is repeatedly engaged [in it] through being devoted to that is *anu*... [text fragment].
"Anuyutto pasuto": "Ālāpasallāpo" means repeated conversation by way of the forms of women, men, and so forth.
There is nothing further to be said regarding the fifth [case].
The commentary on the Bhaddakasutta and others is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Nakulapitusutta 16.
In the sixth [verse], "affliction" (*ābādha*) refers to that which afflicts by cutting off the four postures as if with a saw due to the arising of a discordant feeling;
one who possesses this is "afflicted" (*ābādhika*). He is "pained" by the suffering originating from that [affliction]. "Severely ill" means...
One whose body is completely exhausted by the reckoning of the elements (*dhātu*) is [described as such].

"One who has crossed beyond doubt" (*tiṇṇavicikicchā*) means one who has crossed over these doubts—which consist of sixteen bases and eight bases and are like a perilous wilderness—by means of this [wisdom].
"Free from" (*vigata*) means that [doubt] which occurs in the form of "Is it thus? Or is it not? regarding the process of existence (*pavatti*) and so forth, has been eliminated and cut off.
"Free from doubt" (*vigata-kathaṃkathā*) means one who has abandoned uncertainty.

Because she has abandoned those evil qualities that cause trepidation, and because she stands firm amidst passion and distraction as well as in the virtues such as moral discipline, she has attained self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the state of being fearless, and proficiency; thus she is "one who has attained self-confidence.

Because she has seen [the truth] for herself through direct experience, she does not rely on another, nor is there anything else to be relied upon by her; thus she is "independent of others" (*aparappaccayā*).

"Recovered from illness" means having emerged from the state of being ill and remaining [so]. This designation emphasizes the state (*bhāva*); however, "having been ill and recovered" is merely a demonstration of the literal meaning.
The commentary on the Nakulapitṛ-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Soppa-sutta.

17. Regarding the phrase "emerged from seclusion on the seventh day": here, *paṭisallāna* means withdrawing, retreating, and hiding away from various beings—such as co-residents, pupils, and lay followers—as well as from mental formations such as visible objects and so forth; it is seclusion (*viveka*).

By saying "for the sake of solitude" (*ekībhāvāya*) and so on, he indicates that this is a state of being alone, separated from both body and mind. Furthermore, by the term "from solitude" (*ekībhāvato*), he refers to physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
He speaks of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*). By means of the phrase "through the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma" and so forth, [he shows it] by way of mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*).

"Emergent" (*vuṭṭhita*) means endowed with the arising of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) from those two kinds of seclusion and with the meeting of fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*).
The commentary on sleeping and dreaming is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discourse to the Fisherman (Macchabandhasuttavaṇṇanā) 18.

In the eighth [discourse], "fish-killer" (*macchaghātaka*) refers to a fisherman (*kevaṭṭa*). Regarding the sheep-slaughterers and others: "sheep" (*urabbha*) means rams; one who kills sheep is a sheep-slaughterer (*orabbhika*). The same method applies to the pig-slaughterers and others.
The commentary on the Discourse to the Fisherman is concluded.
9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death (Paṭhamamaraṇassatisutta-vaṇṇanā) 19.
Regarding the phrase "in a village of that name" in the ninth discourse: it refers to a village dependent upon the one named Nātika.

There were two villages belonging to the two sons of Cūḷapiti and Mahāpiti; [the Buddha was staying] in one of those villages. Indeed, a village that serves as the dwelling place for kinsmen is called *ñātiko*; it is simply a village of kinsmen (*ñātikoya*).
In the word *nātiko*, the letter *ña* is replaced by the letter *na*, as in such examples as “*animittā na nāyare*.
It is said that this village was formerly inhabited by their ancestors in common with their own kinsmen (*ñāti*), and for that reason it was known as *Ñātiko*.
Later, it was divided into two parts and occupied by two heirs. *Giñjakā* is so called...
A dwelling made with bricks (*iṭṭhakā*) and indeed with *giñjakā* [bricks] is called a *giñjakāvasatha*.
For that residence was built by piling up and covering it with bricks alone, such that there was no need for plastering work (*sudhāparikamma*).
It is said that in that region the clay was unmixed with gravel, pebbles, sand, and so forth, being hard and fine-textured; even the pottery vessels made from it were likewise.
They were as firm as if made of stone. Therefore, those lay followers had long and broad bricks made from that clay;
having set them down one by one, they constructed the palace using only those bricks, without any other building materials such as doors, windows, shutters, or beams.
Thus it is said: "in a palace made of bricks."

"Night and day" means one night and one day. "The Blessed One’s teaching" refers to the Teacher’s instruction that brings about penetration of the Noble Path. "Much indeed would have been done by me" means: "Much indeed would have been accomplished by me for my own welfare—the purpose for which I went forth.
"In the meantime" means during that much time. "A single alms-meal" means an alms-meal sufficient to sustain oneself for one day.
"As long as the wind that has entered does not go out, or the wind that has gone out does not enter"—this refers to a single [breath].
It is stated as being "like entering and exiting"; this should be understood by way of the commonality of being breath from the nose.
The commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death.
20. "When ten [days] have passed" means when they have elapsed. "Having returned" (patigatāya) means having come back; the sense is "having arrived. Therefore he said, "having set out" (paṭipannāya).

"That would be an obstacle for me" means that not only death as previously described, but also the fact that I have obtained this extremely rare opportunity for attending to the Teacher’s instruction, as well as life itself and the attainment of heaven and liberation—[all these would be obstacles].
"An obstacle would arise for him" means it would come to pass. Therefore he said, "The threefold obstacle," and so forth. "It would fail" means it would go to ruin.
"Sword-winds" are winds that cut the joints and ligaments of the body, like a sword cutting through the limbs and members.
"Desire for action" is the wholesome desire for action that brings about deliverance. "Exertion in application" refers to...
The energy of devotion to meditation (*bhāvanānuyogavīriya*). It is "unyielding" (*appaṭivānī*) because it does not blow back or turn away;
it is the energy that does not fall into intermediate despondency. Therefore he said: "non-discontent and non-recoil.
The commentary on the second *Maraṇassati-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Sāraṇīya-vagga is finished.
3. Anuttariya-vagga: 1–2.
Commentary on the Sāmaka-sutta and others.
21–22. Regarding the first [phrase] of the third [section], "the entire lotus pond" (*kevalakappaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ*):
here, the word *kevala* has the sense of "without remainder," and the word *kappa* has the sense of "all-around. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "the entire lotus pond.
Even for a radiance capable of pervading without remainder, there might be a partial pervasion due to some cause; however, this—
The word *kappa* is taken here in the sense of "all around" (*samanta*) in order to show that it pervades everything.

"Having pervaded with his own radiance" means having pervaded with the radiance issuing from his robes, ornaments, and body; the meaning is that he made it a single radiance, a single light, like the moon.
"Well-disposed" (*samanuñño*) means one who has properly given his consent. Therefore he said, "of equal mind," meaning one whose inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) is the same.
The meaning is as follows: that which possesses harsh speech is "one of bad speech" (*dubbaca*); the action of such a person is "badness of speech" (*dovacassa*).

It is the volition (*cetanā*) occurring in that individual by way of disrespect; its state or existence is "badness of speech" (*dovacassatā*). Alternatively, "badness of speech" itself is "badness of speech-ness" (*dovacassatā*).
In terms of its essential nature, it is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), for the aggregate of formations is primarily volition.
They say this is a designation for the four aggregates that occur in the manner of grasping what is not favorable.
One who has evil persons—such as those lacking faith—as friends is an "evil-friend" (*pāpamitta*); the state of being such is "evil-friendship" (*pāpamittatā*).

This too, in terms of its meaning, should be regarded as similar to "difficult-to-admonish-ness" (*dovacassatā*), for it is by means of that volition that a person becomes an evil friend or associates with the wicked.
That volition is "bad friendship. Alternatively, the four formless aggregates (arūpa-khandha) as they arise in that mode are bad friendship. The second [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Sāmakasutta and others is finished.
3. Commentary on the Bhayasutta.

23. In the third [case], it is called *sambhava* because birth and death arise (*sambhavati*) by means of it; thus he says, "in the arising (*sambhave*), which serves as the condition, for birth and for death.
*Anupādā* means without clinging (*anupādāya*). Therefore he says, "without having clung (*anupādiyitvā*).

It is the destruction of birth and death (*jātimaraṇasaṅkhaya*) because birth and death are completely exhausted (*saṅkhīyanti*) therein; thus he says, "in that which is reckoned as the destruction (*saṅkhayasaṅkhāte*) of birth and death," namely, Nibbāna.

"In Nibbāna. They have transcended all suffering means that they have gone beyond the entire suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*), because with the cessation of the final consciousness, even a trace of the suffering of the round is no longer possible.
The commentary on the *Bhayasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta 24.
In the fourth [sutta], "skilled in attainment" (*samāpatti-kusala*) means skilled in entering into attainment (*samāpajjana*). Therefore, he said, "skilled in entering.
In this context, the word *ṭhiti* (stability) has the sense of the cause included within it; thus, he said that the meaning is "skilled in establishing" (*ṭhapana-kusala*).

“The meaning is: ‘he is able to establish concentration. In that context, ‘he is able to establish’ means he is able to maintain the jhāna for a duration of seven or eight finger-snap moments, because mastery over resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasitā) has been accomplished. ‘According to the limit’ means according to the time previously delimited.
‘He is able to emerge’ because mastery over emergence (vuṭṭhāna-vasitā) has been accomplished. It is fit...”
"Kallita" means that which has become fit; one who is skilled in that fitness, in that state of being fit, is "skilled in fitness" (*kallitakusala*).

"To make laugh, to gladden, to delight. "To make fit" means to make the mind capable by removing the factors antagonistic to concentration and by bringing the cooperative causes into equal exertion for its attainment. Of concentration...

“Skilled in his resort” means that he is skilled and adept because of his application of mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding his resort—the place where he dwells, namely the meditation subject known as his *kammaṭṭhāna*—when concentration is to be accomplished. Therefore, it says:
“Having avoided those states that are unsuitable and unhelpful for concentration,” and so forth. “To bring forth the first jhāna and so on” means the first jhāna and other such concentrations.
To lead forth and bring toward the state of distinction (*visesabhāgiyatā*).
The commentary on the Himavanta Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta.

25. “In the fifth [section], ‘the causes for recollection’ (*anussatikāraṇāni*) means that the recollections themselves are the causes because they are the basis for welfare and happiness pertaining to the present life, the future life, and so forth. ‘Departed’ (*nikkhanta*) means escaped. ‘Freed’ (*mutta*) means released. ‘Emergent’ (*vuṭṭhita*) means gone away.
All of this is said with reference specifically to suppression (*vikkhambhana*). ‘From greed’ (*gedhamhā*) means from the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘This too’ (*idampi*)...”

He speaks of the access concentration obtained by means of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*). "Making it the object" means making it the condition, that is, making it the foundation; such is the meaning.
The commentary on the *Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mahākaccāna Sutta 26.
Regarding the sixth [verse], "in confinement" (*sambādhe*) means in the household life, which is a state of oppression and confusion due to the defilements of craving and so forth.

"Spaces" (*okāsā*) are so called because they constitute the opportunity for the attainment of the bliss of the paths and fruits; thus they are called "spaces. "The attainment of space" refers to the supramundane dhamma.

“*Adhigamāya*” means for the sake of that which is to be attained. “*Visujjhanatthāyā*” means for the sake of purifying the minds that have been defiled by the stains of lust and so forth, as well as by covetousness, improper greed, and the like.

Furthermore, since this purification of the mind, when accomplished, leads to the non-clinging to sorrow and the rest, it is therefore said: “for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,” and so on.

In this context, *soka* (sorrow) is the mental distress, internal burning, and inward brooding caused by the loss of relatives and so forth; it is the state of being sorrowful due to that very same cause.
*Parideva* (lamentation) is the verbal expression through wailing, such as "Where are you, my only son? and so on.
"For the sake of overcoming" means for the purpose of abandoning; for here, "overcoming" refers to the non-arising [of these states] in the future.
"For the subsiding of suffering and grief" means for the subsiding—i.e., for the cessation—of these two: bodily suffering and mental grief.
"The method" (*ñāya*) is that by which one proceeds with certainty toward Nibbāna;
or, it is the Noble Path because by means of it one discerns or penetrates [Nibbāna]. Here, however, the Noble Path is intended together with its preliminary stage.
He said, "It is grasped for the sake of attaining the path accompanied by insight.

By "parinibbāna without conditions," he speaks with reference to nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). This refers exclusively to the unconditioned, deathless element that has not arisen by way of conditions.
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Mahākaccāna Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the First Samaya Sutta: 27.
"He increases" means he brings about an increase based on the turning away of the mind (*manaso vivaṭṭa*). Or, "one who is to be cherished in mind" (*manobhāvanīya*)...
It is cultivated and developed by the mind. And when one directs one's attention and applies the mind, the consciousness becomes free from hindrances.

In this context, the word *bhāvanīya* has the sense of "cultivation" as a passive-objective (karmasādhana). Having stated, "The meditation subject for dispelling sloth and torpor," he spoke the words beginning with "or the perception of light" in order to analyze that very point.
[He also mentions] "or the basis for the arousal of energy," and so forth.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of factors not mentioned here—such as grasping at signs regarding overeating and so forth—is to be understood.
For this has been said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor:
grasping at signs regarding overeating, changing one's posture, attention to the perception of light, dwelling in the open air, having virtuous friends..."
“Appropriate talk. Here, the word *antara* is used as a synonym for the word *antarāya*; thus he says, “without obstacle (*anantarāyena*).
The commentary on the First Samaya Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Second Samaya Sutta.

28. In the eighth [case], the dining hall constructed as a brief pavilion in the shape of a circle is intended by the term "maṇḍalamāḷa"; thus he says, "of the dining hall. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Second Samaya Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Udāyī Sutta.
29. In the ninth [case], "the visible world" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*) as something directly perceived; thus he said, "in this very personal existence.
"For the sake of dwelling in happiness" means for the sake of dwelling in a happiness that is non-material due to the absence of defilements.

"He attends to the perception of light" means that the light of the sun, moon, lamps, gems, fire, lightning, and so forth, which has been experienced both by day and by night, is attended to exactly as it was experienced.

He brings light to mind and fixes it in his heart. He brings it to mind in such a way that, as if for one who has well developed the light-kasiṇa, that light stands present to him at night according to his wish and for as long as he wishes.
By means of this, he establishes the perception of day there; just as by day, so too at night he is free from sloth and torpor. Therefore he said: "As by day, so..."
"Night": having applied the mind according to the method already stated, "he establishes the perception of day," he generates the perception of day as it were.

"Just as by him during the day... so too does he attend to that": just as the sunlight was perceived by him during the day, even so at night he attends to that light in the very same manner seen during the day. And "just as by him at night... etc.
"He attends to it" means that just as the moonlight was perceived at night, he attends to that light during the day in exactly the same manner seen at night;
he fixes it in his mind. "By the open" means by that which is uncovered because it is not veiled by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

"By the unobstructed" means by that which is not concealed. "Together with its radiance" means together with its sign-radiance (*saññāṇobhāsa*). The knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) pertains to the realm of form (*rūpagata*).
"Knowledge and vision" is intended here in the sense of seeing both the divine and the other; thus he said, "of that which is reckoned as the divine eye," and so forth.
"Beyond the exhaustion of life" means after death, subsequent to the termination of the life-faculty. "Emergent" means arisen.
"Because of being smoked" means because of being smoked upwards and upwards, and because of being shriveled. "Broken and mixed with white and black" means shattered and intermingled.
"Blue" (*nīla*) refers to that which has become a transformation of its former color, or it is "bluish-black" (*vinīla*).

The addition of the syllable *ka* in the term "bluish-black" (*vinīlaka*) is said to be for the purpose of lengthening the word, as there is no difference in meaning, just as in the case of "yellow" (*pītaka*) or "red" (*lohitaka*). It is "repulsive" (*paṭikūla*) because it is disgusting.
Or, to show that this syllable *ka* has the sense of "contemptible," it is stated that "bluish-black" (*vinīlaka*) means "contemptibly bluish-black" (*kucchitaṃ vinīlaṃ*). Thus it was said.
“A bad reputation spreads abroad. By means of crows, vultures, and other scavengers, [the body] has broken apart in various places.
“Vissandamānaṃ pubbaṃ” means flowing with pus; the meaning is that it is oozing pus here and there. “Tathābhāvaṃ” means the state of having pus flowing out.
“So bhikkhu” refers to the monk who was mentioned in the phrase, “he who might see a body discarded in a charnel ground. He applies [this reflection to himself].

“Sadisataṃ” (likeness). “Ayampi kho... and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of comparison. “Āyu” is the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*). Here, the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*) follows the destiny of consciousness alone.
“Usmā” is the heat born of karma. “Evaṃpūtikasabhāvo” means that its nature is exceedingly putrid, just like the passing away of vitality and the other factors;
this is the intended meaning. He said “evamevaṃ” (just so) to mean “it will become such,” i.e., it will possess such a state.
"There will be the distinction of being bloated, and so forth.
"Having plucked out, having plucked out" means having torn it away, having torn it away.

"Endowed with the remaining flesh and blood" means that because it has been completely devoured, it is here and there endowed with the little bit of flesh and blood that remains in various places. "Another bone of the hand" refers to it without distinction.
To show that their being scattered is evident from the scattering of the hand-bones, he says, “even the sixty-four varieties,” and so forth.
“Terovassikāni” means those that have passed beyond a year; since they have actually exceeded one year, he says, “those whose year has elapsed.
Here, putrefaction refers to the state of being crumbled due to the loss of solidity through age. To show how that occurs, [he says]:
He said, beginning with “in the open air. “Of many elements” means of the eye-element and so forth, or of the sense-sphere element and so forth.

“For the sake of mindfulness and knowledge” means for the sake of the sevenfold mindfulness described in such passages as “he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning,” and for the sake of the knowledge associated with that mindfulness.
The commentary on the Udāyīsutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Anuttariyasutta 30.
In the tenth [sutta], "inferior" means base or defiled. "Of those living in villages" refers to fools, that is, worldlings (*puthujjana*).
This is "of the ordinary person" (*pothujjanika*). Therefore he said, "belonging to ordinary persons" (*puthujjanānaṃ santaka*);
because it is to be cultivated by ordinary persons, it is said to belong to them. "Unnoble" (*anariya*) means not faultless. For the meaning of "noble" (*ariya*) is the sense of being faultless.
Therefore he said, "not supreme, not pure. Or, it is "unnoble" because it is not to be cultivated by the noble ones (*ariya*). "Not connected with the goal" (*anatthasaṃhita*)...

It is accompanied by various and extensive misfortunes pertaining to both the present life and future lives. And because such [speech] is not based on what is beneficial, he said, "not based on the beneficial.
He said, "not for the sake of disenchantment with the round of existence," because it lacks the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths;
and since dispassion and the other [stages of purification] are impossible in the absence of disenchantment with the round, he said, "not for the sake of dispassion," and so forth.
Regarding "the unsurpassed, the unsurpassable," he said, "This is the unsurpassed.

Regarding "in the elephant," he said, "one should train in the sign of the elephant" (*hatthinimitta*), using the locative case in the sense of a cause (*nimittatthe*). Because it is the domain of the elephant and because it is dependent upon the elephant, the elephant-lore (*hatthisippa*) is taken as "the elephant";
thus it is said, "he trains even in the elephant [lore]. Therefore, it means he trains in the science of elephants.
Thus is the meaning to be understood here. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

Since it was stated that "service" (*pāricariyā*) is expressed through the variation of gender and the variation of case endings, he said, "established in service. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Anuttariya Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Unsurpassed is finished.
4. The Chapter on Devas: 1–4.
Commentary on the Discourses on the Trainee, etc.
31–34. Regarding the first [verse] of the fourth [section], it is said that for those in training (sekha) who have attained a particular quality, there is no such thing as falling away from it;

thus he says, "for the sake of falling away from successive qualities. The meaning is: for the sake of the non-arising of falling away from the paths and fruits that are to be attained one after another.
The third and subsequent verses have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the Sekhasutta and others is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vijjābhāgiyasutta:
In the fifth [sutta], they partake of true knowledge (*vijjā*) by way of association, through such conditions as co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance.
They are called "pertaining to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*) because they go into union with that [true knowledge].

Alternatively, they are called "pertaining to true knowledge" because they function within the sphere of true knowledge, within the constituent part of true knowledge, since they function in a portion of it due to their sharing the nature of true knowledge.

In this context, the eight types of true knowledge consist of insight-knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). According to the former sense, the mental states associated with these are "pertaining to true knowledge."

In the final sense, among those [states], any one single true knowledge (*vijjā*) is itself "true knowledge," while the rest are "pertaining to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*). Thus, both true knowledge and the states associated with true knowledge should be understood as "pertaining to true knowledge.
However, here it is specifically perception (*saññā*) associated with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that is mentioned as "pertaining to true knowledge";
it should be seen that by way of the term "perception," the remaining associated states are also included.
"Knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanāñāṇa*): the perception that has arisen with knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence as its supporting condition;
the meaning is "accompanied by that. The same method applies to the remaining [terms].
The commentary on the *Vijjābhāgiya Sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Roots of Dispute (Vivādamūlasutta) 36.
In the sixth [verse], "one who is prone to anger" (*kodhana*) means one whose nature is to be angry.

Because, due to not having abandoned anger, he is said to be "one who has attained anger," it is therefore stated that "he is possessed of anger. One who has "enmity" (*upanāha*) is "envious" (*upanāhī*); that is, one whose nature is to harbor enmity.
Or it is full of resentment. Regarding "dispute": since a dispute, when it arises, generally arises first between two people, it is said, "a dispute between two bhikkhus.
However, showing by way of illustration how that [dispute] brings harm to many, he said, "How...
and so forth. "In the inner circle" means within the assembly.

*Makkha* (sycophancy) is so called because, even when one proceeds for the purpose of smearing with virtues, it first smears the one who performs the action—just as excrement [smears] one who strikes with excrement—and he who possesses this is *makkhī*.
*Paḷāsa* (envy) means "he slanders"; the meaning is that it snatches away another's virtues as if biting them.
He who possesses this is *paḷāsī*. For a person who is envious takes up the burden of a second [person].
He does not give; having taken an equal share, he speaks excessively. Therefore it is said: "endowed with the characteristic of grasping at the yoke, which is malice.
He envies, thus he is envious (*issukī*). He is stingy, thus it is stinginess (*macchara*); he possesses this, thus he is a miser (*maccharī*).
He is deceitful, meaning he does not speak correctly, because he proclaims himself to be one way when he is actually otherwise; he possesses guile (*māyā*), thus he is guileful.
A deceiver. "Wrong view" (micchā-diṭṭhi) means that his views are wrong, evil, and censured by the wise;

the meaning is that he is possessed of a view that is included within the courses of kamma—having as its basis such [denials] as "there is no giving," and so forth—which is comprised within the category of wrongness (micchatta), and which does not lead to liberation.
Therefore, he says "one who propounds nihilism," and so on.

One who clings to their own view, or who, by oneself, misapprehends what has been grasped—clinging beyond its true nature (sabhāva) and grasping it from another perspective—is called *saṃdiṭṭhiparāmāsī*.
One who holds firmly is *ādhānaggāhī*; that is, one who grasps firmly, meaning one who holds tenaciously with the thought, "This alone is the truth.
One who relinquishes a tenet only upon seeing a valid reason is [called *paṭinissaggī*].
“Relinquishing” means that it is not possible to relinquish [the view] through suffering, hardship, or difficulty, even by showing many reasons;

thus, it is “difficult to relinquish. This is a designation for one who, having firmly grasped the view arisen within themselves as “this alone is the truth,” does not relinquish it even when addressed by the Buddha and others who show the reasons. This is its conventional term.
For such a person, whatever they hear—whether it be Dhamma or non-Dhamma—all of it they withdraw entirely within themselves, thinking, "Thus it was spoken by our teachers;
thus it was heard by us," just as a tortoise, when its hands, feet, or other limbs are touched by anyone, withdraws all its limbs into its own shell.
For just as a tortoise [withdraws] its own limbs, such as its hands and feet, when touched by anyone...
He swallows it right there in his skull, not ejecting it outside;
even so, when told, "Your grasp is not good, let it go," he does not release it, but keeps it within his own heart as he wanders about, taking hold of it like a crocodile.
He grasps it just as crocodiles do not let go of what they have seized.
The commentary on the *Vivādamūla-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Chaḷaṅga-dāna-sutta* 37.
In the seventh [sutta], it is called a *dakkhiṇā* because by means of it one sees and prospers; it is merit consisting of relinquishment (*pariccāga*), and that which serves as its instrument is—
There is also the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*). Here, however, the object to be given is intended. For this very reason, it says:
"he establishes the offering" (*dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti*). "Arisen from here" means arisen from this field [of merit]. "The removal of lust" (*rāgavinaya*) is that by which lust is removed;
it is the practice (*paṭipadā*) that brings about the total eradication of lust. Therefore, it says: "they have entered upon the practice for the removal of lust."

Regarding the verse beginning with “Before giving, he is glad-minded”: before the actual act of giving—that is, from the time one begins gathering the requisites for a gift until the moment of the volition to release it—one should be glad-minded.
One should be filled with joy, thinking, “I shall give a gift that is the cause of prosperity and follows one into future lives.
While giving, one should clarify the mind; while bestowing the object of charity and placing it into the hands of the recipient worthy of offerings, one should [reflect on] its lack of essence...

One should gladden one’s own mind with the thought: “I am taking the essence from what is merely wealth. “Having given, he is elated” means that after relinquishing the object of charity to those worthy of offerings, he becomes elated, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness, thinking:
“I have performed what is prescribed by the wise; oh, how excellent and well done!
“This” refers to this volition prior to the act, the volition at the moment of releasing, and the subsequent volition.
This is the fulfillment of these three types of volition—accompanied by faith, embraced by joy, and resulting in karmic fruit.

"By restraint of virtue" means by bodily and verbal self-restraint. "The hands and feet" refers to the hands and feet of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). "Having rinsed their mouths" means having rinsed the mouths of those very persons; the intention is that one should personally provide them with water for the mouth.
The commentary on the *Chaḷaṅgadānasutta* is concluded.
8–11. Commentary on the Attakārīsutta, etc. (38–41).

Regarding the eighth [sutta], it is said that the energy (*vīriya*) which occurs as the initial commencement of wholesome action is called a "constituent" (*dhātu*) in the sense of maintaining its own nature because of its established intrinsic character.
Thus he says: "The 'initiating constituent' (*ārambhadhātu*) is the energy occurring by way of initiation. It has acquired practice.
"Viriya, having attained strength, disperses its opposites"; thus it is said: "The element of exertion (nikkamadhātu) is viriya whose intrinsic nature is the emergence from indolence.

"The nature of striving" (parakkamanasabhāva) means the nature of advancing further and further through a state of increasing sharpness and intensity, owing to its capacity to disperse even the most powerful opposing states.
Regarding the ninth and subsequent [factors], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the Attakārīsutta and others is finished.
12. Commentary on the Nāgitasutta:
"May I not meet with Yaśas" means: "I do not desire to meet with Yaśas."
"And let not fame come to me" means "let not fame meet with me. By this, he makes manifest his lack of desire for gain and honor.
"By the five kinds of deliverance" refers to the five kinds of deliverance beginning with deliverance by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*).
The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Nāgita Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Devatā Vagga is finished.
5. The Dhammika Vagga.
1. Nāgasutta Commentary 43.

Regarding the first [verse] of the fifth [chapter]: "To bathe" (*parisiñcituṃ*) means that one who bathes by rubbing their limbs with powder, clay, and so forth, or by scrubbing them with a wash-basin, a handful of water, and so on, is said to be "bathing.
One who does not do so, but bathes in the natural way, is likewise included.
Thus he is said to "bathe. Furthermore, no dust or dirt whatsoever adheres to the Blessed One's body because of its smooth, clear skin;
however, for the purpose of experiencing the seasons, the Blessed One merely enters the water.
Therefore it is said: "to bathe his limbs."
"Pubba-koṭṭhaka" means the eastern gatehouse. It is said that the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī was sometimes large and sometimes small.
For instance, in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, it was one *yojana* in extent; in the time of Sikhī, three *gāvutas*; in the time of Vessabhū, half a *yojana*;
in the time of Kakusandha, the measure of one *gāvuta*; and in the time of Koṇāgamana, half a *gāvuta*.
During the time of Kassapa Buddha, it was the size of twenty usabhas; in the time of our Blessed One, it became the size of eight karīsas.
That city was sometimes to the east of that monastery, sometimes to the south, sometimes to the west, and sometimes to the north.
However, in the Gandhakuṭī of Jetavana, it was the spot where the four legs of the couch were established.
It is indeed immovable. For there are four places known as the Immovable Cetiya-sites: the site of the Great Bodhi Throne;
the site at Isipatana where the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion; the site in the city of Saṅkassa where the foot of the staircase was established at the time of the Descent from the Heavens;
and the site of the bedstead’s leg. This Pubba-koṭṭhaka, however, [was established] during the time when the Blessed One Kassapa dwelt for twenty usabhas.
The eastern gate-fortress was there; it is now known simply as "Pubba-koṭṭhaka" (the Eastern Fortress).

In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, the river Aciravatī, flowing around the city, reached Pubba-koṭṭhaka and, breaking through with its waters, created a great lake that was level at the brim and gradually deepening.
Therein, there were separate bathing places: one for the king, one for the citizens, one for the Saṅgha of monks, and one for the Buddhas;
they were delightful, with sands resembling scattered silver bands.
Thus the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, approached this eastern gatehouse of such a kind.
To bathe his limbs. Then the Venerable Ānanda offered him a bathing robe. The Blessed One removed his bright red double-layered upper cloth and put on the bathing robe.
The Elder took the great outer robe into his own hands along with the double-layered cloth.
The Blessed One stepped into the water; at the very moment he entered, all the fish and turtles in the water became the color of gold.
It was as if streams of liquid gold were being poured from mechanical tubes, or as if sheets of gold were being spread out.
Then, having demonstrated the Blessed One’s bathing routine, when he had stepped out [of the water], the Elder presented him with a well-dyed double-layered cloth (*dupaṭṭa*).
The Blessed One, having put that on and fastened his girdle which resembled a streak of lightning, [donned] the great outer robe (*mahācīvara*).
Having contracted [his limbs] by means of the *anta* (the end) and making them resemble the interior of a lotus, he stood holding [them] at both ears.
Therefore it was said: “Having bathed his limbs at the eastern watch-tower, he stood there wearing a single robe.
While the Blessed One stood thus, his body resembled a full-blown lotus flower, with all its petals in full bloom.
The *pāricchattaka* tree shone as if mocking the sky with its splendor, which was blossoming with the rays of the stars;
and his thirty-two garlands of excellent marks, radiant with the halo of his fathom-wide aura,
appeared like thirty-two moons, like thirty-two suns, or like thirty-two successive universal monarchs, thirty-two celestial kings, and thirty-two great Brahmās standing in a row.

And it shone exceedingly, as if [with light]. Because the Blessed One’s body was the color of well-polished gold, with an archway as beautiful as well-purified coral, and with hair and body-hairs resembling a row of perfectly pure blue gems;
therefore, it was beautified here and there by the well-formed streaks of vermilion pigment oozing forth, and was beautifully covered above by a row of seven precious gems like clouds.

It shone like a moving peak of the Golden Mountain. And at that moment, rays of six colors issued forth from the body of the One Possessing Ten Powers and streamed and radiated all around within an area measuring eighty cubits;

it was as if strewn with rows of jewels, jeweled necklaces, and jeweled powders, like a spread-out golden cloth variegated with gems, like a surface painted with streams of flowing lac juice, and as if crowded with the falling of hundreds of meteors.

The vault of the sky was as if strewn with *kaṇikāra* and *kiṅkiṇika* flowers scattered without interval, as if colored by the dust of human skin tossed up by the force of the wind, and as if covered by a canopy of rainbows and streaks of lightning; that place and the wind pervaded it perfectly.
This is what is called the "ground of color" (*vaṇṇabhūmi*). In such places, the physical beauty or the beauty of the virtues of the Buddhas [is displayed].
Or rather, it is appropriate for a capable preacher of the Dhamma to deliver the discourse by filling it out with prose passages, verses, and by bringing forward meanings, similes, and reasons.
For in such instances, the strength of the preacher must be taken into account.
"Making them as they were before" means making them free from water; the meaning is, drying them up.
For when one who has bathed puts on his robe, the corners of the robe tend to bunch up and his requisites become soiled;
however, dust and dirt do not adhere to the bodies of the Buddhas. Just as a drop of water thrown upon a lotus leaf rolls off and passes away, so it is with them.
