Nevertheless, out of reverence for the training, the Blessed One [established] the duties of one gone forth: ... [the duties of one gone forth] ... [continue as per source].
Saying, “It is called this,” he took hold of both corners of the great robe (*mahācīvara*) and stood there covering his body from the front.
“Striking and playing” (*tāḷitañca vāditañca*) means striking and playing; it refers to the striking and playing of musical instruments (*tūriya*).

That which is both great and consists of the striking and playing of musical instruments is “great striking and playing of musical instruments. Thus he said, “With a great [sound],” and so forth. Then—

Or, "the sounding of drums, kettledrums, cymbals, and musical instruments, and the playing of lutes, flutes, gomukhis, and so forth" refers here to the meaning of "sounding, rhythmic percussion, and instrumental music.

One who has gone to the further shore of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is "one who has reached the further shore of direct knowledge" (*abhiññā-pāragū*). The same applies to the remaining terms. For that Blessed One, thoroughly knowing all phenomena...

"Gone" means one who has reached the further shore through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Among these, one who fully understands the five aggregates of clinging is "gone," meaning one who has reached the further shore through full understanding (*pariññā*).

One who abandons all defilements is "gone," meaning one who has reached the further shore through abandoning (*pahāna*). One who develops the four paths is "gone," meaning one who has reached the further shore through development (*bhāvanā*).
One who realizes cessation is "gone," meaning one who has reached the further shore through realization (*sacchikiriyā*). One who enters every meditative attainment is "gone," meaning...
One who has reached the further shore of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-pāragū*). Regarding "Subrahma-devaputta and others":

it is said that this son of the gods, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs (*accharā*), had been sporting in the Nandana grove and was now seated on a prepared seat at the foot of a *pāricchattaka* tree.
Five hundred [nymphs] sat surrounding him, while another five hundred climbed the tree and, singing with sweet voices, caused flowers to fall. These...
Taking them, the others string them together like a single-stalked garland.
Then, having climbed the tree, they die all at once by way of being cut down and are reborn in Avīci, where they experience great suffering.
Then, as time passes, a son of the gods, thinking, "The sound of these women is no longer heard, nor do they drop flowers; where indeed have they gone? reflects upon it.
Even upon seeing that he was to be reborn in hell, he was overwhelmed by grief for his beloved wife and thought, "While these women have gone according to their own karma,

how long is my life-span? Seeing that on the seventh day he too would pass away along with the remaining five hundred and be reborn in that very same place, he was possessed by an even more powerful sorrow.

Thinking, "In this world with its devas, there is no one other than the Tathāgata capable of extinguishing this grief of mine," he went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and standing to one side, said:
"This mind is constantly terrified; this consciousness is constantly agitated."
“When difficulties have not yet arisen, and when they have already occurred—
if there is one who is unafraid, tell me about him when you are asked.
Having spoken this verse, the Blessed One said to him:

“Nowhere else than through the factors of enlightenment, nowhere else than through restraint of the sense faculties, and nowhere else than through the relinquishing of everything do I see safety for living beings.
Thus he taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of that teaching, his sorrow vanished, and together with five hundred nymphs, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having taken his stand, he stood there paying homage to the Blessed One. It was with reference to him that it was said: "The divine sons Subrahma and others who had fallen into suffering.
By the word "others," the divine sons Canda, Suriya, and so forth are included. [He is called] "Arahant" for four reasons: because he is far removed (ārakatta);

because he has slain his enemies (ari) and the spokes (ara) of the wheel of existence; because he is worthy (araha) of requisites and the like; and because he is devoid of secrecy (rahābhāva) in the doing of evil.
By these four reasons.
"The ten kinds of fetters" means the ten kinds of fetters, classified according to those belonging to the lower realm (*orambhāgiya*) and those belonging to the higher realm (*uddhambhāgiya*).
"A resolve that transcends all" means a resolve that functions having surpassed all sentient beings. "The eighth person" refers to one who stands upon the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
He speaks. By the term "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna), the one established in the fruit is intended.
Regarding "gentleness" (soracca): from the statement, "In this context, what is gentleness? It is bodily non-transgression, verbal non-transgression, and both bodily and verbal non-transgression;
this is called gentleness. Furthermore, all restraint through virtue (sīla-saṃvara) is gentleness," it refers to pure virtue.

"Kindness" (*soracca*) is what was stated. "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) refers to the divine abiding of compassion (*karuṇā-brahmavihāra*). "The preliminary stage of compassion" refers to its preliminary stage, namely access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).

"By means of the two kinds of jhāna" refers to this jhāna being twofold, distinguished as *ārammaṇūpanijjhāna* (contemplation upon the object) and *lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna* (contemplation of characteristics).

"By way of the fivefold wrong livelihood" means by way of the fivefold wrong livelihood consisting of scheming (*kuhana*), hinting (*lapanā*), insinuation (*nemittikatā*), flattery (*nippesikatā*), and seeking gain with gain (*lābhena-lābha-nijigīsanatā*).

"Is not smeared" means it does not adhere, either through underlying tendency (*anusaya*) or by making [the object] its objective support (*ārammaṇa-karaṇa*), due to the absence of craving, views, and dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*). The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Nāgasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Migasālāsutta: 44.
Regarding the phrase "with equal destiny" (*samasamagatīti*), it is stated that this is an explanation based on the substitution of the letter *ya* for the letter *ka*: "by way of equality alone."
"Of the same destination. He says, "They will be," using a future tense expression in the sense of the past, explaining:
"'They will be' means they have been born. For she spoke thus with reference to the common destination of Purāṇa and Isidatta.

"Ammakā" refers to a woman; this is a conventional term. Among women, these are synonyms: *ammakā*, *mātugāma*, *jananī*, and *janikā*. Therefore he said: "Being a woman, she was possessed of the very perception of a woman."
"That which is to be penetrated by view has not been penetrated" means that, in terms of meaning and cause, it has not been penetrated by wisdom;
it remains unknown as it truly is, with its roots and thickets unremoved. "Temporary" (*sāmāyika*) here refers to rapture and gladness that liberate from defilements from time to time;
the *m* is used here because the long vowel *ā* has been substituted for the short vowel *a*.
Therefore he said: “‘He does not obtain even temporary liberation’ means that he does not obtain rapture and gladness by means of hearing the Dhamma from time to time.
Regarding the word *pamiṇanti*, since the prefix *pa-* here has the sense of “beginning,” he said: “they begin to weigh. *Paṇīta* means distinguished. Regarding *tadantaraṃ*, he said:
“The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative through a transposition of words; thus, ‘that interval,’ ‘that...’”
"...the cause. Because they arise repeatedly through greed, they are spoken of in the plural as "states of greed" (*lobhadhammā*).
He was distinguished by virtue because he was endowed with the abstention from sexual intercourse.
The commentary on the Migasālā-sutta is finished.
3–6. Commentary on the *Iṇasutta* and others. 45–48.
In the third [sutta], one who is poor (*dalidda*) is called destitute (*duggata*); the state of being such is poverty (*dāliddiya*).
One who has no property of his own (*sakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ*) is "without property" (*assaka*, *asāpateyya*). Therefore it is said: "devoid of what belongs to himself. "The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha."
When it has been said, "The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened one; the Dhamma is well-expounded;

the Saṅgha is practicing rightly," the conviction that arises through an unshakable state, having plunged into the qualities of the Triple Gem and established them [in the mind], is called "conviction through settling" (*okappanasaddhā*).

The wisdom that knows the ownership of kamma through both negative and positive concomitance—thinking, "This unwholesome kamma is not mine; however, this other kamma is mine"—is [the wisdom of kamma-ownership].
The wisdom of being the owner of one’s own kamma. For the threefold misconduct, even when committed by oneself, is not called "one's own kamma" because it destroys one's welfare;

whereas good conduct is called "one's own kamma" because it generates welfare. Regarding the phrase "in the taking of a debt," he says, "I speak of the contracting of a debt," explaining that this locative case is used in the sense of the direct object.
*Kaṭaggāho*: this means grasping something that has already been entirely accomplished. Since that is the attainment of victory, he says "the seizing of victory" (*jayaggāho*). *Hirimano etassa*:

because one possesses shame (*hiri*) toward this, he says "one possessed of a mind associated with shame. The meaning is: one whose mind is associated with shame, which is characterized by a sense of disgust for evil.
One who is ashamed, who trembles, fears, or is afraid because of moral conduct is *ottappī*; [thus he is defined] by means of *ottappa*.
Endowed with. "Spiritual happiness" (*nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ*) refers to the bliss of the third jhāna, because it has cast far away the bait of sensual desire.
"Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to the equanimity of the fourth jhāna; it does not mean any feeling of equanimity whatsoever, which is why he says "the equanimity of the fourth jhāna.
"Aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*) means that his physical and mental energy is exerted and perfected. One who [abandons] the company of crowds...
Having dispelled [distractions] while in the four postures, he becomes solitary by means of the eight bases for exertion;
thus his bodily energy is said to be "aroused. Having dispelled mental congestion, he becomes solitary by means of the eight attainments.
He does not allow a defilement arisen while walking to reach the state of standing, nor a defilement arisen while standing to reach the state of sitting.
Sitting does not allow the defilement that has arisen to reach the lying-down position;

it suppresses the defilement right where it has arisen. This is what is called having initiated mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*). Because it rises alone by virtue of its excellence and its distance from opposing factors, it is called "one-pointed" (*ekodi*);
this refers to one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*). Through association with that, one whose mind is one-pointed is here called "one-pointed" (*ekodi*). [It protects] oneself from opposing factors...

He is *nipaka* because he strikes down, or causes that [defilement] to settle and wither. He is *sato* because he remembers a particular object—such as a division of the body—with preeminent mindfulness.
Therefore, it says, "one whose mind is one-pointed," and so forth.
"My liberation is unshakable" means that my liberation, which is the fruit of Arhatship, is unshakable both by virtue of its own unshakeability and by virtue of having an unshakeable object.
For it is "unshakable" (akuppa) both because it is not shaken by lust and the other defilements, and because its object is unshakable Nibbāna;
thus it is "unshakable" by virtue of having an unshakable object. For this very reason, he said: "Because of having an unshakable object," and so forth.
"Of the fetters of existence" refers to those consisting of sensual lust, ill will, conceit, views, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust for existence, envy, avarice, and ignorance.
Of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*). For these bind beings to states of existence, fasten them down, and yoke them from one existence to another;
therefore they are called "fetters of existence. One whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is supremely free from debt because of the absence of the debt of the defilements (*kilesa*).
For other beings are called "indebted" as long as their defilements have not been abandoned, due to their state of living like slaves.
The fourth and subsequent [sections] have their meaning obvious.
The commentary on the *Iṇasutta* and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the *Khema-sutta*.
49. "One who has lived the holy life" (*vutthabrahmacariyavāso*) means one whose dwelling in the holy life is completed.
Regarding the term "one who has done what was to be done" (*katākaraṇīyo*): here, "what is to be done" refers to full understanding, abandoning, developing, and realizing.

Since these must be performed by means of the four paths, each with respect to the four truths, they should be understood as being sixteenfold. Therefore, it is said: "to be done by means of the four paths."

The three—namely, the aggregates (*khandha*), the defilements (*kilesa*), and the formations (*abhisankhāra*)—are called "burdens" (*bhāra*) because they are like a burden in the sense of causing one to sink down.

One by whom these have been laid down, set aside, deposited, or cast off is "one who has laid down the burden" (*ohitabhāra*). Therefore he said: "Having set down the burden of the aggregates... standing.

"One who has attained his own goal" (*anuppattasadattha*): he has attained his own goal (*sadattha*). And "own goal" (*sadattha*) expresses "one's own purpose" (*sakattha*), with the letter *ka* changed to *da*.

Having done so. For here, arahantship is called "one's own welfare" (*sakattha*) because it depends upon one’s own wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), because it is connected to oneself in the sense of being included within one’s own continuum, because it does not abandon oneself, and because it is the highest state for oneself.
Therefore he said: "One’s own welfare is called arahantship. "Liberated through perfect knowledge" (*sammadaññā vimutto*) means liberated by means of perfect knowing.
The meaning is: having rightly understood suffering and the other truths exactly as they are to be known through unbroken path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), one is liberated.
Therefore he said, "rightly by means of the cause," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding "liberated," there are two kinds of liberation:

the path that is the way out of all mental defilements, and the resolute confidence (*adhimutti*) in *nibbāna*. Resolute confidence in *nibbāna* consists in being inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and tending toward it.
The Arahant is liberated through liberation of mind because his mind is freed from all defilements;
he is liberated in Nibbāna because he is intent upon Nibbāna. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Khema Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Indriyasaṃvara Sutta 50.
In the eighth [sutta], "upanisā" means a cause (*kāraṇa*) because the fruit depends upon it.

"Knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) refers to the vision characterized by knowing things as they truly are. By this, he shows nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*). Nascent insight...

For this is the condition for powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*). "Young insight" (*taruṇa-vipassanā*) is a designation for four types of knowledge: the knowledge of discerning mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa-pariggaha-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of discerning conditions (*paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa*), the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge established after defining what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmaggavavatthāna-ñāṇa*).

"Disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) means that by means of this, one becomes disenchanted. "Powerful insight" refers to the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*) and the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*).
“Knowledge” is a designation for four types of knowledge: the knowledge of desire for deliverance, the knowledge of equanimity towards formations, and so forth.

However, the contemplation of reflection belongs specifically to the side of the desire for deliverance. For it is said: “As long as one has not reached the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, insight is still tender”;
thus, from the knowledge of arising and passing away freed from imperfections onwards, insight is powerful. The noble one becomes dispassionate toward formations.

By this, dispassion is meant—the Noble Path. The "fruit of arahantship" is stated here by way of the highest description. Because restraint of the sense faculties is the cause for guarding virtue, it is said:
"Restraint of the sense faculties is declared to be the preservation of virtue.
The commentary on the *Indriyasaṃvara Sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta 51.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], in the scriptural passages beginning with “Elder monks dwell there, learned, masters of the tradition,” the meaning should be understood according to this same method:

they are called *theras* (elders) because they have attained stability in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). They are "learned" (*bahussuta*) because they have heard much of the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth.

These are the "learned" (bahussuta). They are "those who have mastered the tradition" (āgatāgama) because the tradition (āgama)—consisting of the scriptures (pariyatti)—has come to them through the correct reception [of the teachings] from the presence of their teachers by means of oral recitation and memorization.

They are "bearers of the Dhamma" (dhammadhara) through the retention of the Dhamma known as the Suttas and so forth. They are "bearers of the Vinaya" (vinayadhara) through the retention of the Vinaya. [They are also bearers] of the matrices (mātikā) of those very same Dhamma and Vinaya.
By means of retention, they are bearers of the *mātikā*. There, through inquiry into the Dhamma in various instances, they inquire;

they question, investigate, and examine that by means of inquiry into the meaning. "Venerable sir, what is this? What is the meaning of this?"—this is the demonstration of the manner of inquiring and questioning.
They reveal the meaning of the text already disclosed by showing it in relation to other sections of the canon (*āgama*). And they clarify that which has not been made explicit...
They clarify [the meaning] by analyzing the logical reasoning.

They dispel doubt by providing a definitive determination, according to reality, regarding those passages in the Canon that constitute the focal points for knots—the causes for the arising of uncertainty concerning those things that give rise to doubt.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* 52.
In the tenth [verse], those whose intention is for wealth are "those with the intention for wealth" (*bhogādhippāyā*).

Those whose mind ranges over these [objects] for the sake of wisdom are "those who range over wisdom" (*paññūpavicārā*). Those whose mental adherence (*abhinivesa*) is toward the earth for the sake of a field are "those adhering to the earth" (*pathavībhinivesā*).

Those for whom spells (*manta*) are the foundation and support are "spell-foundations" (*mantādhiṭṭhāna*). In this same manner, the remaining phrases should also be understood. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta*.

53. Regarding the phrase "in the wildernesses" (*jaṅgalānam*): here, that region of land which is not marshy (*anūpa*), being devoid of water and hard and parched, is called a "wilderness" (*jaṅgala*).
Because such [land] abounds there, the entire region of land here is called a wilderness.
They are called "wilderness-born" (*jaṅgalā*) because they are born in that wilderness; [the text says] "of those wilderness-born. For in this way, even those who dwell in rivers [are included].

The inclusion of elephants is made because, just as those to be gathered are included, so too are the gatherers; for here, by the mention of "wild animals" (jaṅgala), they are intended to be included.
By the phrase "those who move upon the surface of the earth," those who move in water are excluded, because their feet are not visible.
Although the term "of living beings" (pāṇānam) is a general expression, it is established as a specific qualification through the proximity of the other word, "tracks" (padajātāni).

He said, "of words with their suffixes (*sapādakapāṇānam*)," meaning they exist. Just as the word *gata* in expressions such as *muttagata*, here too the word *jāta* does not have a different meaning;
thus he said, "word-classes (*padajātāni*) means words (*padāni*). *Samodhānaṃ* means a complete inclusion or being contained within.

Therefore he said, "they go to the placing together (*odhānaṃ*), that is, to the depositing (*upanikkhepaṃ*). *Kūṭaṅgamā* means they approach the peak (*kūṭaṃ*) by way of the opposite end (*pārimantena*).
“Sunk in the peak” (kūṭaninnā) means they are inclined toward the peak by way of entering through the opening in the peak.

“Meeting at the peak” (kūṭasamosaraṇā) means they remain having converged at the peak, both by not entering the opening and by remaining in close contact with it. When the stalk falls, all [the leaves] fall to the ground; thus he said, “they follow the stalk.”
The commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Dhammika-sutta*: 54.
Regarding the phrase "in his native land" (*jātibhūmiyaṃ*): here, "birth" (*jāti*) means the act of being born; the "land of birth" (*jātibhūmi*) is the place where one is born.
Furthermore, this is not called the "birthplace" of the Great King of Kosala and others, nor of the Brahmin Caṅki and others,
nor of Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and others, nor of the eighty great disciples, nor of other beings. However, on the day he was born,
the ten-thousandfold world system became fragrant with heaps of flags, garlands, scattered flowers, perfumes, and powders, like a tree in full bloom.
The Nandana Grove shone brilliantly, yet he remained unshaken, like a drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf;
and many miracles occurred, such as the sight of forms by those born blind and others.

The birthplace of that omniscient Bodhisatta, specifically the support of Kapilavatthu where his father resided, is called the "birthplace" (jātibhūmi). Those belonging to that birthplace are the "jātibhūmakā."

“Lay followers” (*upāsaka*) refers to lay followers residing in their native land. “Root-creepers” (*mūlasantānaka*) are those whose roots remain established after being drawn out, completely pulled out, and spread out.
Since these are in fact nothing other than roots themselves, he said: “‘Of root-creepers’ means ‘of roots.
[This is] because on the day they were born, the weapons shone, and because they were capable of protecting King Aparimita and his sevenfold army from harm.
And because he had received the name Jotipāla, it is said, "by name Jotipāla. He was called Govinda because he was consecrated with the *govindiya* consecration;
the meaning is that he was consecrated with the consecration of being established in the position of a *govinda*. Indeed, that was a rank inherited through the lineage of that brahmin family.
Therefore it is said, "Mahāgovinda by virtue of his office. He finds (*vindati*) cattle and wisdom.
He is called *Govinda* because he "understands" (*paṭilabhati*). He is the "Great Govinda" (*Mahāgovinda*) because he is a great *Govinda*.
For "go" is a designation for wisdom (*paññā*), based on the sense that "it goes toward meaning and awakens. And our Bodhisatta was indeed this very Mahāgovinda.
It is said that he was born as the son of the brahmin Govinda, who was the domestic priest (*purohita*) of King Disampati. Regarding his father...
And after the death of that king, his son Reṇu, along with his seven companions— Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—
these seven kings established themselves in their respective kingdoms so that they did not quarrel with one another.
Having thus installed them and instructed them in their welfare and duty, he became the king of all kings upon the surface of Jambudīpa.
He was like Brahmā to the brahmins and like a god to the householders; he was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected, and he held the position of supreme honor.
Therefore it is said: "He was the domestic priest of the seven kings beginning with Reṇu. These very seven were the Bhāradvāja great kings. For this has been stated:
“Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū together with Bharata,
Reṇu and the two Dhataraṭṭhas— these were the seven Bhāradvājas at that time.
A *purohita* is one who stands before [the king], because he arranges and prepares matters concerning the king’s welfare in this present life and the future life.

“With the foul odor of anger” means with the putrid smell designated as anger. “He has compassion” means he possesses compassion; thus it is said that the jhāna of compassion, including its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), is being described, for which reason he says:
“Established in compassion and in the preliminary stage of compassion. He says “*yetete*” because the letter *y* has been inserted by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
Starting from the state of an Arahant, the seventh is the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*). “With reference to the once-returner” means...
In dependence upon the state of a once-returner. For the five faculties of a once-returner are indeed called "weak" in dependence upon the state of a once-returner.
The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Dhammika Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Dhammika Chapter is finished.
The First Fifty is finished.
2. The Second Fifty.
6. Mahāvagga 1.
Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā 55.
Regarding the first [verse] of the sixth [chapter], "The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared": what was that seat prepared for him at the very beginning?

Was it prepared beforehand, or was it prepared upon seeing the Blessed One? To show that this was the practice of the monks striving in meditation during the time of the Blessed One—that they would sit down only after preparing a Buddha-seat in their own dwelling place—he said, "the monks striving in meditation," and so forth.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, wherever even a single monk resided, [he would prepare such a seat].

In every place, a Buddha-seat is already prepared. Why? Because the Blessed One keeps in mind those who have received a meditation subject from him and are dwelling in a comfortable location, wondering:
"So-and-so has gone away after receiving a meditation subject from me; was he able to produce some distinction, or not? Then he sees that person with his meditation subject...
While he was reflecting on unwholesome thoughts after having abandoned them, [the Buddha], thinking,
"How indeed can unwholesome thoughts overcome this clansman who dwells here having received a meditation subject in the presence of a teacher such as myself,
and cause him to wander in the beginningless round of suffering?"— in order to assist him, manifested himself right there.
Having exhorted that son of good family, he sprang into the air and returned once more to his own dwelling place.
Then, being thus exhorted, those bhikkhus thought: “The Teacher, knowing our thoughts, has come and shown himself standing right here near us.
At this moment, we must seek out a seat, saying: ‘Venerable sir, please sit here, please sit here.’”
“...is called a burden. They remain having prepared a seat; whoever has a bench prepares that.
Whoever does not have one prepares a bed, or a plank, or a stone, or a heap of sand.
Failing to find these, they even gather together old leaves, spread their rag-robes (paṃsukūla) upon them, and stay there.
The seven notes (*sara*) are: *cha* (the sixth), *usabha*, *gandhāra*, *majjhima*, *pañcama*, *dhevatā*, and *nisāda*;
these are the seven notes. The three scales (*gāma*) are: the *cha*-scale, the *majjhima*-scale, and the common (*sādhāraṇa*) scale;
"scales" means groups or collections. In the human world, lute players produce three tunings for each individual note.
There are twenty-one finger-widths (*mucchanā*) [in a lute]. However, they say that in the world of the gods there are fifty finger-widths.
For there, according to each individual string, there are seven finger-widths, and for the intermediate string, one;
thus there are fifty finger-widths in total. For this very reason, it is said in the commentary on the *Sakkapañha Sutta*: "having tuned fifty finger-widths."
This was said by one who wished to demonstrate the lute-playing of Pañcasikha.
"Forty-nine places" refers to seven distinct places for each individual tone, from which the determination of the tone's circularity (*maṇḍalatā*) occurs.
Furthermore, twenty-two varieties of musical intervals (*sutibheda*) are intended, consisting of the specific forty-nine places: three, two, four, four, three, two, and four.
"Exerted too intensely" means exerted excessively for the purpose of pacifying sloth, torpor, and nervous agitation. "Universal" (*sabbatthika*) means applicable in all instances;

or, it is "universal" because it must be pursued by one who is free from both the side of lethargy and the side of agitation. "Tranquillity itself is the sign of tranquillity. The same applies to the remaining [terms].
Regarding the phrase "through the destruction of lust, he is one free from lust": here, because an outsider...

"One who is free from lust for sensual pleasures" does not mean one who is free from lust through its destruction; rather, it means one who is not entirely devoid of lust because lust has merely been suppressed.
An Arahant, however, is free from lust precisely through its destruction; therefore it is said, "because he is free from lust through its destruction.

This same principle applies to hatred and delusion as well. Regarding the phrase "desiring gain, honor, and fame": here, "gain" (lābha) is so called because it is obtained or acquired; it refers to the four requisites.
It is a designation. "Sakkāra" (hospitality) means that which should be performed respectfully.
For it is the requisites themselves—whether excellent or most excellent, beautiful or most beautiful—which, having been prepared and made ready, are called "sakkāra";
as well as the act of showing respect toward oneself by others, or worship with flowers and so forth. "Siloka" means the speaking of praise. Desiring that gain, hospitality, and renown...
The meaning is "while causing [them] to proceed. For this very reason, he said: "longing for the acquisition of the four requisites... and so forth.
*Thūṇaṃ* refers to a post known as a *thūṇa*, which is driven into the ground for the purpose of binding cattle. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Soṇa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Phaggunasutta 56.
In the second [verse], "he honored from all sides" (*samantato adhosi*) means he showed respect by way of every limb through the manner of trembling and moving.
It is said that this is the proper duty (*vatta*): even one who is very ill, upon seeing an elder, should show respect by rising from his seat.
However, he should be told, "Do not move, do not move. Since that movement is a demonstration of the manner of rising, he says, "He demonstrates the manner of rising.
Regarding the phrase "These seats are ready," he speaks first with reference to the seat already prepared.
For during the time of the Buddha, even at the dwelling place of a single bhikkhu, [the thought would arise]: "If the Teacher should come..."
"Let a seat be prepared"—this means that at the very least, even a mere wooden plank or a layer of leaves has been prepared.
"Is it bearable? Is it sustainable?"—he asks this to inquire whether the pain can be endured, or whether one is able to maintain one's posture.
"Painful sensations in the head"—these are powerful sensations in the head produced by winds that are unable to escape from anywhere.
The commentary on the Phaggunasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Chaḷabhijātisutta: 57.

Regarding the third [sutta], concerning the phrase "six classes" (*abhijātiyo*): here, the prefix *abhi-* is merely a grammatical particle and does not indicate a specific meaning; thus he says, "six births. The same principle applies to the term *abhijāyati* ("is born into").
They kill sheep, thus they are *orabbhikā* (sheep-butchers). In this same way, *sūkarikā* (pig-butchers) and others are to be understood.

They cry out (*rodenti*) because of their cruel occupations, shedding tears for beings who are bound [to them]; thus they are *ruddā*. By changing the letter *r* to *l*, they become *luddā* (hunters).
By this term, all other hunters and fowlers are also included; he calls them "of dark birth" (*kaṇhābhijātī*) because of their addiction to evil deeds.

"Bhikkhus" refers to the bhikkhus in the Buddha’s dispensation. It is said that, with the intention that they enjoy things through their own desire and craving, he calls them "thorn-livers" (kaṇṭakavuttikā), saying that they eat by putting thorns into the four requisites. Why is this?
Because his misconception is that they consume refined requisites; yet even the requisites obtained through right means [are not enjoyed with craving].
He says that while eating, they are adopting a course contrary to the Ājīvaka doctrine by as if throwing thorns into their requisites before consuming them.
Alternatively, there were certain renunciants named Kaṇṭakavuttikā who were devoted to the practice of self-mortification to an extreme degree;
for they lived as if walking upon thorns, and thus they were called "Kaṇṭakavuttikā. This very...
And with reference to the distinction of meaning, he said: "These ascetics are 'thorn-livers' (kaṇṭakavuttika).

Those of the red caste (lohitābhijāti) are called the Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single garment (ekasāṭaka). It is said that because of their observance of vows—such as refusing to eat while standing or refusing to bathe—they are whiter than the previous two groups.

"Disciples of the naked ones" (acelakasāvaka) refers to the disciples of the Ājīvakas. It is said that because of the extreme purity of their minds through the Ājīvaka doctrine, they are whiter even than the Nigaṇṭhas. And by doing so, he makes his own providers of requisites even more venerable than the Nigaṇṭhas.
The male and female Ājīvakas are called "the white-born" (*sukkābhijātī*). They are said to be whiter than the previous four classes.

For Nanda and the others had established themselves by bringing such a mode of life as that of the Ājīvakas to its highest excellence; therefore, they are called "the supremely white-born" because they are whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas and the Ājīvaka disciples.
"They would hang it up" means they would bind a portion of flesh—either with sinew or by some other means—to a man's hand or hair by way of hanging it down;
by this, he demonstrates what is called the "dharma of the caravan leader.
It is said that when a caravan leader had entered a great wilderness, he took the meat of oxen that had died along the road and [gave it] to all the members of the caravan.
“Having eaten this, so much must be paid as the price,” he would hang a portion [of the meat] there. There were those who ate ox-flesh and those who did not;
among those who ate it, there were both those capable of paying the price and those incapable.
The caravan leader, for the sake of ensuring that all the merchants held the price for which the ox had been purchased, forcibly took a portion [of the meat].
Having given the root, he takes it back;
this is the nature of the teacher. "Being of a dark birth" means being born into a low family.

Regarding "a dark nature," he says, "being of a dark essence, he is born," using the accusative case in its absolute sense; that phrase contains the meaning of the underlying cause, for it means "he produces."
This is the meaning. Therefore, "he generates dark states" means he produces the black states of the tenfold immorality.
Regarding "he generates bright states," the meaning should be understood here by this same method.
For he thinks, "In the past, because I did not perform meritorious deeds, I was reborn in a low family; now I shall perform merit," and thus he performs the bright state known as merit.
“Neither black nor white is Nibbāna”: if it were black, it would yield a black result, just like the tenfold unwholesome states of misconduct;
if it were white, it would yield a white result, just like wholesome kamma such as giving and virtue.
Because it yields neither of these two, it is said to be “neither black nor white. And in this context, what is called Nibbāna is Arahatship.

It is intended [here] by the expression "he is born to it" (abhijāyati). For that is called Nibbāna because it is born at the end of the extinction of defilements (kilesa), just as one speaks of "the destruction of lust" (rāgakkhaya), "the destruction of hatred" (dosakkhaya), and "the destruction of delusion" (mohakkhaya) because they are born at the end of the destruction of lust and so forth.

Alternatively, it is Nibbāna because it causes the extinguishing (nibbāpana) of defilements by way of their subsiding. He is born to that; he produces it. For here too, the cause is included within the term itself.
The meaning of the word "is born" (*jāyati*) is [attainment]. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, having taken the sense of "reaches" (*pāpuṇāti*) for this term "is born," it is stated:
"he reaches Nibbāna. "Being of the bright birth-class" means having been born into a bright, high-born family.
The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Chaḷabhijātisutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Āsavasutta*. 58.
In the fourth [sutta], “by restraint” (*saṃvarena*) means by means of restraint as the cause. “Here” (*idha*): this word “here” (*idha-saddo*) in its entirety...

It is said, "‘Here’ means in this teaching," which illustrates that for a person restrained by the restraint of the sense faculties, the teaching serves as a support and precludes the state of being otherwise.
"Having reflected" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means having reflected (*paṭisaṅkhāya*). The word *saṅkhā* is seen in the senses of knowledge, a portion, designation, enumeration, and so forth;

for instance, in such passages as "having reflected, he indulges in one [thing]," it is seen in the sense of knowledge. In such passages as "the conceptual proliferations of perception and volitional formations (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*) are active,"...
In such passages as “the reckoning (saṅkhā) and designation (samaññā) of this or that phenomenon,” it refers to a concept (paññatti).
In such passages as “it is not easy to reckon (saṅkhātuṃ),” it refers to counting (gaṇanā). But here it should be understood as knowledge (ñāṇa). For this very reason he said:

“The meaning is ‘having recognized and having reflected. The construction is: “reflection on danger (ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā)” means reflection upon danger (ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇā). “Sampalimaṭṭhaṃ” means rubbed or polished.
“By way of the minor details (*anubyañjana*)” means by way of the various parts such as the hands, feet, looking forward, looking around, and so forth.
For that is called a “minor detail” because it is a secondary manifestation (*anubyañjana*) of the defilements for one who attends to it improperly (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).

“Grasping at signs (*nimitta-ggāha*)” means the grasping of the sign of a woman or a man, or of a sign such as the sign of beauty, which serves as a basis for the defilements. “By way of the discourse on the burning (*ādittapariyāya*)” means in the discourse on the burning.
It should be understood according to the method already stated.
Just as a woman’s faculty is called the "female-faculty" (*itthindriya*), this is not so;
rather, because the eye itself is the faculty, it is the "eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriya*). Therefore he said: "the eye itself is the faculty. Just as a tortoise that dwells permanently in a pit...
It is called "the tortoise in its hole" because its mode of existence is bound to that place; thus, restraint is the restraint of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya-saṃvara*).
Therefore he said: "Restraint in the eye-faculty is the restraint of the eye-faculty.
But is there not actually neither restraint nor non-restraint in the eye-faculty? For mindfulness or negligence does not arise depending upon the sensitive matter of the eye (*cakkhu-pasāda*).

Furthermore, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye, then, after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) arises and ceases, performing the function of adverting. Thereafter, eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing;
thereafter, the resultant mind-element performs the function of receiving; thereafter, the resultant mind-consciousness-element [performs the function of investigating].

The investigating function [of the bhavaṅga] ceases after having arisen; then, the functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by roots, performing the function of determining, arises and ceases, immediately followed by the impulsion (javana).

Even therein, neither restraint nor non-restraint exists at the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), nor at the moments of any of the preceding processes such as adverting and so forth. However, at the moment of impulsion—
If immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness arises, there is non-restraint.

However, when virtue and the other [faculties] have arisen, there is restraint; therefore, he asks why it is said that "there is restraint in the eye-faculty," and replies: "For even though this [restraint] arises in the javana-consciousness... it is called 'eye-faculty restraint.'"

This is what is meant: just as when the four gates of a city are left unguarded, even though the inner houses, doors, courtyards, and chambers are well-secured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded;
for once thieves have entered through the city gate, they may do as they please—exactly so it is when lack of virtue and other such faults arise in one's mental speed (javana).
When there is non-restraint, the doors are unguarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), and the other process-consciousnesses.

However, just as when the city gates are closed, even though the houses and so forth within are unguarded, nevertheless all the goods inside the city remain well-protected and well-guarded; for when the city gates are shut, there is no entry for thieves.

In the same way, when the impulsions (javana) regarding virtue and so forth have arisen, the sense-door is well-guarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), and the other process-consciousnesses.
Therefore, even though it arises only at the moment of the impulsion, it is called "restraint of the eye-faculty.

A person endowed with such restraint is said to be "restrained"; thus he says, "endowed" (upeto). This very meaning here is stated to be more excellent because it is seen later in the text. Hence he says, "For thus," and so forth.
By the phrase "they go" (*yanti ādeso*), he shows that a change of number has been made along with a change of gender;
or else, this is a particle used in the sense of a plural. "Causing vexation" means causing mental vexation, or producing bodily and mental suffering.

The "fever of the result" (*vipāka-pariḷāha*) refers precisely to the results that follow from the burning [of defilements], which have the aforementioned defilements as their cause. Now, as for how it is here...

The taints and other afflictions that cause distress—the fevers of the defilements—arise; in order to demonstrate this, it was said, "In the eye-door," and so forth. That is indeed easy to understand.

Furthermore, in this context, the following distinction should be understood: the means of restraint, that which is to be restrained, the restraint itself, from where that restraint arises, where the restraint occurs, how the restraint is practiced, and what the fruit of the restraint is.
How so? For "wise reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*) is the means of restraint. The eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) is that which is to be restrained.

Mindfulness (*sati*), included by the mention of "restraint," is itself the restraint. "Of one who is unrestrained" (*asaṃvutassa*) indicates the limit of restraint; for restraint is the opposite of non-restraint. Here, the domain of restraint is established by the mention of that which is to be restrained.
Indeed, the eye-faculty is the restraint; it restrains [the mind] regarding the object of form (*rūpārammaṇa*). Thus, this meaning is established even without being explicitly stated.
The fruit is the absence of the fever of defilements caused by the taints (āsava). This should be applied accordingly to the ear-door and the other doors.
"In all cases" means in every door, namely, both the mind-door and the five sense-doors.

In such passages as "reflecting wisely on the robe," etc., "wisely" (yoniso) refers precisely to the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa) performed according to [the purpose], such as "for the warding off of cold," and so forth.
Reflecting: "Such" means of this kind, a desirable object. "Relishing through the longing for existence" means for one who relishes an object cultivated by way of the longing for existence.
"Robe" refers to any robe whatsoever, such as an undergarment and so forth. "Uses" means he makes use of it by way of wearing it as an undergarment and so forth.
"Only to the extent that" is a restriction regarding the measure of the purpose. [The purpose] is precisely the warding off of cold and so forth.
For this indeed is the purpose for which a yogi makes use of robes:

"Against cold" means against the cold that has arisen either from a disturbance of the cold element or from a change in the weather. "For the warding off" means for the sake of warding it off, for the sake of dispelling the discomfort caused by it.
"Against heat" means against the heat produced by the warmth of fire. "Gnats and so forth" are well known. Again, "only as far as" [means]...

It is the restriction of the quantity [of robes] to a fixed purpose. For the purpose of using a robe is fixed as the covering of the private parts (*hirikopīna*) for one who uses it; the other [purposes] occur only occasionally.

"Private parts" (*hirikopīna*) refers to the private area. For that limb by which, when uncovered, modesty (*hirī*) is disturbed and destroyed—that being the cause of the disturbance of modesty—is called "the shameful part" (*hirikopīna*); it is for the sake of covering that part that one uses the robe.

“Almsfood” (piṇḍapāta) refers to whatever kind of nutriment there may be. It is called “almsfood” because it falls into the bowl of a bhikkhu through wandering for alms (piṇḍolya), or because it is the falling together (pāta), the gathering, of the portions of alms-food obtained here and there.
“Neither for sport” means not for the sake of play. “Neither for intoxication” means not for the purpose of the pride of strength, the pride of youth, or the pride of manhood.
“Neither for adornment” means not for the sake of [beautifying] the limbs and members of the body.

For the purpose of nourishing; "not for the sake of adornment" means not for the sake of their own beauty, but for the purpose of achieving a radiant complexion—this is the meaning. These [four] should be understood as being, respectively, for the purpose of abandoning delusion, fault, shape, and color-attachment, which are the underlying supports.
Alternatively, the first pair is for the purpose of preventing the arising of defilements in oneself, while the other is for the sake of others as well. All four are [for this purpose].
It should be understood that these are stated for the purpose of abandoning devotion to the pleasure of sense-desires. "Of the body" means of the material body (*rūpakāya*).
"For its stability and maintenance" means for the sake of continuous persistence and for the sake of preventing the interruption of its occurrence;
it is for the sake of making the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) persist for a long time. "For the cessation of affliction" means for the sake of the subsiding of the suffering of hunger.

"For the support of the holy life" (*brahmacariyānuggahāya*) means for the purpose of supporting the holy life of the path of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, by this means.
"I shall terminate old feeling" (*purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi*) means I shall terminate old feeling that arises due to the condition of not having eaten.
"And I shall not produce new feeling" (*navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi*) means [new feeling] that arises due to the condition of having eaten.
"I shall not produce it. For he consumes food solely for the purpose of its non-arising.

Herein, "feeling arising due to the condition of not eating" refers to the feeling characterized by the aforementioned hunger; for that arises by way of increasing more and more in one who does not eat.
"Feeling not arising due to the condition of eating" likewise has hunger as its characteristic.
Pains such as the burning of limbs and aches have ceased their occurrence. For that [pain], having arisen due to the condition of eating, will not arise again as it has not yet arisen.
Their distinction from cruelty lies in the fact that they are not caused by cruelty.
"There will be my sustenance" means there will be the maintenance of my four postures. "For the sake of sustenance" (yāpanāya) means...
By this, the maintenance of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is stated; here, "maintenance" refers to the non-interruption of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
This is the distinction between them. "Faultlessness and comfortable living": faultlessness arises from avoiding improper seeking, accepting, and using [of requisites];

comfortable living arises from moderate use. This is because, by reason of unsuitable or excessive food, there is an absence of faults such as discontent, lethargy, yawning, and the reproach of the wise.
Or it is blamelessness (*anavajjatā*). Through the condition of eating what is suitable and in moderation, there arises bodily strength, resulting in a comfortable dwelling (*phāsuvihāra*).
Or, by avoiding food that fills the belly to satiety, there is no occurrence of the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of drowsiness, and so forth;

thus, there is blamelessness. By eating a meal less than four or five mouthfuls, one brings about fitness for the four postures (*iriyāpatha*), resulting in a comfortable dwelling. For this has been said:
“Having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;
this is sufficient for a well-disposed dwelling for a bhikkhu who is resolute.
To this extent, the discernment of the purpose and the middle way of practice have been illustrated by the words, “And there will be sustenance for me.”
The explanation of the grasping of the purpose: for sustenance indeed employs him in the application of nutriment.
A comfortable dwelling, which is the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness, is the middle way because it avoids the two extremes.
"Recluse’s lodging" (senāsana) means both a place for lying down (seyyā) and a seat (āsana); that is, a monastery or similar place where one lies down, reclines, sits, or remains seated.

"Requisites for the robe and lodging": "For the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate and delighting in seclusion. Here, "climate" itself, in the sense of being a hardship (*parissaya*), causes bodily affliction and mental distraction;

the meaning is: for the purpose of warding that off, for the purpose of not allowing what has not yet arisen to arise, and for the purpose of pacifying what has already arisen. Alternatively, it refers to the aforementioned climate and the manifest perils such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
And there is the danger concealed by lust, hatred, and so forth, as well as the danger of the climate; for the purpose of dispelling these, and for the sake of the comfort of solitude.

Just as the concealment of private parts with a robe is a necessary requirement when using a robe, so too is this [the use of medicine] a fixed necessity; therefore, it is stated again, "only so far as.
Regarding "requisites of medicine as a support for the sick": it is a support for the sick because it acts as an antidote to disease; from that...
Thus, because it is a substance permitted by a physician, it is "medicine" (*bhesajja*); and because it serves as an accessory for sustaining life, it is an "equipment" (*parikkhāra*).
Therefore, it is "medicinal equipment for the support of the sick" (*gilānapaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra*).

"Of those afflicted" (*veyyābādhikānaṃ*) means of those arisen from affliction—that is, from the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*) and from diseases produced thereby, such as leprosy, boils, and pustules. "Of feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*) means of painful feelings (*dukkha-vedanā*).
"By means of the state of supreme non-affliction" means by means of the state of supreme freedom from suffering. The construction is: "I partake [of food] so that all that suffering may be abandoned.
Thus, in this context, the commentary on the Pāḷi should be understood in brief.

"Also because of the arising of the nine feelings" means not only is there the fever of karmic result in the future, but also, due to overeating, there is [the suffering of] the stomach-cloth and so forth.
It should also be understood from the arising of new feelings as if they were fresh.
For one who practices meditation, "wavering" means the abandonment of the meditation subject; thus it is said: "it wavers, it trembles, it abandons the meditation subject.
Regarding the passage, "He is patient with cold and heat," the story of the Elder Lomasavaṅga should be told here.
It is said that while the Elder was dwelling in the meditation hall of the Piyaṅgu Cave on Cetiyapabbata during the interval between the rains,
at a time when snow was falling, he spent his time in the open air, contemplating the Lokantarika hell without ever abandoning his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
And in the summer season, as he attended to his meditation subject outside on the walking path after his meal, sweat poured from his armpits.
They were released. Then a pupil said to him, "Venerable sir, sit here; it is a cool place.
The Elder replied, "Friend, it is out of fear of heat that I am sitting here," and having reflected upon the Great Niraya of Avīci, he sat down right there.
And in this context, "heat" should be understood as the heat of fire, since the heat of the sun will be mentioned later. By way of the heat of the sun—
This is the story that was told.
And even one who does not receive food or drink for two or three times,

if he reflects upon his own rebirth in the realm of the hungry ghosts throughout the beginningless cycle of existence and does not waver, he certainly does not abandon the meditation subject, despite the contacts of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and sun.
Even if he is touched [by a snake], if he does not waver upon reflecting on his rebirth as an animal, he certainly does not abandon his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Even when touched by the contact of a crawling reptile, the Elder Padhāniya certainly does not abandon his meditation subject, for he reflects on how, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he has previously undergone this many times in the mouths of lions, tigers, and other such beasts.
In this way, he should be understood as one who "is patient with hunger... [and] even the touch of reptiles.
It is said that while the Elder was listening to the Dhamma on the Noble Lineage in the Kaṇikāra Meditation Hall at Khaṇḍacela Monastery, a venomous snake bit him.
Although the Elder knew it had happened, he sat there with a serene mind and continued listening to the Dhamma alone; the force of the poison became paralyzed.
The Elder, beginning with the ordination hall, reflected upon his virtue and, thinking, "I am pure in virtue," gave rise to rapture (*pīti*).
Simultaneously with the arising of that rapture, the poison turned back and entered the earth.
There and then, the Elder attained one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), and by developing insight (*vipassanā*), he reached Arahantship.

However, one who, upon hearing even a course of speech consisting of the final offense—whether it be harshly spoken by way of abuse or simply because it was ill-spoken—does not waver, but reflects instead on the virtue of patience, like the Elder Abhaya the Dīgha-bhāṇaka;

such a person should be understood as "one who is patient with harsh and ill-spoken courses of speech. It is said that the Elder, due to his contentment with requisites and his delight in meditation, [remained undisturbed].
He preached on the practice of the Great Noble Lineage (mahāariyavaṃsappaṭipadā), and the entire great village came out;

great honor accrued to the Elder. A certain other great elder, unable to endure this, reviled him, saying, "The Dīgha-bhāṇaka is making a clamor all night long, saying, 'I am preaching the Noble Lineage!
Both of them then returned to their respective monasteries.
As they traveled, they proceeded along a single path for the distance of one *gāvuta*. Throughout that entire *gāvuta*, he continued to revile him.
Then, at a place where the paths to two monasteries diverged, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka stood there, paid homage to him, and said, "Venerable sir, this is your path.
He went on as if he had not heard it. The Elder also went to his monastery.
Having washed his feet, he sat down. His pupil said to him, "Venerable sir, why did you not say anything at all while he was reviling you for an entire league?
The Elder replied, "Patience alone, friend, is my burden; it is not impatience.
Even when a single word was uttered, I saw no separation from my meditation subject."
"Speech itself is the path (vacanapatha) for those who wish to make that meaning known; it is the means," thus he said, "speech itself is the path of speech.
Or, in the sense of being unpleasant, it is "intense" (tibba). For that which is not pleasant is called undesirable and intense.
"He is of a nature to endure" means he has the inherent disposition to endure the aforementioned feelings. [Regarding] the Elder Padhāniya at Cittalapabbata...
It is said that after he had spent the night in meditation, wind arose in his belly.
Being unable to endure it, he rolled over and turned about. The Elder Piṇḍapātika, who was standing by the side of the walking path, said to him:
"Friend, one who has gone forth should be patient. He replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and endured it.
He lay down motionless. The wind cut through him from the navel up to the heart.
The Elder, suppressing the pain and practicing insight, attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmī) in a moment and passed away into final Nibbāna.

Thus, in all cases—in the passage beginning with "one who, touched by heat, longs for coolness"—it should be understood that the outflow of sensual desire (kāmāsava) arises due to such signs as heat and so forth. There is no cold or heat in the state of a happy destination (sugati).
The intention is that there is no undesirable cold or heat. When there is the grasping of a self, there is the grasping of "mine";
thus he says: "The grasping 'it is cold for me,' 'it is hot for me,' is the taint of views.
"I am an ascetic" means thinking: "I am an ascetic; what does it matter to me whether I live or die? This is the intention.
"Having reflected" means having reflected upon the purpose for entering the village and so forth.
"He withdraws" means he moves away from approaching the vicinity of elephants and other such creatures. "A place" (*ṭhāna*) is that wherein they stand;
a "place of thorns" (*kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna*) is a place of thorns, meaning the location where thorns exist. "Infested by non-human beings" refers to being frequented by non-human beings.
"Defiled" means accompanied by danger. "Becoming the basis for an undetermined [offense]" means being the cause for an undetermined training rule (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*).
"Due to the classification as courtesans, etc. means due to the classification as courtesans, widows, women of loose conduct, young girls, eunuchs, taverns, and bhikkhunīs.
"Equal" means the same; the meaning is not uneven. "Or he did" means he committed such improper conduct. "By what is termed the restraint of virtue" (*sīla-saṃvara*).

What is virtue as avoidance? For by avoiding unsuitable seats, the avoidance of improper conduct is expressed. And the avoidance of the resort of improper conduct is the restraint of virtue through the nature of virtuous behavior (*cāritta-sīla*).

Thus, when the Blessed One was analyzing the restraint of virtue in the passage, "He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," he demonstrated the perfection of conduct and resort by saying, "There is improper conduct; there is an improper resort," and so forth.

The proper conduct (*ācāra*) and the field of activity (*gocara*) have been shown by way of analysis. From the statement, “One avoids a fierce elephant,” it should be understood that even the avoidance of elephants and so forth constitutes the virtue of conduct (*ācārasīla*), as it is carried out in accordance with the word of the Blessed One.

“For this reason also”: for this further reason—that is, because [these states] arise from improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and because they are accompanied by greed and the other [defilements].
The meaning is that this thought is unwholesome for reasons such as being the opposite of the wholesome (*kusalappaṭipakkha*).

In this same manner, the meaning should also be understood regarding [the terms] "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) and so forth. And here, by the phrase "unwholesome" and so on, he shows the disadvantage of sensual thought pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*);

by the phrase "resulting in suffering" (*dukkhavipāka*), he shows that pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*). Furthermore, in the phrases "it leads to self-affliction" (*attabyābādhāya saṃvattati*) and so forth, [the same distinction applies].
In this same manner, the discernment of danger should be understood.

The non-endurance of an arisen sensual thought means not allowing such a thought to arise again. It is appropriate to say that its abandonment, removal, bringing to an end, and disappearance are what is meant;
thus, after stating in the Pāḷi, “he does not endure an arisen sensual thought,” it says, “he abandons it,” and so forth.

To show that meaning, he said, "What does one who does not tolerate [them] do? and so forth. Here, it is shown that "abandoning" (*pahāna*) refers specifically to suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and not to eradication (*samuccheda*); thus, the meaning is presented by way of suppression alone.
By the phrase "as they arise again and again" (*uppannuppanne*), either the state of their arising is being grasped, or a complete inclusion of those evil thoughts is intended.
Regarding these, he says "as soon as they have arisen" with reference to the first [type]; the meaning is "just as they are born.
He says "even a hundred times, whenever they arise" in order to show that the inclusion of "without remainder" occurs when there is a desire for elaboration (*byāpani*).
"Thought of relatives" (*ñātivitakka*) refers to thoughts based on worldly affection, such as: "Our relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity," and so forth.

Thought concerning relatives (*ñātakavitakka*) is thought that arises with reference to one's kinsmen. Thought concerning the country (*janapadavitakka*) is thought that arises with reference to one’s native land by way of worldly attachment, such as:
"Our country has abundant food, rich crops, and is delightful. Thought associated with asceticism (*pariļāhavitakka*) is that which is connected with the practice of austerities, such as thinking:
"Through the exertion of squatting and other such practices, beings will be happy and immortal in the future life once suffering has been worn away."

Thought concerning immortality (*amaratthāya vitakko*). Or, taking that as its object, it is "immortal-thought" (*amaravitakko*) because it is accompanied by the view of the Eel-Wriggler (*amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhi*), being both immortal and a thought.

"Associated with concern for others" (*parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyutto*) refers to a thought connected with worldly affection—a semblance of compassion—that arises through rejoicing and so forth toward others such as one's attendants. "Associated with gain, honor, and renown" (*lābhasakkārasilokappaṭisaṃyutto*)...
It is associated with robes and so forth, with gain, with honor, and with fame by way of making them the object [of thought].
"Associated with non-disparagement" refers to the arisen thought: "Oh, may others not despise me;
may they not hold me in low esteem; may they treat me with respect, like a stone parasol."

Because it has the nature of conceiving sensual desires and because it is preeminent in leading to the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) is called a "mode of longing";

thus it is said: "In this context, sensual thought is the influx of sensual desire. "Its particularity" means the particularity of the influx of sensual desire, with the intention that it has the nature of existence (*bhava*).
It is called "dispelling" (*vinodana*) because one dispels—meaning one removes from one's own mental continuum—sensual thought and the rest by means of it.
He said, "By means of 'dispelling,' which is designated as the restraint of energy.

From the statement, "The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation," it follows that the non-attainment of true knowledge and liberation—and consequently the failure to transcend the entire suffering of saṃsāra—is the disadvantage of non-cultivation. By way of the opposite of what was stated...
And the benefit of meditation should be understood by way of [the Buddha] being the Blessed One’s own legitimate son and so forth.

"Praising" means extolling that very difficult task because the abandoning of the taints (*āsava*) is difficult to achieve. "Abandoned precisely through restraint" means they were abandoned only by means of restraint.
Therefore it was said: "One does not perceive them as abandoned when they have not actually been abandoned."
The commentary on the *Āsavasutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Dārukammikasutta*. 59.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "a bed crowded with children" (*puttasambādhasayana*) means a bed crowded by children. Here, by the term "children," the taking of a wife is intended.
It is like a turmoil among children and wives. By this, he shows the defilement of the mind caused by their being overcome with sorrow due to illness and other such afflictions.
By the phrase "those who enjoy sensual pleasures," however, he shows the mind being overcome by lust. By both [of these], he shows the state of a distracted mind.
"Kāsika sandalwood" refers to brilliantly shining sandalwood; it is said that it is exceptionally radiant in color and luminous.
They make it even more delicate for that very purpose. Therefore he said, "delicate sandalwood" (*saṇhacandana*);
the meaning is "Kāsī cloth and sandalwood. Regarding "garlands, scents, and ointments": one wears garlands for the sake of beauty and color, and for the sake of fragrance;
one uses scents for the sake of fragrance; and one uses ointments for the sake of coloring the skin and for the sake of loveliness.
"By one who possesses": by one who approves of gold and silver, that is, both gold itself and whatever wealth remains.
This expresses the state of being utterly greedy for all sensual pleasures.
The commentary on the *Dārukammika-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Hatthisāriputta Sutta 60.
In the sixth [sutta], one who drives an elephant is a *hatthisārī*; his son is *Hatthisāriputta*.
It is said that he was the son of an elephant trainer in Sāvatthī, and having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and mastered the Three Piṭakas, he [excelled] in subtle matters...
He was skilled in various meanings, such as the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana). Therefore it is said:
“While the elder bhikkhus were discoursing on the Abhidhamma, he would interject his own discourse from time to time.

In this context, “he would interject his own discourse from time to time” means that he would insert his own explanations into the intervals of the continuous flow of discourse being spoken by the elders.

The meaning [is as follows]. "By the five kinds of association" means by these five associations: association through hearing, association through seeing, association through conversation, association through sharing enjoyments, and physical association. "Eaters of husks":
for that which grows in a place of husks is called "husk," using the name of the cause for the effect (kāraṇūpacāra). "Sippiyo" refers to oysters; "sambukā" refers to conch shells.

"He spoke in praise of the state of a householder": it is said that during the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, there were two friends who lived in harmony with one another and practiced their recitations together.
One of them, becoming dissatisfied, conceived a desire for the life of a householder and informed the other.
The latter, showing him the disadvantages of the household life and the benefits of going forth, exhorted him. He—
Having heard that and being delighted, on another day when a similar thought arose, he said this to him:
"Friend, such a thought arises in me; I shall give this bowl and robe to you.
Out of greed for the bowl and robe, he showed the advantages of lay life to him and spoke of the disadvantages of the going-forth. Upon hearing this, he—
Having turned his mind away from the state of a householder, he took delight only in the life of renunciation.
Thus, because he had been told by a virtuous bhikkhu at that time about the advantages of the householder’s state, he now left the order six times;
but on the seventh occasion, having gone forth, while Mahāmoggallāna and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika were discussing the Abhidhamma, [he listened].
From time to time he would pose questions. Then the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika rebuked him.
Being unable to stand firm in the teaching spoken by the Great Disciple, he left the order and became a householder. Now, this man had been a lay friend of Poṭṭhapāda;
therefore, after leaving the order, two or three days later, he went into the presence of Poṭṭhapāda. Then he—
Seeing him, he said, “Friend, what have you done? You have turned away from the teaching of such a Teacher as this!
Come, it is now time for you to go forth. Taking him with him, he went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone forth at that place, he attained arahantship. Therefore it was said: “Having gone forth on the seventh occasion, he attained arahantship.”
The commentary on the Hatthisāriputta Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Majjhe Sutta: 61.

Regarding the word *manta* in the seventh [verse], it is an indication by means of the elision of the letter *ya*; or else, this is a nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental. Therefore he said:

“Having understood both extremes by means of that”: because it is produced through contact—that is, because it is produced through mutual contact during the union of the two [parents]—and because this body originates from contact according to the sequence:
“With contact as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging;
with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth.”

It is said: "Because it is produced by way of contact. Regarding the phrase "one extreme," here this word *anta* (extreme/end) is seen used in the senses of end, interior, boundary, absence, portion, verse-filler, proximity, and so forth.

For instance, in such expressions as "full of ends" (*antapūro*) or "full of the belly" (*udarapūro*), the word *anta* means "end. In such passages as "They wander in the world, concealed by their retinues;
impure within, yet appearing beautiful without," it means "inside" or "interior. In the passage "The end of the waist-band decays... it means "portion" or "part."
In such passages as “the edge of the jungle, or the edge of the path, or the edge of a rock, or the edge of water,” it means a boundary.
In such passages as “This, monks, is the end of livelihoods,” it means something base or inferior. In such passages as “This indeed is the end of suffering,” it means non-existence;

for the destruction of all conditions is called the “end” (koṭi) because it is the non-existence of suffering. In such passages as “The three ends,” it means a portion. [Now, please consider the Sutta...]
In such passages as, "Master the verses, or the Abhidhamma, or having requested an opportunity for the Suttantas," it functions as a filler for the meter.
In such passages as, "A village lodging is one that has entered the vicinity of a village," it means "in the vicinity. But here, it refers to a constituent part;
thus, "this is one constituent part."

*Sakkāya* is a collection of phenomena existing in the ultimate sense; it refers to the five aggregates of clinging. Therefore, he said, "the round of existence in the three realms. The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the middle sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Purisindriyañāṇa-sutta*.

62. In the eighth [case], one is "destined for the states of misery" (*āpāyika*) because one is fixed in the states of misery by means of karma that leads to such states through the process of rebirth;
the same principle applies here to the term "hell-bound" (*nerayika*).

One is "a dweller for an eon" (*kappaṭṭha*) because, having arisen in the Avīci hell, one remains there for an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*), which is designated as a "life-span eon. One is "incurable" (*atekiccha*) because one cannot be cured by means of avoiding rebirth in hell.
"Unbroken" means not broken even in part. From the moment it is split, a seed no longer serves the purpose of a seed.
"Unrotted" means not rotten due to soaking in water; for a rotten seed does not serve the purpose of a seed.
"Not damaged by wind or sun" means not damaged by wind or sun, nor reduced to a state of saplessness. For a sapless, withered seed does not serve the purpose of a seed.
It is not suitable. Although one should say "sārādānī," the shortening of the vowel *ā* was made in the Pāḷi, hence it says "sāradānī.
It is called "sārādāni" because of taking the essence (*sāra*); that is, those from which the essence has been taken, or those whose essence remains established.
For a seed that has lost its essence is not suitable for the purpose of a seed. "Well-stored" means kept in a granary according to the rule for four months.
“Laid out comfortably” means well-arranged. “In a fertile field” (*maṇḍakhetta*) refers to a field of high quality that has not been pierced by defects such as salinity or alkalinity.
Regarding “*abhido*,” he says it is a particle synonymous with the prefix *abhi*; thus, “*abhiaḍḍharattan*” [is explained].
Alternatively, *abhido* means “of which there is no piercing. When one ought to say “*aḍḍharattaṃ abhidaṃ*,” the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
*Addharattaṃ* (midnight) expresses either absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*) or it has the sense of the locative case.
Therefore, *abhido addharattaṃ* means "at the time of midnight that has not passed" (*abhinne addharattasamaye*).

For when the moon is situated to the east or west of the center of the sky on the full-moon day, the time of midnight is said to be "passed" (*bhinnā*); but when it is situated exactly in the middle, it is said to be "not passed" (*abhinna*).
Regarding "Suppabuddha, Sunakkhatta, and others": it is said that Suppabuddha the Sākiyan,
having conceived resentment toward the Teacher for two reasons— namely, "He has gone forth after abandoning my daughter" and "Having ordained my son,
he has taken his place as an enemy"— one day thought, "I shall no longer go to a place where I have been invited to eat..."
Thinking, "I will give [him nothing]," he blocked the path and sat in the middle of the street drinking liquor.
Then, when the Teacher arrived at that place surrounded by the community of monks, they announced, "The Teacher has arrived. He said, "Tell him to go on ahead;
this man is not older than I, nor shall I give him the way. Again and again...
Even though he was being addressed, he remained seated just as before. Since the Teacher could not obtain the road from his maternal uncle, he turned back from that very spot.
He, too, dispatched a secret agent, saying, "Go, and having heard what he says, come back. As the Teacher was returning, he smiled;
when asked by the Elder Ānanda, "Venerable sir, what is the reason for manifesting a smile? the Teacher replied:
He said, "Ānanda, do you see Suppabuddha? "I see him, Bhante. "That man has committed a grave deed in that he did not give alms to a Buddha such as I am;
on the seventh day from now, he will sink into the earth at the foot of the palace on the lower terrace," he declared.
Sunakkhatta, too, had previously approached the Blessed One and asked about the practice for the divine eye.

Then the Blessed One explained it to him. Having developed the divine eye and increased his range of vision, as he looked out, he saw young gods and goddesses enjoying celestial splendors in the Nandana Grove, the Citralatā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the Missakavana Grove.
Seeing them, [he thought]: "For these beings, with such a [form of existence]..."
Thinking, "For those established in the perfection of their own bodies, will their voices indeed be sweet?
he approached the One of Ten Powers with a desire to hear their voice and asked about the preliminary practice for the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*).

However, the Blessed One, knowing that "there is no supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the divine ear-element" in him, did not explain the preliminary practice. For the Buddhas [do not teach what is useless].
They explained the preliminary practice for that which was yet to come. Having harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, he thought:
"I first asked the ascetic Gotama about the preliminary practice for the divine eye, and he told me, 'Let it succeed or not;
