let it happen or not. But I, by means of my own personal effort, have accomplished that and [now ask about] the preliminary practice for the divine ear-element."
I questioned him, but he did not tell me. It was certainly because of envy and stinginess that he thought:

“This royal renunciant, having developed the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of penetration of minds, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, will become my equal. Thus it was on account of these things that he did not tell me.
“...he does not speak,” thinking thus, he bound himself with even greater resentment; having cast off his saffron robes and returned to the life of a householder, he still did not remain silent.
But having slandered the One of Ten Powers with what was untrue and empty, he became a denizen of the states of misery.
The Blessed One explained that as well. For it has been said: “In this way too, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son...”
"Even when addressed by me, he would depart from this Dhamma and Vinaya, becoming one bound for the states of misery. By this it is said:
"The Blessed One also knew others, such as Suppabuddha, Sunakkhatta, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of Kokālika and others should be understood.
"Susīma the wanderer" refers to a wise wanderer of that name who was skilled in the Vedangas. [This refers to] those of other sects.
For those who have lost their gains, honor, and fame think: "The ascetic Gotama has not attained the pinnacle of gain by virtue of his birth or lineage;
rather, he is a supreme poet who composes verses for his disciples and provides them with bonds of poetry.
Having mastered these, they engage in introductory discourses, expressions of thanks, and formal recitations for their supporters. Thus they speak.
They bring gains to those who have faith. "If we were to know even a little more than what the ascetic Gotama knows, we could incorporate our own doctrines therein and speak to our own supporters.
Then we would become even more successful in gaining gains than they are. Who indeed, having gone forth in the presence of the ascetic Gotama..."
Thinking, "He will be able to learn it very quickly," and seeing that Susīma was capable, they approached him and said:
"Come, friend Susīma, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama.
Once you have mastered the Dhamma, you should teach it to us; once we have mastered that Dhamma, we shall explain it to householders."
"In this way, we too shall be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped, and shall obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Then, the wanderer Susīma, having accepted their words, approached Ānanda;
having approached him, he requested the going-forth. The Elder took him and, approaching the Blessed One, reported this matter to him.
The Blessed One, however, reflected: "This wanderer lives proclaiming himself 'I am a teacher independent of others' according to the tenets of the sectarians;
yet he says, 'I wish to practice the holy life under this very path.
Is he perhaps inspired by faith in me, or rather by faith in my Dhamma discourse or that of my disciples? Then, even in that single instance...
Knowing that he lacked faith, [the Buddha] observed: "This man has gone forth into my teaching thinking, 'I shall deceive the Dhamma.

His coming here is not pure; what will his outcome be? Seeing that although he had gone forth thinking, "I shall deceive the Dhamma," he would nevertheless, after striving for only a few days, attain Arahantship, [the Buddha said]: "Therefore, Ānanda..."
“Let them ordain Susīma. It was with reference to him that this was said: “Who is known by the Blessed One in this way? The wanderer Susīma.

Regarding the minister Santati: it is said that at one time, having returned after pacifying a rebellion on the frontier of King Pasenadi, the king was pleased with him and, granting him sovereignty for seven days, gave him a woman skilled in dance and song.
He gave [the gift]. Having remained intoxicated by liquor for seven days, on the seventh day—adorned with all his ornaments and mounted upon the back of a noble elephant—he went to a bathing place.
Seeing the Teacher entering through the gateway for alms, he bowed from the very back of the elephant’s neck while still shaking his head. The Teacher smiled and said, “Who indeed...”
“Venerable sir, what is the reason for breaking into a smile? When asked thus by the Elder Ānanda, [the Blessed One], explaining the cause of his smile, said:

“Ānanda, do you see the minister Santati? This very day, adorned with all his ornaments, he will come into my presence and, at the conclusion of a four-line stanza, having attained Arahantship, will attain Parinibbāna. Therefore it was said: “Thus...”
“Who is known to the Blessed One? “The minister Santati.
The commentary on the *Purisindriyañāṇa Sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Nibbedhika Sutta*.

63. In the ninth [sense], it is called a "mode" (*pariyāya*) because it proceeds by taking its own fruit as its own possession, or because it enters into the state of being the cause for that fruit; thus, it is said here that "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is what is meant. For example, in the passage:
"I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) made of unwashed cloth," the word *guṇa* has the sense of a layer (*paṭala*).
In the passage: "Time passes, nights fly by, and the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned," the word *guṇa* has the sense of a heap (*rāsa*).
The meaning of "strand" (*guṇa*) [is as follows]: In the passage, “A hundredfold merit is to be expected from a gift,” it has the sense of benefit (*ānisamsa*).

In the passage, “One should make an end and a cord, and many strands for a garland,” it has the sense of binding (*bandhana*). Here too, this same sense is intended; thus he said, “Strands in the sense of binding.
In the case of the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāma*), there is also the sense of binding by way of being a condition for the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*).

Or, the meaning of "delight" (*rāsa*) or the meaning of "quality" (*guṇa*) should be understood. Or, "cognizable by the eye" means they are to be known by consciousnesses that have the eye-consciousness as their door.

The same method applies to "cognizable by the ear" and so forth. "Being desirable objects" means they are of a nature that is inherently an desirable object, or they have attained the state of being an desirable object.
"Pleasant" (*kamanīya*) means they are to be desired. "Increasing the mind" means they are captivating. By this—
Even by way of imagining, it includes the state of being a desirable object. "Born of what is dear" means having a nature that is to be cherished.
"Connected with sensual desire" means that which is to be approached and bound by sensual lust; it is to be associated with it. Therefore he said, "making it an object," and so forth.
Alternatively, "lust of intention" (saṅkapparāga) is the lust that arises toward what has been intended as beautiful and so on. Thus, herein, the sensual object (vatthukāma) [is explained].

Having set aside [the other types], "sensual desire as defilement" (kilesakāma) was mentioned because the state of being sensual desire is established for those [objects] by virtue of that [defilement] alone.

Since even sensual desire as defilement exists in various ways—distinguished by its association with pleasant feeling, views, and so forth, and by the diversity of its modes of occurrence—it was said, "having variegated and manifold objects," in order to distinguish it from that;
the meaning is that they have objects such as visible forms and so on of many different kinds.
"In this regard, the wise subdue desire": herein, those who are steadfast and wise subdue desire and lust for these objects.
"Of that same nature" means having that same character; in terms of meaning, it is said to be "conformable to that sensual pleasure.

A "portion of merit" (*puññabhāga*) is a division or section of merit. One who is produced by that, or exists therein, is "one who partakes of merit. "One who partakes of demerit" (*apuññabhāgiya*)...
The same principle applies here as well. Since it is the result itself that is the cause of differentiation, he says "conventional result" (*vohāravipāka*).
"Comprehensive" means common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome. "Volition that coordinates" is volition characterized by the coordination of associated mental states.
"Beating the chest" means having struck one's chest. "A single-word [mantra]" refers to a spell consisting of a single word; hence he says, "or a single-word mantra," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Nibbedhika-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Sīhanāda-sutta*. 64.
Regarding "the powers of a Tathāgata" in the tenth [sutta]: these are the powers belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata, not shared by others. But are they not...?

Do some [knowledges] arise even for disciples? Certainly they do arise; however, those such as the Buddhas’ knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa*) and so forth do not arise for others at any time in such a manner, and thus they are not shared with others.

Indeed, it is with reference to this aforementioned characteristic that the designation "unshared" is established specifically for the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) and so on, because of their non-commonality.
Just as the powers of previous Buddhas came about through the attainment of merit, so too they are called "Tathāgata-powers" because they have come about in that same way.
This belongs to a bull (*usabha*), thus it is "bull-like" (*āsabha*); it is the pre-eminent position. "Foremost cry" means the best cry.

Regarding "both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching": here, the knowledge of penetration is that which is developed by wisdom and brings about one's own noble fruit (*ariyaphala*). By compassion...
The knowledge of teaching is that which has been developed and brings the noble fruits to disciples. In this regard, the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is twofold:
that which is arising and that which has arisen. For that [knowledge] is "arising" from the Great Departure until the path of Arahatship;
it is called "arisen" at the moment of the fruition (*phala*). From the Tusita heaven until the path of Arahatship on the Great Enlightenment Seat (*mahābodhipallaṅka*), [it is arising].

That which has arisen at the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇa*) is called "arisen. That which arises from the time of Dīpaṅkara Buddha up until the path of Arahatship is called "arisen at the moment of fruition.
Knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is also twofold according to its occurrence:
that which occurs up until the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña is called "occurring at the moment of fruition. Among these—
Penetration-knowledge is supramundane; teaching-knowledge is mundane. Yet both of these are not shared by others;
they are the very own-knowledge of the Buddhas alone.
"He understands the possible as possible" means he understands the cause as a cause, because the fruit resides therein.
Because it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that, it is therefore called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*).
The Blessed One, understanding that "whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are the grounds;
and whatever states are not the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are the non-grounds (*aṭṭhāna*)," [taught this].
One understands, as it truly is, what is possible and what is impossible.
"Samādiyantī" means "undertakings" (samādānāni); however, since these are undertaken and then performed, he says "of those undertaken and performed.
Alternatively, "kammasamādāna" simply means "kamma"; by this, he shows that there is no new meaning for the word "samādāna" beyond that of "kamma."

As in the compound *muttagata* (fallen from the stream), the word *gata* [is understood]. "Destinations" (*gatī*) refers to the destinies such as hell and so forth. "Bases" (*upadhī*) refers to the individual existence (*attabhāva*).
"Time" (*kāla*) refers to the time when karma is ready to ripen. "Application" (*payoga*) refers to the activity that serves as the condition for the arising of the result.
"Of the four jhānas" is said in the sense of burning up their opposites and in the sense of closely contemplating the object.
Of the fine-material-sphere jhānas. This is stated according to the fourfold method. Of the eight liberations: of the eight liberations beginning with “possessing form, one sees forms.
Of the three kinds of concentration: of the three concentrations beginning with that accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*).
Of the nine successive attainments: of the nine beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.

Regarding the "gradual attainments" (*anupubbasamāpatti*): here, the name "concentrations" (*samādhi*) applies to the eight [meditative states] in their sequence, and they are also called "attainments" (*samāpatti*) because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).
However, because that [one-pointedness] is absent in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is not given the name "concentration.

"A state conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgiyo dhammo*) refers to the leaping toward sense-desires and so forth by one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so on while possessing only weak proficiency.

The "state partaking of distinction" (*visesabhāgiya-dhamma*) is the leaping forward of perception and attention from the first jhāna and so forth—when one has emerged from them while they are still familiar—toward the second jhāna and so forth.

Thus, the leaping forward of perception and attention from the sense-sphere realm toward the second jhāna and so forth are shown as states partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiya*) and states partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiya*), respectively.
Furthermore, by the word "dhamma," the fact that those [states] possess the intrinsic nature of the jhānas is indicated.
Thus it was said. Therefore, he refers back to that very meaning already stated by way of its causal nature.

"Purification" (vodāna) means purification in the sense of proficiency. For that is called "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) because, having emerged from the first jhāna and so forth, it serves as the condition for the attainment of the second jhāna and so on.
As for those who say, "There is no canonical text stating 'emergence from the attainment of fruition through cessation' (nirodha)," [the answer is:]...

They say this. They should be refuted by means of this canonical text: “For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition by way of proximity-condition for the attainment of fruition.
The commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
7. The Chapter on Devas (Devatāvagga). 1–3. Commentary on the Discourses on the Fruit of Non-Return and Others.
65–67. The first [sections] of the seventh [chapter] are clear in meaning. Regarding the third:

that which exists in the highest conduct (*abhisamācāra*), the supreme conduct, is "pertaining to higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārika*); it is the practice of the duties (*vatta*). Therefore, he said: "consisting of the highest conduct," and so forth.
"Virtue prescribed by the rules for trainees" (*sekha-paṇṇatti-sīla*) means virtue prescribed by way of the *sekhiya* rules.
The commentary on the *Anāgāmiphala-sutta* and others is concluded.
4–5. Commentary on the *Saṅgaṇikārāma-sutta* and others (Suttas 68–69).
In the fourth [sutta], "crowd" (*gaṇa*) refers to a gathering or assembly; this is "crowd-association" (*gaṇasaṅgaṇikā*). It is called a "delight" (*ārāma*) in the sense that it is to be enjoyed.

"Of this" refers to one who delights in the company of a group. "Company" (*saṅgaṇikā*) means the gathering together of one's own circle; "group" (*gaṇa*) means the gathering together of various people.
The rest here is easy to understand. The fifth [sutta] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the *Saṅgaṇikārāma-sutta* and the others is finished.
6. Commentary on the Samādhisutta 70.

Regarding the sixth [sutta], it is said that "paṭippassambhana" (subsiding) and "paṭippassaddhi" (subsided state) are identical in meaning: "Not one who has attained subsiding" means not one who has attained the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*).
In the white side [of the teaching], regarding the terms "peaceful" (*santa*) and so forth, it is due to the peace of the factors (*aṅga*) and the peace of the object (*ārammaṇa*).
It is "peaceful" because all defilements have been stilled; it is "sublime" in the sense of being unassailable;
it is "attained through subsiding" because it has been obtained by the subsiding of defilements, or because the state of the subsiding of defilements has been attained;

it is "attained by one whose defilements have subsided" because it has been attained by an Arahant whose defilements have subsided; and it is "attained through singleness" because it is reached by means of singleness.
The meaning should be understood in this way.
The commentary on the Samādhi-sutta is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the Sakkhibhabba-sutta and following.
71–74. "In each respective distinction" means in each respective distinction that is to be realized.

"Capable of being a witness" (*sakkhibhabba*) means one who is capable of acting as a witness through direct experience; the state of being such is "witness-capability" (*sakkhibhabbatā*). That is "witness-capability.
"When there is mindfulness as a basis" means when there is mindfulness as the cause. What is the cause here? Either direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) or the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge.
Alternatively, at the conclusion, it should be understood that either Arahatship by means of the sixth direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is the cause, or insight (*vipassanā*) is the cause for Arahatship.

For that which consists of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), such as the experience of psychic power described as "the state of being capable of realization" in various contexts, has direct knowledge as its cause.

Now, if the experience of the various supernormal powers and so forth is itself direct knowledge, then in that case, the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññāpādaka-jjhāna*) [is the cause].

It is the cause. Even for Arahantship, it is the cause for one who, having established a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, thinking, "When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere?", brings about the sixth direct knowledge (abhiññā). And this [longing] is not common to all;
however, by way of being common, insight (vipassanā) is the cause for Arahantship. Alternatively, when there is a sphere (āyatana)...

The meaning here should be understood as follows: "When the cause, known as the decisive support (upanissaya), for each respective specific attainment exists. Regarding the states conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya*) and so forth:
"When perception and attention accompanied by sensual desire (*kāma*) assail one who has attained the first jhāna, that is concentration conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya*).

When mindfulness in accordance with that state remains established, that is concentration conducive to stability (*ṭhitibhāgiya*). [When it is] accompanied by the absence of applied thought (*avitakka*)," and so on.
When perceptions and acts of attention associated with distinction occur, it is concentration partaking of distinction.
When perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment and conjoined with dispassion occur, it is concentration partaking of penetration.

Having explained all the attainments in this manner, the meaning of those partaking of decline and so forth should be understood. In that context, "one who has obtained the first jhāna" refers to one who...

He is one who has attained the first jhāna, which is still weak. When perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire (*kāma*) occur, then for one who has emerged from that state, perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire continue to occur and prick him by way of the object.

Because of those perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire—which have not transcended sensual desire and which leap into sensual desire—that concentration of his first jhāna [is weakened].
It declines and falls away; therefore, it is called "conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgiya*).
"In accordance with that" (*tadanudhammatā*) means its nature conforms to that. "Mindfulness stands still" is said with reference to wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*).

For one whose inclination consists in finding gratification and delighting in the first jhāna—seeing it as peaceful and sublime because its nature conforms to the first jhāna—[his mindfulness stands still].
By way of attachment (*nikanti*), that first-jhāna concentration neither decreases nor increases; it becomes a factor of stability (*ṭhitikoṭṭhāsika*).

Therefore it is said: "concentration partaking of stability" (*ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi*). "Accompanied by non-thinking" (*avitakkasahagatā*) means that for one who attends to the second jhāna—which is without thinking—as peaceful and sublime, [the concentration] is accompanied by non-thinking by way of its object.
"Perceptions and acts of attention proceed" (*saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti*)...
They urge and incite one who has emerged from the first jhāna that is well-mastered, for the sake of attaining the second jhāna.
Because of the application of perception and attention directed toward the second jhāna above that, this concentration of the first jhāna is called "partaking of distinction" (visesabhāgiya),
since it serves as the proximate cause for the arising of the second jhāna, which is its superior state.
"Accompanied by disenchantment" means that [the mind] is accompanied by the knowledge of insight—which is termed "disenchantment"—in one who has emerged from that very first jhāna after attaining it.
For insight-knowledge becomes disenchanted and weary when the factors of jhāna appear with their various distinctions;
therefore, it is called "disenchantment. "Occurring" means for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna.

They urge and prick. "Connected with dispassion" means connected with Nibbāna, which is designated as dispassion. For insight-knowledge is called "connected with dispassion" because it proceeds from the thought:
"It is possible to realize dispassion, Nibbāna, by means of this path.
The perception and attention associated with that [insight] are likewise said to be "connected with dispassion. Of those perceptions and attentions...
By virtue of this, the concentration of the first jhāna is called "conducive to penetration" (nibbedhabhāgiya) because it serves as the proximate cause for the realization of the Noble Path.
They are "conducive to decline" (hānabhāgiya) because they partake in decline; or, they possess a portion of decline, which means they belong to the category of falling away.
In this same manner, that which is "conducive to stability" (ṭhitibhāgiya) should be understood. The eighth and subsequent [categories] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Sakkhibhabbasutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Devatāvagga* is finished.
8. The *Arahattavagga*.
1–3. Commentary on the *Dukkhasutta* and others (75–77).

Regarding the first [sections] of the eighth [chapter], there is nothing further to be said. In the third [section], "the three bases of hypocrisy" refers to the three bases of hypocrisy consisting of:

the seeking of requisites, indirect hinting (*sāmantajappana*), and the adoption of specific postures (*iriyāpatha*). "Having raised up" means by such [claims] as: "He is a great householder, a great ship-owner, a great master of charity," and so forth.

“Taking up” refers to speaking after having adopted [the view]. “Having cast down” refers to speaking after having disparaged [someone] by saying, “What is the use of this man’s life? He is merely one who eats seeds.
The commentary on the *Dukkha-sutta* and others is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Sukhasomanassa-sutta*.
78. Regarding the fourth [section], among the aforementioned phenomena and so forth, because his suffering—the sign of defilement—is non-existent, it is said:
"He dwells abundant in happiness and gladness. One who has much physical pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental gladness (*cetasika-somanassa*) is "abundant in happiness and gladness.
That by which the fruit is, as it were, mixed is the "womb" (*yoni*), meaning a decisive cause. "His" refers to the one previously mentioned.
For a bhikkhu. "Complete" means without deficiency and without remainder.
The commentary on the *Sukhasomanassa Sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Adhigama Sutta*.
79. "Coming" (*āgamana*) means that by this [mental attention], wholesome or unwholesome states come; it is the cause for the arising of wholesome and unwholesome states.
In this context, "wholesome" refers to one who is skilled in coming. Thus, when one attends to mental objects (*dhamma*), knowing that "wholesome or unwholesome states increase," one is so aware.
"Going away" (*apagamana*) means that by this [mental attention], wholesome or unwholesome states depart.
He is skilled in that regard because he is skilled in the means of avoiding them—that is, skilled in departing from them.
One who knows thus: "When one attends to mental objects in this way, neither wholesome nor unwholesome states increase," is skilled in means.

This should be understood as being endowed with the wisdom of immediate application (*ṭhānuppattika-paññā*), which consists in knowing the appropriate course of action for the purpose of remedying an urgent task or a danger that has arisen.
The commentary on the *Adhigamasutta* is finished.
6–7. Commentary on the *Mahantattasutta*, etc. 80–81.
In the sixth [sutta], "when defilements have arrived" (*sampatte*) means when the defilements have come upon one. The seventh is self-evident.
The commentary on the Mahantattasutta and others is concluded.
8–10. Commentary on the second Nirayasutta and others (82–84).

In the eighth sutta, by the phrase "through bodily immodesty and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes verbal immodesty and mental immodesty. The ninth and subsequent suttas are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the Dutiyanirayasutta and the others is finished.
The commentary on the Arahattavagga is finished.
9. The Sītivagga.
1. Commentary on the Sītibhāva Sutta 85.
In the first [verse] of the ninth [sutta], "coolness" (*sītibhāva*) refers to *nibbāna* or the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"He restrains" (*niggaṇhāti*) means he restrains the mind that has become agitated by excessive energy (*accāraddhavīriya*) and so forth, by way of protecting it from the side of restlessness (*uddhacca*). "He exerts" (*paggaṇhāti*) means [he exerts it] by way of [excessive] laxity of energy (*atisithilavīriya*) and so forth.
One uplifts the sunken mind by way of protecting it from falling into indolence. "Encourages" means that one satisfies or inspires with wisdom the mind that is proceeding evenly in its course;

or, when the mind—due to weakness in the application of wisdom or because the bliss of tranquility has not been attained—lacks zest and does not leap forward into meditation, then one reflects upon the grounds for spiritual urgency, such as birth and so forth.

He encourages and inspires. He looks on with equanimity: when, however, the mind is neither sluggish nor agitated, is not dissatisfied, proceeds evenly toward the object, and has properly entered the flow of development, then—without performing any function of exertion, restraint, or encouragement—he looks on with equanimity, just as a charioteer does when the horses are proceeding evenly. He is indeed equanimous.
[He] exists. "One who is intent on the sublime" means one who is resolved upon, inclined toward, and leaning toward the sublime and supreme path and fruit.
The commentary on the *Sītibhāva-sutta* is finished.
2–11. Commentary on the *Āvaraṇa-sutta* and others.
86–95. In the second [case], "one who lacks desire" (*acchandika*) means one devoid of the wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of being "without desire. "One of weak wisdom" (*duppañña*) means one who is deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*).
However, even if the wisdom of the life-continuum is complete, one for whom that life-continuum does not serve as a condition for the supramundane is likewise "one of weak wisdom."

"Unable to enter into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states" means that he is unable to enter—that is, to attain—the Noble Path, which is designated as the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
In the phrases "not through obstruction by karma," and so forth, the meaning should be understood as the opposite of "unable. The fourth and subsequent [sections] have their meanings obvious.
The commentary on the Āvaraṇasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Sītivagga is finished.
10. The Ānisaṃsavagga.
1–11. Commentary on the *Pātubhāvasutta* and others (96–106).

Regarding the first and subsequent sections of the tenth [chapter], there is nothing further to be said. In the eighth [section], one who possesses loving-kindness (*mettā*) is called "possessing loving-kindness" (*mettāvā*).

The state of being such is "the state of possessing loving-kindness" (*mettāvatā*), which is the practice of loving-kindness; it is by means of that. Furthermore, that state of possessing loving-kindness is service performed by way of loving-kindness.
He said: "By service joined with loving-kindness. They serve because their holy life (*brahmacariya*) has been practiced imperfectly.
This is because the service that must be performed for the Teacher by a disciple who has served him—including everything up to the Dhamma—has been properly accomplished.
The meanings of "new" and so forth are self-evident.
The commentary on the *Pātubhāvasutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the *Ānisaṃsavagga* is concluded.
107–116. The eleventh chapter is of plain meaning.

Part One: The First Fifty.

The first chapter of the Section of Sevens (Sattakanipāta) is clear in its meaning.

4. Commentary on the Puggala Sutta 14.
Regarding the fourth [type] of the second [section]: "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutto*) means liberated from both sides, that is, from both parts (*ubhohi bhāgehi*).

This is according to the method of *ekadesasarūpekasesa* (retaining one part of a similar group). The plural form "from two parts" (*dvīhi bhāgehi*) is used here in the sense of the instrumental case as well as the ablative. It is also [to be understood] by way of repetition (*āvutti*) and so forth.
"This rule should be understood," he said, [beginning with] "by the formless attainments" and so forth.

By this, [he refers to] the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga, which proceeds thus: "He is 'liberated in both ways' because he is liberated by the liberation of suppression through the attainment, and by the liberation of eradication through the Path";
and the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Mahārakkhita, which proceeds thus: "He is 'liberated in both ways' because he is liberated from the mental body and from the physical body."
It should be understood that the combined summary of these three Thera-vāda positions has been made here:

namely, the position of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya, which maintains that one is "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated once through the liberation by suppression during attainment, and once through the liberation by eradication via the Path.
And herein, in the first position, by means of two...
One who is liberated from both parts is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). In the second explanation, one is "liberated in both ways" because they are liberated from both sides;
in the third explanation, one is "liberated in both ways" because they are liberated twice by means of two parts—this is the distinction between them.
"Liberated" (*vimutta*) means liberated from the defilements (*kilesa*), or the sense is that they are liberated from the body through the suppression and eradication of the defilements.

He is one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Although here even the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—just like the immaterial-sphere jhāna—is said to possess two factors and to have reached imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*), one who attains Arahantship by making that [fine-material jhāna] the proximate cause is not called "liberated in both ways," because he is not liberated from the body of form (*rūpakāya*).
For that [Arahantship] is liberated only from the body of defilements (*kilesakāya*).
It is not by means of the form-body; therefore, one who has emerged from that [formless attainment] and attained Arahantship is not "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
Thus he said: "Of the four formless... there are five kinds. In the phrase "of the formless attainments," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
The expression "non-returners who have attained Arahantship" refers to their former state; for one who has already attained Arahantship is no longer a non-returner.
It is so named. Having described the eight liberations beginning with “one possessing form sees forms,” and ending with the attainment of cessation, it is said in the *Mahānidāna Sutta*:

“But when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells having touched these eight liberations with his body, and having seen them with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This, Ānanda, is called a bhikkhu liberated in both ways.
Although this is stated there, it was spoken specifically regarding the most excellent type of liberation-in-both-ways; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
However, in order to include all those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), he stated, "It is fivefold," and then said, "But here the canonical text... [etc.
...is presented according to those who have attained the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*). Furthermore, in the *Kīṭāgiri Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*:
"And what, monks, is the person liberated in both ways? Here, monks, a certain person..."
“Those liberations that are formless, transcending forms—having touched them with the body, he dwells therein;
and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This, monks, is called a person liberated in both ways.
Thus, by way of the formless attainments, four types of those liberated in both ways are described, and the best among them is stated because it possesses the characteristics already mentioned.

Among those five types mentioned above, the first four are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) in a figurative sense, because they do not enter cessation as the pinnacle of the meditative attainments. However, a non-returner who has attained the eight meditative attainments,
enters that [cessation], emerges from it, and then, having developed insight, reaches Arahantship— he is called the "foremost among those liberated in both ways" in the literal sense.
"And what kind of person? and so forth is the *Puggalapaññatti* (Designation of Persons) scripture. Therein, "what" (*katamo*) is a word of inquiry.
"Person" (*puggalo*) is a word to be inquired about in its specific sense. "Here" (*idha*) means in this teaching. "A certain one" (*ekacco*) means one.
"Dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body" means having entered the eight attainments and having acquired them through the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
"He dwells... and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed. This means that through insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), he sees the conditioned phenomena;
and through path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*), having seen the four truths, all four taints are utterly destroyed. "Having seen" means by reason of seeing.
For it is not that one sees the taints with wisdom; rather, because they are destroyed by the cause of seeing, it is said that they are "destroyed having seen."
Because its destruction depends upon vision. For thus vision is said to be the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

"Liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) means liberated specifically by wisdom alone, not by the preeminent concentration consisting of the eight liberations which serves as its basis; such a person is "liberated by wisdom.
This noble one has not yet attained the eight liberations and is [freed] from all taints.
"Delivered"—this is its designation. For even when the form-sphere jhāna-liberations have been attained, one is not yet "supported by preeminent concentration";

thus, it is said that the state of being "liberated in both ways" does not occur on account of those alone. However, if there is even a single formless-sphere jhāna, one is indeed called "liberated in both ways.
It is for this reason that, by means of a portion of the eight liberations capable of conferring that name, [the term is applied].
It is said that he is "one who has attained the eight liberations.

For a designation applied to a whole is also seen to apply to its parts, as in the expression "a heap of spears," because of the complete exhaustion of the taints without remainder. This is by way of the negation of the eight liberations themselves, and not by way of the negation of the material jhānas which constitute only a part [of them].
For in this way, even though there is an absence of the material jhānas which are parts [of the set], there is still the negation of the eight liberations.

It is established that [the state of being] "not existing" [does not apply]. For even when there is but one meditative absorption (jhāna) of the formless realm (arūpāvacara), one is indeed called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).
"Having realized the limit of what is touched" (phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikato): "the limit of what is touched" (phuṭṭhanta) means the end of those things touched;

the intended meaning is the time immediately following the formless absorptions (arūpajjhāna). This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). It refers precisely to that time immediately following the touch.
It is said that it has been realized by means of the method for realization;

or, this is a neuter gerundive, as in such expressions as "he sat to one side. For by one who is liberated from the material body and from one portion of the mental body through the liberation of suppression by means of formless jhāna, the liberation termed cessation is, as it were, looked upon and made manifest.

It exists, yet it has not been realized by means of the body. However, when certain taints (āsava) have been exhausted by taking cessation as the object, it is realized by him through that [cessation];

therefore, because he realizes the cessation to be realized exactly as it was contemplated by means of the mental body (nāmakāya), he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī), but not "liberated," because some taints have not yet been fully destroyed.
Therefore it is said: "First he touches the contact of jhāna; afterwards he realizes cessation, Nibbāna.

This refers to the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), namely: those four who have attained the state of a body-witness (*kāyasakkhi*) by emerging from each of the four formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*), having reflected upon conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has reached the highest path after emerging from cessation (*nirodha*).
"It is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā that ‘there are likewise five kinds even in the case of the body-witness’ (kāyasakkhi).
‘Some taints’ (āsavā) refers to those taints to be abandoned by the lower paths.
‘One who has reached the end of vision’ (diṭṭhantaṃ patto) means one who has attained immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated as ‘vision’."
“Because it has been seen, it is attained”—this is also a reading. By this, he illustrates that cessation is attained through the vision characterized as the seeing of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore he said, “Formations are suffering,” and so forth. Therein, “by wisdom” means by path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*).

One who has attained vision is one who, starting from the stage of the first fruit up to the stage of the highest path, possesses that vision. Therefore he said, “He too is sixfold, like the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*).”
...“it occurs. Just as the one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), so too this dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*) should be understood as being fivefold:
namely, four who have emerged from the four formless jhānas and attained the state of one who has reached vision (*diṭṭhippatto*), plus himself as the fifth.
The same method applies to the one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*). “This is suffering”: this much is suffering, there is no suffering beyond this. [He understands] it as it really is.
"He understands" means that, setting craving aside, he understands the five aggregates of clinging as the truth of suffering according to reality.

Furthermore, because craving gives rise to and produces suffering, and from that [craving] suffering originates, he understands it as it truly is: "This is the origin of suffering. Moreover, because this [craving] is both suffering and its origin...
And having reached Nibbāna, it ceases and enters into non-occurrence;
therefore, one does not understand "this is the cessation of suffering" as it really is. However, the Noble Eightfold Path leads to that cessation of suffering;
by means of that, one understands "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" as it really is. Up to this point, at different moments—

The determination of the truths (saccavavatthāna) has been shown. Now, in order to show that [determination] within a single moment, the passage beginning with “proclaimed by the Tathāgata” is stated.
“Proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means made known, understood, and made manifest by the Tathāgata at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
“Dhammas” refers to the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths. “Vodiṭṭhā honti” means well-seen (sudiṭṭhā). “Vocaritā” means well-practiced (sucaritā), [that is,] by means of wisdom (paññā).
The meaning is: "well-caused to practice. "Ayam" means "this person of such a kind is one who has attained right view.

"Liberated by faith" (saddhāya vimutto) means liberated by way of believing. By this, he shows that even for one who is not liberated in every respect, there is a state of being liberated by mere faith.
Alternatively, "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutto) means intent upon faith (adhimutto). But what of these?

Is there a difference in the abandoning of the defilements? No, there is not. Then why does the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) not reach the level of the one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto)? It is because of the difference in their progress (āgamanīya).

For the one who has attained vision, while suppressing the defilements during his progress, is able to suppress them without pain, without difficulty, and without fatigue; but the one liberated by faith [suppresses them] with pain and with difficulty.

One who is wearying is able to suppress [the defilements]; therefore, the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) does not reach the level of the one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta). Thus he said, "For this," and so forth.
"Of one who has faith" means: of one who has faith in this way: "This practice certainly brings about the destruction of the defilements, because it was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Furthermore, because for him, through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) and so forth, by way of abandoning the perception of permanence (niccasaññā),...

In the cultivation [of the path], one perceives successive distinctions; thus, there is direct personal realization (paccakkhatā) in each respective stage. Therefore, it is said, "as if for one who has faith. The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that same state.

Furthermore, by the expression "cultivation of the preliminary path," it is shown that through the diversity of the approach, there is a diversity of wisdom among those who have attained vision and those who are liberated through faith.
In the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā* as well, it is stated: “There is no difference among them in the abandoning of defilements; there is indeed a difference in their wisdom. Having said this, it concludes:
“It is precisely because of the difference in their progress that one liberated by faith does not reach the level of one who has attained through vision.
That which bears and determines an object according to its true nature is *dhamma*; that is, wisdom (*paññā*). That *dhamma*, which is reckoned as wisdom—
One is a "follower of the Dhamma" (dhammānusārī) because one recollects that which has proceeded with the Dhamma as its supreme forerunner. Therefore, he says "the Dhamma," and so forth.
"Preceded by wisdom" means having wisdom as its primary factor. He extends this same method to the meaning of "one recollects faith; one develops the path preceded by faith.
One is a "conveyor of wisdom" (paññāvāhī) because one carries wisdom along; that is, one causes wisdom to proceed with particular excellence.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “He develops the Noble Path preceded by wisdom. Or, it carries the person or leads them toward Nibbāna;
thus, it is “wisdom-bearing” (*paññāvāhī*). Regarding the term “faith-bearing” (*saddhāvāhī*), the meaning should be understood here according to this same method.

The discussion on those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) and so forth refers to the discourse that should be stated starting from the point of their arrival among those liberated in both ways and the rest.
Therefore, because it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, the meaning here should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
The commentary on the *Puggala-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Udakūpama Sutta 15.

Regarding the fifth [simile], "by those that are exclusively dark" refers to the phenomena of fixed wrong view, namely: the doctrine of non-existence (*natthikavāda*), the doctrine of no-cause (*ahetukavāda*), and the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*).
Therefore, it was said: "It was spoken with reference to fixed wrong view. "In this way, a person..."—for this reason, once...
"Sunk, he is indeed sunk. For they say, like Makkhali Gosāla and others, that there is no rising again from this existence.
"The food of the fires of hell below and below" means that one sinks further down. "Good is faith in wholesome things":
thinking, "This faith in wholesome states is truly well-acquired," one emerges; by that much wholesome merit alone, one emerges.
...so it is named. The same method applies to the terms “sādhu hirī” and so forth. *Caṅkavāra* refers to a washermen’s alkaline strainer, or a liquor strainer.

Thus, regarding the term *puggala*: having once emerged by means of these qualities such as faith—thinking, “In this way, faith is good”—one sinks back down again due to the decline of those very qualities, just like Devadatta and others. For Devadatta [fell from] the eight attainments...
Although he had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañca abhiññāyo*), because he acted as an adversary to the Buddhas, he fell away from those virtues;

having committed the deed of shedding blood and the deed of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, at the breaking up of the body, immediately after his death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) in the second moment of thought, he was reborn in hell.
Kokālika, having slandered the two chief disciples, was reborn in the Paduma hell.
"It neither decreases nor increases" means that it does not decrease even when there is insufficient [food], nor does it increase even when there is sufficient food.

Both of these points should be illustrated by way of both the householder and the homeless one. For instance, a certain householder might have a weekly or annual meal provision set aside when it was insufficient;
later, even when it is sufficient, he continues to take only that much, such as the weekly meal and so forth.
He practices. Even a homeless one may take up the recitation or the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) at the beginning when he is not yet capable;
however, a wise person, having attained sufficient strength and energy, does not go beyond that. Thus, regarding the individual:

by means of this stability of faith and the other faculties, the individual is said to be "standing after having emerged. "Having emerged, he flies away" refers to the once-returner (sakadāgāmī) individual.
Having arisen through the thinning of the defilements, one who proceeds facing the direction that must be reached is said to "cross over.
"One has reached a firm footing" refers to the person who is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). These seven types of persons are illustrated by the simile of water.
It is said that seven foot-trading merchants, while traveling along a long road, encountered a river full of water on their way.
They reached [the water]. Among them, the man who was afraid of the water, having entered first, sank right where he had stepped in and was unable to stand up again;

he inevitably became food for the fish and turtles. The second man, having sunk at the place of entry, rose once, but then sank again and was unable to rise; he became food for the fish and turtles right there within the water.
The third, having submerged himself, emerged and stood in the middle of the river; he was unable neither to return from this side nor to go to the far shore.
The fourth, having emerged and stood there, looked toward the ford for crossing. The fifth, having looked toward the ford for crossing, swam across.
The sixth, seeing him, went to the further shore and stood in water reaching only to his waist.
Having gone to the opposite shore, he bathes with scented powders and the like, puts on fine garments and such, anoints himself with fragrant ointments,
adorns himself with garlands of blue lotuses and other ornaments, and having entered the great city and ascended the palace,
he partakes of the finest food.
In this context, these seven types of persons are like the leg-traders; the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) is like the river;
the drowning right at the place where the first man, who was afraid of the water, stepped in is like the person of wrong view drowning in the cycle of existence;
and the man who, having emerged, then drowns again is like the person who, having emerged by means of the arising of faith and the other [faculties], sinks back down through their decline.
The "person established" (*ṭhitipuggala*) is like one standing in the middle of a river, representing the stability of faith and the other faculties;

the "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) is like one looking toward the ford for crossing; the "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*) is like a person leaping across, because he still leaps due to the whirlpools of defilements and sensual desires;

the "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) is like a person who has crossed over and stands in water reaching only to the waist, because he is no longer subject to returning; and the "arahant" is like one who, having bathed, has reached the further shore.
Just as a man standing on dry land, having crossed over the four floods, stands upon the ground of Nibbāna, so too should the Brahmin whose taints are destroyed be understood;
and just as that man on dry land, having entered the city and ascended the palace, partakes of the finest food,
so should the one whose taints are destroyed be understood as spending his time having entered the meditative attainment (samāpatti) that has Nibbāna as its object.
The commentary on the Udakūpama Sutta is finished.
6–9. Commentary on the Aniccānupassī Sutta and following. 16–19.

Regarding the sixth [sutta], having stated, "In this case, one who is 'equal at the head' (samasīsī) is spoken of," and having thus analyzed that state of being equal at the head, that which is intended here—
To show this, he said, "He is fourfold," and so forth. By way of disease, one who has the same end as his disease is a *roga-samasīsī*. This same method applies to the others as well.

"All at once" means in a single moment. When, upon the occurrence of any one of the eye-diseases or other ailments, one established insight thinking, "If I do not recover from this, I shall attain Arahantship," then for him, both Arahantship and the disease [arise simultaneously].
When emergence occurs at one and the same time, this is called "the simultaneous peak of the illness.

"The conclusion of the posture" refers to the transition to another posture. This concerns one who, having resolved upon any one of the postures such as standing and so forth, established insight with the thought, "I shall reach Arahantship without disturbing this very posture.
Then, for him, both the attainment of Arahantship and the disturbance of the posture [occur simultaneously].
It occurs all at once; this is called "that which shares the same end as the postures" (*iriyāpathasamasīsī*). Regarding the term "that which shares the same end as life" (*jīvitasamasīsī*):

here, pride is the head of obstacles, views are the head of misapprehensions, restlessness is the head of distraction, ignorance is the head of defilements, faith is the head of resolution, energy is the head of exertion, mindfulness is the head of establishment, concentration is the head of non-distraction, and vision is the head...

Among the seventeen "heads" mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*—namely, "wisdom is the head of occurrence," "the life-faculty is the head of existence," "liberation is the head of death," and "cessation is the head of formations"—two heads are intended here: the "head of occurrence" and the "head of defilements.
This is because of the statement: "The exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after. Of these two, the "head of defilements" [is as follows]:
The path to arahantship brings ignorance to an end; the death-consciousness brings to an end the life-faculty, which is the head of the process [of existence].

In this regard, the consciousness that brings ignorance to an end is not able to bring the life-faculty to an end, and the consciousness that brings the life-faculty to an end is not able to bring ignorance to an end.
The consciousness that brings ignorance to an end is one thing; the consciousness that brings the life-faculty to an end is another.
He for whom these two "heads" reach their simultaneous completion is called one whose head is level with his life.

But how is this simultaneous? By way of equality of turn. For at whichever turn the emergence from the path occurs—there being five reviews on the path of stream-entry, five on the path of once-returning, five on the path of non-returning, and four on the path of Arahantship—[the two heads reach completion together].

When one, having established oneself in the nineteenth knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa), descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and attains final Nibbāna, this exhaustion of both the "heads" (i.e.,
the beginning and end of the cycle) is also equal by virtue of this equality of the twelvefold sequence. For the sequence of reviewing,
which must be accomplished immediately after the path-consciousness that provides the equal occurrence of the twelvefold sequence, serves for the very exhaustion of the defilements.

It deserves to be called "the last. Because of the statement, "When liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated,'" the exhaustion of the defilements is said to be accomplished by the completion of the reviewing [knowledge].
Thus, through the equality of this sequence of stages, the equality between the exhaustion of the defilements and the exhaustion of the life-span should be understood.
For this very reason, it was said: "But because of this... [etc. ...therefore it was said thus."

One who attains final nibbāna by means of the complete extinction of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) in the interval, without having exceeded the midpoint of the life-span, is an *antarāparinibbāyī*.

Therefore, he said: "He who [attains it] in the five Pure Abodes," and so forth. "In the middle" (*vemajjhe*) means in the midst of the life-span in whichever of the Aviha realms, etc., one has been reborn.
One who attains final nibbāna there after having reached and exceeded the midpoint of the life-span is an *upahaccaparinibbāyī*.

Therefore he said, “He who right there,” and so forth. Because he attains final nibbāna with ease—due to his sharp faculties—without exertion, without application, and without effort, and without becoming weary, he is one who attains nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*). Therefore he said, “He who among them,” and so forth.
In the phrase “of those very persons,” the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). “Without application” means without excessive application, that is, without difficulty.
One who attains final nibbāna with exertion and application, wearying himself through effort, is one who attains nibbāna through exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).

One whose stream of craving and the stream of the round have been directed upwards, or who has gone upwards because the stream of the Path is to be attained by going upwards, is one who goes upstream (*uddhaṃsoto*).
One who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm by way of rebirth-linking is one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*).

In this regard, however, a fourfold classification should be understood. For one who, starting from the Aviha heaven, purifies the four divine worlds and goes to Akaniṭṭha to attain final nibbāna, is called an "upstreamer bound for Akaniṭṭha.
Such a person, while dwelling in the Aviha heavens for a thousand aeons, being unable to attain arahantship there, goes to Atappa; and even there, two...
Dwelling there for a thousand eons, if he is unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Sudassa;
dwelling there also for four thousand eons, if he is unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Sudassi;
dwelling there also for eight thousand eons, if he is unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Akaniṭṭha, where he dwells.

One attains the highest path. In this regard, one who goes from the Aviha realm to either the second or fourth divine world and there attains final nibbāna is called an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota), but not one "bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.

One who, having passed away from the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), attains final nibbāna in the Akaniṭṭha realms is called "bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm," but not an "upstreamer. One who [goes] from among the four lower...
Having been reborn right there in various worlds of the gods, he attains final nibbāna; this one is neither an "upward-streamer" nor a "goer to Akaniṭṭha.
Furthermore, among those born in the Aviha heaven, there are five types: three who attain final nibbāna in the interval—by attaining it before reaching the midpoint of their lifespan;
one who attains final nibbāna upon landing; and one who is an upward-streamer, distinguished by whether they attain final nibbāna without exertion or with exertion.
There are ten [types] in Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī; thus, there are four decades, making forty.

In Akaniṭṭha, however, there is no one who goes upstream (uddhaṃsota); there are four—three who attain parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin) and one who attains parinibbāna upon arrival (upahaccaparinibbāyin)—and eight when divided by those who attain parinibbāna without exertion and with exertion, making forty-eight non-returners (anāgāmin). There is nothing further to be said regarding the seventh and subsequent heavens.
The commentary on the *Aniccānupassīsutta* and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Niddasavatthusutta*:

Regarding the tenth [sutta], he says "the grounds for the ten-fold designation" (*niddasādivatthūni*), explaining that this is a formal exposition (*niddesa*) where the word "etc. (*ādi*) has been elided from the phrase "the grounds for the ten-fold designation and so forth" (*niddasavatthūnīti*).
“Niddasa” means one who does not have ten [years] now; that is, he is "niddasa. "Pañha" refers to the matter desired to be known.
The inclusion of the word "kira" (it is said) is to show that the claim "he is no longer ten years old" is merely their opinion.
Furthermore, the term "niddasa" is a mere expression used to indicate that, just as his status as "nibbīsa" and so forth is intended, his status as "ninna-vādi" is likewise intended.
The passage beginning with “not only this” has been stated. “Wandering in the village” means wandering for alms in the village.
This is not a designation for the followers of other sects (*tīrthika*), because that characteristic is absent among them;

nor is it a designation even for one in training (*śaikṣa*) within the Dispensation, so how much less for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)? To show for whom this is a designation and by what reason, [the text says]: “This is for one whose taints are destroyed,” and so forth.
It has been stated. For him, the state of being without rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*) is the direct cause; the others, which have come down in the Canon, are causes by way of succession.

"Taking up the training" (*sikkhāsamādāna*) means the correct undertaking of the training. However, that [undertaking] should be understood as its fulfillment; thus he said, "in the fulfilling of the three trainings.
Alternatively, "taking up the training" is the guarding of the training correctly from the very beginning.
And that [training] is delimited by its meaning through Pūraṇa, because it is entirely non-existent when not guarded, and because it is fully perfected when guarded.
"Strong desire" means firm desire. "The future" is intended as the time of the immediately following days and so forth, not as a future existence;
thus he says, "in the future, on the next day and so forth. For one who fulfills the training therein...

“Devotion” means having affection that has not vanished. “Discernment of phenomena” (dhammanisāmanā) is the thorough contemplation of the phenomena belonging to the three planes by way of their impermanence and so forth;

thus it is said, “This is a designation for insight” (vipassanā). “In the removal of craving” refers to the suppression of craving accomplished through the power of the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution.
“In unification” refers to dwelling in seclusion, which is established by the departure from the company of crowds and the company of defilements.
“Exertion of energy” (*vīriyārambha*) refers to the undertaking of the right effort (*sammappadhāna*). Since that constitutes the complete cultivation of energy in every respect, he said:

“in the fulfillment of physical and mental energy. “In mindfulness and in circumspection” means both through acting with mindfulness (*satokāritā*) and acting with clear comprehension (*sampajānakāritā*);
for it is precisely by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that the exertion of energy succeeds. “Penetration by view” (*diṭṭhipaṭivedha*)...
It is for the penetration of right view of the path. Therefore he said, "in the seeing of the path.
The commentary on the Niddasavatthu Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Anusaya Vagga is finished.
3. The Section on the Seven Vajjī Factors. 1. Commentary on the Sārandada Sutta. 21.

In the first [sutta] of the third [section], it is called a *cetiya* because it is a place of mental devotion due to its nature as a divine abode (*devāyatana*), and because it is a site of veneration for the world.
It was so. As long as—this single phrase is used indefinitely to express a measure of time.
Since time is intended here, he said, "for as long as a period of time. "Frequent gatherings" means constant gatherings.
To show that state of constant gathering, he said, "of the day," and so forth. "Abounding in gatherings" means having many gatherings. "Cessation" means contraction.
In order to demonstrate by way of contrast the meaning already stated in the passage beginning with “Only growth,” it was said: “For those who do not assemble frequently,” and so forth.
“Agitated” means disturbed and not serene. “Having split” means having divided themselves into factions and become separate.
“With the assembly drum” means with the drum that announces the assembly. “Or having eaten half” means or having eaten their fill. “Sinking” means declining.
*Suṅka* is the portion to be given to royal officers by those traveling with goods after having taken them through mountain passes, river fords, village gates, and so forth.
*Bali* is the tax obtained from the harvested crops and other sources, such as a sixth or seventh part.
*Daṇḍa* is the monetary fine to be collected according to the offense, such as ten or twenty kahāpaṇas. *Vajjidhamma*...

The Dhamma of the Vajjian kings. Now, in order to show in detail the dangers and benefits regarding the promulgation of what was not previously promulgated and so forth, as well as their opposites, the passage beginning with “Of these” is stated. “Capable of service” means capable of attending upon [the Saṅgha].

Regarding the phrase “the ancient Dhamma of the Vajjis,” it is said that formerly, when the Vajjian kings were presented with someone brought before them saying, “This is a thief,” they would say: “Seize him...”
Without saying, "He is a thief," they hand him over to the judges of the court. Having investigated the case, if he is not a thief, they release him.
If he is a thief, they themselves do nothing but hand him over to the magistrates; these too, having investigated the case, if he is not a thief, release him.
If he is a thief, they hand him over to those who uphold the legal codes (*suttadhara*). These too, having investigated the case, if he is not a thief—
They hand it over. If the thief gives it to the *aṭṭakulikās*, they do exactly the same and pass it on to the commander-in-chief;
the commander-in-chief to the viceroy; and the viceroy to the king. After the king has investigated the case, if the person is not a thief, he releases him.

But if he is a thief, he causes the written record of the tradition (*paveṇipaṇṇaka*) to be read aloud. In that regard, [it says]: "This is the punishment for the name of whoever committed such-and-such an act."
It was written down. The king, having compared his actions with that [document], imposes a corresponding punishment.
Thus, people do not find fault with those who conduct themselves by adopting this ancient Vajjian custom.
Those born into the eight families that have come down through tradition, who refrain from following wrong paths, are the eight great men of the *aṭṭakula* (the eight clans).

"Honoring" means rendering assistance. "Having established a sense of respect" means having established a sense of respect toward them individually, thinking, "These are our elders. "They will honor" means they will honor properly.
Since that proper honoring is preceded by their being pleased with them, he said, "they will love them with affection. "Humble service" means prostration.
“Dassenti” means they show the burden of a heavy mind. “Sandhānetuṃ” means to connect and join [the parts] so that the continuity is not broken.
“Pasayhakārassa” means of one who acts with force. Granted that because of growth there is worthiness of honor, it is stated as “growth and decline”;
however, the meaning should be construed according to the sequence already mentioned. Or, in the text, since it is said: “Only growth is to be expected, not... [decline].”
Since it was stated [previously] as "decline," it is therefore stated in that same sequence as "increase and decline.
When evil kamma has not found an opportunity to ripen, or when there is no occasion for the ripening of that kamma, there is no room for the assault of a deity.
However, when that [kamma] has found an opportunity, there may be an occasion for the assault of a deity; thus he said: "They increase... [unarisen... evil unwholesome states."
By this very same principle, the meaning should also be understood here in the phrase "happiness that has not yet arisen.

The fact that the enemy force was seen to be twice or three times as strong is a demonstration of its terrifying nature; in such ways, the assistance of the deities at the head of the battle is to be understood.
"Unwanted" means undesirable. "From obstruction" means from prevention. "Dhammiya" means not departing from the Dhamma; herein—
They are called "lawful" (*dhammikā*). *Vāja* refers to the practice of wandering in the forest by dragging dogs and other animals for the purpose of killing deer, pigs, and so forth;
those engaged in that are *vājikā*, or hunters who kill deer.
The commentary on the Sāraṇada Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta 22.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to attack" (*abhiyātukāmo*) in the second [sutta]: here, the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of "overpowering," as in the case of words such as *anabhividituṃ* ("not to comprehend").
Thus he says, "desiring to go for the purpose of overpowering. Regarding the term *Vajjirājāno*: from the beginning, they were called "Vajjis" because "these are to be avoided" (*vajjetabbā*).
Based on the speech that had come forth, the kings who received the name "Vajjīs"—or the kings of the Vajji kingdom were called "Vajjirājāno.
However, the designation "Vajjī" for the kingdom should be understood by way of the royal princes residing therein. "By royal power" means by the majesty inherent in their status as kings.
That majesty of these republican (gaṇa) kings was well-known in the world due to their mutual concord. It was long-lasting.
And it was said, “It speaks of their state of concord. It is called *anubhāvo* because it brings about (*bhāveti*) or increases (*vaḍḍheti*) that which belongs to those who possess it;

*ānubhāvo* is simply *anubhāvo*, meaning majesty or splendor. Furthermore, that majesty of theirs became manifest in the world through their excellence in mounts such as elephants and horses, and through the abundance of food there; thus it was said, “By this... [it] speaks. By means of the keyhole.
"Through the keyhole. "An arrow" (*āsana*) means a shaft. "They will cause to pass over" means they will cause it to exceed [the mark].
"Arrow after arrow" (*poṅkhānupoṅkha*) means following the arrow (*poṅkha*) after the arrow; the meaning is that they make another arrow follow upon the track of the first arrow's shaft.
"Unfailing" (*avirādhitam*) means unerring. "I shall cut off" means I shall cut off the lineage of the clan by way of uprooting it.
*Ayana* means increase; its opposite is *anaya*, which is why it is called "decline" (*avaḍḍhi*). The ruin or destruction of kinsmen is "kinsman-destruction" (*ñātibyasana*).
"By the Ganges" means near the Ganges. "A market town" (*paṭṭanagāma*) means a village that is a cart-station. "Therein" means in that market town.
"Born from a powerful blow" means that intense anger has arisen. "To me" means for my sake. "By going" means by the act of departing. At that moment, there was neither cold nor heat.
"Facing him in battle" means by engaging directly and straightforwardly in combat.
The words beginning with "Enough" were spoken to show both conciliation and personal giving. Here, even "sowing dissension" is considered a means [to achieve one's goal].
It was stated: “except for causing a schism in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, the fact that war is not a proper means has already been made clear.
“This” refers to this statement: “except for deception and except for causing a schism in the Saṅgha.

“Having found the method in the discourse” means having found the means through this discourse of the Blessed One beginning with: “As long as... [there will be] decline. “Out of compassion” means out of favor toward the Vajjian kings.
The king, having sent that same man, [sent] all of them... [and so on]... "he caused them to bring [the matter]. The king asked him, who had come into his presence:

"Teacher, what did the Blessed One say? He replied: "Sire, just as it is impossible for anyone to seize the words of the ascetic Gotama by force, nevertheless, it may be possible through conciliation or by creating dissension. Then the king [addressed him].
“‘Our elephants, horses, and other livestock will be lost through deception; I shall seize them by means of causing a schism.
What shall we do? he asked. ‘In that case, Great King, initiate a discussion regarding the Vajjis in the assembly.
Then I shall say: "What have you to do with them, Great King? Let these men live by performing agriculture, trade, and so forth with their own property."'”
Having said, "The kings," I shall depart. Then you should say, "Sir, why does this brahmin oppose the conversation concerning the Vajjis? At midday, I will send them a gift;
having had that accepted as well, you should charge me with a fault and—without even subjecting me to imprisonment, flogging, or the like—merely shave my head.
"Make me into a ball and carry me out of the city; then I will say, 'I had the walls and moats built around your city;
I know which places are strong and weak, and which are shallow and deep; before long, I shall now straighten it.
When you hear that, you should say, 'Let him go. The king did everything accordingly.
When the Licchavis heard of his departure, they said, "That brahmin is a rogue; do not let him cross the Ganges.
Thereupon, some among them said, "He is doing this because he was speaking about us," to which others replied, "In that case, let him come!
He went there, and upon seeing the Licchavis, when asked, "Why have you come? he related the situation.
He reported this. The Licchavis said, "It is not right to impose such a heavy penalty for a mere trifle," and asked, "What office do you hold there?
He replied, "I am the chief minister of justice. "Then let that very office be yours," they said.
Consequently, he administered justice even more effectively. The princes learned their craft in his presence.
Having thus established his virtue, one day he took a Licchavi aside and asked, "Are the boys plowing?
"Yes, they are plowing. "Have they yoked two oxen? "Yes, they have yoked two oxen.
Having said this much, he turned back. Then another person asked him, "What did the teacher say? Not believing what was told to him...
Thinking, "He does not speak to me according to reality," he broke away from him.
On another day, the brahmin led a certain Licchavi aside, asked him, "With what sauce did you eat?
and then turned back. Another person questioned that man as well; not believing him, he likewise broke away. On yet another occasion, the brahmin...
One day, having led one Licchavi aside, he asked, "It is said that you are extremely poor. "Who said so? "A certain Licchavi by such-and-such a name.
Then, having led another aside, he asked, "It is said that you are of a timid nature. "Who said so?
"A certain Licchavi by such-and-such a name. In this way, by telling what had not been said by one person to another, [he did so] three times.
The king had the assembly drum beaten so that the kings, having broken with one another for years, would act in such a way that two did not travel along the same path.
The Licchavis, being told, "Let the lords assemble! Let the heroes assemble!
did not assemble. The brahmin sent a message to the king, saying, "Now is the time; let him come quickly."

He sent word. Upon hearing this, the king had the drum of his army beaten and set out. When the people of Vesālī heard it, they beat their own drums, saying, "We will not let the king cross the Ganges. Having heard that, [the king's men] said, "Let the brave kings go," and so forth, and did not assemble.
[The Vesālīans] beat their drums, saying, "We will not allow him to enter the city; we shall close the gates."
They had [messengers] sent out, but not even a single one assembled. Having entered through the doors as they were opened, he brought them all to ruin and disaster and departed.
With reference to this, it was said: "The king, too, having sent that very person, broke them all apart and, having gone, brought them to ruin and disaster."
The commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the First Sattaka Sutta 23.
In the third [sutta], *aparihānāya hitā* means "conducive to non-decline"; or alternatively, they are called *aparihāniyā* because one does not decline by means of them.
Thus, showing the meaning stated in brief in detail, he said, "And here too," and so forth.

Therein, the phrase beginning with "from that" refers to the words spoken and the discourse delivered in the teachings received from various directions. Because the monastery boundary (*vihārasīmā*) was crowded, the *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* ceremonies were suspended.

"One who is perishing" means one who is being destroyed both according to the text (*pāḷi*) and according to the meaning (*attha*). "Causing to be cast out" means by way of making [the text] proficient.
And by way of commenting on the meaning, they are those who uphold [the teaching],
such as the monks in Sāvatthī who prescribed that a *pācittiya* offense must be confessed, or like the Vajjiputtakas who did so by illustrating the ten points.
"Not acting thus" means not crushing either a new formal agreement (*katikavatta*) or a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), thereby departing from the Dispensation according to the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Illuminating even the minor training rules and not abolishing them—just as the Venerable Mahākassapa did:
"Listen to me, friends, let the Saṅgha hear. We have training rules that have passed into the hands of householders.
Even householders know: 'This is permissible for you, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans; this is not permissible for you. For even if we [were to abolish] the minor and lesser rules..."
"We shall abolish the training rules; there will be those who say: 'The ascetic Gotama laid down the training rules for his disciples only for a period of smoke;
as long as their Teacher remained, they trained in these rules.
But since their Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, they no longer train in these rules. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha..."

And just as the Venerable Mahākassapa established this principle: "The Saṅgha should not ordain what has not been ordained; it should not abolish what has been ordained; and it should practice by undertaking the training rules exactly as they have been ordained," [the assembly] attained a state of stability—meaning they reached a state of firmness and non-retrogression within the Dispensation.
By those who act as elders means by those who accomplish the status of an elder (*thera*).
By means of the qualities such as virtue (sīla) and the qualities of one beyond training (asekkhadhamma). "Many nights" means that having gone forth, they have known [the truth] for many nights.
