Establishing others in the qualities such as virtue is what constitutes being a leader in the Dispensation; thus he said, "they cause them to proceed in the three trainings.
They do not give instruction because [the recipients] are not fit vessels. "Lineage discourse" refers to the exposition of right practice handed down through the succession of teachers.

A discourse on the Dhamma. A "discourse on the Dhamma that is essential" refers to the framework of teachings such as the *Sutta on Higher Consciousness* (*Adhicitta-sutta*), which constitutes the core of the Dispensation by bringing about serenity, insight, the path, and the fruit, and which provides skill in the factors of enlightenment and the state of unsurpassed coolness.
"Initial advice" means, by the word "initial," [the instruction]: "In this way you should look forward; in this way you should look around; in this way you should bend [your limbs]..."
"Thus you should extend [your limbs], and thus you should wear your outer robe, bowl, and robes"—in this way he includes the instruction.

"Rebirth-giving" (*punabbhavadāna*) means rebirth (*punabbhava*), by the elision of the final member of the compound. "The others" refers to those who are not dependent on requisites and do not have their eyes fixed on material gain; they do not fall under the power of craving.
"In forest regions" means in parts of the forest included within the wilderness. But is craving not blameworthy wherever it occurs?
Having in mind such an exhortation, he says: "In regard to lodgings within inhabited areas," and so forth.

By this, he shows that the longing (*pihā*) and other states mentioned in the passage "for one who establishes longing for the unsurpassed liberations" refer to a state of attachment to forest lodgings, which belongs to the side of what should be cultivated.

"By oneself" (*attanā*) means by one's own accord. By this, he refers to those well-behaved monks who, even without being urged by others, [act] out of their own inherent disposition toward the future.
This shows that they desire both his arrival and the well-being of those who have arrived.
"By this very method" means by this practice. "The grasping of the Dhamma not yet grasped" means the acquisition of the scriptural Dhamma not previously mastered.

"The recitation of what has been grasped" means the thorough reflection on the meaning of what has been acquired; for this word *sajjhāya* has the sense of reflection (*cinta*). "They come" means they approach.
They sit down by means of the preparation of seats and so forth.
The commentary on the First Sutta of the Septet is finished.
4–6. Commentary on the Second Sutta of the Septet, etc.
24–26. "Even while doing so" (catutthe karontoyeva) means even while speaking the aforementioned frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

Although it is not frivolous talk [in this specific case], the restrictive term is used to show that he was intent upon that [talk] at that time. "One who makes a limit" (*pariyantakārī*) means one who speaks having set a limit;
for it is said: "One who speaks words that possess a limit. "One who speaks little" (*appabhasso*) means one who speaks in moderation.
Because it must be spoken in an absolute sense; the noble silence is the attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
"He simply sleeps" means that when falling asleep, seeing no danger therein, he simply sleeps and does not dispel it by changing his posture and so forth.
"Thus he remains associated" means that, according to the method already stated, he dwells precisely associated with the socializing of a group. [Those who are] immoral and of evil desires.
Regarding the names: they are themselves devoid of virtue; because they possess a desire for the esteem of qualities they do not have, they are "evil-desirous" (*pāpicchā*).
Because they make friends with evil persons, they are "evil-friends" (*pāpamittā*). Because they always move together with them, they are "evil-companions" (*pāpasahāyā*).
Because they are inclined toward them through such inclinations and so forth, they are "devoted to evil" (*pāpasampavaṅkā*). The fifth and subsequent terms have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the *Dutiyasattakasutta* and others is finished.
7–11. Commentary on the *Saññāsutta* and others, 27–31.

Regarding the seventh [sutta]: it is called "contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā*) because one contemplates [things] as impermanent by means of this; it is insight (*vipassanā*) proceeding in that manner.
However, because it is indeed cultivated by means of the perception that has been cultivated together with the [respective] contemplation of impermanence and so forth, it is therefore said:
“the perception associated with the contemplations of impermanence, etc. These seven are also mundane insight (*vipassanā*), because they proceed by way of [the formula] “impermanent,” and so on.
But here, two [kinds of insight] are included by virtue of the passage: “This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations.”

It should be understood that they are supramundane. For since Nibbāna is described there as "dispassion" (*virāga*) and "cessation" (*nirodha*), the perception of dispassion (*virāga-saññā*) here may also have Nibbāna as its object, just like those aforementioned perceptions. The rest here is easy to understand. The eighth discourse and the following are of plain meaning.
The commentary on the discourses beginning with the *Saññā-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Vajjisattaka-vagga is finished.
4. Devatā-vagga. 5.
Commentary on the First Mitta-sutta.
36. Regarding the fourth [precept], "he reveals his own secret to him":
this means that without telling another person a matter suitable for keeping secret, he discloses it only to that specific individual. "He does not disclose his secret to others":
this means that he conceals it by not revealing it in such a way that others would come to know the secret told by that person.
The commentary on the First Friend Sutta is finished.
6–11. Commentary on the Second Friend Sutta and following, 37–42.
In the sixth [sutta], the characteristics of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) are shown by the statement: "He is both dear and pleasing. A virtuous friend...

For he is one who is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, endowed with learning, endowed with generosity, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.
Therein, through the perfection of faith, he has conviction in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment, as well as in karma and the fruit of karma;
therefore, he does not abandon the welfare and happiness of beings, which are the cause of that enlightenment.
Through perfection in virtue, one becomes dear to beings, respected, worthy of esteem, a reprover, one who censures evil, a speaker who is patient with what is said.
Through perfection in learning, one becomes a speaker of profound discourses connected with truth, dependent origination, and so forth.
Through perfection in generosity, one becomes few in desires, contented, secluded, and unattached. Through perfection in energy...
He is one who has aroused energy in the practice for his own benefit and the benefit of others. Through the perfection of mindfulness, he is possessed of established mindfulness.
Through the perfection of concentration, he is undistracted and possesses a concentrated mind. Through the perfection of wisdom, he understands things without error.
Examining with mindfulness the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, he understands with wisdom what is beneficial and what is harmful for beings.

Having known things as they truly are, one becomes single-minded through concentration (*samādhi*) in that regard; then, by means of energy (*vīriya*), one restrains beings from what is unbeneficial and enjoins them to what is beneficial.
Therefore it is said: "Beloved... [and so forth] ...he enjoins. The seventh and following verses have their meaning obvious.
The commentary on the second *Mittasutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the Devatāvagga is finished.
5. Mahāyaññavagga 1. Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisuttavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Stations of Consciousness)
44. In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], because the particle is used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*), "seyyathāpi manussā" means "just as humans.
There is indeed a distinction, even though there is no difference in the external cause, because of the internal differentiation.
They are "diverse-bodied" (*nānattakāya*) because there is diversity in their bodies, or because their bodies are diverse. By this method...

The meaning should be understood in the remaining phrases as well. "Of them" means of humans. They are called "possessors of diverse perceptions" (*nānattasaññino*) because they possess various perceptions.
They are called "fallen ones" (*vinipātikā*) because they have fallen away from the mass of happiness; this is because, despite being gods, they lack divine prosperity.
Alternatively, they are called "fallen ones" because there is no non-falling (*nipāta*) for them into the states of misery (*apāya*). Therefore, he said: "freed from the four states of misery."
"Like that of Piyaṅkaramātā and others": it is said that at dawn, the female spirit (yakkhinī) Piyaṅkaramātā, having heard the Elder Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma, [said]:
"Make no noise, Piyaṅkara! The bhikkhu is reciting verses of the Dhamma."
“Even if we were to understand but a single verse of the Dhamma, let us practice it for our own welfare:
‘We shall exercise restraint toward living beings; we shall not speak falsehood knowingly;
we shall train ourselves in our own virtuous conduct, so that we may be released from the womb of a *pisāca*.’”

Having thus persuaded her son, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) on that very day. As for Uttara’s mother, however, she became a stream-enterer simply by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One.
They are called *brahmakāyikā* because they exist in the *brahmakāya*, which is the assembly of Brahmas produced through the first jhāna, or the host of Brahmas.
They are called *brahmapārisajjā* because they exist in the retinue of Mahābrahmā, standing in the position of his attendants. [Of Mahābrahmā...]

They are called *Brahmapurohitas* because they stand in the position of chaplains (*purohita*) to Brahmā. They are called *Mahābrahmās* because they are great Brahmās by virtue of their long life, beauty, and other qualities.

Although all three types [of these deities] are born there after having reached it by means of the first jhāna, the following was stated—beginning with "But the *Brahmapārisajjas*"—to show that this distinction exists due to the different modes of occurrence of the jhāna. "By the limited" means by the inferior. That...
Its inferiority is to be understood from the inferiority of zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors. Or, it is inferior merely by having been attained.
"Of an aeon" (*kappassa*) means of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*). It is "middling" because it exists in the middle between the inferior and the superior.

Its middling nature is to be understood from the middling nature of zeal and the other factors. Or, it is middling when, having been attained, it has not been well-cultivated. "Half-an-aeon" (*upaḍḍhakappa*)—
It is half an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*). "More extensive" means that it is larger in measure than the Brahmā-pārisajja devas and more sublime in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For it is indeed most sublime by its very nature; however, in this context, it is immeasurable.
For, although there is a difference in intrinsic nature between the bodies of the Parittābha and so forth, and the Parittasubha and so forth, they are [described] solely by way of their unity.
Because they are defined as such, they are called "a single body. "Exquisite" means superior. That superiority should be understood as the superiority of zeal and the other [factors].
Alternatively, it is "exquisite" because it has been well-cultivated or brought to mastery, being considered as having been "led to the state of excellence" (*padhānabhāva*).
Here too, an "aeon" (*kappa*) should be understood specifically in terms of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
Because a great aeon (*mahākappa*) is impossible to fulfill. "Thus" (*iti*) means in the manner already described.

"They" (*te*) refers to the three kinds of Brahmās mentioned as "the Brahmakāyika gods. "By the unity of perception" (*saññāya ekattā*) means because they possess a single nature by virtue of being endowed with three roots (*tihetuka*);

for there is no other distinction in that [perception] based on its associated mental states (*sampayutta-dhamma*). By the word "thus," he shows that those who have diverse bodies but a single perception are included.
"By means of a staff-torch" (daṇḍaukkāya) means by means of a torch-staff. "It wanders, it runs" means it wanders about, running as if scattered.
"Two aeons" (dve kappā) means two great aeons (mahākappa). This same method applies to those that follow hereafter. "Here" (idha) means in this sutta.
By the mention of the Ābhassara [heaven] alone, all the Parittābha and Appamāṇābha [deities] are also included, according to the principle of the highest limit.
“Sundarā pabhā subhā; tāya kiṇṇā subhakiṇṇā”—this is how it should be stated. By shortening the vowel of the word *bhā* and changing the final letter *ṇa* to *ha*, it is expressed as “*subhakiṇhā*.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), since the word *subha* is a synonym for radiance that is steady and uniform, the meaning is given as “strewn or scattered with beauty (*subha*)”; here too, [the same applies to] the final letter *ṇa*.
The production of the sound "ha" is indeed desirable. Its radiance does not break apart because it is of a single solid mass.

They belong specifically to the fourth station of consciousness because the body and perception are of one form. They are called "Vehapphala" (Abundant Fruit) because they yield fruits such as vast, peaceful happiness, long life, and beauty.
"Therein" means in that station of consciousness.
They stand on the side of the turning away because they do not return.

Having stated that "they are not present at all times," the passage beginning with "even for a hundred thousand eons" was spoken in order to clarify that very quality of not being present at all times.
This is because the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās who arise after sixteen thousand eons pass away into final Nibbāna, and others do not arise there while the world is empty of Buddhas.
That place becomes empty; therefore, the Suddhāvāsa deities are not present at all times. The planes of the Suddhāvāsas are like the sites of military encampments.
By this very sutta, which illustrates that the Suddhāvāsas are among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*), their status as stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) is also illustrated.
Therefore, the Suddhāvāsas are included within the fourth station of consciousness among the seven stations of consciousness, and among the nine...
They resort to the fourth abode of beings among the abodes of beings.

"Subtlety" is due to having reached a state of extreme subtlety as residual formations (*saṅkhārāvasesa*). Because there is an absence of the function of consciousness that is clearly manifest, it is not consciousness;
yet because it is not entirely without consciousness, it is "not non-consciousness. Therefore, [it exists] amidst those [beings] who possess the function of pervasive consciousness.
It was not stated among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).
The commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Stations of Consciousness is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Requisites for Concentration (*Samādhiparikkhārasutta-vaṇṇanā*).

45. "In the second [case], 'requisites for concentration'": here there are three kinds of requisites. For in the passage, "The chariot has virtue as its equipment, meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels," it is an ornament that is called a requisite (*parikkhāra*).
In the passage, "It is well-equipped with the seven requisites of a city," it is a retinue that is called a requisite.
In the passage, "Requisites for the sick... [and so on] ...requisites for life," it is... [the means of subsistence].
“Requisite” (sambhāra) means equipment (parikkhāra). Since that is intended here, he says: “the requisites for path-concentration.

An accompanying equipment (parivāra-parikkhāra) is also certainly appropriate. For the path-factors such as right view and so forth are called equipment because they surround and prepare (abhisaṅkharaṇa) right concentration by way of being its co-nascent and other conditions.
“Equipped” (parikkhatā) means surrounded. This is called noble right concentration.
This noble right concentration is called "surrounded by seven factors," just as a wheel-turning monarch is surrounded by seven treasures.
It is "upanisā" because it is approached and relied upon; "saha upanisāya" means "with its upanisā.
Thus, "an object with its upanisā" means precisely that which has its retinue. For here, the collection of phenomena that serves as the cooperative cause is intended by the term "upanisā."
The commentary on the *Samādhiparikkhāra-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the First Fire Sutta (Paṭhama-aggi-sutta) 46.

Regarding the third [sutta], "in the sense of not burning": although the three fires beginning with the fire worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya-aggi*) are indeed desired even by the brahmins, [the Blessed One] spoke thus [to distinguish them].
They do exist; however, they are merely desired by those [beings], and they do not actually accomplish the welfare of beings.
To show those who do accomplish the welfare of beings, it was said: “Āhuna is so called,” and so forth. In this context, bringing [offerings] and sacrificing—that is, worshipping—is called “āhuna.
Parents are worthy of that āhuna. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Worthy of offerings (āhuneyyā).”

“Monks, this is a designation for mother and father. And because they are worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) due to their great helpfulness toward their children, right conduct toward them brings them benefit and happiness;
likewise, wrong conduct toward them brings them harm and suffering. Thus he said: “Toward them... [they] arise.”

This matter is to be understood by means of the story of Mittavindaka. For Mittavindaka, having been told by his mother, "Dear son, today, having observed the Uposatha, listen to the preaching of the Dhamma in the monastery all night; I will give you a thousand [pieces of gold]," he undertook the Uposatha out of greed for wealth.
Having gone to the monastery and observed that "this place is free from fear," he [climbed] onto the Dhamma-seat...
Having slept the entire night while lying on the ground, he went home. His mother prepared gruel early in the morning and offered it to him;
he drank it after first taking a thousand pieces of gold. Then the thought occurred to him, "I shall accumulate wealth.
He became desirous of setting out upon the ocean by ship. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, in this family there is four hundred million in wealth..."
“There is no need; enough with going,” she said, trying to stop him. But disregarding her words, he continued on his way.
She stood in front of him. Then, becoming angry and thinking, “This woman stands before me,” he struck her with his foot, stepped over her as she fell, and went on.
The mother rose up and said, “My son, you who have committed such an act against a mother like me—do you truly imagine that there will be happiness for you in the place where you have gone?
As he boarded the ship and traveled on, on the seventh day the ship stopped. Then those men said, “Surely there is a wicked person here; cast lots!”
They said, "As the voting sticks were being distributed, they fell to him alone three times. They gave him a raft and cast him into the ocean.

He went to an island and, while enjoying prosperity together with *vimāna*-petīs, was told by them, "Do not go further and further ahead," yet he continued on, seeing prosperity twice as great, then twice as great again.
Gradually, he saw one man wearing a razor-wheel. That wheel appeared like a lotus flower.
He said to him, "Ho there! Give me that lotus you have fastened on.
"Sir, this is not a lotus; it is a razor-wheel. "You are deceiving me," he said, "have I never seen a lotus before?"
Having said this, he remarked, "You do not wish to give me red sandalwood paste, ornaments, and lotus flowers.
He thought, "This man too has performed an action similar to what I have done, and now wishes to experience its fruit.
Then, saying to him, "Take it, you! he hurled a discus at his head. Thus it was said:
“From four he attained eight, from eight sixteen;
from sixteen thirty-two—thus one who has encountered the wheel of immoderate desire;
for a person struck by craving, the wheel spins upon his head.”
"He" refers to the husband, the master of the house. "In the same manner as before" means by way of being a condition for non-consummation. Here is the story:
During the time of the Buddha Kassapa, the wife of a lay follower who was a stream-enterer committed adultery.
Seeing her doing so with his own eyes, he said, "Why do you act in this way? She replied, "If I were to do such a thing, this dog of mine would devour me..."
Having said, "Eat," she died and was reborn as a *vemānika-petī* in Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake;

by day she experienced prosperity, but by night she suffered misery. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, while out hunting, entered the forest and eventually arrived at Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake, where he enjoyed prosperity with her. She deceived him, and at night—
He experienced suffering. Having understood this, [the king] thought, "Where indeed is he going? and followed closely behind.
Standing not far away, he saw a dog emerging from the Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka ditch, gnawing at him with a "paṭapaṭa" sound;
he cut it in two with his sword, and there were two. When he cut them again, there were four; when he cut them again, there were eight; and when he cut them again—
When it was cut, sixteen [pieces] remained. She said, "What are you doing, Master? He replied, "What is this?
She said, "Instead of doing that, spit a lump of saliva onto the ground and rub it with your foot.
He did exactly that, and the dogs vanished. It is said that this "fist-technique" (muṭṭhiyoga) was the means by which those dogs disappeared—namely, the lump of saliva.
Having spat on the ground, she rubbed it with her foot; on that day, her [rebirth] karma was exhausted. The king, becoming remorseful, began to depart.
She said, "My lord, my karma is exhausted; do not go. The king went away without even hearing her.

*Dakkhiṇā* means the four requisites being given, because by means of these, welfare and happiness are seen (*dakkhanti*); one who is worthy of that *dakkhiṇā* is a *dakkhiṇeyya*, namely, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The commentary on the First Fire Sutta is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Second Fire Sutta and following. 47–48.
In the fourth [sutta], having prepared a sacrificial enclosure and for the sake of a great sacrifice, [he offered] both animate and inanimate things...
And because the sacrificial implements had been prepared, it is said in the Pāḷi: “A great sacrifice has been set out.
That equipment was prepared for them in such a manner; thus he said: “‘Set out’ means ‘presented.

“A hundred young bulls” refers to a hundred young bulls that have reached the state of youth, but are not yet very strong. Moreover, they were merely calves, not trained oxen or draft animals. “Goats”—
“Taruṇameṇḍakā” means young goats. “Upanītāni” means brought forward for the purpose of being set down. “In the sense of harming” means in the sense of injury.
“Upavāyatū” means may a soft, cool breeze blow, approaching and quenching the distress of the body. The rest is easy to understand.
In the fifth [case], there is nothing further to be said.
The commentary on the second *Aggi-sutta* and others is finished.
6. Commentary on the second *Saññā-sutta*: 49.
"Scraping with a hair-comb" refers to the dregs discarded after scraping the skin by those who are scraping the skin.

“I-making” (*ahaṅkāra*) is the act of making “I,” as in “I am this. “Mine-making” (*mamaṅkāra*) is the act of making “mine,” as in “this is mine. Therefore, he said, “from the view of I-making,” and so forth.
“Three kinds” refers to the three types of conceit (*māna*) by way of being superior, equal, or inferior.

In such passages as “the grouping of form is of one kind,” the word “kind” (*vidhā*) is used in the sense of a category or division. “In what kind do they say a person is virtuous? In what kind... [and so on].
In such passages as "they call one possessed of wisdom," it is the prefix *vi-* [that is intended]. In the passage, "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of *vidhā*. Which three?
The conceit 'I am superior' is a *vidhā*," it is conceit (*māna*) that is called "*vidhā*. Here too, conceit alone is intended. For conceit is so called because it burns;
since it burns in a threefold way according to the inferior and other grades, it is called "*vidhā*" because of burning (*dahanato*) and scorching (*upadahanato*) in that manner.
The commentary on the second Saññā-sutta is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the Methuna-sutta and others, 50–51.
Regarding the seventh [sutta]: "here" means in this world; "a certain one" means one person; "whether a recluse or a brahmin" refers to one by virtue of mere renunciation.
Whether a recluse or a brahmin by birth alone. "The attainment of the couple" means that which is to be entered into by two [persons] together;
the meaning is sexual intercourse. "He does not enter into it" is the connection [of the sentence].
"Anointing" is rubbing with unguents. "Massaging" is kneading. "He relishes" means he accepts. "He finds gratification in that" means he delights in the anointing and so forth. "He desires" means...

*Ichati*: desire. *Vittiṃ tuṭṭhiṃ*: satisfaction. "This too" (*idampi kho*): here, "this" (*idaṃ*) refers to the aforementioned relishing and so forth, spoken of as a single unit by way of its constituent parts such as the "bite" (*khaṇḍa*).
The word *pi* has the sense of conjunction, referring to what is about to be said; the word *kho* has the sense of emphasis. This is what is meant:
that which belongs to one who merely claims to be a celibate practitioner, even though there is no actual mutual sexual intercourse with a woman...

Anointing, bathing, massaging, and so forth. This too, because it brings about the state of being broken and so on for that holy life (*brahmacariya*), is "broken," "perforated," "flecked," and "mottled.
By thus falling into such states as being broken, he leads an impure holy life, not a pure one; he is fettered by the bond of sexual intercourse, not unfettered. Therefore...
Showing that there is no liberation from birth and so forth for him, he says, "This is called," and so on.
*Sañjagghati* means he laughs with a loud laugh due to the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Saṃkīḷati* means he sports by way of physical contact.
*Saṃkelāyati* means he dwells constantly fondling women. *Cakkhunā* means with his own eye. *Cakkhuṃ*... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The eye of a woman. "He gazes upon" means having approached, he gazes or looks at.
"Through a wall" means beyond a wall. Likewise, "through a fence": they say that a wall made of clay is a *kuṭṭa*, while one made of bricks is a *pākāra*.
Or, any wall reaching a person's height or measuring one and a half ratanas is a *kuṭṭa*; anything taller than that is a *pākāra*. "Of him" means...
"Of one who has declared himself a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). "In the past" means prior to the undertaking of the vow.

"By means of the strands of sensual pleasure" means by means of the components of sense-desire. "Endowed with" means well-endowed, joined together. "Possessed of" means fully equipped. "Sporting" means playing or being attended upon.
"Having made a resolve" means having wished for. Regarding "by virtue of moral conduct" and so forth, it refers to the undertaking of restraints, observances, and the like.
Virtue (*sīla*) is so called by way of non-transgression; the vow (*vata*) is likewise virtue, or rather, it is virtue as it is practiced through difficult conduct.

Alternatively, virtue has the characteristic of abstaining from various things considered improper, while the vow is the specific performance of duties such as eating at certain times for one who has undertaken those various observances.
In every respect, austerity (*tapas*) is difficult conduct. Abstinence from sexual intercourse is the holy life (*brahmacariya*); such is the commentary on the text here.
[These] are to be understood. The eighth [sutta] is self-evident.
The commentary on the Methunasutta and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the Dānamahapphalasutta.
52. In the ninth [section], “he gives a gift thinking ‘good is giving’” means he gives a gift thinking, “Giving is indeed good and beautiful.
For when one has given a gift and reflects upon it, joy, rapture, gladness, and so forth arise, while greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, and so forth are kept at a distance.
Now, by means of this gift, through the nourishment of favorable states and the removal of opposing states—
And because it serves both as an adornment for the mind in cultivation and as an accessory, it is said: "He gives that which has become an ornament and an attendant.
One is called a "non-returner to the jhānas" because, having attained jhāna, one does not arise again below the noble ones reborn in the Brahma-world.
Giving with the expectation, "I shall enjoy this after passing away," is [a gift] characterized by hope for the fruit in the next world.
Because it arises through the influence of previous conduct and is accompanied by an exceptional experience, it is called "the supreme gift of craving";

thus he said, "First, the gift of supreme craving. Because a gift is praised by the Buddhas and others, and must be given while establishing a sense of reverence and esteem, it is called "second, the gift of esteem. [It was given] by his ancestors, his father and grandfather...

It is said that the "third gift is that of moral shame and dread" because one must give by establishing moral shame and dread on the basis of the common nature of one's own person, thinking, "It is indeed unbecoming to abandon what has been previously given and done. Giving while perceiving thus:
"I am cooking, these others are not cooking; it is not right for me, while cooking, to fail to give to those who do not cook," one gives without remainder.
“Having prepared it, he gives,” thus it is said: “The fourth is the gift without remainder.
Because a gift should be given to those worthy of offerings by one who possesses the perception:
“Just as those ancient seers had those great sacrifices, so may this enjoyment of my gift be for me,” it is called “the fifth, the gift to those worthy of offerings. “This gift of mine...”
"By giving, the mind becomes serene," and so forth; for one who gives having thus generated rapture and joy, the gift is called "the access of joy" because it results in an abundance of joy.
Therefore, it is said: "The sixth is the gift of the access of joy.
The commentary on the *Dānamahapphala Sutta* is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta 53.
Regarding the tenth [sutta], the phrase “Having completed the rains residence and performed the *pavāraṇā*... he set out” is stated according to the opinion of the reciters of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
However, the reciters of the *Majjhima Nikāya* say: “When the time for entering the rains residence was approaching, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, departed from Jetavana...”

He set out on his journey. Because he had departed at an improper time, the King of Kosala and others began to try to stop him, for it is the custom of the Buddhas to wander only after the *pavāraṇā* ceremony.
Anticipating Puṇṇā’s correct practice, the Blessed One said, "What will you do by reason of my turning back? Then Puṇṇā... [and so forth] ...went forth. Here, the merchant—
Hearing that "the Blessed One has turned back because of Puṇṇā," he freed that slave-girl and established her in the position of his daughter.
She requested the going-forth and went forth; having gone forth, she applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
Then the Teacher, knowing her state of having commenced insight, uttered this illuminating verse:
“Fill yourself with the true Dhamma, like the moon on the fifteenth day;
with perfected wisdom, you shall bring an end to suffering.
At the conclusion of that verse, she attained arahantship and became a renowned female disciple. The rest here is easily understood.
The commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāyañña Vagga is finished.
The First Fifty is finished.
6. Abyākatavagga 1–2.
Commentary on the Abyākata Sutta, etc., 54–55.
The first [sutta] of the sixth chapter is easily understood. In the second, [the Buddha speaks of] that which produced his personal existence in a past life.

"Kamma" refers to the fivefold cycle of kamma together with its requisites as it has been handed down: "In the previous existence of kamma-becoming, delusion is ignorance, the exertion is volitional formations, attachment is craving, the approaching is clinging, and volition is becoming.
"May there be no present selfhood for me now" refers to the present [existence] together with consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
He speaks of the fivefold round of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). "That which exists" (*yatthika*) means that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
Therefore he says "become" (*bhūta*); for it is called "become" because it is produced by conditions.

"I abandon that" means that by abandoning the desire and lust bound to it, I abandon and relinquish it precisely by way of establishing its nature as not arising again in the future. "The yellowed" (*haritanta*)...
It is simply green. The word *anta* (end) is used here as a suffix to extend the compound, as in the expression “the forest-end discourse” (*vananta-suttanta*).
The meaning is that it extinguishes [the fire] by resorting to the all-green grass and so forth. *Pathanta* means a great highway. *Selanta* means a mountain. *Udakanta* means water.
Or, “a delightful portion of ground” refers to a secluded, open area of land free from grass, shrubs, and the like.
"Without nutriment" means without conditions, without clinging. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Abyākata-sutta and others is finished.
3. Commentary on the Tissa-brahmā-sutta.
56. But in the third [case], since such places are secluded yet limited and too far away, he said:
"The very last and most remote. Those that exist at the end are "terminal" (*antima*); those that are terminal are themselves "remote" (*pariyantima*).

By both terms, he demonstrates excessive distance. "Establishing in the act of attention" means causing the faculty to function with evenness, bringing it to a state of equilibrium of the faculties (*indriyasamata*).

It is so named. Concentration associated with insight-consciousness, even though it lacks the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*), is called "signless" (*animitta*) because it is devoid of the signs of permanence and so forth;
thus he says, "The 'signless' is strong insight-concentration.
The commentary on the *Tissabrahmā-sutta* is finished.
4–7. Commentary on the *Sīhasenāpati-sutta* and others (57–60).

In the fourth [verse], "vile" (*kucchita*) refers to the ignoble miser (*kadariya*). Indeed, there is nothing as vile or utterly base as stubborn stinginess, because it acts as a negation of all that is wholesome, which is the very foundation of all virtue. The remainder here, including the fifth verse and those following, is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the *Sīhasenāpati-sutta* and others is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Pacalāyamāna Sutta* 61.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "you should attend to the perception of light": whether by day or by night, you should attend to the light of the sun, fire, moon, gems, and so forth, as "light.
This is what is meant: [attend to] the light of the sun, moon, and so on, both by day and by night.
You should attend to what has been perceived precisely according to the manner in which it was perceived; you should fix it in the mind.

Just as for one who has well-developed the kasiṇa of light, that light of the kasiṇa stands present at night whenever and for as long as desired, by means of which you may establish the perception of day there, and you may become free from sloth and torpor as if it were actually daytime. Therefore he said: "Just as..."
"By day and likewise by night. Thus, "with a mind open" means with a mind that is not shut off, because it is not shut off by the veil of sloth and torpor (*thina-middha*).
"Unenveloped" means not bound on all sides, not covered over. "Together with light" refers to the light of clear knowledge (*saññā-obhāsa*).

Whether it be the light for dispelling sloth and torpor, the light of the *kasiṇa*, or the light of the preliminary work (*parikamma*), it is the light [that serves to remove] the defilements (*upakkilesa*).
All this light, as it were, is born of knowledge. Those duties which, if not performed, make a person utterly destitute must necessarily be done.
As for those which may be omitted when circumstances do not permit, they are called "duties" (karaṇīyāni) because they ought to be performed when the opportunity arises;
thus he said, "the other duties. Alternatively, they are called "duties" (karaṇīyāni) because they are actions that deserve to be done.
They also say that other duties [are included].
Controversial talk proceeding in such a manner is as follows: "You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya.
How could you understand this Dhamma and Vinaya? You have entered upon a wrong course; I am [the one who has entered the right course]."

The discourse that proceeds thus: “You have practiced rightly; what is consistent for me is inconsistent for you; you said later what should have been said first, and you said first what should have been said later;
your habitual practice has been overturned; your argument has been refuted; you are defeated.
Go forth to seek release from your position, or provide an explanation if you are able. In this context, “what is consistent for me” means:
The meaning is: my words are coherent, well-connected, endowed with purpose, and endowed with reason. Alternatively, "coherent" means not contradictory in their sequence.
"Incoherent for you" means your words are incoherent and ill-connected.
"That which was long-practiced by you has been overturned" means that which was well-mastered through your long-standing practice has, by my single word alone—
"Turned back and standing overturned"—the meaning is that you do not understand anything at all.
"A charge has been brought against you"—I have brought a fault upon your doctrine. "Go for the sake of escaping the challenge"—go, wander about;
the meaning is that go and train yourself by going here and there. "Or refute it, if you are able"—if you yourself are capable, then now...
The meaning is: "explain it thus.
It is called *taṇhāsaṅkhaya* (the destruction of craving) because craving is completely exhausted therein; [it means] "in that [destruction].

And regarding the term *taṇhāsaṅkhaye*, he says "taking that as its object" to show that this is a locative case used in the sense of an objective domain (*visaye bhummam*). "By way of having a liberated mind" means by way of the mind being dissociated from all defilements (*saṃkilesa*).
"In the later stage, the 'path' (paṭipadā) is the realization of the Noble Truths. Since that path has the range of practicing the Dispensation as its domain and must be personally realized, he asks:
'Teach me the preliminary path in brief. "Because it has transcended the limit known as destruction and decay due to its unshakable nature, it is 'ultimate' (accantā).
That very state is the 'ultimate goal' (accantaniṭṭhā) because its intrinsic nature is such that there is no further decline."

Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘one whose goal is absolute’ and ‘one whose goal is constant. For there is no such thing as the impairment of vision regarding the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma) that has been penetrated.
Because absolute security from the four yokes (yoga) belongs to him, he is ‘one who has attained absolute security from the yokes’ (accanta-yogakkhemī).
Because he has completed the holy life (brahmacariya) of the Path and because its nature is not subject to decline, he is ‘one who practices the holy life absolutely’ (accanta-brahmacārī).”

One who is a complete practitioner of the holy life (*accantabrahmacārī*). Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'one who constantly practices the holy life'. "The consummation" refers to the consummation of the holy life of the Path and the consummation of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

"The five aggregates" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*). For here, with reference to the whole of personal existence (*sakkāya*), it says "all phenomena" (*sabbe dhammā*).
This was stated because the object of insight (vipassanā) is intended here. Therefore, the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu) should also be understood as belonging to that same category.
Thus the Blessed One said: “They are not fit for misapprehension. They are not suitable for misapprehension—that is, for the clinging (ajjhosāna) that thinks, “This is mine, this is my self.
In such phrases as “It is indeed sufficient to become disenchanted, sufficient to become dispassionate,” the word *alaṃ* also carries the sense of being appropriate.
He said, "It is not appropriate," meaning that it does not hold true. "They occur" means they come into being.

Even though these two purifications—the third and the fourth—are wisdom consisting of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-paññā*), nevertheless, because they involve the seeing of mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) together with its conditions, when there is the grasping of conditions, [mentality-materiality] is impermanent due to having conditions;
through the impermanence of mentality-materiality, there is suffering; and what is suffering is non-self (*anattā*). This is the meaning.
"The three characteristics are indeed very clearly manifest," thus he said: "One directly knows [them] as 'impermanent, suffering, non-self' by means of full understanding through knowledge.

Likewise, with the phrase "by means of full understanding through investigation," he applies this to name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in the sense that it is not fit for adherence because of its impermanent nature and so forth;

it does not refer to the qualities that are the requisites for direct knowledge and wisdom. For the three characteristics, which are already implied by the meaning of the former [full understanding], [are here applied].
[The text] grasps [the object] because that [insight] consists in the discernment of specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa-sallakkhaṇa*).

By means of the second [type of insight], through the imposition of the three characteristics upon it according to its own nature, there occurs the state of "comprehension" (*sammasana*) by way of the application of those three characteristics. Because it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness and is merely a direct impact, it is even slight;

yet, because the discernment of form (*rūpa*) is coarse, [the author] shows the discernment of the formless (*arūpa*). And while showing this, because feeling (*vedanā*) is proximate [to that discernment], specifically—

He demonstrates [this] by producing it through the mode of feeling of the Elder, due to his being stained by the essence of pleasure and his mind being attached to the gratification of existence (*bhava*).

"Fading away through destruction" (*khayavirāga*) means the fading away consisting of destruction, which is the crumbling of formations (*saṅkhāra*); that *nibbāna* by depending upon which there is a complete fading away from all formations is "absolute fading away" (*accantavirāga*).
"Also in the case of the contemplation of cessation" (*nirodhānupassimhipi*) refers even to the term "contemplation of cessation."
Having indicated that "the same method applies," he explains it in part by saying, "Cessation also... is indeed twofold.
He states that the relinquishing of the aggregates occurs by way of the abandoning of the defilements bound to them;
for in whatever manner insight abandons the defilements, in that same manner it is fit to be described as abandoning the aggregates which are the signs of those [defilements].
It says: “For it... [as before]... relinquishes. “As an object” means by way of making it an object through the accomplishment of its function.
For in this way, the absence of both leaping forward (*pakkhandana*) and relinquishing (*vossagga*) in other states that take Nibbāna as their object—distinct from the Path—is established.
Or rather, it is by two reasons: by relinquishing and by leaping forward. “It” refers to the Path. The relinquishing of all aggregates.
It should be understood by way of the abandoning of defilements bound up with that [object].

Or rather, it is said "the mind leaps forward" (pakkhandati) with reference to the consciousness associated with the path, because the path abandons both defilements and the aggregates by means of their total eradication.
Therefore, leaping forward, relinquishing, and relinquishment should be understood respectively according to the functions of insight and the path.
"One who possesses both" refers to one who possesses insight (vipassanā) and one who possesses the path (magga). For, according to such statements as "By the contemplation of impermanence,
one abandons the perception of permanence," just as the relinquishment and renunciation of defilements is obtained through insight,
so too must the relinquishment and renunciation of the aggregates that are to be produced by those defilements in the future be stated.

The relinquishing of the plunge (*pakkhandanapaṭinissagga*), however, should be understood by way of the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*), which is the absolute cause found on the path.
On the path, moreover, both of these are obtained in their primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) because they have arrived through the proper method (*ñāyāgata*).
Therefore he said: "A person possessing both," and so forth. According to the intention of the questioner: "Nothing in the world..."
Regarding the phrase "he clings," it is said here that he rejects clinging by way of sensual clinging (kāmupādāna), thus stating, "he does not cling by way of craving (taṇhā).
Alternatively, since there can be no clinging by way of views (diṭṭhi) in the absence of clinging by way of craving, it is stated simply as "by way of craving.
"He does not misapprehend" means he does not take it up; or rather, [it refers to] misapprehension by way of views, such as [thinking] "it is permanent," and so forth.
He does not misapprehend it. "He spoke in brief" means he spoke without elaboration, according to the listener's inclination.
The commentary on the *Pacalāyamāna Sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Mettasutta*.
62. "In the phrase *navame mā, bhikkhave, puññānaṃ*, the word *mā* is a particle used as a prohibition.
The word *puñña* occurs in reference to the fruit of merit in such passages as: 'Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) that this merit increases.
It also occurs in such passages as: 'Monks, when a person immersed in ignorance performs a meritorious volitional formation (*puññaṃ saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti*),' and so forth."

In such passages as “consciousness is bound for merit,” it refers to the wholesome volition (kusalacetanā) that constitutes the bases of meritorious action—namely, the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving, the basis consisting in virtue, and the basis consisting in meditation—as taught in the Sutta: “Bhikkhus, there are these three bases of meritorious action. However, here [in this context], it refers to the rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) which is a specific type of happy destination, as in the case of wholesome deeds pertaining to the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere. In such passages as “consciousness is bound for merit,” it refers to the rebirth-existence that constitutes a particular kind of happy destiny.

In such passages as “Bhikkhus, there are these three bases of meritorious action: the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving, the basis consisting in virtue, and the basis consisting in meditation,” it refers to wholesome volition. But here...

It should be understood as wholesome states belonging to the three planes. Regarding the phrase "he was afraid," there are two kinds of fear here: the fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*) and the fear of trepidation (*sārajjabhaya*).

In this context: "Bhikkhus, even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, and dwell for a long time in lofty palaces—even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part experience fear, agitation, and terror..."

The fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*) is mentioned in the passage beginning with "they fall into [it]. The fear of trepidation (*sārajjabhaya*) is mentioned in such passages as "there was indeed fear, there was trepidation, there was horripilation.

Here too, it is precisely the fear of trepidation. This is the meaning here: "Monks, for a long time there has been restraint of body and speech, the fulfillment of duties and services, sitting alone, lying down alone, mastery over the sense faculties, and the ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*)."
"Do not be afraid; do not fall into fear or terror" regarding those merits that must be practiced continuously by a bhikkhu— such as the restraint of the mind, mindfulness and clear comprehension,

and the exertion of energy through application to the meditation subject— for these [merits] bestow the happiness of Nibbāna in the future life, despite the fear of obstructing certain forms of happiness in this present life.
"Do not fear on account of merits. Here, this is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
Now, showing the reason why one should not fear from that [merit], he said, "Of this happiness," and so forth.

In that context, the word *sukha* occurs in the sense of the root of happiness, as in such passages as, "The arising of Buddhas is a happiness; dispassion toward the world is a happiness. And because... [the passage continues].
In such passages as, "Mahāli, form is pleasant, it is followed by pleasure, it has descended into pleasure," it refers to a pleasant object (*sukhārammaṇa*).
In such passages as, "To this extent, monks, it is not easy to reach by description how far the heavens are pleasant," it refers to the state that is a condition for pleasure (*sukhapaccayaṭṭhāna*).

In such passages as, "The accumulation of merit is pleasant," it refers to the cause of pleasure (*sukhahetu*). In such passages as, "These states are dwellings pleasant in the present life," it refers to... [the dwelling itself].
In the phrase "without affliction" (*abyāpajje*), it refers to non-affliction. In such passages as "Nirvana is the supreme happiness," it refers to Nirvana.

In such passages as "With the abandoning of pleasure," it refers to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). In such passages as "Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, peaceful, this is indeed spoken of as happiness," it refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhāvedanā*).
In such passages as "Ānanda, these two feelings have been described by me in a figurative sense as pleasant feeling and painful feeling," it refers to desirable pleasures.

In such passages as “The ripening of merit is pleasant,” it refers to desirable ripening. Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to desirable ripening. Regarding the terms “of the desirable” (*iṭṭhassa*) and so forth:

it is “desirable” (*iṭṭha*) because it is to be wished for and because it is the opposite of the undesirable. It is “lovely” (*kanta*) because it is desirable, because it is cherished by the mind, and because it enters [the mind].
It is “dear” (*piya*) because it is to be loved and because it satisfies. It is “endearing” (*manāpa*) because it is to be esteemed and because it increases the mind.
And the meaning should be understood as "and what is pleasing. Regarding the expression "merits, merits":
this statement is a designation and a name for happiness, for the desirable result.

By saying "merits, [which are] this very happiness," he speaks of the figurative treatment of the cause as non-different from the fruit. Having heard that the fruit of merits performed and accumulated is necessarily to come to pass...
He exhorts them to perform meritorious deeds with diligence and respect, and inspires in them a sense of earnestness toward such practice.

Now, illustrating the exceedingly sublime ripening of merit experienced for a long time—which had been concealed by other existences—by means of the meritorious deed he himself performed during his time as Sunetta, making that matter more evident, he says: "I recall..."
He said, “I recall,” and so forth. Therein, “I recall” (*abhijānāmi*) means I know by means of distinguished knowledge;
I awaken to it through direct experience. “For a long time” (*dīgharattaṃ*) means for a long period. “Of merits” (*puññānaṃ*) refers to wholesome states such as giving and the like.

“Seven years” (*satta vassāni*) means seven years. “Loving-kindness mind” (*mettacittaṃ*): it is called *mettā* because one is moistened (*mijjati*); the meaning is that one is made smooth. It is that which exists toward friends (*mitte bhavā*).
It is called *mettā* because it proceeds toward a friend (*mitta*). From the perspective of its characteristics and so forth, however, it has the characteristic of proceeding in a mode of welfare;
its function is to provide welfare; its manifestation is the subduing of ill-will; and its proximate cause is the perception of beings as being agreeable.

Its perfection is the pacification of ill-will; its failure is the arising of affection. "Having developed a mind of loving-kindness" means a mind accompanied by loving-kindness; it is expressed by way of the term "mind."

"Samādhi is said [to be attained]" means having both arisen and increased the concentration of loving-kindness (*mettā-samādhi*), which is the divine abiding of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*).

"Seven eons of dissolution and evolution" refers to seven great eons (*mahākappa*). By the mention of dissolution and evolution, the periods of subsistence during dissolution and subsistence during evolution are also included.
"This world" refers to the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*). "While it was dissolving, indeed" means while it was dissolving; *sudam* is merely an expletive particle.

The meaning is "when it is failing. Some also read, "It is said that [this occurs] at the time of the world's dissolution (*saṃvattaṭṭhāne*). *Kappe* means "at the time. For by the term *kappa*, time is expressed;
when time is exhausted, everything indeed comes to an end. As it is said: "Time devours all beings, including the Brahmās themselves.
Because it is stated, "May I go to the Ābhassara realm," the emergence of the *kappa* here is according to the mode of destruction by fire (*tejo-saṃvaṭṭa*).
It should be understood as follows: "One who goes to the Ābhassara realm" means that by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) there, one goes to the Ābhassara Brahma-world;

thus, one is "one who goes to the Ābhassara realm. "When [the world] is evolving" (*vivaṭṭamāne*) means when it is being established. "I am reborn in an empty Brahma-palace" means that because no other being has been born there, it is empty—that which is designated as the plane of the first jhāna.
The Brahma-palace arises first; I am reborn there, I arrive there, by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

He is called "Brahmā" in the sense of being distinguished from beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and in the sense of being born from the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) through the cultivation of qualities in various ways.
Because he is greater than the *Brahmapārisajja* and *Brahmapurohita* deities, he is the "Great Brahmā" (*Mahābrahmā*).

Because he stands having overcome them for that very reason, he is "the Overcomer" (*abhibhū*). Because he is not overcome by anyone through any quality whatsoever, he is "the Unconquered" (*anabhibhū*).

*Aññadatthu* is a particle used as an emphatic expression. He is a "Seer" (*dasa*) because of his seeing; the meaning is that he is capable of seeing the past, future, and present, and thus sees with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) whatever is to be seen. [He surpasses] the other Brahmās by the power of his own development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

The phrase "I am a master" (*vasavattī*) should be connected with "my mind abides under my control. At that time, it is said, although the Bodhisatta was already an attainer of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he observed the welfare of beings and the fulfillment of his own perfections;

thus, generating a preference for those very two levels of jhāna, he wandered from one existence to another by way of the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā-brahmavihāra*). Therefore it is said: "Seven..."
“...for years... [and so on] ...a lord of power.

Thus, having demonstrated the greatness of the ripening of merit pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with “thirty-six times” in order to show the ripening of merit pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Therein, “I was Sakka” means thirty-six times.
For thirty-six times, without being reborn elsewhere, he was continuously Sakka, the lord of the gods and king of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Regarding the phrase "he was a king" (*rājā ahosi*), he is called a "king" (*rājā*) because he delights the world through four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy.
He causes the wheel-treasure to turn, he proceeds by means of the four wheels of prosperity, and by those [wheels] he [overcomes] others...

He causes [the wheel] to turn; and because he possesses the turning of the wheels of postures for the welfare of others, he is a *cakkavattī*. Here, "king" (*rājā*) is the general term, while "wheel-turner" (*cakkavattī*) is the specific one.
He acts according to the Dhamma, thus he is "righteous" (*dhammika*); the meaning is that he conducts himself by way of the proper method and equanimity.
Having obtained the kingdom through the Dhamma alone, he has become a king, thus he is a "Dhamma-king" (*dhammarājā*), [referring to] the tenfold wholesome Dhamma.
He is called *dhammika* because he is devoted to the royal duties that are not censured. He is called a *dhammarāja* because he gladdens the entire world by means of that very *dhamma*.
Alternatively, he is *dhammika* through performing the *dhamma* that benefits others, and a *dhammarāja* through performing the *dhamma* that benefits himself.
Since a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) acquires sovereignty through *dhamma* and justice, and not through what is contrary to *dhamma*, it is therefore said:
“Because he has obtained sovereignty in accordance with the Dhamma, he is a ‘Dhamma-king.
Because it extends to the edge of the ocean in the four directions, it is called ‘the four-cornered’; thus he said, “In the east... [and so on] ...
the lord,” referring to the great earth on various islands therein. “The Victor” means one who has conquered that which is to be conquered, such as desire, anger, and the like.
The meaning is: having conquered and standing victorious over both the internal rival kings and the external host of enemies.

Although there is indeed no battle for a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) with anyone, he is nevertheless described as "one who has won the battle" because of the accomplishment of victory that must be achieved through combat.
Or, the realm is endowed with the fourfold marvelous quality.
Having attained a state of steadfastness (*thāvariya*) toward this king that cannot be shaken by anyone— a state of firm devotion— or having attained a state of steadfastness, a state of stability,
for his own kingdom through his righteous conduct, he is one who has "attained the steadfastness of the realm" (*janapadatthāvariyappatto*).
For when a cruel king oppresses the world with taxes, punishments, and the like, people abandon the central provinces and flee to mountains, oceans, shores, caves, and so forth.
Relying on [the borderlands], they establish their dwellings in the frontier regions.
When King Atimuduka is oppressed by thieves who plunder wealth with violence, his people abandon the frontier and establish their dwellings in the midst of the central provinces.
Thus, under such a king, the country does not attain stability.
"Endowed with the seven treasures" means being possessed of the seven treasures beginning with the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*).

For among them, the Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) conquers what is unconquered by means of the wheel-treasure; he traverses the conquered realm with ease by means of the elephant and horse treasures;
he protects the conquered realm by means of the counselor-treasure (*pariṇāyakaratna*); and he experiences the pleasure of enjoyment through the remaining [four] treasures. First...

His application of the power of energy is fulfilled by the preceding [jewels], his application of the power of counsel by the latter [jewel], and his application of the power of sovereignty is perfectly complete through the jewels of the elephant, the horse, and the householder.
He experiences the pleasure of enjoyment through the jewels of the woman and the gem, and the pleasure of lordship through the remaining ones.
Specifically, for him, the first three succeed through the influence of kamma produced from the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*), while the middle ones...

By the power of karma produced from the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha-kusalamūla*), and by the power of karma produced from the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha-kusalamūla*) as the final one.
"Brave" (*sūra*) means possessing capability; the meaning is "fearless," which is why he says "the fearless. "Factor" (*aṅga*) means a cause.
That cause by which they might be called "heroes" is the "hero-factor" (*vīraṅga*). Therefore he says, "This is the name for energy (*vīriya*). As far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains...
Because it revolves like a wheel, it is said to be "bounded by the ocean and having the Cakkavāḷa mountain as its limit.

By the phrase "without punishment" (*adaṇḍena*), the non-infliction of both monetary fines and corporal punishment is expressed. By the phrase "without weapons" (*asatthena*), the non-engagement of an army in combat is expressed;
thus, in order to show both of these, the words beginning with "not by punishment" (*na daṇḍena*) and so forth were spoken. This is what was stated.
There were those who, having committed offenses, would seize even a hundred or a thousand beings; they ruled by means of fines and punishments.
Those who administered cutting and tearing [punishments] ruled by means of the sword and punishment. But I, having abandoned both kinds of punishment, dwelt without punishment.
Those who harmed others with a one-edged blade or other weapons ruled by means of the sword.

They are indeed said to "cause [others] to do. But I, without causing even as much blood as a tiny fly might drink to flow from anyone by means of the sword, having been welcomed by rival kings with the words, "Come, Great King," and having thus conquered the earth in the manner described, I dwelt there;
having completely conquered it, I lived as its sovereign.

Thus the Blessed One, having made himself a witness by body and having proclaimed the greatness of the ripening of merits, now spoke the passage beginning with “Behold, the ripening of merits,” demonstrating that very same matter through the composition of verses.
“O seekers of happiness” (*sukhesino*) is a term of address; by it, he calls out to beings who are in search of happiness.
In the original text (*pāḷi*), however, where one would have said “Behold! (*passatha*), it says “Behold! (*passa*).

It should be understood that "the proficiency of speech" (*vacanabyatti*) has been accomplished. Because they place a weapon upon the chests of men and carry away desired wealth and so forth, or because of their violent conduct, they are "violent persons" (*sāhasika*);
their action is "violent action" (*sāhasikakamma*). One who is a lord over the earth is "the earth";
thus he said, "the master of the earth" (*puthavisāmika*).
The commentary on the *Mettasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Bhariyāsutta*. 63.

In the tenth [verse], "loud-sounding" and "great-sounding" means that because they have risen upwards (*uddhaṃ uggatattā*) and because they are spread out widely (*uccaṃ patthaṭattā*), they are great and indistinguishable (*avinibbhoga*).
They speak while making sounds that cannot be grasped by separating them.

For even the sound of speech, when produced simultaneously by many people, is difficult to understand in terms of its meaning or its specific phonemes; it reaches the range of hearing merely as a great roar.
"In the catching of fish" means either in seizing [them] after plundering the fish, or in the plundering of the fish themselves.
For at the place where the fishermen have set down their baskets of fish, the great multitude gathers and makes a loud clamor, crying out, “Give me another fish here!
Give me a fish-spear! You have given a large one to him, but a small one to me!
It was with reference to this that it was said: “At the place where the fishermen have lowered their baskets of fish and stood.”
Even when a net has been cast into that place for the purpose of catching fish, the fishermen and others raise a great clamor, saying, "Has it entered?
Has it not entered? Is it caught? Is it not caught? It is with reference to this that it was said: "In the net... there is a great clamor.
"Duty to be performed" (*kattabba-vatta*) refers to the tasks to be done, such as the tending of the feet. "Harsh" (*khara*) means by way of the mind.
And harsh in speech. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the Bhariyā-sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Kodhana-sutta.
64. Regarding "causing enmity" (*sapattakaraṇa*): it means that which is to be done by enemies (*sapattehi*). "One who is prone to anger" (*kodhana*) means one whose nature is to be angry.
"This one who is angry" (*kodhano ayam*): here, *ayaṃ* is merely a particle. "Overcome by anger" (*kodhapareta*) means followed by anger, or overwhelmed by it.
"He becomes ill-favored" (*dubbaṇṇo va hoti*): even if he is naturally handsome or adorned and prepared [with ornaments], by way of facial distortions and so forth—

He becomes ugly indeed. To show that for one overcome by anger this result is certain both now and in the future, the restrictive term “or disfigured” (*dubbaṇṇo vā*) was used, and then it was stated again as “overcome by anger.
“Having a nature of disgrace” means having a state of ill-repute. “Producing harm” means producing harm for oneself and for others. “From within” means...

"From within" means from the mind. "People do not understand that" means this great multitude of fools does not know that which is called anger—a cause of fear consisting in the arousal of the mind toward the production of harm—which has arisen from within, inside one's own mind.
"Yattha" (wherein) is a nominative form used in the sense of a locative; it refers to the time when anger overcomes [one].
The connection is: "then that man becomes utterly blind. Alternatively, *yaṃ* is a word expressing the reason;
because anger, when arising, "overcomes" (sahate) the man—that is, it masters him—therefore he then becomes utterly blind. This is the meaning:

"when he is angry," due to the absolute syntactic connection between the words *yaṃ*, *taṃ*, and *tadā*. Or else, *yaṃ* refers back to the action (*kiriyā*). Regarding the word *sahate*, this is [the function] of anger...
"Sahana" means overcoming; the meaning is that this is the blinding darkness of existence (*bhava*). Alternatively, when anger overcomes or masters a person, then for him there is blinding darkness.
Consequently, one who is angry does not know the goal (*attha*);
one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.
“Bhūna” means growth; the destruction of that is “ghāta. Those [things] which have this [destruction] are “bhūnahaccāni. Therefore he said, “those whose growth has been destroyed.
To clarify the very same meaning expressed by the word *dama*, he spoke the words “by wisdom and energy, by views,” showing [this];
thus he said, “By what kind of self-mastery (*dama*)? for the word *dama* has many meanings. [As it is said: “Tamed by truth, endowed with self-mastery...”

In the passage, “A master of the Vedantas, one who has lived the holy life,” self-restraint (*dama*) is spoken of as the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), because it is said that “one tames the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth.

In the passage, “If there were truth, self-restraint, generosity, and patience—if more than these were found here,” wisdom (*paññā*) is self-restraint, because it is said that “it tames and abandons defilement (*saṃkilesa*). [And in the passage: “By giving, by self-restraint, by self-control, by speaking the truth...”
In the passage, "There is merit; there is the arrival of merit," the Uposatha observance is *dama* (taming), because it "tames bodily actions and so forth by means of fasting.

In the passage, "Punna, being endowed with this *damūpasama* (taming and pacification), you will be able to dwell in the Sunāparanta country," *dama* refers to patience as endurance (*adhivāsanakkhanti*), [which subdues] anger, resentment, malice, and so on.
Having established that [it] "tames" and "dispels," in the passage, "There is no taming here for one who desires pride,
nor is there wisdom for one who is unconcentrated," the term *dama* refers to the factors conducive to concentration, such as the factors of enlightenment,

because it is said, "The mind is tamed by this. Here too, based on the statement, "One should cut that off by means of taming, through wisdom, energy, and view," the words "wisdom," "energy," and "view" are expressed by the word *dama*.
The commentary on the Kodhana-sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Abyākata-vagga is finished.
7. Mahāvagga.
1–2. Commentary on the *Hiriottappa-sutta* and others. 65–66.
The first [sutta] of the seventh [chapter] is self-evident. In the second, "three dissolutions" refers to the three types of dissolution:

dissolution by water (*āposaṃvaṭṭa*), dissolution by fire (*tejosaṃvaṭṭa*), and dissolution by wind (*vāyosaṃvaṭṭa*). "Three limits of dissolution" refers to the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, and Vehapphala [heavens].
There are three limits of destruction. For when an eon is destroyed and perishes by means of fire, then everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by fire.
When it is destroyed by means of water, then everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water.
When it is destroyed by means of wind, then everything below the Vehapphala realm is dispersed by wind. As for its extent:
At all times, even a single Buddha-field perishes. There are three kinds of Buddha-fields:

the birth-field (*jātikkhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākkhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakkhetta*). Among these, the birth-field extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*);
it is that which trembles when the Tathāgata undergoes such events as his conception. The field of authority extends as far as a thousand million world-systems.
Wherever the *Ratana Sutta*, the *Khandha Paritta*, the *Dhajagga Paritta*, the *Āṭānāṭiya Paritta*, and the *Moraparitta*—the power of these protective spells (*paritta*) prevails.
Their sphere of influence is infinite and immeasurable, as it is said: "or as far as he might wish.
Thus, among these three types of Buddha-fields, one—the field of authority (*āṇā-khetta*)—is subject to destruction.
When that [world-system] is destroyed, the field of birth is likewise destroyed.
It perishes all at once, and it re-forms all at once.
"Three roots of dissolution" refers to the three causes of dissolution, namely lust, hatred, and delusion. For among the unwholesome roots, beginning with lust—
The world perishes when these [defilements] are predominant. For when passion (*rāga*) is more predominant, it perishes by fire;

when hatred (*dosa*) is more predominant, by water; and when delusion (*moha*) is more predominant, by wind. Some, however, say that when hatred is more predominant, it perishes by fire, and when passion is more predominant, by water.

Regarding the "three tumults" (*tīṇi kolāhalāni*): they are the tumult of the eon (*kappakolāhala*), the tumult of a Buddha (*buddhakolāhala*), and the tumult of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattikolāhala*). These are the three tumults.

In that context, the sound proclaimed by the deities, beginning with “At the end of one hundred thousand years, there will be the emergence of the aeon,” is called the *kappakolāhala* (the uproar of the aeon).

Deities wander along the paths of men, crying out: “At the end of one hundred thousand years from now, the world will be destroyed; friends, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity.”
“There will be a Buddha at the end of a thousand years”—this is what is known as the "Buddha-proclamation. Devas cry out:

“At the end of a thousand years from now, a Buddha, having appeared, will wander about teaching the Dhamma, surrounded by the Jewel of the Saṅgha who practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma.
And: “At the end of a hundred years, however, a Wheel-turning Monarch will appear.”

There is what is called the "clamor of the wheel-turning monarch. Deities proclaim: "In a hundred years from now, a wheel-turning king, endowed with the seven treasures, lord of the four continents, accompanied by a thousand followers, and capable of traveling through the air, will arise.

Because they do not endure for long, they are "not stable," meaning they lack stability due to their short duration, like bubbles on water and so forth. They are "devoid of consolation," meaning they lack any comfort, like drinking water in a dream or like sandalwood paste smeared over one's body.
"Upakappanamegha" refers to the cloud that destroys the eon (*kappa*).
For at the time when the eon is destroyed by fire, first of all, the great eon-destroying cloud arises and pours down one great rain over a hundred thousand million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
People, joyful and delighted, bring out all their seeds and sow them. But when the crops have been reduced to mere hoofprints of cattle—
When the rain-god utters a cry like that of a donkey among those born [in the sky], not even a single drop falls;
at that time, the rain is utterly cut off. Therefore it was said: "At that time, the seed sown... [not] even a single drop does the god rain.
Having heard the words spoken by the deities, beginning with, "After the passing of one hundred thousand years, the emergence of the world-age (kappa) will occur," for the most part—

Both humans and earth-deities, having become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and possessing hearts softened toward one another, perform meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and are reborn in the world of the devas;
thus, [the world] becomes empty starting from the Avīci hell.
"The five kinds of seeds" refers to root-seeds, trunk-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seed-seeds—these are the five.
Seeds have been produced. In this context, "root-seed" refers to *vacā*, *vacatta*, turmeric (*halidda*), ginger (*siṅgivera*), and so forth.
"Stem-seed" refers to the *assattha* tree, the *nigrodha* tree, and so forth. "Joint-seed" refers to sugarcane (*ucchu*), bamboo (*veḷu*), reeds (*naḷa*), and so forth.

"Apex-seed" refers to the *ajjuka* plant, the *phaṇijjaka* plant, and so forth. "Seed-seed" refers to early grains such as rice (*vīhi*) and so forth, as well as later grains such as mung beans (*mugga*) and black gram (*māsa*).

Because it serves as the specific cause for the production of something dissimilar when other conditions are present, the word *bīja* (seed), which is conventionally established for a noble fruit capable of sprouting,
is applied to the roots and so forth as well for the sake of establishing that same meaning. Therefore, in order to exclude [the application of the term] to the roots and so on,
it is stated with the qualification "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*), just as one says "matter-matter" (*rūparūpa*) or "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
Just as medicinal herbs, trees, bamboos, reeds, and so forth, have their limit in the ripening of their fruit.

In the phrases “yaṃ kadāci” and so on, *yaṃ* is merely a particle. *Kadāci* means “at some time. *Karahaci* is a synonym for that same word. *Dīghassa addhuno* means “of a long time. *Accayena* means “by the passing of. The rest here is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Hiri-ottappa-sutta* and others is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Nagaropama Sutta 67.

In the third [case], *paccantima* means "bordering" (*paccanta*). In such passages as, “The chariot has virtue as its equipment (*parikkhāra*), meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels,” the word *parikkhāra* is used in the sense of an ornament;
thus he said, “adorned with the ornaments of the city. It may also have the sense of a retinue.
It is indeed appropriate [to say "seven requisites of concentration"], as in such cases as [the phrase] "the seven requisites of concentration.
*Nema* refers to a spot of ground not struck by pillars and the like; thus he says "deep pits," meaning they have entered deep into the earth.
"Well-settled" means they have been properly placed after being buried in the ground.
“Anupariyāya” means that by which one goes around; it is itself a path, thus it is an *anupariyāyapatha*, a road that runs along the perimeter of a rampart.
Those who mount an elephant or cause it to be mounted are called *hatthārohā*.
For this includes everyone who, by whatever means, prepares a man for the act of mounting an elephant, as they perform that service for the elephant. Therefore he said, “all of them,” and so forth.
In this context, "elephant trainers" (*hatthācariya*) refers to those who instruct the elephants and their riders. "Elephant physicians" (*hatthivejja*) refers to elephant doctors (*bhisakka*).
"Elephant keepers" (*hatthibandha*) refers to those who protect the feet of the elephants. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes those who provide barley and other provisions for the elephants.
