The same principle applies here to "horsemen" (*assāroha*) and "charioteers" (*rathika*); "charioteers" (*rathika*) are those engaged with chariots, namely, the protectors of the chariots.

The *āṇirakkhā* are the protectors of the chariot’s linchpin. They are called *dhanuggahā* because they take up bows or cause others to take them up; they are archers and instructors in the art of archery.
Therefore he said: “The archers are the teachers of archery. They are called *celakā* because they go to battle with a cloth banner (*cela-paṭākā*).
Thus he said: “Those who go at the front of the battle carrying the victory-banner. Just as...
When the army is thus stationed, they cause it to waver and toss it here and there by means of making it tremble; thus they are called *calaka*.
Like hawks and other birds, they tear at the enemy host as if it were a lump of meat, cutting it apart with their boldness as great warriors and departing by leaping up;
thus they are called *piṇḍadāyaka*. In the second interpretation, they "tear at the mass" (*piṇḍe dayanti*), as if leaping up amidst the crowd of people.
"Gacchanti" means "those who give alms"—this is how the meaning should be understood. "Uggatuggatā" means exceedingly exalted by way of strength, speed, prowess, and so forth;
the sense is "highly uplifted. "Pakkhandanti" means entering the enemy army without being hindered due to their own heroic and brave nature;
the sense is that they are like great elephants endowed with strength, speed, power, and prowess.
"Great elephants. "Brave in solitude" means those who, being brave by their very nature, engage in battle while remaining alone. "With quivers" means equipped with arrows.
"A shield for protection" refers to a shield bound with leather, or a wooden board made of leather. "House-slave warriors" means warriors who are one's own slaves.
"Characterized by leaping forward" means characterized by leaping forward toward an object that is credible, thinking, "It is indeed so. "Characterized by serene confidence" means...

Faith characterized by conviction (*okappanā-saddhā*) has the characteristic of being convinced regarding an object that is to be believed in; it is the act of resolving after having entered into and leaped upon [the object].
Faith characterized by clarity (*pasāda-saddhā*) is the state of being clear and confident regarding an object that inspires confidence.

"This is the conformable dharma" (*anudhamma*) means this is the dharma that accords with the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "Abounding in disenchantment" (*nibbidā-bahula*) means abounding in weariness [with the conditioned]. Faith.

"It binds the provisions for the journey" means that this thing called faith binds the pack of provisions for a being who is traveling along the great road by way of death, entering upon the great wilderness, and plunging into the great abyss; it provides the travel-rations.
For having generated faith, one gives gifts, guards morality, and performs the observance-day rites. Therefore, this...
It is said: “Faith binds the provisions for the journey. *Sirī* means sovereignty (*issariya*).
For when sovereignty is present, wealth comes indeed from both land and water. Therefore it is said: “Sovereignty is the abode of wealth.
Faith is the second companion of a person as he goes to the world of the gods, the world of humans, and even to Nibbāna.
Faith is the companion; it accomplishes the task of a friend. In the phrase "a bowl of food, etc.," the word "etc.
(ādi) should be understood as including a second wife and so forth. "Possessing manifold flavors" means having many inherent natures, or performing many functions. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Nagaropama Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Dhammaññū Sutta (68).
In the fourth [verse], one who knows the Dhamma—namely, the discourses, verses, and so forth—is called *dhammaññū*.

By virtue of being skilled in the meaning through the words that clarify the meaning of various other discourses and phrases, such as those spoken in the form of discourses, verses, and so on, he understands the meaning.

One who knows is "one who knows the meaning" (*atthaññū*). One who knows oneself is "one who knows oneself" (*attaññū*), in the sense of knowing one's own measure thus: "I am so much in virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
One who knows the measure is "one who knows the measure" (*mattaññū*), because they know the proper measure in receiving, using, seeking, and relinquishing.
In the *Niddesa*, however, by means of the knowledge of measure in receiving alone, the knowledge of measure in using and so forth is implied.

The phrase "it happens" indicates simply knowing the proper measure in receiving. One who knows the time—thinking, "This is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for the attainment of yoga"—is called "one who knows the time. In that regard, five years is the time for recitation, ten years for questioning;
however, this is too restricted for one of very sharp wisdom, as such a period of time [would be insufficient] for him.

Because it is impossible to master [the entire teaching] at once, the time for formal recitation (*uddesa*) is ten years, twenty years for inquiry (*paripucchā*), and beyond that, one should apply oneself to the practice (*yoga*).
He is "one who knows the assemblies" (*parisaññū*) because he knows the eight kinds of assemblies, beginning with the assembly of kṣatriyas.
There are four kinds beginning with the assembly of bhikkhus; furthermore, the human assemblies beginning with the kṣatriyas are themselves fourfold.

Others say that there are eight kinds [of persons] by taking this [text] into account. Furthermore, in the *Niddesa*, the inclusion of the fourfold assembly beginning with the assembly of Khattiyas should be regarded as merely illustrative.
“For one who attends upon this person, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase;
therefore, this person is to be attended upon. By the opposite, another is not to be attended upon.”

One who knows persons to be associated with and not to be associated with is "one who knows the higher and lower among persons" (*puggalaparoparaññū*). For it is in this way that one is said to know the higher and lower—that is, the superior and inferior—among those persons.
Furthermore, in the *Niddesa*, it should be understood that the very exposition of persons to be associated with and not to be associated with constitutes the discourse on recluses (*samaṇakathā*).
The commentary on the Dhammaññū Sutta is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Pāricchattaka Sutta, etc., 69–70.
In the fifth [sutta], *patitapalāso* means one whose leaves have fallen. Here, the first refers to the state of being like a withered leaf (*paṇḍupalāsataṃ*), and the second—

Having stated that the first [stage] is the state of being withered leaves (*paṇḍupalāsata*) and the second the state of green leaves (*pannapalāsata*), the third as the state of having become a web (*jālakajātatā*), and the fourth as the state of having become a skeleton (*khārakajātatā*),
these are what is recited in the Canon (*pāḷi*). However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, specifically in the commentary on the *Mahāgovinda-sutta*, having cited this very same canonical passage,
it is shown that after stating the first as the state of withered leaves and the second as the state of green leaves, the third is the state of having become a web, and the fourth—
And the state of being covered with a network [of flowers] is shown. For it is said there:
"When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, they go to attend upon it for one year; from the time it becomes pale and withered, they become joyful. As it is said:
'Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra of the Tāvatiṃsa devas becomes pale and withered...'"
At that time, monks, the gods of the Thirty-three are delighted, thinking: "The Pāricchattaka coral tree is now pale-yellow;

before long it will become covered with leaves. When the Pāricchattaka coral tree of the gods of the Thirty-three is covered with leaves, when it has produced buds, when it has produced shoots, and when it has produced blossoms...
It becomes a bud; it becomes a bud, monks. At that time, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are delighted, thinking:
“The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has now become a bud; before long it will be in full bloom with all its blossoms.
In the *Līnatthappakāsinī* as well, the meaning is shown here in this way: “pannapalāso” means fallen leaves. “Khārakajāto” means...
“With buds that have become small”: for those very small buds with blue petals are called “khārakas.
“Covered with a network” means that by means of those same small buds, it has become entirely like a net, having produced a network. Some, however, explain the meaning as:
“‘Covered with a network’ means it has become like a single net. It is said that when the *pāricchattaka* tree takes up the *khāraka* buds—
It is entirely covered in sprouts, and those sprouts are brilliantly radiant with the color of glowing coral.
Because of that, it stands shining forth in every way. "Become a cluster" means a great mass has formed.
"Become a bud" means the state of being about to open immediately after the needle-like tip has emerged. "In full bloom" means completely blossomed and fully opened.
And this sequence is shown according to the usage of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas; no contradiction on the part of the Master is to be suspected here.
"The wind that plucks" (*kantana-vāta*) is the wind that cuts flowers due to the condition of the meritorious deeds of the devas. "It plucks" (*kantati*) means it cuts.
"The wind that receives" (*sampaṭicchana-vāta*) is the wind that catches the flowers as they are being cut. "Gathering" (*cinanto*)...
"Arranging it in various ways" means making it dense by way of the arrangement of diverse decorations. "Of a certain deity" refers to deities who are not well-known by name or clan.
"A mass of dust" (*reṇuvaṭṭi*) means a collection of dust. "Striking the pinnacle" means striking the summit of the Sudhamma hall.
"The power of spreading forth" refers to the spreading of the fame of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, reaching as far as the Brahma-world.
This is the majesty. "Based on the going-forth" means that the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) pertaining to the going-forth is also shown;
this is the intended meaning. The meaning in the phrases "based on the first jhāna," and so forth, should be understood in this same manner.
However, in this context, there is a delimitation from both sides because the delimitation has been shown as being below virtue and above Arahantship.
"It was said for this reason" means that for that reason these words beginning with "The fourfold purification of virtue is dependent on going forth" were spoken.
The sixth [section] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Pāricchattaka Sutta* and others is finished.
7. Commentary on the Bhāvanā-sutta 71.
In the seventh [sutta], because it is stated that one who is "not devoted to development" (*bhāvanam ananuyuttassa*) does not accomplish the goal, the term *sambhāvanattha* is used.
Here, the sense of *sambhāvanattha* is the sense of possibility, meaning "perhaps this might be so. For in common worldly usage, such is considered smooth or elegant speech.
The word *hoti* (is) is not used alone, but is spoken together with another number;
such speech is considered polished in the world, as in the expression, "two or three drops of water.

*Sammā adhisayitāni* means that she, without causing them any injury herself by means of her feet or other limbs, properly covers them from above for the purpose of warding off external dangers such as wind and so forth.
[The eggs] have been laid. Here, the prefix *adhi-* has the sense of "above" or "on top.
"Causing them to take up heat" means causing them to take up heat by means of the warmth of her own body for the purpose of exhausting their raw moisture and oiliness. Therefore he said, "made warm.
"Well-impregnated" means thoroughly impregnated in every way with the odor of a cock. Therefore he said, "made to take on the smell of a cock."

And here, it should be understood that right spreading and right perfuming are accomplished by the power produced by the accomplishment of right laying out and right spreading; for the other two succeed through right laying out alone.
Indeed, there is no separate cause for right spreading or right perfuming apart from right laying out.
It is stated [in this way] because the other two also succeed only together with that.
"By performing the threefold action" means by performing the threefold action consisting of right lying down and so forth.
Although no wish such as "O, may it be thus for me" might arise, nevertheless, because the cause has been accomplished, one is indeed capable [of success].
The construction is: "they emerge from the shell. To the question "Why are they capable?", he says: "For because of that... and so forth.
"Itself" refers to the eggs. They "ripen," meaning they reach maturity and the state of being fit for emergence.

Just as the thinning of the shell is the cause for light becoming manifest within, so too, through the thinning of the shell and the hardness of the claws, the tips of the nails, the mouth, and the beak, [the embryo emerges].

And it should be understood that the statement of the cause refers to the exhaustion of unripened oil. "Therefore" means because the light is manifest within and because it has itself reached maturity.
"The application of the simile" means the correct presentation of the meaning of the simile by means of the thing illustrated. "That" refers to the application of the simile.
"Thus" means in the manner now being described. "By way of the meaning" means by correlating and joining it with the meaning of the simile.
The sharpness of knowledge should be understood by way of its accomplishment through associated states;
for the sharpness of knowledge arises from its own nature and from its inclusion of mindfulness, its hardness from concentration, and its clarity from faith.

The "time of transformation" (*pariṇāmakāla*) is the time of powerful insight (*vipassanā*). The "time of growth" (*vaḍḍhikāla*) is the time of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*). For at that time, the insight that serves as the counterpart to conformity (*anuloma-ṭṭhāniyā*) is said to have "conceived," because the embryo of the Path (*magga-gabbha*) has been conceived therein. "Of that same nature" (*tajjātika*) means suitable for that application of insight.
The Teacher strikes the eggshell of ignorance, and the teaching likewise [strikes] that which resides within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
It strikes the eggshell of ignorance, not allowing it to remain in its place.
"Olambaka-saṅkhātaṃ" means what is designated as the *olambaka*-cord; for "pala" is the name of that cord.
Having moved it, one raises it up beneath the timber in order to detect defects. One who removes a boil (*gaṇḍa*) is a *palagaṇḍa*; by this [the term] "with the *pala*"...

He shows that in the phrase “gaṇḍahāra palagaṇḍo,” there is an indication by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound. "In the place of grasping" means in the place where it is to be grasped with the hand. It is a brief expression because bodily misconduct and so forth are properly cast off by means of this; thus, "the brief expression for going forth" (pabbajjā-saṅkhepa) is simply "going forth" itself. The complete destruction of the taints (*āsava*) is intended here as the benefit of insight (*vipassanā*).

By means of the winter season—which functions as the cause—or in the sense of the locative case (i.e., "in the winter"), the meaning is "during the winter. "They subside" means they have their fruits stilled.
Therefore he said, "they become rotten. The Dispensation (*sāsana*) is like the great ocean.
"Because of its unfathomable depth. Like a boat, the practitioner of yoga crosses over the great flood. "Like traveling around" means like traveling here and there all around.
"Of those being chewed up" means of those whose bonds are being carried away by water as if by one who is eating them.

"The state of attenuation" is the state of weakness due to the inability of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) to continue their activity. "By means of the joy and gladness of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*)."
By means of the rapture and gladness arising from insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

"While it is being cleared away" means while the meditation subject of insight is being cleared away through the successive stages of the path, or while it is being cleared away by the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*). It is being cleared away by equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
Its weakness is illustrated by the statement: "The fetters are easily pacified; they become putrid."
The commentary on the Bhāvanāsutta is finished. 8–9.
Commentary on the Aggikkhandhopama-sutta and others. 72–73.
In the eighth [verse], "passatha nū" means "look indeed. "Mahantaṃ" means vast. "Aggikkhandhaṃ" means a mass of fire.
“Burning” (*āditta*) means set ablaze. “Blazing up” (*sampajjalita*) means flaming on all sides, emitting sparks of flame.
“Become a mass of fire” (*sajotibhūta*) means having become a single mass of radiance due to the flames rising up on every side.
“What do you think of that?”—he asks this in order to obtain their consent, asking: “What do you think of this matter which is now being stated by me? Regarding what is here...
The Teacher brought forth the simile of embracing a mass of fire and the simile of embracing a maiden; in order to clarify that meaning, he said, "I announce," and so forth.

"Of one who is immoral" means of one who lacks virtue, who is devoid of moral conduct. "Of one who is of evil nature" means, precisely because of immorality, one whose disposition is base and whose character is inferior.
"Of one whose conduct is impure and suspicious" means being impure due to lack of purity, and thus being suspicious.
"Of one whose conduct must be guarded. For when an immoral person sees something even slightly improper, others become suspicious, thinking, "This must have been done by such-and-such a person.

Furthermore, seeing monks consulting together about some business, he must guard his own conduct out of his own suspicion, thinking, "Could it be that they are consulting because they know of the deed I have committed? Thus, he is one whose conduct must be guarded. "Of one whose actions are concealed": [this refers to...]
Of one whose conduct is to be concealed because it is shameful; "not a *samaṇa*" means not a true ascetic.

One who claims to be a *samaṇa* through the false pretension, "I too am a *samaṇa*," during the taking of voting sticks (*salākā*) and other such occasions. One who is not a practitioner of the holy life (*abrahmacārī*) due to his lack of noble conduct;

one who claims to be a practitioner of the holy life through the false pretension, "I too am a practitioner of the holy life," during the observance days (*uposatha*) and other such occasions. By means of a putrid action...
Because he has entered into the interior of a failure of virtue, he is "putrid within.

Because his six sense-doors are moistened by the constant flow of defilements such as lust, he is "lustful. Because he is covered with the refuse of lust and other defilements, and because he must be discarded by those possessed of virtue, he is "born of dregs.
"With a hair-rope" means with a rope made of hair; for that is indeed very rough. "He should rub" means by way of friction.
*Ghaṃseyya*: "Teladhotāya" means sharpened with oil. "Paccorasmin" means upon the breast;
the intended meaning is "facing the middle of the chest. "Ayosaṅkunā" means with a pair of tongs. "Pheṇuddehakaṃ" means having skimmed off the froth again and again;
the meaning is "having repeatedly raised up the froth. Thus, in brief, the commentary on the text here should be understood. The ninth [offense] is self-evident.
The commentary on the *Aggikkhandhopama-sutta* and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Araka-sutta*. 74.
In the tenth [sutta], "paritta" means limited. Therefore he said, "little, slight. It is the state of being a condition for the non-interruption of continuity.
Here, it is intended that the "essence" (rasa) refers to life; thus he said, "even because of the limitedness of its essence.
For it is dependent on that [life-force], as stated in the words: "Monks, whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.
It is also limited by the limitedness of the moment. In the ultimate sense, the moment of life for beings is extremely limited, lasting no more than a single moment of consciousness.

Just as a chariot wheel, though it is rolling, rolls upon only one part of its rim, and though it is standing still, stands upon only one part, even so the life of beings lasts for only a single moment of consciousness;
as soon as that consciousness has ceased, the being is said to have ceased. As it is said: "In a past moment of consciousness, he lived; he does not live, nor will he live."
In a future moment of consciousness, one has not lived, does not live, and will not live. In the present moment of consciousness, one has not lived, lives, and will not live.
“Life and the personal existence, and all pleasure and pain—”
Joined with a single state of mind, the moment passes swiftly.
"All those aggregates (khandhas) that have ceased for one who is dying here, or for one who is still living—all are alike; they have gone without reconnection."
“Not born by what is unborn, he lives by means of the present;
with the breaking up of the mind the world is dead—this is the ultimate designation.
Lightness means being light. Therefore it was said: “Because it arises and ceases quickly, it is light. Limited lightness.
Both of these, moreover, are synonyms for "little. For that which is little is both limited (*paritta*) and light (*lahuka*).

However, since "life-span" (*āyu*) is intended here, it is said to be "short" (*rassa*). Regarding the phrase "by means of wisdom" (*mantāya*), this locative expression is used in the sense of the instrumental;
thus he says: "It is to be understood by means of wisdom; the meaning is 'it is to be known by means of discernment' (*paññā*). Or alternatively, *mantāya* means "one should deliberate" (*manteyya*).
It is said; the meaning is that it should be reflected upon and examined with wisdom (*paññā*).
It should be known through wisdom—that life is fragile and characterized by much suffering and so forth.

And having known this, one should cut off all worldly attachments (*palibodha*), perform what is wholesome (*kusala*), and lead the holy life (*brahmacariya*). For there is no non-death for one who is born as a woman.
Whether for a little more than a hundred years, or a little less than a hundred years—living for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years—one with such a long lifespan is extremely rare.
One must go here and there to see someone and say, "So-and-so lives for such a long time. In this regard, Visākhā...
A female lay follower lives for two hundred years; likewise do the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the Brahmin Bāvari, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa.
The Elder Anuruddha, however, lived for one hundred and fifty years.
The Elder Bakkula lived for one hundred and sixty years; he was the longest-lived of all, and he too—
He did not live for two hundred years.
The commentary on the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
8. Vinaya Chapter: 1–8.
Explanations of the First Discourse on the Bearers of the Vinaya, etc., 75–82.
The first and second [discourses] of the eighth [chapter] are of obvious meaning. In the third, one is established in the characteristics of the Vinaya.
By means of a sense of shame, one stands firm in the characteristic of discipline (*vinaya*).

For one who lacks shame, even if he is very learned, might—out of a high regard for gain—misrepresent the tradition, proclaim what is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya as the Teacher’s instruction, and thereby cause great calamity to the Dispensation, even bringing about a schism in the Saṅgha or a rebellion within the Saṅgha.
But one who possesses shame, being conscientious and desirous of training, [does not do so] even for the sake of life.
Without contradicting the *tanti*, he illuminates the Dhamma and the Vinaya alone, establishing the Teacher’s instruction as something venerable.

Thus, one who possesses a sense of shame (*lajjī*), not abandoning nor stepping away from the Vinaya, stands and is firmly established in the characteristics of the Vinaya by virtue of that sense of shame. Regarding the term "unshakeable" (*asaṃhīro*):
here, one who is "shakeable" (*saṃhīro*) is one who—whether in the *pāḷi*, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), or from below or above—[is moved].
When questioned according to the sequence of the words, he falters and flounders;
he is unable to stand firm and, whatever is said by the opponent, he grants assent to it, abandoning his own position and adopting that of the other.
But one who, when questioned according to the sequence of the words—whether in the canonical text (pāḷi) or in the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), or by way of inversion from bottom to top—is...
He does not expand upon it nor does he waver; like one grasping a single hair with a pair of tongs, he replies, "This is what we say;
this is what our teachers say. He in whom both the text and its interpretation remain without being exhausted or depleted—like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel—is called [a master].

He is unshakable. However, because he does not concede whatever is said to him by another, and because he does not relinquish the unerring meaning grasped after having well-determined it for himself, it is said:
"He is unable to be made to relinquish what has been grasped.
The fourth and subsequent [qualities] are easy to understand.
The commentary on the first *Vinayadhara-sutta* and others is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Satthusāsana-sutta*. 83.

In the ninth [verse], *vivekaṭṭho* means secluded. Therefore he said, “having become distant. *Satiavippavāse ṭhito* means established in the non-abandonment of mindfulness regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
He stands without abandoning mindfulness. "With mind directed" means that, through lack of regard for both body and life, his mind is directed toward Nibbāna;
it is inclined toward it, slanted toward it, and leaning toward it.
The commentary on the Sutta of the Teacher’s Instruction is finished.
10. Commentary on the Sutta on the Settling of Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇasamatha-sutta) 84.

Regarding the tenth [section]: "Legal issues" (*adhikaraṇāni*) are so called because legal issues (*adhikarīyanti*) are settled therein. What are they that are settled? They are the methods of settling (*samatha*).
How are they settled? By means of the methods of settling. Therefore, it is said: "Legal issues [are settled] by way of those methods of settling. Thus he says: "Legal issues..."
"...they settle," and so forth. "Of those that have arisen, of those that have arisen" means of those that have occurred, of those that have occurred.

"For the purpose of settling" (*samathattha*) means for the purpose of calming (*samanattha*). It has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Saṅgīti-sutta* of the *Dīgha Nikāya*. Herein, this is the method of detailed explanation:
first, regarding legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), the dispute among monks who are contending over eighteen grounds as to whether it is "dhamma" or "not-dhamma"—this is [the first type].

This is called a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). The accusation, the reproach, and the formal charge of those who accuse another of a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), or a failure in conduct, view, or livelihood (*ācāra-diṭṭhi-ājīvavipatti*), is called a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
The seven classes of offenses—five found in the *Mātikā* and two in the *Vibhaṅga*—are called a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). That which belongs to the Saṅgha...
The performance of the four types of formal acts, beginning with the act of obtaining permission (*apalokana*), is what is called a legal issue concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

Among these, a legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two means of settlement: by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
When it is being settled by resolution in the presence of the parties alone, it may be resolved either in the very monastery where it arose or elsewhere.
Whether while they are traveling on the way, or having arrived at the place where it was handed over to the Saṅgha,
it is settled either by the Saṅgha, or— if the Saṅgha is unable to settle it— by persons authorized by a committee right there. And while this is being settled,
that which constitutes presence before the Saṅgha, presence before the Dhamma, and presence before the Vinaya [is maintained].
The presence of the person [involved] is what is called "settling in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*).
In this regard, the presence of the performing Saṅgha by way of the harmony of the Saṅgha is "presence of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasammukhatā*).

Because the matter to be settled is factual, it is "presence of the Dhamma" (*dhammasammukhatā*). The settling of that matter exactly as it ought to be settled is "presence of the Vinaya" (*vinayasammukhatā*). And whoever disputes, and by whom...
They dispute; the presence of both of these adversaries face-to-face constitutes *puggalasammukhatā* (presence of the persons).

However, in this case, when the matter is settled by a committee (*ubbāhikā*), *saṅghasammukhatā* (presence of the Saṅgha) is waived. Thus, first of all, it is settled by means of *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties).
But if even this does not settle it, then the monks appointed to the committee say: "We are not able..."
Thinking, "May it be appeased," they hand it over to the Saṅgha itself. Then the Saṅgha appoints a monk endowed with five qualities as the distributor of voting tickets (*salākaggāhāpaka*).

Having had the voting tickets distributed by one of the three types—those who distribute in secret, those who distribute openly, or those who whisper into the ear—the assembly that has gathered determines, by a majority, those who speak according to the Dhamma.
In the way those who speak according to the Dhamma say, so is the legal issue settled;
it is settled by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority). Therein, *sammukhāvinaya* is of the method already described.
As for the performance of the formal act of *yebhuyyasikā*, that is what is called *yebhuyyasikā*. Thus, a legal issue arising from a dispute is settled by two methods of settlement.

A legal issue concerning an accusation is settled by four means of settlement: by presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by recollection (*sativinaya*), by being of sound mind (*amūḷhavinaya*), and by the verdict of the majority (*tassapāpiyasikā*).

When it is being settled by presence alone, having heard the words of both the one who accuses and the one against whom the accusation is made, if no offense exists, both are to be excused; if one does exist, then this [procedure] applies here.
An offense is thus settled when it has been adjudicated. In that regard, the characteristic of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) is exactly as described by the aforementioned method.

However, when a monk whose taints are exhausted is accused of a groundless failure in virtue and requests a *sativinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness), and the Saṅgha grants him a *sativinaya* by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), then [the dispute] is settled by *sammukhā-vinaya*.
And it is settled by means of a verdict of past insanity. But once a verdict of past insanity has been granted, no further reproach against that person can take root.

When a monk who was insane is being questioned by the monks regarding unmonastic transgressions committed under the influence of insanity, saying, "Does the venerable one remember committing such an offense? he replies, "Friends, this was done by me while I was insane."

Even while saying, "I do not remember that," if he is pressed by the monks and again requests *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer deluded) so that there may be no further pressing, the Saṅgha grants him *amūḷhavinaya* by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*).
Then the matter is settled both by *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and by *amūḷhavinaya*. Once *amūḷhavinaya* has been granted, regarding that person...

In such a case, no formal charge based on that [accusation] gains ground against anyone. However, when one who is being charged with a *pārājika* offense or an offense bordering on a *pārājika* evades the matter by speaking of something else—being a person of evil character who exaggerates his own wickedness—one should consider:
"If this man has not cut off the root [of his offense], he will conduct himself properly and obtain reinstatement; but if he has cut off the root, then this very [evasion]..."

If the Saṅgha, thinking "there will be no [grounds for] expulsion," carries out a *tassapāpiyasika* (action for the worse) against him by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha kamma*),

then it is settled both by the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and by the *tassapāpiyasika*. Thus, a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by four methods of settlement.
A legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled by three methods of resolution:

by presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*), and by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). For this [type of issue], there is no settlement by means of presence alone.
However, when a monk confesses a light offense either in the presence of a single monk or in the midst of a Saṅgha or a group, then the legal issue concerning the offense [is resolved].
It is settled by means of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what is admitted).

Regarding that, first, in the case of *sammukhā-vinaya*, the presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom it is confessed constitutes "presence of persons" (*puggala-sammukhatā*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
At the time of confession before an individual or a group, "presence of the Saṅgha" (*saṅgha-sammukhatā*) is lacking. As for that which is here [said]: "I..."
When one has confessed by saying, "Venerable sir, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense," and when asked, "Do you see [it]?

he replies, "Yes, I see it," the act of instructing him, "You should exercise restraint in the future," is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa* (acting according to what has been confessed). In the case of the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, the request for probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth is the confession;
the granting of the probation and so forth is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa*.
But when monks who have become partisans and are quarrelsome, having committed much unbecoming conduct unworthy of a recluse,

later develop a sense of shame and perceive the fault in making one another confess their offenses— thinking, "If we make each other confess these offenses, this legal dispute might lead to harshness or violence"— then, at that time...

When the monks perform a legal act by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka-kamma*), then a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is settled both by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by covering over as with grass.
For in that case, as many as have come within arm’s reach do not reopen the matter—
without having made their views known by saying "this does not please me," nor by saying "this is a wrong action, it should be done again"— and they even fall asleep.
Setting aside all grave offenses and those connected with householders, all other offenses are cleared.
Thus, a legal issue concerning an offense is settled by three means of settlement.
A legal issue concerning business is settled by one means of settlement, namely, by resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*). Such are these four legal issues.
These seven methods of settling (*samatha*) settle [disputes] according to their respective suitability. Therefore it was said:

“For the settling and pacification of disputes as they arise, face-to-face settlement (*sammukhāvinaya*) should be granted… [and so on] … up to covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Settling of Disputes is finished.
The commentary on the *Vinayavagga* is finished.
Thus ends the elucidation of the meanings not [otherwise] explained in the commentary on the *Sattakanipāta* of the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the commentary on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
